Uniform Title: Vimalāvatītantra Author: Vimalaśiva Manuscript: NGMCP 1-431 Reel Number: A186/10

Description: This is a work on *siddhānta* ritual composed by Vimalaśiva, who lived in the thirteenth century. He proudly declares that he took the vow of residing his entire life in Kāśī (Varanasi). The first chapter deals with the accomplishment and fruits of worship (*pūjāsiddhi*). The second chapter concerns the procedure for preparing the sacrificial fire (*vahnikārya*) and the third, the oblations offered therein (*homa*). The fourth deals with the seasonal offering to the deity of the sacred thread (*pavitra*), and the next with the offering of the *dāmana* garland. The fifth chapter treats the rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The text continues to elaborate on the details regarding initiation. It includes several interesting internal purification practices linked to the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the movement of the *kuṇḍalinī*. The rules of right conduct (*samayācāra*) for initiates of various types are enumerated, along with other matters concerning their duties and those of Śaivas in general, both as householders and renunciants. Various initiatory rites are described for different types and levels of initiands.
Notes: Revision 0: December 17, 2013.
Country of Publication: India. Oṃ namaḥ śivāya.
He who maintains the stability of a living being and provides for its preservation and favor, yet does not become attached to it, is not overcome by others; indeed, he shines forth like Jupiter.

Having heard from the Guru the doctrine concerning Śiva— the immortal, whose primordial impurity has been burnt away by the fire of reality— we shall now perform the rites for worship, fire-oblation, the sacred thread, and the ancillary limbs, as prescribed in the Smṛtis.

It is appropriate that the initiation and consecration of the Bodhipāṛidha [temple] possess a path whose meaning is profound, deep, firm, soft, and hidden, resting upon a foundation that is pure and unfathomable.

Having remembered this established conclusion, I shall illuminate it with rays of light; I shall speak against the one who obstructs the supreme Dharma, the Śivācārya, the Sun-like Teacher, the Purifier.
Then, having arisen— whether pure or always impure—
one should perform the eight-limbed yoga beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma), [visualizing] the lotus situated in the center of the heart.
With one-pointed concentration, one should meditate on the supreme light, the subtle and imperishable *haṃsa*,
as Sadāśiva, who may be visualized as the size of a thumb-joint or as something gross.
Having known Śiva— the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, who is both the effect and the cause— as the Reality,
yoga consists in the one-pointedness of mind upon Śiva alone through the cessation of other mental modifications.

The restraints (yama), observances (niyama), postures (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and absorption (samādhi) have as their object that which is eternal, unconditioned, and accessible to the solitary [yogi].
Thus,
that which consists of the day and night, along with its primary and secondary branches and sub-branches, is the entire Veda; thereafter,
from the mass of light consisting of the foremost [deities] such as Agni, there arises the morning bath and so forth.
One should discard husks, impurities, insects, and the like, and go outside.
Having once cast aside the two threads upon that [person], he whose face is gentle, who has restrained his speech by day and night, and who has maintained the sacred girdle—
whether in shade or in darkness, or during the rainy season or in the heat— [he attains success].
One may act according to one's pleasure or with a favorable face, even in situations involving fear for one's life.
One who is pure should not look at the stars or the moon; one should perform purification oneself and follow the conduct of one who is being purified.
And one should properly grind apāmārga,
karañja, khadira, and arjuna— each eight finger-breadths long— and mix them with water to form a paste.
One should prepare a seat made of *bhukṣya*, *śūrmyā*, *plakṣa*, *jambu*, mango, *kuma*, and so forth;
it should be of the smallest size, two feet in width, moist, excellent, and scented with fragrant substances.
[The ground] is strewn with Piśāca-dhava, vānira, nimba, eraṇḍa, ākulī, grasses, kāśa, aṅguli, kuśa, dhātrī, and excellent varuṇa and other [plants].
2a) The Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Māhendra, Māruta, [Māna],
Mānasa, Mārtagaurava, and Nitya— these are the eight baths; among these, I shall speak of the others.
Having bathed in water with the mantra "Aghorebhyaḥ," one should perform the general ritual there, having composed oneself and visualizing the ocean as being filled with nectar.
Having dug a pit eight finger-breadths deep at the *astra* [point] and having discarded the earth from below, one should proceed to the heart [point].
Then, having filled the pit with the head [of the earth], one should place it on the bank of the water.

Having sprinkled the grass, roots, and so forth with the *śikhā* mantra and protected them with the *varma* mantra, one should wash from the navel down to the feet three times with the *bhakṣya* mantra. Thus it is said in the *Bhava*.
One should anoint one's limbs with water over which the *avyaya-astra* mantra has been recited seven times;
then, entering the water with *dūrvā* grass in the mouth, one should perform the six-faced invocation, the foot-stroking, and so forth.
Having meditated upon the radiant weapon-mantra within one's heart, one should bathe while contemplating it at dawn,
midday, and evening, even during sleep.
One should worship the twilight [deity] in the form of a blazing weapon, and then again with earth containing Shesha;
having taken a small amount of earth with the heart-mantra and the words for bathing, one should apply it.
Then, for the sake of purifying all his limbs with the fourfold [purification],
he should take even more earth from a northern or eastern direction while standing in the midst of water.
One should divide the left hand into three parts and the right hand into one part; then,
one should consecrate them once with the mantras beginning with the Heart and ending with the Armor.
One should cast the weapon seven times with the Astra-mantra and ten times with the Mūla-mantra; having recited the Astra-mantra, one should hurl it toward the ten directions with force.

One should offer half a portion of the recited *śiva-mantra* into the water with the root mantra, and the other half for the purpose of rotating the arms as a hundred-fold pilgrimage; or alternatively, one may obtain [the merit] by means of the root mantra alone.
Having recited the mantra over the four limbs beginning with the head— namely the arms, the face, and the two thighs— one should then place it upon the crown of the head.
Having immersed the breath (*prāṇa*) in water joined with [the mantra] *vāri*, as before,
and having meditated on Śiva in the heart and bathed, one should look at the sun and offer it with that [mantra].

With water on his head, free from distraction, anger, and haste, he should perform each [rite] with both hands joined in the gesture of the water-pot (kumbha-mudrā), like the rays of the moon and sun.
The stream of nectar flows into the refuge with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
thereafter, water is cast in the cardinal and intermediate directions with the *astra* mantra to remove obstacles.
One should expel the five impurities with the chest and [offer] water right there with the mudrā;
one should worship with the previously mentioned yoni-mudrā—this is known as the ritual bath (*māntra-snāna*).
3a) By means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by the mind, and by the root-mantra [which has] fallen [into place],
through the piercing of the aperture of the suṣumnā, [the breath] is established at the "end of twelve" (dvādaśānta).
One should mentally bathe all the limbs with divine nectar;
then, having established the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) at the drop (*bindu*), one should proceed with the ritual of immersion (*aṅgāhana*).
Having performed the earthly bath and the Agneya bath that instantly destroys sin,
and having put on other garments, a mortal should resort to the two-fold stage of life.
Having bathed, one should always place on the head a hundred flowers, white mustard seeds, blue durva grass, and blazing kusha grass, along with *laka* and *canā*.
If Kilivśaśa burns as if consuming everything, the husband of Malakṣmī is slain.
The Varuṇa-bath.
Having washed his feet and hands with water, Dakṣodha Dvaśikha sat facing either the north, the south, or the east, with both knees between his two hands.
One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water that has been drawn out, is silent, pure, filtered through a cloth,
free from impurities, not noisy, clear, and sweet-tasting.
One should stand while touching the mantra-limb and beholding [it].
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the reality of the self (ātmatattva). Oṃ hīṃ, svadhā to the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva).
3b) Oṃ hūṃ, svadhā to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
Having washed each hand with the right hand and sipped water using the Brahma-tīrtha.

Oṃ haḥ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ. Having rubbed both [feet] twice with the root of the thumb while the fingers are closed, one should touch all the limbs with the heart-mantra using the thumb and ring finger; or else, using the three middle fingers for the mouth and the index finger and thumb for the two nostrils, in the sequence of left and right.
Likewise, having washed each ear twice with the thumb and ring finger,
and having washed the fingers [as before], one should touch the navel with the little finger and thumb,
the heart with the middle of the hand, the head with all the fingers, and both shoulders in the same manner, without washing the fingers, as it has been taught.

In the *Śrīpauṣkara*, one should touch the right limb, and then touch the left limb. Then, with the *astra* mantra, one should wipe from the lower half of the left hand up to the lower half of the right hand, visualizing it as burnt:
*oṃ hauṃ śaktaye vauṣaṭ*.
Having flooded [the area] with nectar:
*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva*. *Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva*.
Oṃ hau, homage to the one whose body is wisdom.

4a) Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva. [This is] for the hollowed palms. From the beginning of Kāla up to the end of the thumb, and from the heart-mantra up to the weapon-mantra, [one should recite] with the root mantra.
Having performed the supreme consecration (*paramākṛtya*), one should veil the fourfold [limbs] beginning with the seat with armor (*varman*) at the navel;

the heart at the heart, the head at the head, the crest (*śikhā*) at the crest, and the armor (*kavaca*) on all limbs. With the weapon (*astra*) mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ* directed toward the ten directions, one should perform the snapping of fingers (*choṭikā*) while destroying [obstacles], having performed the supreme consecration.
The great mudrā of the tooth-power (ḍantaśakti) brings about the attainment of dreams. [This is] the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa). And it has been said:
"Whenever the mantra-practitioner performs the rite consisting of the mantra, at that very time the power-point (śāktabindu) should also be applied here upon the limbs."

Then, having gazed at the syllable *glāṃ* and so forth, and having joined [the offering] located at the *bindu* with the *tīrtha* [of the hand] by means of the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the *adbhava* mudrā, one should consecrate [it] from the heart up to the root-mantra (*mūla*) with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*),
veil it with the armor-mantra (*varma*), protect it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and transform it into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *śakti* and *dhenu* mudrās.

Alternatively, having enchanted it with the *prarocya* mantra and concealed it, one should protect it and cast it upon the head facing east. As it is stated in the *Śārḍhatriśatikā*: "One should apply the weapon-mantra (*astra*) to the body; one should cast the *kṣāmra* [mantra] toward the front, which dries up the body; one should join it with the *vartma* and the *ātman*."
4b) Having always engaged the wise ones against the nets of obstacles and evils,
he then, having wrapped himself in a calf-skin and holding his nose with his left hand, [proceeded].
Having performed the *prāṇāyāma* and recited the *saṃhitā* from the *mūla-mantra* to the *astra-mantra* three times, one should perform the *nyāsa* beginning with the mind (*manas*).
Then, having enveloped oneself with the *varma-mantra*, one should place the middle of the *darbha* grasses in the hollow of the hands and, using water with *kuśa* grass,
perform the *avibhāvatī* [meditation] at the heart.
Having meditated upon the twilight [deity] situated for five ghaṭīs in absolute solitude,
one should likewise [meditate upon] Brāhmī, who has four faces, eight eyes, and four arms.
She holds a water-pot and a staff in her right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in her left;
she is sattvic, seated upon a swan and a lotus, and possesses matted hair and a sacred thread.
Having hair and wearing red garments and so forth, she is the manifest protectress,
light, and situated in the center of a vast red maṇḍala extending for hundreds of millions of leagues.
In the morning, O best of beings, one should meditate upon the goddess Vaiṣṇavī residing in the heart, accompanied by the syllable Tāra, youthful, white in complexion, with one face and two eyes.
Seated upon Tārkṣya and the lotus, dressed in white garments and adorned with ornaments,
she is encircled by a forest garland, wears a crown, and possesses four arms.
5a) Holding a conch and a discus in her left [hands], and a mace and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her right,
she resides within two hundred million white mandalas.
At midday, one should meditate on the Rājasa form, situated on the forehead, characterized by paralysis and trembling,
fierce, with a downward face, three-eyed, slightly aged, and mounted upon a bull.
Clad in a tiger skin, dark-complexioned, with a serpent as her sacred thread,
she has made her abode in the *brahmarandhra* and is adorned by the crescent moon within her matted locks.
Four-armed and adorned with a garland of tridents, she holds [the trident] in her right hand;
in her left, she holds the Śakti of Fear, while [another] half-moon is on the shoulder of the Guru’s attendant.
She is the witness of all actions, situated in their midst,
within a pure mandala extending for forty-one million yojanas.
Then, at midnight, one should contemplate another [form]: Śyāmā, or Rūpavarjitā, who is established in the supreme reality at the end of the twelve [fingers], the all-pervading Śivā.
Thus, having meditated upon the twilight [deities] consisting of the three qualities and so forth according to the sequence of time,
one should remember oneself as independent, entered into the expanse of their circle of light.

Having placed water in the left hand, one should pour it over the heart three times with the right hand while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*; then, moving it from back to front and letting the water drip down, one should cast it upon the head while meditating as before with the *saṃhita-mantra*. This is how it should be done.
5b) Then,
O Vasiṣṭha, that water used for sprinkling,
which is auspicious and the very form of Dharma, remains in the right hand, being filled by the *pūraka* breath.
Then, through the practice of *kumbhaka* [retention of breath], let them enter the nostrils;
having caused the destruction of internal sins, that sin becomes like soot.
Having expelled [the impurity] by means of exhalation through the right nostril,
one should visualize it in the hand and strike it with the Astra-mantra ending in *kūṃ phaṭ*.
One should join the palms in reverence;
then, when there is impatience [with the breath], that is *recaka* (exhalation) due to the forceful expulsion of the breath, while *pūraka* (inhalation) is its restraint.

One should neither exhale nor inhale, like a full jar during breath-retention (*kumbhaka*). However, if possible, one should offer a handful of water (*arghāñjali*) facing the sun while reciting the root mantra ending in *svāhā*. Having stood up and offered this, one should sit down before the Three-eyed Goddess.

Upon a lotus, she is white in color, possessing one face and four arms; her right hand is extended toward the mouth, while her left rests upon a lotus held in the hand. She is adorned with matted hair, a crescent moon, and a sacred thread, and possesses four arms.
Holding an excellent rosary in her left hand, she stands with a lotus in her right hand and displays the gesture of fearlessness.

6a) Having meditated upon the Gāyatrī in the heart, one should sprinkle [it] with the joined palms (añjali) for the sake of attaining the fruit of the four Vedas; then, with the [mudrā] facing upward (ūrdhvamukha):
"Oṃ tat maheśāya vidmahe, vāgviśuddhāya dhīmahi, tan naḥ śivaḥ pracodayāt"—thus [recite] the Anuṣṭubh.
Having performed circumambulation clockwise and having recited the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer it to the form [of the deity].
Having recited the root mantra eight hundred times for the satisfaction of the *pūgīphala* and other offerings, starting from one and so forth.

One should satisfy the mantra-deities, beginning with Dhruva and ending with Agni, who have gentle countenances, using the tips of *kuśa* grass from all the fingers; thereafter, one should satisfy the sages (*ṛṣis*) at the throat with barley-grains.

In the case of Kāmeśvara, one should join the fingers at the joints of the middle phalanges with the tips of the Kuśa grass; likewise, for the Lord of the Human World, one should join them at the roots of the little fingers.
Facing the east, with the base of his hand joined [to the previous mudrā], he should visualize even the multitude of spirits;
facing the south, he should become one whose mind is fixed on the deities and the pretas by means of the sacred thread (apavīta).
With the thumb at the root of the [ring] finger, the base and tip of which are bent, one should perform [ablution] with sesame seeds;
then, at a common sacred site (tīrtha), the Brahma-tīrtha is located at the base of the thumb.
The lunar *sāvitrī* is prescribed on the palm of the left hand, and the solar one on the right. 6b) Oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā || Oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya svāhā || Oṃ hrīṃ śirase svāhā ||
Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ haiṃ, svāhā to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ haḥ, svāhā to the weapon (astra).
The mantras.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Ādityas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Vasus! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Rudras!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Sādhyas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Maruts! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Bhṛgus! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Aṅgirases!
The gods.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Atri; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vasiṣṭha; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pulastya.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kratu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhāradvāja. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viśvāmitra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pracetas. [The Sages.]
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanaka! Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sananda! Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanātana!
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanatkumāra! Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Kapila! Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Pañcaśikha! Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Ṛbhu! [These are] the humans.
7a) Oṃ hāṃ, to the beings of space, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hāṃ, to the beings of wind, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hāṃ, to the beings of fire, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hāṃ, to the beings of water, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hāṃ...

To the earth and the elements, Vauṣaṭ! Oṃ Hāṃ, to Kavyavāla, Svadhā! Oṃ Hāṃ, to Anala, Svadhā! Oṃ Hāṃ, to Soma, Svadhā! Oṃ Hāṃ, to Yama, Svadhā! Oṃ Hāṃ, to [Agni], Svadhā! Oṃ Hāṃ, to Ājyapa, Svadhā! Oṃ Hāṃ, to Somapa, Svadhā!
O gods and ancestors!
Oṃ hā& svadhā to the father Īśa. Oṃ hā& svadhā to the grandfather Sadāśiva.
Oṃ hāṃ! To the peaceful great-grandfather, svadhā!
The specific deities and ancestors; by householders, their own deceased ancestors [should be honored] by means of [reciting] names, lineage (*gotra*), and so forth.
Oṃ hā&! To all kinsmen, teachers, lords of the directions, perfected ones, mothers, grahas, rākṣasas, and so forth—svadhā!
Oṃ hā&! To all those who dwell in the worlds beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Agni, svadhā!
Are these [factors] each individually [a cause]? No.

7b) Then, being dexterous and wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītin*), having cast the *tarpaṇa*-kuśa grass upon the ground with the Astra-mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, and having thrilled the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) with that mantra using the Heart-mantra in the mode of withdrawal (*saṃhāriṇī*), one should perform the correct sipping of water (*ācamana*); this is the "binding of the twilight" (*sandhyābandhana*).
Having performed the morning twilight ritual with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
one should always daily present the *arghya* to the Sun and worship him once.
Having meditated upon the sky-linga and so forth as being like Śiva, otherwise it is not accomplished.
The two hands are marked with sandalwood and akṣa; RĀM is at the base of the form of the victim, and SAT is on the fire.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to the heart. Oṃ arka, homage to the head.
Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, obeisance to the flaming crest-lock (śikhā).
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the armor (*kavaca*); having assigned the vowels to the little finger and the other fingers: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the eyes (*netra*); [on] the palms of the hands.

Oṃ raḥ, salutation to the weapon (*astra*). Having joined the two thumbs and performed the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), [one should perform] the triad beginning with the sprinkling (*āsana*) at the navel.
Having performed the placement of the heart-mantra and others in the heart and other locations, of the eye-mantra in the two eyes, and of the weapon-mantra in the directions, she is supreme.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the syllable *daṃsauṃ*, prepare the general water-offering (sāmānyārgha), sprinkle the ritual substances with that water, and then meditate upon oneself as having the form of the Sun and worship [it].
8a) Oṃ aṃ, homage to the seat of the Sun. [In the center of the lotus: Oṃ haṃ khaṃ, homage to the Sun-form Khaṣolska.
Above that, one should worship the red-formed goddess situated on the head, who holds a white lotus in her hand, has two eyes, and is adorned with red ornaments.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ śaḥ, homage to Sūrya.
Having clearly visualized [the deity] as radiant and red, appearing like a spoken word, [one should recite]:
*oṃ aṃ sūryāya namaḥ*.
Having performed the placement, the storage, and the confinement of his heart and other limbs, one should perform the supreme [consecration].

Oṃ AṂ. Having offered red sandalwood and other substances with the mantra "To the suns" (sūryāyebhyaḥ) and so forth, one should worship three times with the root mantra and offer incense and other articles.
Oṃ saṃ, salutation to Soma; [he is] situated in the east. Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Budha; [he is] fair-complexioned in the south.
Oṃ vṛṃ, obeisance to Bṛhaspati; in the west, [the seat] has the luster of gold. Oṃ bhāṃ, obeisance to Bhārgava; in the north, it is white. Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Aṅgāraka.
In the southeast, red: Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara. In the southwest, dark blue.
Oṃ raṃ, homage to Rāhu.
8b) In the northwest, [one should place] Kṛtāñjali, who is black: Oṃ kaṃ, obeisance to Ketu.
One should worship the Lord who holds an axe, a trident, a snake, and a sword.
Having meditated upon Rāhu and Ketu as being struck by arrows, with their right hands raised and their left hands filled with fear.

Having offered the sacrificial oblations and other items to the Sun and others, having bowed down, and having established [the deity] in both its manifest and unmanifest forms, one should, at the time of Śiva’s dismissal (visarjana),
unify the Sun who resides in the heart with Śiva by means of the root mantra.
Alternatively, having meditated upon Sadāśiva as entirely red.
Oṃ hauṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ haḥ, salutation to Śiva-Sūrya.
One should worship the three winds.

Alternatively, having recited the root mantra of Śiva one hundred and eight times or more, ending with "svāhā," one should offer [the oblation] to the Sun with that root mantra; such is the worship of the Sun.
With his mind perfectly concentrated, he held the *argha* water, which was of the nature of the mantra and consisted of the syllables *ar-vya-kā-ra*.
Having sprinkled the door with water empowered by the weapon-mantra, one should worship the gatekeepers in the western [door].
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. He is dark blue, pot-bellied, and elephant-faced;
in his left and right hands he holds a *laḍḍuka*, an axe, a rosary, and his own tusk; and on the right, he is seated holding a *laḍḍuka* and a battle-axe.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī.
To the north of that [deity] is Śuklā, seated, holding a book and a rosary in her left and right hands respectively.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to Mahālakṣmī! She is golden-hued and seated, holding a *śrīphala* fruit and a lotus in her left and right hands, [which are] between those two.
Above the Udumbara tree: Oṃ Hīṃ, homage to Nandin.
One should protect the three-eyed, matted-haired [deity], with his right and left hands placed [upon them].
Holding a rosary and a trident, standing upon a lotus:
Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā.
[She is] white, standing upon a makara, holding a blue lotus and a vase with her right and left hands respectively; to the north of that, on the southern branch.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla. He is black, with formidable fangs, wearing a sacred thread, with tawny matted hair standing upon his head; in his right and left hands, he holds a trident and a skull-bowl respectively. To the north [is the deity].

Oṃ hā& namaḥ to Yamunā. She is seated upon the back of a dark tortoise; her right and left hands hold a blue lotus and a water-pot respectively, and she is positioned on the northern branch to the right of that [deity].

Having performed the purification of the path for these gatekeepers, as well as the offering of incense, lamps, and food, and having proclaimed the command of Śiva, one should perform ten recitations of the *namasva* mantra for the sake of guarding the gates.
9b) Having gazed with eyes fixed on the sun [of wisdom], and having performed the *didhyāntārāca-mudrā* while reciting the seven-weapon mantra (*saptāstrajapta*),
one should strike the weapon stationed in the sky with three blows upon the left foot, and likewise those stationed on the ground.
Having driven away the obstacles in three ways, he raises his left leg with its branches [the toes].
Having entered the middle of the threshold, one should place the form of the weapon-mantra for the sake of protection.
Oṃ hā& salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the site.

Tundira holds a *śruva* ladle, a rosary, a *śruk* ladle, and a water-pot in his right and left hands; he is purified by the gaze and other rites from the *nairṛta* direction, and [the vessel] is cleansed from the tip of the *gaṇḍuka* with the *śāstra* mantras.
Having obtained permission from Śiva, the silent practitioner should proceed with the Gaṅgā and other mantras,
using water purified by ninefold cloth and consecrated over his limbs.
One should fill the vessels purified with the weapon-mantra (astra) either with the Gāyatrī or with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
The collection of all substances, beginning with the jar-eyed one (*gaḍukākṣa*) and so forth.
Having gathered these for the purpose of worship, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the subsequent rites.
Having offered [the seat] with the heart-mantra of Gaṇaguru, they sit comfortably upon the seat of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Having merely performed the placement of the armor and the weapons.

10a) Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, homage to Consciousness (caitanya). [One should visualize] oneself as resembling a steady lamp, with a flower in the right hand, and having performed the withdrawal [of the elements] into the heart-sun, moon, and fire.
Having visualized [the deity] situated in the center of the mandala of power, one should form the "tortoise" hand-gesture.
Oṃ hlāṃ, to the Nivṛtti-kalā, haḥ hūṃ phaṭ!

The seed of the elements such as earth, rooted in passion, hatred, merit, demerit, and delusion; protected by the lords of knowledge and ignorance; having the principles beginning with *kalā* as its trunk; having the five subtle elements such as form as its branches; having the perception of objects as its sprouts; having the manifold expansion of dispositions as its flowers; and consisting of intellect, determination, and volition—[this is the tree of transmigratory existence].
The fruit is to be enjoyed by the person, who is like a bird; it consists of the essence of the relationship between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer.
With the first half-verse of the *Pūraka* hymn, one should contemplate the body in the form of a banyan tree, with roots above and branches below, yet devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruit.
Oṃ hrīṃ pratiṣṭhāyai haḥ hūṃ phaṭ! [He becomes] smooth, with leaves, flowers, and fruits in the latter half.
Oṃ hūṃ, to the portion of knowledge (vidyākalā), haḥ hūṃ phaṭ!
10b) By means of the first two types of *kumbhaka*, [the yogi] quickly dries up and burns [the body] with the fire of time (*kālāgni*) arising from the big toe of the right foot.
Oṃ hūṃ, to the Śānti-kalā, haḥ hūṃ phaṭ! [The weapon] is dissolved in the ten directions from the ashes for the sake of emergence within the half-repha. Oṃ hauṃ, to the Śāntyatīta-kalā, haḥ hūṃ phaṭ!
And with the latter half [of the mantra], having meditated upon the sky as resembling pure crystal, one should contemplate the Self—

consisting of the digits (kalās) beginning with Śāntyatītā, possessing a subtle form, radiant, and devoid of the gross body and senses— within all [the centers] by means of the Praṇava, specifically in the locations of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the middle of the eyebrows, the palate, the throat, and the heart.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with streams of white, yellow, and silver nectar flowing from the ocean of the Kuṇḍalinī power, which resides at the dvādaśānta and ends with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of the Self (ātmamūrti). One should meditate upon the subtle form as white or protective, its hands, feet, and other limbs being undivided. As it has been said:

One should install the form within oneself, remembering it as possessing four measures (catuṣkala), endowed with tranquility, resembling the rising orb of the sun, and having the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
One should place within the center of the *liṅga* the form called Ātman, possessing its own white radiance;
Śiva [is formed] with Sadāśiva by means of the body of Vidyā, and with Īśa as the face of men, and with Aghora as the heart.
Having contemplated Śiva with the trunk of meditation, which is filled with all [attributes] through the union of the secret [organ] on the left, we pay homage.
Having correctly performed the placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other centers, and having mentally realized oneself as the supreme form of Śiva,

one should discard the flower held in the hand at the conclusion of the limb-nyāsa. Having performed the Mahāmudrā with the mind, and having offered the water for the arghya-vessel and so forth within the heart, one should meditate upon a lotus [seat] while reciting the kavaca-mantra, and therein [visualize] the supporting bases (ādhāra) and so forth.

When the body has reached its end and the mind has dissolved into the tranquil Śiva, one should worship as desired by means of substances through the movement of the left channel (vāmanāḍī), and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times or more, one should offer it.
And so it is said:
The reality known as Ānanda, numbering thirty-six, becomes eight hundred through the threefold division beginning with Aparā, and then half of that, and again half of that, respectively.

Again, having established the innate fire (*sahajāgni*) at the navel and Śiva within the sacrificial pit as before, one should satisfy him with the oblations of the black nectar drawn in by inhalation through the right channel as previously described; then, having offered the *pūrṇā* oblation for the limbs as well, such as milk-rice and other offerings— 11b).

Having bowed and offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, having worshipped the Śiva-liṅga in the image (*mūrti*), having stabilized it, and having united it with Śiva residing in the heart, one should offer the eight concluding oblations (*aṣṭakṛt-āhuti*). Having worshipped the internal fire (*svātmanāgni*) and dismissed it along with its wings (the flames), one should transfer the merit of the Śiva-homa to Śiva residing in the heart. Then, having worshipped the one residing in the image with the root mantra, [one should recite] the eight-syllable mantra: *namaḥ śivāya*.

Having spoken thus and offered the *arghya* and other oblations, one should then contemplate the Lord Madhūmakṣya in the form of a drop (*bindu*) in the center of the forehead by means of the central breath-movement (*madhyacāra*).
Having become Śiva both externally and internally, and having worshipped Śiva, one should instill the realization: "I am the worshipper. This is the supreme state of mind.
Thus ends the impurity of the self.

With the two hands joined and turned upward, one should place them at the region of the heart; then, with the *nīva* [mudrā], perform three claps of the palms and snapping sounds in the ten directions, as well as the enclosure (*prākāra*). Alternatively, having fashioned a moat around the heart with the *varma* [mudrā], one should form the net of spears (*śaktijāla*) and the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) with both hands.
"One should expand by means of power" refers to the purification of the substratum.

Having sprinkled each of the substances with water from a vessel containing the fragrance obtained by the heart-mantra, which has been empowered by reciting the Astra-mantra twenty-one times and joined with the *vardhanī* vessel, one should first take a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or earth in the palm of the hand.
12a) The vessel for the *argha* offering to Śiva should be circular, free from blemishes or cracks,
and made of materials such as conch, mother-of-pearl, horn, or leaves of the *palāśa* or lotus.
Having washed it with the Astra-mantra, ending with *vauṣaṭ*, and having filled it with the nectar-drops from the *vardhanī* vessel using the Heart-mantra and the Astra-mantra, ending with *bhūḥ*.
Rice, barley, sesame, and beans—these are the grains with their husks removed.
The eight-limbed *arghya* is prescribed here along with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*).
When that has been prepared, provided with *kuśa*, *dūrvā*, and other materials, and worshipped with either a brief or extensive *āsana* like unto Śiva,
one should perform the imposition (*āropaṇa*) of the two forms together with their limbs, beginning with the enveloping by mantras (*mantraguṇṭhana*).
With the *sakala* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should consecrate the self as Śakti; with the armor (*varman*) mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, the substances;

with the *vāmana* mantra, the garment; with the *bharaṇa* mantra, the ornaments; and with the *naivedya* mantra, the food offering. Then, one should consecrate the remaining flowers and other substances with the *gāyatrī*.

Having performed the mental placement (*nyāsa*) of Śiva, Sadāśiva, Vidyā, Kāla, and Puruṣa in the eastern, southern, western, and northern mandalas respectively, [one should place them] in the heart. 12b)
Then, in the west, [one should place] bowls that are well-established, very peaceful, radiant, made of non-earthly substances, and arising from jewels, as well as black ones.
The earth [element] is the half of the big toe, divided fivefold by the Sadyojāta;
the north is the blue-bodied [Nīlāṅga]; and the thread is the length of a pala above.
In the south, two *palas* of tawny ghee with the *aghora* mantra recited three times;
in the east, three *palas* of white curd with the *nara* mantra recited twice.
In the center, one should place copper and milk;
with a single-minded focus, having added a *pala* of *kuśa* water from the northeast, one should pour it into the vessels with the *Gāyatrī* mantra and consecrate them.
I shall perform [this] for Śiva; otherwise, it would be different.
Then, having first cast each preceding root into the middle, one should touch [the object] with the hundred and eight roots;
this is the brief summary of what was stated regarding bathing.
Cow dung, a thread from a garment, curd, milk, and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya), touched with the heart-mantra, possess supreme and great qualities.
The five products of the cow.

Having placed milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, sugar, and scented water along with *kuśa* grass in the directions of the center, east, south, north, west, and northeast, one should consecrate them— one, two, three, four, five, and six times respectively— with the mantras beginning with *Dadhivīśa* and others, following the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*) for the former and the order of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*) for the latter; that is, from the sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*) up to the scented water, using the mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta* and ending with the *Gāyatrī*.
"One should recite the mantra" refers to the five nectars.

13a) Having sprinkled the flower-vessel with the Weapon-mantra (astra) and worshipped it with the Heart-mantra (hṛd), while ringing the bell— which has been honored with the Weapon-mantra— with the left hand, one should fumigate all the ritual substances and perform the veiling (guṇṭhana) and other rites.
Purification of substances.
Then, having worshipped oneself like Śiva, having offered a drop of water on the head with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
having recited the root mantra ten times and offered it, having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā*, and having cultivated the realization "I am Śiva."
During bathing, worship of the gods, fire-offerings, eating, yoga practices, necessary duties,
and recitation of mantras, the wise man should always maintain restraint over his speech.

Thus, having adopted the silence observed [in this way], one should—by means of the short, long, and protracted [utterances] in sequence—raise the root [mantra] three times as far as the *dvādaśānta* and then lead it back; this is the purification of the mantra (*mantra-śuddhi*).
Having sprinkled with the Astra-mantra a small portion of the previously prepared offering vessel (puṭaka) that has been partially revealed, having worshipped it with the Gāyatrī,

and having worshipped Sadyojāta and the others in sequence with the root mantra ending in "svāhā" using the general arghya water, one should place the right hand over the vessel, recite the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, take [the substance], and stand facing the northeast direction.
Having offered the remains of the garland to Caṇḍa with the heart-mantra.

13b) Having washed the pedestal and the *liṅga* with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having sprinkled them with the water of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should place a flower upon them.
Having thoroughly sprinkled the site for the worship on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should draw a lotus; this is the purification of the locus (liṅgaśuddhi).
Thus it has been said:
Thus, when the fivefold limbs of the mantra-signs—the substance whose locus is the self—are purified, one should worship Maiva by name; otherwise, it shall not come to pass.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.

Having visualized what was previously mentioned in the northwest, one should perform the eight rites; [then] for the worship of Īśa, the *arghya* [is offered with] "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Gurus. One should recite the eight [verses] in the northeast as before.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti).
Having the form of the ocean of milk, appearing like a sprout from a seed, she is seated upon the Tortoise-stone.
Oṃ hā& namaḥ to Ananta. In the center, rising from that [base], is the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), resembling a white, upright lotus bud.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dharma. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jñāna.
14a) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vairājña. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya.

[One should visualize] the forms of white, red, pale yellow, and black, each with a hundred petals and so forth, showing their mutual backs, having the shapes of the [eight] seats, and situated from the lotus-knot (padmagranthi) to the northeast (Īśāna), starting from Agni. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Adharma; black and white. *Hāṃ*, obeisance to Ajñāna.
White and red.
Oṃ hā& salutation to Avairāgya (Non-detachment). He is reddish-white.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lack of sovereignty; the limbs are white and black.

From the east to the north: *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the lower covering; *Oṃ*, obeisance to the upper covering. [One should contemplate] the form of Raktā and Śvetā, whose nature is darkness (*tamas*), in the center, consisting of the qualities of *rajas* and *sattva*, in the space between the south-west, the north-east, and the zenith.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lotus seat. Having worshipped the white, full-blown [lotus] in the center: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Padmā. One should display the lotus mudrā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the pericarp.

[One should visualize] fifty white-colored seed-syllables within [the lotus]; the root is yellow, the middle is red, and the tip is white; in the center of the sixty-four filaments and so forth is: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā.
14b) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī.
Oṃ hā& salutation to Valavikalaṇī. Oṃ hā& salutation to Valapramathanī. Oṃ hā& salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī. Oṃ hā& salutation to Manonmanī.

The eight red [deities] are situated on lotus seats upon the tips of the filaments located in the petals starting from the east and ending in the northeast. They hold chowries in their left and right hands; they are seated on the auspicious throne of Śiva-Śakti, possessing four digits of power (kalās), and are both Śiva and Śakti. They hold chowries and grant boons and fearlessness, or alternatively, they grant boons and fearlessness while holding chowries. Adorned, they wear matted hair and the crescent moon, and possess three eyes; and so too the ninth.
The two white [deities] are to be worshipped in the pericarp: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Namaskārā.

One should form the *namaskāra-mūrdhā* [mudrā]. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc, upon the tip of the white, radiant, and fair lotus leaf. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar disc.
On the tip of the filament of the white lotus: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the fire-maṇḍala*. *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala*.
15a) At the tip of the pericarp are red and white [lotuses]. Oṃ hauṃ, homage to the circle of power (śaktimaṇḍala).
Oṃ hauṃ, homage to Śiva, the lord of the circle of power.

For the seven crooked [powers] extend through the lower and upper forms of the object of speech; in the middle is the seat, which pervades the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Śuddhavidyā.
One should perceive the embodied form of the Lord as pervading the end of the *bindu*;
this is the previously mentioned [form] for the encircling of the *liṅga* above that. And it has been said:
The syllable "haṃ sa" enclosed by the heart-mantra (hṛd) proceeds in succession from the heart-lotus.
Emerging from the *vibhidyā*, it is known as the *vinda* consisting of the embodied mantra.

Having uttered the syllable *plūṃ*, which is radiant and reaches the end of the hand, one should place that *vidyādeha* (knowledge-body) upon the unmanifest form of the Great Soul, who is beyond the material nature (*aprākṛta*).
Īśāna and Śāntyatītā constitute the face-lotus; Puṃs and Śānti are the heart; Ghorā and Vidyā are the left [side]; and Pratiṣṭhā and the other [Nivṛtti] are the secret [organ].
The state of being born as one who has just turned away [from worldly existence] is the feet; the path of the worlds is the skin;
the state of being phonemes is the blood; and that which consists of mantras is the flesh covered with veins.
Seated in the lotus posture, with skin, bones, marrow, semen, and so forth as his ornaments, possessing ten arms,
three eyes representing vision, action, and will, and five faces, he is worshipped by the digit of the moon of knowledge.
Resembling pure crystal and endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Peaceful, though youthful, adorned with a mass of matted hair and the crescent moon,
he holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness along with a khaṭvāṅga staff, a spear, and a trident in his right hands.
Holding a citron and so forth, a hand-drum, a blue lotus, and an akṣa-bead in his left hands,
he extends [his power] as far as the Śakti, pervading the Linga even in times of distress.
In the south is the excellent Oṃkāra, who is short and holds a citron;
likewise, he holds a skull-topped staff, a hand-drum, and a trident for the sake of the Three-eyed Goddess.
Facing them are blue lotuses, and upon them are the weapons held in the hands of the five-faced deities beginning with Īśa, such as the noose, the goad, and the trident.

Then, having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the fire-mantras, one should meditate upon the five causal deities beginning with Brahmā, who reside in the heart; as they dissolve into one another until the end, one should utter the mantra of the All-Creator, which rises like a fierce sun from the root of the heart.
One should meditate upon Śiva— the omniscient, partless, all-pervading, consisting of knowledge and bliss, self-luminous—

as resembling the orb of the sun falling from the *dvādaśānta* (the space twelve finger-breadths beyond the crown), appearing like ten million moons on the forehead, and filling the circle of the quarters with a mass of celestial nectar.
16a) Then, having visualized [the fingers] joined at the thumbs and reaching to the tips of the little fingers in the añjali gesture;

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva. Thus, one should perform the stabilization and so forth by means of entry into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) within the image of the deity. As it has been said:
The letter A, the letter U, the letter Ma, and the Bindu;
the Half-moon, the Nirodhī, the Nāda, and the end of Nāda.
Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and likewise Unmanā;
the net of bonds extends up to the end of Samanā, while Supreme Śiva resides at the end of Unmanā.

When the thumb is pressed down, with the fingers slightly bent and the nails dry and powdered, this is the *jalit* mudrā for invocation (*āvāhana*); for installation (*sthāpana*), the ring finger is likewise bent.
When the thumb and fist are raised and joined within the hollow of the hands, that is the Liṅga-mudrā; by means of it, Lord Śambhu becomes present through the heart-mantra.
One should perform a firm restraint with two fists, the thumbs tucked inside, conceived as being composed of the entire self,
until the dismissal of the Lord.
When the [deity] has been invoked with the name ending in the acute accent (udātta) and has been brought face-to-face (sanmukhī) by means of the *āvāhana* mantra,

then, having struck [the deity] with the *kālakarṇī* weapon-mantra, having formed the *liṅga-mudrā* and the salutation (*namaskāra*), and having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the heart-mantra and the others, one should effect the supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) by means of the root-mantra and the power-mantra (*śakti*).
One should meditate on the name as being situated between the staff and the portion, free from the speed of the serpent, possessing the single color of Śiva, outside the mouth of the Brahma-portion.
Then, having meditated upon Śiva with a smiling face for a mere moment, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ hau! Welcome to you, O Blessed One, free from all impurities."
Oṃ hā&! "Welcome, my child, to us," having thus honored him with these auspicious words;
Oṃ hā&! Homage to Śiva—svadhā, svāhā.

With the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and flowers, respectively, to the two lotus-feet, the mouth, and the five parts of the head, while facing [the deity] and performing the rites clockwise and counter-clockwise.
In the *ācamanīya* [water for sipping], one uses the *tatpuruṣa*, *aghora*, *vāmadeva*, *sadyojāta*, and *īśāna* [mantras] ending with *īśāna*.
For the *arghya* [offering], one uses *īśāna*, *tatpuruṣa*, *aghora*, *guhyaka*, and *jāta*.
The meaning of "left" and "right."

And here, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), one should offer the *argha* with water drawn up by means of the *uttolitāstramudrā*; then, having raised the *viśeṣārghya*, one should uncover the *liṅga* within it and wash it.
17a) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śiva.
One should divide [the portion] with the *dyuta* mantra: *oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ*. Having extracted [it], one should recite: *oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*.
[The practitioner] should drive away the Mlecchas with mustard seeds and other substances. Having raised [the deity] with "Oṃ Hāṃ Śiva, arise," he should cause him to stand up.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva. Having washed the limb with lukewarm water, one should bathe it individually with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the nectar [of the elements], and so forth, using incense and water for rinsing (ācamana) ending with "svāhā" while reciting the root mantra. Then, having rubbed it with fragrant powders and the like, one should hold a jar filled with water in the left hand.

Having offered flowers and *arghya* at the *liṅga*, and having removed them, one should pour water from the conch-mudrā— filtered through the washed hands— into the vessel (*gaḍuka*) as desired; then, at the conclusion, having bathed [the deity] with scented water and other substances according to one's capacity, and having wiped [the image] with a clean cloth, [one should apply] sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, and *durvā* grass.
Having offered with devotion, whether mentally or physically, ornaments such as golden loincloths, waist-bands, sacred threads, and earrings, as well as variegated garments;
"Oṃ hāṃ, O Śiva, please be seated. Having been addressed thus, he sits down and worships him with three handfuls of excellent flowers, along with incense and other offerings.
Having performed the arrangement of the worship, having fumigated [the area], and having sipped water (ācamana), one should perform the *ārātrika* with fourfold pure hands.

Having worshipped it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*), and having slowly moved it three times from right to left while mixing it with the ringing of the bell, one should fan the flame upward with the *astra-mantra* ending in *svāhā*.
Then, having meditated upon the Lord with joy and bowed down, he said, "O Blessed One, give your command; I shall worship the limbs of enjoyment.

Having thus spoken, having drawn the white [form] from his own heart into [the deity's] heart by means of the heart-mantra, he [placed] the fair-colored head from the five heads into the northeast (Īśāna) of the fire-altar by means of the head-mantra.
One should place the red crest-mantra on the crest at the southeast;
the black armor-mantra on all limbs at the northwest.

One should worship the weapons with the Astra-mantra on the petals of the directions starting from the east and ending in the north, beginning at the ten hands. Of these [deities], who are adorned by the Guru (Bṛhaspati), the Sun, the Moon, and the crescent moon, and who stand upon lotuses and arrows—
with their right and left hands displaying the gestures of granting boons (*varada*), the power (*śakti*), the trident (*triśūla*), and fearlessness (*abhaya*)— in some places they are single-faced.

Having performed the entire supreme worship of Śiva, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, along with the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), incense, and food offerings, using their respective mantras;
Having offered a handful of flowers with the root-mantra at the base for the sake of Śiva, and having rendered it supreme, one should contemplate the unification of the heart and the other limbs.
As it has been said:
Whether joined with Yama or even acting independently by herself, Prakṛti performs the task; the Lord does not act. Therefore, Prakṛti is the cause.

Then, having worshipped Śiva with flowers and other offerings according to one's own inclination, and having offered a lamp, food (naivedya), and water for the hands with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, water for sipping (ācamana) with the mantra ending in *svadhā*, and mouth-fresheners such as camphor and betel-leaf with the mantra ending in *svāhā* while holding them in the hand, one should consecrate [the deity] with a mirror, umbrella, chowries, and so forth.
Oṃ hā& obeisance to Dravyadā (the Giver of Wealth).
Having performed the sipping of water (ācamana), having displayed the *pūrvandravya* mudrā, and having consecrated [the materials] with the *dhenu-mudrā*,
one should place the purifiers such as *kuśa* grass upon them with the essence of all reality (*sarvatattva*).
As it has been stated in the Śrī-Brahmasambhu:
When one's own speech, mind, and body have acted through negligence,
the supreme bathing with pure water is said to be the appropriate remedy.

Then, having offered durva grass, unbroken rice, and incense, and at the conclusion of the recitation, having presented a handful of flowers with the root mantra, one should cause [the deity] to rejoice by means of the great mudrā.
Thereafter, having meditated upon the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow— being praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others, and being well-pleased—
one should take up a rosary made of Rudrākṣa, Putrajīva, Prasthūra, crystal, Kuśa grass, or similar materials.
One of the commentaries and so forth.
Having requested [the deity] for the sake of recitation.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the rosary (mālā). Having worshipped it and fumigated it with incense, one should display the *mālāmudrā*. Then, placing the rosary upon the middle, ring, and little fingers of the right hand—whereby the fruit is multiplied by hundreds, thousands, lakhs, and crores according to one’s desire—one should count the beads starting from the thumb and index finger, reciting [the mantra] a hundred times or more.
The root of calculation is the eightfold error; one should avoid accepting numbers and so forth that are free from such faults when crossing over the *melu*.
For it is thus:
Then, beginning with the *praṇava*, one should mentally recite the mantra "Śivāya" followed by "namaḥ," with the inner self absorbed in Him.
One should not transgress Meru, the cause of creation and destruction, even when bound;
yet for one who has transgressed it, there is no fault, provided they string together the final garland of the courtyard devoid of Meru for the sake of the rider who fears the *tāra*.
Having joined mouth to mouth, or with Meru facing upwards.
19a) Or, with threads made of linen cloth and the like, the *nāgapāśinī* [noose] is visibly formed;
it has two purposes, follows the manner of a cow's tail, and is free from defects such as holes.
One should apply the mantra with a rosary made of old bones, broken at the neck, and consisting of irregular vajras; by means of such a rosary, the *traṃmasa* [mantra] is accomplished.
One should recite the mantra, which is faultless and abounding in virtues, using a rosary of forty beads;
[the sequence] from the little finger to the tip of the index finger consists of three groups of three.
At the base of the thumb, one should place [the hand] downwards; then, moving upwards again, from the index finger to the little finger, it should be positioned on the right hand as before.
One should count by means of twenty-seven joints, known as the "garland of hands";
one may begin from the middle of the thumb or from whichever [joint] one prefers, and thus lead [the breath] along.
One who abandons neither the middle nor the non-middle [fingers], or else, from the time [of the breath] onwards, having placed the ten [syllables] on the right hand,
one should then assign the armor (*varma*) and the heart (*hṛdaya*); having worshipped the form therein with women...
Above that, one should place the weapons (astras) along with the silver-encased protective coverings, using the mudrā arising from the knees placed on the ground.
Oṃ. O Guardian of Secrets, accept this recitation performed by me;
through your grace, may it lead to my success as it rests within you.
Having recited this while standing at night,

one who desires victory and nourishment should stand in the southeast corner, holding a hand-gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) together with unhusked rice, *kuśa* grass, and water, resembling the full moon.

Having meditated upon the fruit of the worship, one should offer the worship, the recitation, and oneself into the *kumbha* through exhalation (*recaka*), saying "I offer," and then present it with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* or *namaḥ*.
One should apply the mantra to the *śakti* within the principle (*tattva*) that is supreme among the auspicious.
In the supreme reality which is free from conceptual proliferation, mantra becomes fruitless.
A mantra is not perfected by mere recitation, nor does it grant fruit when merely offered as an oblation;
and if unworshipped, it does not fulfill one's desires; therefore, one should practice this triad.
Then:
Oṃ! O God, whatever we do, whether good or evil deeds, may Śaṅkara, who abides in the state of Śiva, destroy that for me—Hūṃ Kṣa!
Thus concludes the expiation.
Oṃ! Śiva is the giver of the head, Śiva is the enjoyer, and this entire world is Śiva.
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; he who is Śiva is indeed delusion itself.
Thus it is for one desiring liberation. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda Tantra*: "Those who desire liberation should perform recitation equal to the breath throughout the day;
for the upward-moving breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the day, and the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) is the night."
Having correctly established the self, the mind, the mantra, Śiva, and likewise Śakti,
one should conquer the mantra, its commentary, and the solar mind.
Relying upon the garland of mantras like a jewel,
the mantra-deity Prabhāvatī is clearly manifest to others who hear it, generating an understanding of the words.

In the commentary, it is said that for rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*), the mantra should be whispered (*upāṃśu*); for pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it should be recited with the mere movement of the lips, making it audible only to another.

The vocal [recitation] is known to be one part; another is ten million times superior to that, wherein through the connection of the syllables of the words, meaning follows from meaning, word follows word.
In the contemplation of all sounds, one who possesses equanimity of mind shall attain liberation through the *sat* (Being);
or else, those who recite mantras may attain the powers such as *aṇimā*, or even that which is devoid of these, by means of the middle and other [vowels].

Then, having recited the mantra ten times for the subordinate deities (ājñā), having offered it, honored them, and meditated upon them, he— having performed the flower-offering, the sipping of water (ācamana), the hymn of praise, and so forth, and having paid homage with due respect— for the purpose of worshipping the deities of the [inner] circle,
should place the Veda in the western part of the northern petal of the central lotus, conjoined with the light of Aghoralocana.

One should worship the deities in the form of Nātha and others in the central portion, those in the form of male and female deities such as Ghumeśvara and others in the eastern portion, and those in the form of Durgā and others.
And the bull in the illustrious Mṛgendra.
On the petals of the southern lotus, in the eastern and western sectors, there are the forms of a woman and a man;
the light of the Aghora-eye is in the center and nowhere else.
In this manner, the teacher too, remaining firm in that vow, should indeed act for a short time, avoiding the final siege;
he should remain with his senses restrained, desiring to know the self, for the sake of someone’s forgiveness and so forth.

Oṃ kṣuṃ hūṃ hraḥ, homage to the Great Tiger, whose face is distorted and whose eyes are tawny. Oṃ kṣuṃ, homage to Padma. Oṃ duṃ, homage to Durgāsana. [These three, beginning with Siṃha, are in the center.]

Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the form of Durgā. Above that, one should visualize her form as golden-hued, standing upon a lion with its back resting on a buffalo, her feet in the *ālīḍha* posture, three-eyed, adorned, and ten-armed; holding in her right hands a sword, an arrow, a spear, a trident, and a discus, and in [the left] a shield and a bow.
Having visualized the supreme [deity] accompanied by Kuśa grass, nooses, and *kuśarā*, [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ śaḥ mahādurge caṇḍikātyāyani svāhā*.
Having performed the pervasion with the root mantra and having established the presence [of the deity] through the *toraṇa* and other rites: Oṃ hrīṃ durge, homage to the heart.
Oṃ hrīṃ dūrge, svāhā to the head. Oṃ hūṃ durge, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Oṃ hraiṃ durge, hūṃ to the armor (*kavaca*). Oṃ hrauṃ durge, vaṣaṭ to the three eyes.
Oṃ hraḥ! O Durgā’s weapon, blaze forth, blaze forth! devour, devour! Hūṃ phaṭ! Homage!
Having arranged [the mantras] as before, one should perform the supreme consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*). [Recite: *oṃ bhagavati bhadrakālike svāhā*.

Having performed the preliminary services (*upacāra*) with the Heart-mantra and the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth as before, one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*) as before; however, in front of the Goddess, one should worship the Eye (*netra*).
[Recite: *oṃ bhagavati kātyāyani namaḥ*. *oṃ bhagavati mahiṣāsuramardani namaḥ*. *oṃ*...

Salutation to the Blessed One dwelling in the Vindhya mountains. Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One who moves at will, the bringer of delight. [In the directions starting from the east: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Aindrī.

Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the goddess of the southeast. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the goddess of the south. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the goddess of the southwest. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the goddess of the west. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the goddess of the northwest. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the goddess of the north. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the goddess of the northeast.
21b) Quiescence of the eastern direction and so forth.
Oṃ gauṃ, salutations to Gaṇapati, the form of Rudra, the lord of the Gaṇas.
Haraṃ raṃ. Oṃ, homage to Hari-dasva, the one of great speed, the sovereign lord of the seven horses. [The chariot].
Oṃ, homage to Puṇḍarīka, the protector against heat. [The parasol].
Oṃ, homage to Daṇḍa, who has the form of a great iron bar, the warder-off of all evil ones.
The center of the parasol: Oṃ, homage to the Lord of Obstacles, the one born from Prajñā, who holds a banner in his hand;
[homage to] the banner.
Having worshipped with offerings such as recitation (*japa*) and others, and having established [the deity] within the image, one should dismiss it like the sun by means of the root-mantra (*mūla*).
Alternatively, having meditated upon the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) as being endowed with the seat, the image, the root-mantra, and the limb-mantras, one should perform the sacrifice.
The worship of Durgā.
Having worshipped Śiva with three *añjali*s, performed three circumambulations (*pradakṣiṇa*), and offered prostrations with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*) and so forth, one should say:

"O Blessed One, accept the fruit of the merit of my worship, recitation (*japa*), and other rites: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*. Then, having offered the remaining ritual actions, one should say: "O Blessed One, from this day forward..."

Having offered eight flowers with one's own mantras into the center of the Śiva-linga, having propitiated it, and having recited [the mantra] again, one should think: "I must perform this rite which is to be honored by others and is without end; therefore, O Command, come here. Then, having recited [the mantra] again...
Having made the offering, one should announce:
"Oṃ! Whatever has been done by me through delusion—whether deficient or even excessive—may all that become complete for me through your grace, O Lord."
And so forth.

Then, from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, ending with *svāhā*, one should offer the *arghya* with the root mantra; and from the weapon-mantra (*astra*) to the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), ending with *svāhā*, one should offer the *arghya* with the weapon-mantra and others while facing away, using the hand and the *nārāca* [weapon].
Having raised the *mudrājñā* [mudrā of command] with the thumbs and ring fingers held like flowers in both hands,

one should join the limbs of the form (*mūrti*) to their respective locations. Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra and employed the *mahāmudrā* and other gestures, one performs the dismissal (*visarjana*) at the principal *liṅga* with the request, "Forgive me."

Having honored Śiva on the sacrificial mound with the *arghya* offering, one should unite Him, who resides within the heart-lotus, with the Śiva residing in the heart by means of the root-mantra and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā]; thus it is independent [of external supports].
And so it is said:
Having meditated on her as risen like a flash of lightning, one should perform the dissolution (laya) into their respective places.
When the mantras have gone to the place of dissolution, the root-mantras also go to dissolution.
Then one should meditate on the root mantra as having dissolved into the throbbing *bindu*; the *bindu* dissolves into the *nāda*, and the *nāda* enters the power of consciousness (*vijñāna-śakti*).
The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is dissolved in the Supreme; he who is established in the space of the heart (hṛd-vyoman) from whom the mantra is born, into that very place it is dissolved.

Thereafter, the Goddess [should worship] the Gurus and the Gaṇas with the Virūpākṣa-arghya using their own mantras; [she should worship] Vardhanī, Ambikā, Astra, Brahmāstra, Yamunā, and the rest with the general arghya. Having performed the worship in this manner, she should dismiss them with the heart-mantra and the general arghya.

Having placed the deity within a vessel, having assigned the seat of Caṇḍa and the root-mantras to the image with the heart-mantra, and having worshipped them in the Śāna [shrine], one should raise the deity, offer him his used garland (nirmālya), dismiss him with the heart-mantra, and worship the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) as one would Śiva.
And it has been said:
Or one should worship the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), the Koṭikātra, or one's own Saṃhitā.

Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Nandā. Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Bhadrā. Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Surabhi. Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Suśīlā. Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Sumanas. Having worshipped [the goddesses] on the top of the head, at the front right and left, behind, and in order upon the four hooves.
Oṃ! O Saurabhī, Mother of the World, Bestower of nectar upon the gods; accept this morsel, O Giver of Boons, and grant me my desired object.
Oṃ! You have been honored by Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Jahnu;
O Kapilā, may whatever evil deed has been committed by me also come to an end.
Oṃ! You who arose from the churning of the nectar of immortality, O fragrant one, sustainer of the world!
Accept this morsel from me; this is my supreme vow.
Regarding food and drink: one should give three mouthfuls.
Oṃ, may cows always be before me, and may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart as well, and may I dwell in the midst of cows.
One who is self-controlled and pure should recite this mantra, known as the *nārājana*, three times daily.
Liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva;
then, having performed three circumambulations, one should offer salutations.
The worship of Kapila.
One should not perform divine rites while seated in the presence of one’s own guru; rather, having entered the Kula of Śiva, one should prostrate before him.
Or, through the yoga of meditation, one should worship the Guru as Śiva himself, established within the heart.

23b) One should properly worship the sandals placed upon the pedestal for the absent [guru]. Likewise, having abandoned the gaze toward other well-known [teachers], one should bow with devotion and offer a special *argha* [offering] to the Guru.
Having established [the deity] within the image, one should dismiss it without further attachment;

or else, after the *gaṇas*, one should dismiss [the deity] and perform another *argha* offering. Then, having removed the *nirmālya* and purified the ground, one should sip water (*ācamana*), perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and [protect] the earth with the *astra* mantra.

If there is an excess or deficiency of even one [syllable], for the sake of pacifying that defect, one should recite the *Saptaviṃśatisaṃhitā* twenty-one times or the *Aghora-mantra* twenty-one times, and then determine the auspiciousness of all [the rites]. Thus,
worship performed for the sake of attaining the splendor and power of the infinite light existing from the dissolution (*vilaya*) up to the end is of little essence.
Whatever various maṇḍala one contemplates, it immediately attains equality with its presiding deity due to its identity with the object to be accomplished.

In the abbreviated rite, however, from the doors up to the worship of the Guru, one should offer the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) with the Heart-mantra in the center and at the points from Agni to Īśāna; the remaining seats, such as those for the Mūrtis, are as before. This has been stated in the *Śrīpūrva* [Tantra]:
Ananta, Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, and Padma— this is the sixfold seat.
In the common *svayaṃbhū* rite, having assigned the two wings as the *kāraṇāsana* and the *mūrti*, and having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the *sādi* mantras,
one should worship with the *gāyatrī*.
Or as by others: "The Praṇava, Mātṛkā, Māyā, Dhyāna, the six-syllabled [mantra], Prasāda, and Vahurūpa—these are remembered as the seven common [mantras]."

One desiring the Kāmika [type of Linga] should fashion the Linga from clay or other materials that are free from impurities, soft, and pure, using a mold or other instruments, measuring three finger-breadths in height.
For the purpose of purification through sprinkling, using the general *argha* water held in the hand, one should perform the sprinkling and other rites;
once the *liṅga* is purified, one should contemplate the *Śivatattva* and its Lord (*Īśvara*).
In the middle, one should contemplate the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) along with its lord Viṣṇu;
and in the lower portion, the principle of the self (ātma-tattva) along with Brahmā, the lord of the rivers.
Having then performed the placement of these [syllables] for the sake of purification with *hūṃ hīṃ hāṃ* while reciting the *Sambara* mantra,
one should touch the root, middle, and tip of the *kuśa* grass and thereby consecrate the linga.
Then, one should place the seats—divided into five parts each—at the base, middle, and top; these are to be installed upon pedestals for the form known as the Mūrti-liṅga.
Then, having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs according to the previous procedure by means of pervasiveness,
one should release him without further expectation and cast that flower into the water.
24b) Having performed another [rite], one who is initiated obtains his desired fruit in a single year; he should worship the *liṅga* without [the usual] mantra.
Earthenware and so forth.
In every case here, in whatever rite no mantra is found,
one should recollect the Heart-mantra there at the prescribed time, according to the rules.
Whatever may arise at every moment, all that [should be contemplated] with the heart;
through that, concentration, retention, meditation, victory, and the state of Śiva are attained.
Whether in one's own form or in the form of the Guru, on the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in water, in fire, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
in a fixed linga, or in a mobile [linga], [one should worship] externally in their presence.
Sacrifice performed upon a linga possessing auspicious marks is superior to all these;
it becomes a single-pointed concentration, free from dependence on external objects.
The supreme means of attaining Yoga is by means of the mere object of concentration;
[it may be] in the heart-lotus, at the navel, or on the mountain of the head.
Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to such locations as the head and so forth;
it is the continuous flow of the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*) by taking a location or an object as its support.
That meditation, unmixed with other mental states, is the heart of liberation;
it consists of the constant worship of the Lord at Vārāṇasī, by one whose intellect has been purified through the power of that city.
They designate that form of fire, which is an essential component of the sacrifice, by names such as Vimala and Śambhu.
The first [chapter]: The Accomplishment of Worship in Vimalāvatī.
Grantha 372.
By which [knowledge] one's stainless nature, known as the eye of wisdom, is not obscured;
and by whose true presence, for a being born in the ocean of existence, [suffering] has passed away.
Having recognized that Lord, the Destroyer of Cities, who by His grace destroys even that darkness which is otherwise difficult to restrain,
this fire-rite (agnikārya) is now being written.

Desiring to perform the fire-oblation (homa) with all the ritual substances and assistants, one should first, with devotion, prostrate fully with eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma) before Śiva, the Supreme Intellect, and say: "O Lord, grant me your permission;
I shall now perform the fire-rite."
Having thus honored the vessel of fragrant offerings and performed a circumambulation, he approached,
beholding the articles required for the fire-oblation situated in the direction of the fire.
One should consecrate it according to the group of prescribed rites, as in the worship of the northern face;
and that [mandala] should be either a five-pointed star or a circle measuring one cubit.
In the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites as prescribed by the ritual manuals,
[the altar] should be constructed with well-baked bricks, or without them if such materials are unavailable.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as prescribed in the scriptures, with five, three, or one girdle (mekhalā).
The girdles of the five types of pits should consist of six, five, four, three, and two [units] respectively.
Or it may be three finger-breadths wide, with three corners, six sides, or one finger-breadth;
therein, the splendor of Śiva is augmented by the root-mantra, and there is gazing with the eye.
Sprinkling and fumigation are performed with the Astra-mantra ending in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*;
sprinkling is performed with the Varma-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* or *vaṭ*.
One should dig the two doors with the Astra-mantra; perform the filling and leveling of the heart [of the site] with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
perform the sprinkling with the Varma-mantra ending in Vauṣaṭ; and perform the solidification with the Astra-mantra.
The cleansing of the armors is on the other side of the vessel. Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śāntyatītā; in the center.
Oṃ hyaiṃ, obeisance to Śānti; in the east.
Oṃ hrūṃ, homage to Vidyā; to Yāmī.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Pratiṣṭhā; in the north.
Oṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛtti; in the west.
The conceptualization of the *kalāmaya* [fire] with flowers; the wrapping of the triple-thread with armor (*varman*).
*Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the *kalāmaya* pit (*kuṇḍa*). [This is] the worship.
Alternatively, one may draw three lines with their tips pointing north and a single line facing east using a blade of kusha grass as a measuring tool.
26a) One performs the vajrification with the Astra-mantra using three kusha blades in the shape of a vajra;
one forms the crossroads with two kusha blades from the Heart-mantra, having their tips pointing east and north.
These eighteen purificatory rites are the root; the syllable *Hrūṃ* is their cause, residing in the heart.
With the *varman* mantra and *kuśa* grass, one should perform the rite at the four necks of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using a bamboo staff.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī, the mistress of speech.
Having placed a seat in the center of the sacrificial pit: Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Vāgeśvarī.
Oṃ hau& vāgīśvarāya namaḥ. This is the worship. There is either the invocation of Vāgīśā or not, as the venerable Kṣemarāja has said.

Therefore, satisfied by the supreme savor of the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the most excellent Guru— by the command of Śiva, intent upon the auspicious speech directed toward the essence of Śiva, and having ascended by his own power— produces through his own splendor the entire sequence beginning with fire as being identical with the single self-luminous radiance of Śiva.

Then, having extracted a piece of charcoal from a fire produced in a fire-drill, or from the sun, or from a house, or from a bird’s nest, and placed it in a worthy vessel, one should purify it through inspection and other rites using the Astra-mantra.

26b) Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire (Vahni-mūrti). Having grasped the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), which has the luster of a green gram (*mudga*) and a [single] spoke, with the *pūraka* [breath-retention], and having [grasped] that which has the luster of the sun with the *bindu*-fire by means of the *kumbhaka*, [one should contemplate it] again at midday with the navel-fire (*nābhyagni*).

Having unified this solar form as it arises with the *bindu*, [one should say]: "Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the fire-caitya. By means of the *recaka* breath through the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*), one should place the blazing, revolving fire into the vessel;
then, having consecrated it with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and performed the three rites beginning with the veiling (*guṇṭhana*), [one should say]: "Oṃ..."

"Hā&! Salutation to Agni. Having worshipped [the fire] and taken it up with both hands, one should rotate it three times clockwise over the sacrificial hearth (kuṇṭha) while the knees rest upon the ground. Then, having visualized Vāgīśvarī and Saumyā as being united in the directions of Īśāna, Śiras, Vāyu, and Agni, [one should recite]: "Oṃ Hā&."

Salutation to the seed-syllable of Śiva. One should meditate upon the seed-syllable being cast, like a seed by the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśa), into the womb-channel of Vāgeśī; thus it should be cast facing the inner self (*vibhādhyātma*).
Then, once that seed has moved from the heart to the navel, there is its confinement within a hut (*kuṭīkaraṇa*) and its covering with a garment (*paridhānasaṃvaraṇa*).
27a) Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Vāgīśvarī; for the ritual rinsing of the mouth.
