Having covered it with a shield and with wood, and having washed it with a fan.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire of the womb. [This is] the worship.
One should sprinkle with the Astra-mantra, but one should not perform worship with the Agni-mantra.

Having tied a ring of kuśa grass over which the Astra-mantra has been recited seven times on the right hand, [one should pray]: "O Vāgīśī, destroy the afflictions of the womb for the sake of obtaining a son and a husband."
Having worshipped with the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should offer five oblations ending in *svāhā* with the *hṛdaya* mantra during the first month for the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*).
Having worshipped with the left hand, one should offer oblations with the head.
Oṃ hāṃ puṃ puryaṣṭaka-dehāya namaḥ. One should offer a drop of water containing living beings along with *kuśa* grass; this is the *puṃsavana* rite.

In the third terrible [rite], having performed the sacrifice, one should offer twenty oblations for the purpose of severing and extracting the arrangement of the faces, the crest, the sides, and the limbs.
One should assign the *Ṛṣabha*, *Gāndhāra*, and [the other notes] to the forenoon, midday, and afternoon of the day;

then, having performed the rite for the mouth (*mukhakṛtyā*) in the eastern direction with three *tattva*-offerings in succession, the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*) and the opening of the eyes (*nayana*) take place in the sixth month.

27b) Having offered oblations into the fire with *kuśa* grass using the armor-mantra (*varma-mantra*) that is not to be worshipped by men, he— by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*)— should immediately destroy the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*). Having sprinkled the interior and exterior of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he should recite "vāg asī" and then dismiss [the deity].
Having visualized a braid of *kuśa* grass as a ceremonial bath-offering (*snānālaṃkāra*) and having worshipped it with the heart-mantra,

one should offer five fuel-sticks— measuring a finger-joint (*karanni*), smeared with ghee, and consisting of the tips, the roots, or both root and tip— with the weapon-mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ* and followed by *svāhā*, in order to remove saliva.

Having placed kuśa grass with its tips pointing east and north in the four directions of the pit using the Astra-mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*) upon them using the Varma-mantra.
For it is said thus:
Tightly knotted with thirty blades of darbha grass, they should reach the length of an arm;
they may be either braided, circular, or broad, as known by those learned in the ritual.

The sacrificial enclosures (paridhis) are always said to be made from the wood of the *tan-māna*, *nāma-ja*, *sādra*, or *sat-palāśa* trees; their circumference should equal the span of the middle finger.
Then, on the enclosing sticks (paridhis): Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā; in the east.
Oṃ hā& obeisance to Viṣṇu; in the west.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkara; in the south.
28a) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta; in the north.

Upon the seats, starting from the east and ending in the north in the four cardinal directions, and outside of those from the northwest (Vāyu) to the northeast (Īśāna), are the eight world-protectors (Lokapālas): Candra and the others, ending with Īśāna, and Agni and the others, facing inward. [One should worship] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Nairṛta, and Diti with the Heart mantra. Outside the enclosure (paridhi) in the southern pit (kuṇḍa).
On a bed of *kuśa* grass spread over dried cow dung:

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of sacrifice. Likewise, in the northern direction, having worshipped the *praṇītā* vessel filled with water, *kuśa* grass, and a purifier (*pavitra*), [saying]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the slayer of the enemies of sacrifice. O, O!

Having caused the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) to station themselves by the command of Śiva, one should proclaim: "Protect this Agnikumāra! Then, grasping with both hands the *śruk* and *sruva* ladles—which are free from defects such as missing limbs, which are of the nature of the power (*śakti*) and Śiva, purified by inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and other rites, and provided with *kuśa* grass—one should [place them] in the fire with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) in order to remove their wooden state.
Having heated the roots, middles, and tips of the *kuśa* grass three times, one should scratch their roots, middles, and tips with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva along with the Intellect for the sake of liberation, and having worshipped the Power (*śakti*) in the *śrucī* ladle and Śiva in the *śruva* ladle, one should wrap them with the Armor-mantra (*varman*), using either the triple-stranded *kuśa* or a cloth, on the left side.

Having placed those two [blades of] kuśa grass with their tips upward and their bases downward for the purpose of protection, one should take the "Kapila" ghee— which has been purified by reciting the scripture—
contained in a vessel of copper or similar metal that has undergone the fourfold purification. Having meditated upon the fire as the form of Brahman,
one should circumambulate it three times over the sacrificial pit while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, and then place it in the corner of the pit near the fire.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Brahmā!
One should perform the heating by casting a drop of clarified butter onto fire with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass,
while maintaining the visualization of oneself as having the form of Viṣṇu.

Oṃ hīṃ viṣṇave svāhā. Thus one should cast [the oblation]; this is the act of placing upon the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*). Holding oneself over the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and meditating on oneself in the form of Rudra, [one recites]: Oṃ hūṃ rudrāya svāhā. Then one should cast [it]; this is the act of stirring (*uśana*). Alternatively, at the conclusion of the placing upon the fire, one performs three rotations of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in the measure of a ladle (*dhyaghṛta*) within the pit. Then...

Taking the middle *brahmagranthi*—which is one span long and reddish—with the thumb and ring finger, one should wash it with the *varma* mantra ending in *svāhā* and cast it three times into the mouth; then, in the same manner, one should cast it again into one's own mouth with the *hṛdaya* mantra ending in *svāhā*. These are the *utplava* and *saṃplava* rites.
Having thrown a *kuśa* torch into clarified butter held in the heart-vessel, one should cast it into the fire; this is the purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).

29a) Regarding *varmaṇā*: having produced fire by rubbing together blazing *kuśa* grass, one should cast that *kuśa* into the fire; this is *añjana*. Regarding *astreṇa*: having kindled [the fire] with blazing *kuśa* grass, one should cast [it] into the fire; this is *udyotana*.

Having cast a *kuśa* grass knot of the size of a span into the center of the heart, and having meditated upon the right and left [channels] as the white and black fortnights respectively, as well as the three channels of Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Suṣumnā, one should take up the sacrificial ladle (*śruva*) in the left portion.

Oṃ hāṃ, to Agni, svāhā! [Offer] ghee into that very [mouth], the right eye of Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, to Soma, svāhā! Into the left eye, [offer] ghee with *hāvāma*. Oṃ hāṃ, to Agni and Soma, svāhā! Into the middle eye, [offer] ghee with *hāmadhya*. Oṃ hāṃ, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! Into the mouth of Agni.
Hā at the third division; thus in the bright fortnight.

In the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), however, one should serve the Vāma [tradition] according to the following sequence: *oṃ hāṃ somāya*, *oṃ hāṃ agnaye*, *oṃ hāṃ somāgnibhyām*, *oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte*. This sequence, joined with *svāhā* and *hūṃ*, is as previously described. In the *Śrīmṛgendrottara* and the *Śrīsvacchanda*, however, it is otherwise, as follows:
29b) Thus indeed is the procedure for the bright fortnight; in the dark fortnight it would be otherwise.
When the moon occupies the solar portion, it is indeed called "fire," as before.
One should cause the oblation to fall into the midst of the fire of the sun,
because on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the moon enters into the midst of the sun. Then,
having consecrated her with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) externally, one should perform the veiling and other rites with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), and by the casting of its drops (bindu), [the other].

Having taken clarified butter with the *sādhya-śruva* ladle, [one offers it] with: Oṃ haṃ sadyojātāya svāhā | Oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya svāhā | Oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā | Oṃ hyaṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ īśānāya svāhā | This is the illumination of the faces (*vaktradīpana*).
Oṃ haṃ hiṃ, svāhā to Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva! Oṃ hiṃ huṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva and Aghora!

Oṃ huṃ hyaṃ, svāhā to Aghora and Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ heṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna. This is the joining of the faces. Oṃ hauṃ hyaiṃ huṃ hiṃ haṃ, svāhā to Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta. [From the southeast corner to the northwest corner...]
30a) But for these two, [the eyes] are always directed outward; otherwise, it is indeed different.
And it is said: "In the application of the terrifying face, one should perform the *sadya* and other rites with the *saṃvaras*;
subsequently, having understood the activity through the *yadvaśāna* and so forth, one attains oneness."

Having meditated upon the five faces of the fire, one should perform the desired rite in the principal face at the top; the upward-facing mouth should be located in that position. Having internalized the other faces, that [fire] should be of the same measurement as the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Śiva, Rudra, Agni, Āditya, Brahmā, Indra, Acyuta, and the others,
as well as those whose mouths are the sacrificial fire— he is the remover of fear for all the gods.
Thus, in the tenth [chapter] on the birth-rite (jātakarman), having worshipped with the Īśa [mantra] and offered oblations with the Astra [mantra].

Having recited, "Oṃ hāṃ! You are the Śiva-fire; you are the seat," and having worshipped Vāgīśī, he offers ten oblations to each with the word *svāhā* at the end, and then dismisses her. Rising up, taking the *śruk* and *sruva* ladles together with the *kuśa* grass while maintaining meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and placing a flower on the tip of the *śruk* filled with clarified butter, he gazes at it with his face turned downward.

Having placed the *śruva* spoon down, and having held it with the right and left hands in sequence from front to back at the level of the navel— counting thirty [times]— one should slowly move it across to the end of the left breast and the end of the heart.

Or, having brought [the mantra] to the end of the mouth or to the root of the ear, one should offer the "Full Oblation" (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, which fulfills all desires and bestows prosperity on the joints; this is the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). Thus are the rites for the conception, the male gender, the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth, and the naming. As it has been said:
The Śiva-fire, consecrated by the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras),
is indeed the most excellent for the rites of initiation, the daily obligatory duties, or even for rites performed for specific desires.

One should daily cause the fire to be awakened for the rites prescribed for Kuṇḍanī, such as the drawing of lines and so forth; however, in the case of obligatory daily rites, one should not awaken it from sleep.

In the consecrated [fire], however, one should not pour water into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) daily; having previously consecrated it with water, one should then extract a small portion of fire for the purpose of incense and other offerings and preserve it in another location.
As it has been said:
The sacrificial oblations of cooked rice and cakes are purified by the five consecratory rites;
O Śivā, the oblation (homa) performed in the fire that has been invoked becomes [efficacious] even if [the deity] was not formally summoned.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Agni.
Having worshipped and meditated upon the sixteenth [digit] for the sake of nourishment, and having offered oblations, [one should recite]:
"O Agni, you are the splendor of Īśvara, because you are the supreme purifier."
"Therefore, having established him within the lotus of your heart, I shall satisfy him.
Having thus supplicated, one should visualize the channel (nāḍī) emerging from the right nostril entering the left nostril as fire.
Having meditated upon Śiva with his limbs (sāṅga) within the fire, and having worshipped the fire— which has assumed the form of the deity— by offering food (naivedya), sacred threads (pavitra),

recitation (japa), and so forth; and having entreated the fire with the words, "O Blessed One, you are the fuel for us by means of whatever substances are available," [one should worship] the tongues of the fire.
Having made the mental resolve, one should offer clarified butter and other substances with the *saṅkalpa* and the *śruva* ladle; *mṛgī* mudrā for *anyayāva*, *yava*, sesame, rice, and so forth;
with the fist for parched grain (*lāja*) and other such items; and likewise for other substances with the *vārāhī* and *saṃkhinī* mudrās according to the nature of the material. As it has been said:
In the absence of ghee, the oblation should be performed with black sesame seeds. Likewise:
"An oblation consisting of sesame seeds soaked in ghee bestows all desires. One should offer it when the fire is not blazing; and honey should be offered in the case of a binding [of a vow]."
When the fire is blazing and licking [the offerings], the oblation succeeds;
it is glossy, turning to the right, and its sound is muffled by the Vedic chants.
Because it always rises upward like a flame, that auspicious [fire] has a concentrated crest;
then, having recited the root mantra ending in *svāhā* ten times, one should offer oblations for the ten parts as well.

Having offered [the oblation] completely, having worshipped the space in front of the deity, having gratified and dismissed [the deities], and having offered three morsels of food to the God with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and one morsel each to the fires, having offered water for rinsing the mouth and so forth, and having praised [the Lord], one should circumambulate from left to right with devotion and honor the sacred ash (*bhasma*).

Oṃ hāṃ bhūḥ svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā | Oṃ svaḥ svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā. Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, having worshipped Śiva with the eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpī*), and having dismissed [the deity], one should also offer to the deities stationed outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Then, having offered to Caṇḍa and Caṇḍādyā, [one performs] up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having satisfied [the deity] with the Astra-mantra and offered eight expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-āhuti*), [one offers]: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ agnīsomābhyāṃ svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, [one says]: *oṃ hāṃ hūṃ agnaye namaḥ*. Agni...
One should release it.
Having prepared two mandalas in the corner of the sacrificial pit fire, [one] at the edge of the western mandala: *Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Bhadras*; in the east:
*Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Mothers*; in the south.
32a) Oṃ hā& namaḥ to the Gaṇas. In the west.
Oṃ hā& homage to the yakṣas! In the north.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the planets; in the northeast (īśa). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the asuras; in the southeast (agni). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the rākṣasas; in the southwest (nairṛtya).
Oṃ hā& namas to the Nāgas; [this is] in the northwest.
Then, within the mandala: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the constellations (nakṣatras) in the northeast.
Oṃ hā& namaḥ to the zodiac signs. [In the southeast.]
Oṃ hā& salutation to all the Viśvedevas. [Direction: Nairṛtya.
Oṃ hā& namaḥ to Kṣetrapāla in the northwest (vāyu).
The inner fold.
Then, in the east: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Indra. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nairṛtya. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kuvera. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna. Oṃ hāṃ.
Salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. As before.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nīlalohita. In the center.
Having performed worship with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā* and concluding with a libation of water, one should offer the *bali*.
The outer enclosure: Oṃ, those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, who abide in the realm of Rudra, and those who are gentle—[to all of them].
Those who dwell in gentle places, the Mothers of fierce form, those who are lords of the Gaṇas,

and others who have become obstacles residing in the cardinal and intermediate directions— may you all receive this bali offering with pleased minds; may you grant me success and always protect me from the three states of existence.
Oṃ, svāhā to those dwelling in the ten directions beginning with the east, including the lords of the directions, the elemental mothers, the hosts of mātṛs, the Rudras, the kṣetrapālas, and so forth.
Oṃ hā& svāhā to the crows and others who violate their commitments!

Having stated that each offering (*bali*) should be made outside the mandala, starting from the right and ending in the center, one should release them all with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). Then, having gone near Śiva, one should perform the dedication of the ritual action (*karmārpaṇa*) and so forth as before.
Alternatively, the fruit may be achieved through the root-mantra, water, and so on, or by the final offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) of the oblation.
Alternatively, according to the view of Līlāvatī, even in that [rite], having washed the fire on the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or the altar (sthāṇḍila) and so forth,

one should gaze at it, sprinkle it, and strike it; having removed the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda), and having sprinkled [the remaining] three fires and unified them, one should install the consciousness (caitanya) of the fire.
Having worshipped Sadyojāta and the others, offered five oblations with the root mantra,

and performed the naming ceremony, one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and its girdles (mekhalā) with water using four auspicious kuśa blades while reciting the Varma-mantra, and then plant them in the directions starting from the east.
Having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Ananta, and having fully honored and satisfied the fire;

then, for the purpose of satisfying Śiva, having invoked Śiva into the center, having satisfied him and offered the *pūrṇāhuti*; having presented the offerings such as the *naivedya*, having applied the sacred ashes (*bhasma*), having performed the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and having worshipped and dismissed Śiva.
Having offered the oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt along with the bali offerings, one should dedicate the ritual action.
On the fourteenth day, on the fifteenth day of both fortnights,
during the solstices, the equinoxes, Rāhu’s eclipse, Vyatīpāta, the Aṣṭakās, and so forth.
One should perform rituals such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblations (homa), however, with double the usual effort.
Having thus completed the morning rites according to the rules without sloth,
one should listen to the True Guru with devotion, reflect upon it, and then teach it.
Avoiding the full moon, the first day of the lunar fortnight, the fourteenth, and the eighth days of the year;
as well as the seventh, the ninth, and the three *aṣṭakā* days;
and those [times] declared [inauspicious] such as twilight, eclipses, portents, comets, and the burning of the quarters.
Having worshipped Śiva and the gurus in the maṇḍala with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,

Having first prostrated and performed other such acts of reverence toward the scripture situated on the leaf-stalk machine (śārayantra), as well as toward the Lord who is the Guru of Knowledge, one should thereafter recite it until the Guru has given his approval.
Upon its completion, having rested well and bowed down, one should again proceed beyond that.
At midday, having performed the external rites as before, he should go home with his friends;
he must observe strict vows during the rainy season, [abstaining from] Arundhatī and Śavita, and engage in bathing and other such acts in rivers, streams, lakes, or ponds.
It would be best if located within the house, middling if in a lotus pond, and inferior if in a long canal and so forth; however, it should be near a well for the sake of stability.
One should always face the east when bathing for the removal of impurities;
however, during a ritual bath, both the religious student and the householder should likewise face the north.

One should never bathe in water while wearing dry clothes, nor on dry ground while wearing wet garments; nor should one perform any ritual action while standing upon dry clothing that was previously beneath those [wet] clothes.
Bathing with the ashes of the fire-god (Āgneya) bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon husbands;
it is performed with the burnt remains of pure cow-dung by means of the auspicious fire (Śivavahni).
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), he should take [the vessel] with his right hand in a fist;
having purified it as before with the *nivṛtti* and other kalās, he should consecrate it again.
Then, with the left hand, he should [hold it] while the right hand performs the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having taken [the weapon-mantra] from the head down to the feet, one should perform it otherwise.
34a) Then, there is the bath for removing impurities, the ritual bath, and furthermore the consecration bath; in sequence,
one should smear [the body] from the head downwards with the [mantras] beginning with Īśa, using the hand marked with Hrīm.
For the sake of liberation, one should abandon the presence of the Guru and others with both hands;
then, having performed the three *tāla* strikes with the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the circumambulation.
Bathing, clothing, and the sacred thread—whether white or saffron-colored—are impure; one should wipe them with earth, shake them out, and beat them upon the ground.
The Māhendra bath is victorious; it likewise consists of the destruction of impurities.
It is like a shower of sunbeams, possessing form through the coming and going of the seven steps.

A donkey with ears like those of a horse, arising from dust, should be addressed by a man with eyes closed like those of an elephant; that [act] should be performed through the recitation of the mantra.
With minds alone,
they mentally invited Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, and the other sacred rivers that were present nearby.
Or likewise, one may obtain earth from a good battlefield;
with that, one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) to the body, beginning with the head, using unguents.
This is indeed the "earthly bath," which destroys all evil deeds;
being pure, one should bear the feet of the guru upon one's head while uttering the name of Śiva.
34b) Recalling the mantra from its state of impurity, one should [attain] reverence through that mental activity.
Having performed the bath and other rites from these [substances] as desired— even if the rite is deficient in minor parts—
one should then wash [the body] with water mixed with earth.

Since one might lose one's garments and other belongings during bathing or fall from one’s staff while walking, one should proceed with care; on the path, one should avoid the lower vital organs (marmas) by means of the weapon [of mindfulness].

Standing in the midst of the cage of missiles (astrapañjara), with eyes like those of a cowherd boy, one should sip water (ācamana) therein; at the end of the mantra, one should go to the abode of Sadāśiva.
In that regard, one should first worship Śiva in a linga, or on an altar (sthaṇḍila) and so forth; even by worshipping on an altar, one quickly attains the desired goal through the mantras.
But what is more difficult to abandon than rites such as the invocation of deities?
It is the husband, under the pretext of supporting others, who brings reproach from kings, thieves, and the public.
Because of the fickleness of the semen, the *liṅga* is therefore superior;
just as worship performed upon a *liṅga* in the presence of the Preceptor [is effective], so it is here.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should indeed offer that supreme, complete [flower-offering];
having first worshipped Śiva according to one's capacity, one should present the eightfold flower-offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā).
The seat of Śiva (śivāsana), the image (mūrti), and its head, along with its five limbs— thus,
one should offer flowers to these eight [deities] individually with eight separate mantras.
And one should perform the prescribed rite when the preceptor has returned from a pilgrimage site.
When the worship of the worshipped must indeed be performed with haste at that time, then,
O Śivā, one should proceed from the gatekeepers onwards by means of the previously mentioned purification of the elements alone.
Having thus performed the midday ritual, one should eat; otherwise, it is not so, according to the scriptural injunction regarding expiation even for a learned man desiring liberation. For example:
"Without having completed that [ritual], bathing, eating, and the worship of the deity [are forbidden]."
Established upon the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), they abide as the presiding deities over the mantras.
If five muhūrtas have passed after performing the midday rites,
the auspicious mantras become inauspicious for one who eats.
When he was led to the house smeared with cow dung and the rites of the hearth-offering and so forth were performed, the master of the household,
who possessed only enough for the maintenance of life, bowed down.
One should eat in the evening and in the morning according to that rule; what is the intention behind this?

In that regard, having washed one's feet and hands and performed the assignment of limbs (*nyāsa*), one should consecrate water seven times with the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, using the *varma* mantra, one should protect oneself from the right and left sides with ashes or water.
On page 35b: One should draw two lines with their tips pointing east and two lines with their tips pointing north, in succession, facing [the center].

Thereafter, having purified the vessel for pure food by means of inspection and other rites, one should place upon it the Ghorasaptaka mantra, which resembles ten million moons, and the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra. Having sprinkled the food with water from the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, the devotee should place his right hand over the food as before and [recite] the Mṛtyuñjaya-jayā.

Having thus incited [the recipient's interest], one places the cooked rice and other offerings in another vessel and [performs the ritual] with water dripping from the lower part of the mouthful (*gaḍūṣa*).
Oṃ, svāhā to Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya, the secondary vital airs!
Having offered [the oblation] with the Astra-mantra and meditated upon the blazing fire within the stomach, [one recites]:
"Oṃ, you are the spreading of the nectar; svāhā!"
Taking water for the purification of the self: Oṃ, svāhā to the out-breath (prāṇa).
With the thumb, index finger, and middle finger: Oṃ apānāya svāhā.

With the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger: *oṃ samānāya svāhā*. With the thumb, ring finger, and little finger: *oṃ udānāya svāhā*. With all fingers except the index finger: *oṃ vyānāya svāhā*. With all fingers: [the final offering]. Having thus made five mouthfuls with very small intervals between them.

36a) The Ācārya faces east with a golden vessel; the Sādhaka faces south with a silver one; the Putraka faces west with a copper one; and the Samayin faces north, having touched the vessel with his left hand at the moment of the auspicious gaze.

One should eat with small morsels, avoiding the word "mouth. According to worldly custom, one should first perform the preliminary rite facing east, south, west, or north respectively. Upon encountering hair or other such things, one should remove only that much, wash the hand, touch ashes, and [use] a vessel made of bell-metal or other non-sacrificial materials.

No. When the vessel has been purified seven times with ashes and the *aghora* mantra has been recited seven times, one should avoid placing the hand in milk, salt in the hand, or tasting clarified butter (*ghṛta*). One should avoid stale substances and the like.

One should not eat while making noise, nor with the left hand placed [on the lap], nor without having washed the mouth, nor with food still in the hand; and at the beginning, one should not drink water. Then...
At the conclusion of the meal: *oṃ amṛtāpidhāne asi svāhā*. Having taken a mouthful of water for rinsing and sipped it, [one says]:
*oṃ kālāgnirudrāya svāhā*. Having sprinkled the big toe of the right foot with water flowing from the tip of the thumb of the right hand, one should form the *parigha-mudrā*.
Having placed the little finger of the left hand at the navel region,
one should join that very finger with the thumb of the right hand.
Having spread out both hands, one should place the right thumb upon the mouth;
this is declared to be the *parigha* [mudrā], which destroys even wicked food.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditated upon Śiva with great joy, one should perform the purification of the mouth by means of ash, *harītakī*, earth, and so forth.
One should pay obeisance to Śiva and the Guru; this concludes the eating of alms-food for the sake of peace.
One who is free from desire, a celibate student, one seeking knowledge, and one who supports his teacher [are exempt].
The Devavratin, the Tapasvin, and the Sadhetabhikshuka are recorded as such;
therefore, a householder should not set his heart upon consuming [forbidden] food.
A householder may incur sin by taking a second wife while the first is still living,
by approaching a Śūdra woman, by approaching the wives of others, or likewise by approaching prostitutes and the like.
They should be known as fallen; they are not fit for the householder's stage of life—those who desire to practice the purifying *mādhūkara* alms-round.
Having bathed with pure ashes, put on a loincloth,
bound his matted hair, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon Śiva and his Guru.
Having bowed down, one should purify the vessel according to his command; silently bowing,
[one should use] a vessel made of copper or bronze, or a fresh cup made of *palāśa* leaves.

One who has made the alms-bowl free of desire, having performed the purification by spitting and so forth upon it, and having covered it with a cloth of *kapāsa* cotton—[one should place] that which resembles blazing fire within it.

Upon that garment, [one should place] a terrible armor; likewise, on a staff equal to oneself and on a white umbrella, [these should be placed] when surrounded and gathered together in a shallow bowl (*sarāva*).
When the coals have been extinguished and the people have finished eating,
having gone to the houses of the twice-born and others, one should remain with a downward gaze; when it is said,
"Give alms," then Gaurī is worshipped by the mere striking [of the ground].
He waited for that duration of time, neither less nor more,
until the sacrificer returned from his home once again to offer alms.
Even when urged, he should never turn back from that place;
there alone he should accept alms, having rejected what is fresh and defiled.
He should not accept alms placed in bronze or similar vessels, nor from a despised woman, nor from mines;
he should not take alms from one who delights in begging, nor from one who is censured.

One should not accept alms consisting of abundant food from a Śaiva, from those such as the Svayambhū-pāśupatas, or even from one who merely bears the external marks (liṅgin), nor from one who is overly refined.
And also from where women are clever in jesting and the like.
A peacock’s egg constitutes one *bhikṣā*; four times that is a *puṣkala*;
and four *puṣkalas* are prescribed as an *hantakāra*.
Having thus performed the begging of alms,
he should return to his own hermitage with whatever has been obtained, while forming the resolve for the welfare of all people.
Having deposited that [image], sprinkled it with dust, and empowered it with the Astra-mantra, one should divide it three times as before;
then, having offered a portion separately to the Guru and separately to Śiva.
Having consumed the remainder, such as the eight morsels and so forth, while recollecting the Lord and the mudrā,
and having partaken of the contact and the great sacrificial food (mahāviṣya), one should thereafter conduct oneself accordingly.
One should always perform atonement for eating;
one should await the evening meal while listening to discourses on that [topic] and avoiding wicked people.
At that time as well, having ascended to a high place, one should perform the necessary duties,
such as purification, sipping water (ācamana), bathing, or cleansing the waist.
Or else, having wiped all the limbs with pure and soft cloth,
one may perform a bath without washing the head, using either cold or warm water.
One who performs ritual actions partakes in the fruit of practicing the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and the water-offering (arghya).
The power of Śiva, though one, becomes manifold through limiting adjuncts such as time;
one whose heart is veiled by knots [of ignorance] should worship Śiva with [offerings] such as cloth.
If one is sprinkled with bathing water, milk, or other such substances by a devotee,
one should bathe or wash oneself from above the navel as well as below it.
Then, having performed the purificatory rites for the feet, one should cleanse them again with soft powders made from barley and wheat, mixed with water and clarified butter.
Then, being one whose self is the mantra and who eats only at dawn, he should meditate on Śiva within his heart;
having seen [the deity] on the left side, he places the best [of offerings] upon the back of the right hand.
Having placed his knees upon a wooden plank, with his back straight and his chest forward,
he should lie down, joined with meditative cultivation, in the sleep of yoga.
One should worship Mukti, Airyāmya, Śiras, and Guhya; previously [worshipped] there, Turaṅgada; then Namo Nandīśvarāya, Itiṣeta, Yoni, and Dhruva, and so forth.
For him, there is no fear whatsoever from the Kuṣmāṇḍa kings;
by means of silence, he quickly attains the path, and he burns away the sin of the head as if it were an oblation offered into the fire.
The bed, water-pot, ashes, the ascetic's staff, clothing, seat, support,
sacred thread, and so forth— none of these, nor anything else, should be touched by one who has not attained purity through seniority.

Even a householder may sleep comfortably in the quarters of a servant during the month of Śrāvaṇa; one should use medicinal herbs in the month of Bhādrapada, a physician in Āśvina, and the blue-throated Lord (Śiva) with one's food in Kārttika.
During travel, one should remember the Three-eyed Lord; while lying down, the Lord of the Mountain-dweller; during sexual union, the Lord of Umā; and at the time of death, Śiva.
Then, at midnight, the practitioner should worship the previously mentioned goddess with water and other offerings collected during the day, which are free from demonic influence.

A family touched by the sun becomes purified; even at night, it shines with purity like the rising sun. Having risen, one should again recite before oneself the remainder of what was left unsaid during the night.

One should perform the prescribed rites daily without deceit; the rule is one that must be observed. One should wait for the imperishable state, remaining vigilant while the body is still subject to departure.
Consisting of eternal bliss, pure, the power of Śiva by the command of Śiva,
like the sun upon the lotus-stalk of the lineage of the Gauḍas, he was marked on his shoulder by his preceptors as a treasure-house of excellent qualities.

The compassionate Guru, a lion uniquely capable of splitting the head of the elephant of sloth— the leader of the host of vandāvas— has accomplished this Siddhānta; he who is like Indra in luster, pure as Śiva, and whose conduct is the very essence of Kāśī, performed this work for the sake of the fire-ritual.
39a) The second [section], the ritual procedure for the fire oblation (homavidhi) in Vimalāvatī.
The number of knots is 216.
Because the worlds, the elements, the senses, and the vital breaths have all arisen from Śiva and are well-established within Him,
they are eternal; thus the disciple, having prostrated before the pure Śiva— who destroys the loss of all years and who is born from the source of the serpent-vehicle— spoke to Him.

At the beginning of Āṣāḍha and other months, the best, middling, or lowest retreat (adhema) should be observed for two fortnights by the preceptor and others every year while [the deity] is asleep or departed, for the sake of accomplishing the goal.
From the beginning with Agni up to all the gods,
the preceptor [should teach] the Sūtra and its meaning in sequential order to widows, Brāhmaṇa women, maidens, and others.
It should be free of hair, uncut, spun,
very even, smooth, auspicious, new, ninefold, and washed with water from the *sadyojāta* mantra.

With the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with the juice of Madana fruit and fragrant substances, [one should bathe] with water that is neither too thick nor too thin, not burnt, and free from impurities.
Furthermore, it is knotted on the left with well-purified, fashioned threads of Śiva;
likewise, the mass of hair and so forth held by Aghora is dyed.
With red sandalwood, Kashmiri saffron, musk, moonstone, yellow orpiment, or the powder of realgar— or with any one of these among them— [one should perform the rite].
39b) In the *tatpuruṣa* compound, it is not so; thus by this [rule], it has been perfumed.
In "tastranyastadhruva" and so forth, the *prakṛti* (base form) and other elements reside within the joints (*granthi*).

In the Kali age, the primary [materials] are cotton and silk; other items include wool and the like, as well as lotus bark, lotus fibers, and those produced from muñja grass, kṣema-grass, and so forth.
It fulfills the needs of both the wealthy and the poor according to their circumstances;
therein, the fragrant *pavitra* should be very small, consisting of a single knot.
Vacā, campaka, saileya, the two types of haridrā,
mustaka, śaṭhī, kuṣṭha, surā, and māṃsa— thus it is joined with all these medicinal herbs.
Each one of all these is free from measure and weight;
it is the preeminent purifier, which is triple and ring-shaped.
The talliṅga may be equal to that [measurement], or it may have a hollow of six or eight finger-breadths;
the dimensions of the liṅgas range from one cubit up to nine cubits, along with their respective intervals.
Increasing by twenty-eight [units] successively by tens,
up to one hundred and eight, [the measurement applies] from the top of the liṅga to the base (garbhaka).
For manifest [deities], the measurement from the navel to the tips of the feet is nine units for the lowest [grade];
the best should be one hundred and eight [units], and the middling should be half of that.
The smallest [number] is twenty-seven; in some cases, it is half of thirty-six;
[it may also be] fifty, thirty-six, or forty-three.
The intervals between the knots are equal, measuring eighty-one and twenty-eight [units] respectively.
It should be provided with ten knots, or else with a number of knots equal to the [number of] threads;
however, in that which is known as the Gaṅgāvatāra, four knots are tied.
Furthermore, four [sections] should be made according to the measurement of the width;
thus it is completed until there are again two knots.
This remaining form of Śakti rests upon the edge of the pedestal;
therein, the primary [form] of the Sun is the fourfold purifiers (pavitra).
It is said that the eight parts of the wooden frame should be arranged here according to their beauty,
with one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, ten, or eighteen spokes.
With twenty-eight threads of Rudra and Arka, the creators (Dhātṛs) and others beginning with Pañca are established;
each one is a mark of Brahmā, located in the directions starting from Indra and extending to the elements.
O Śiva, like the sun, one should offer a single vessel-mouthed [vessel] for oneself and one's own group,
or likewise four or eight for the gurus.
Or else, one [mantra] is prescribed for their husband, or nine for the limbs;
however, there are none for Śiva, Agni, Vidyā, Caṇḍa, or the Doorkeeper, as in the case of Śiva himself.
Similarly, the inner twelfth fold and the outer eleventh fold of the Guru rest upon the single heart; this is the auspicious [teaching] in the Vidyādhara tradition.
This has been stated: each one of these, such as Sūrya, Kumbha, Agni, Caṇḍīśa, Vidyā, and the others, possesses fruit like that of Īśvara.
There should be ten portions of scented [substances], one hundred and nine of *kaṅkanī*,
one for oneself, and then twenty for the principal preceptor.
The seven descents of the Gaṅgā, as well as Kaṅkaṇika and the others, are as previously described;
thus, in their unity, they are characterized by countless ages, seasons, and fortnights.
If, among those who have died in such pure places and the like, Indra has departed from his station,
or if the sacrificial vessel is lost by fate, or the purifying thread is lost on the full moon of Āśvina or Kārttika;
Alternatively, having recited the *ghora* mantra according to the prescribed rite, one should offer it when only the defects have been removed;
for by the absence of the three-fold *piṇḍa*, all [defects] vanish, even if there is only one [remaining].
Then, having performed the daily rite on the thirteenth or seventh lunar day,
and having performed the occasional bath during the twilight prayers, initiations, and other such occasions;
One should not wear new clothes during an intercalary month; one should worship the Sun, yet he who acts like an ordinary person does not honor the door, the vehicle, or himself.
For the sake of one's own purification, one should worship the final [syllable] on the left;
one should place the hand upon the root and fix the hand of the Destroyer upon the head.
Having meditated, "I am Śiva, the primordial omniscient one," one performs the purification of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa-śuddhi).

One should hold in the hand the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), which measures one span (*vitasti*), has thirty-six ribs, and is topped with a point; it is shaped like a braid (*veṇī*) and consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having prepared the vessel for the arghya offering and taken it, the Guru should go to the northeastern direction of the sacrificial pavilion and then consecrate it with the *kūrcavat* mantra.

One should spread out parched rice, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, flowers, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains— appearing as blazing weapons consecrated seven times with the Astra-mantra— while reciting the Astra-mantra itself.
One desiring to cure should bring the sick person together;
then, from the base of the weapon-increasing [vessel], the direction of Nirṛti extends for a hundred [fathoms].
One should worship Brahmā and Mahālakṣmī, who fill my abode with great jewels, in the water; one should remember her in the form of a pavilion.
Having offered a libation with the *saḍutthaṃka* mantra, one should place the jar of Death facing west, situated upon a bull and resting on seven grains of rice. It should be described [as follows].
Having touched with his right hand that which is smeared with gold, the one who is the sole lord of sacrifice and the power of knowledge, located always in the southern direction of this river;

Having installed the Vardhanī vessel, which faces west, containing the Lion-throned Goddess who crushes obstacles, together with the Mūrti-mantra upon the *satru* (enemy) stone; one should then worship the ancient [deities] within the Kumbha,
as well as their Kriyā-śakti and the Āluka.
Oṃ haḥ, homage to the one who brandishes the weapon, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ haḥ, homage to the embodiment of the weapon, hūṃ phaṭ!
Having placed [the vessel] upon the vardhanī.

Oṃ haḥ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ. As before, perform the invocation. Oṃ haḥ astra-hṛdayāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ haḥ astra-śirase hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ haḥ astra-śikhāyai hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ haḥ astra-kavacāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ astrāya.
HŪṂ PHAṬ NAMAḤ.

Having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* and other rites, one should worship [the deities] on the decorated jars or on the sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*), using the *praṇava* and the heart-mantra as seats, according to the power of the directions: "Oṃ hāṃ! Salutation to Indra, the thousand-eyed, yellow-colored, mounted upon Airāvata, holding a thunderbolt in his hand, the lord of the eastern direction. Oṃ hāṃ! To Agni, the tawny-colored..."

Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Eastern Quarter, who holds a spear in his hand. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Yama, the Lord of the Southern Quarter, who is blue in color, mounted upon a buffalo, and holds a staff in his hand. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Nirṛti, the Lord of the South-Western Quarter, who is black in color, mounted upon a dog, and holds a sword in his hand.

42a) Oṃ hā& salutation to Varuṇa, who is white in color, mounted upon a sea-monster (makara), holding a noose in his hand, the lord of the western direction. Oṃ hā& salutation to Vāyu, who is smoke-colored (dhūmra-varṇa), mounted upon a deer (mṛga).

Salutation to Dhvajapāṇi, the lord of the quarter of Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kubera, who is fair-complexioned, whose form is three-eyed, who holds a mace in his hand, and who is the lord of the northern quarter. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna, who has three eyes, who is white-complexioned, who is mounted upon a bull, who holds a trident in his hand, and who is the lord of the northeastern quarter. Oṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to Brahmā, who has four faces, is white in complexion, is mounted upon a swan, holds a lotus in his hand, and is the lord of the upward direction. Oṃ Hāṃ! Salutation to Viṣṇu, who is dark in complexion, wears a forest garland, is mounted upon Garuḍa, holds a discus in his hand, and is the lord of the downward direction.
Then, taking the *vardhanī* vessel followed by the water-pitcher (*kalaśa*), reciting the root mantra:

"Oṃ! This Śiva-sacrifice has commenced; by the command of Śiva, it must be protected from those who would oppose it by the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) with focused minds. O Śakra, you must [protect] in your own direction for the pacification of obstacles."
O Vadhyanetra, by the command of Śiva, you must not engage in the work of execution.

At the time of such-and-such a worship, one should cause [the names] to be heard individually by their own names. Having first caused an unbroken stream of water to circulate from the east to the northeast, and having subsequently placed the *vardhanī* vessel in the south, [one should place] the *śakti* and so forth, facing east or northeast.
Up to the limit of the *śakti*, having worshipped the full seat (*pūrṇāsana*) as Śiva, along with the weapon (*astra*) in the *vardhanī* vessel together with its limbs;

then, touching the water-pot (*kumbha*) with the thumb of the heart-mantra, one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) should [hold] the *vardhanī* with the fist, while one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) should hold the *vardhanī* with the fist—thus performing everything like the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*. Om.

"For you are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this is your immovable form. This is your sword of knowledge (jñāna-niṣtriṃśa); therefore, accept it, O refuge of Soma. Having offered the hundred and eight roots of the sacrificial swords—or a tenth part of that number—into the *vardhanī* vessel of the weapon-mantra (*astra-vardhanī*), [he should proceed].
Oṃ! This sacrifice, which was initiated by me, has not yet reached its conclusion; therefore, it must now be protected by you until its completion.
Oṃ! Salutations to Umā, who possesses the form of the bhaga, and to Śaṅkara, who bears the form of the liṅga and bestows grace upon his devotees.
43a) Having informed the teacher of the assembly as before, and having honored him by bathing him with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances,
and having worshipped him and prepared the fire, one should accomplish the *dvayacarū*.
The procedure for that, joined with the single *jādi* [mantra], is proclaimed by means of its stated utterances;
having placed the vessel washed with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should deposit the *viśve* within it.
The knower of the ritual should worship Śambhu with the seat and other offerings in due order;
having meditated upon Him as being filled with that [essence], he should finally cast the flower-offering.
The practitioner of mantra, having sprinkled it with water until it is completely purified, should place unhusked rice and other grains into a cooking pot and set it upon the stove.
In the southeast, having consecrated the vessel and facing east while reciting the *śiva* mantra, the practitioner of mantras should cook the *caru*; there is no need for moving or striking it.
Having performed the heart-mantra and the armor-mantra, Śani, the knower of ripening,
should slowly draw [the deity] forth with the mantra-saṃhitā ending in *svāhā* or *vaṣaṭ*.
Having worshipped Dhruva, Kṛṣṇa, Āsana, and Āmiṣa with a ladle filled with ghee while [the vessel] is heated and then cooled,
one should begin the sprinkling with that [ghee].
One should cast the oblations into the fire with the mantra ending in *svāhā*, saying "O weapon! (*heti*) over that sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Then, the practitioner of mantras should consecrate it with the *saṃhitā* mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*.
Then, one should cause [the disciple] to be inspired according to their capacity with the *mudrā* ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should divide the accumulated sins three times for the sake of the deity, the fire, and oneself.

Having invoked Śiva into the fire and offered libations as before according to the Saṃhitā, and having performed the oblation following auspicious signs and other rites, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, the purificatory materials (*pavitra*), sprinkled with *argha* water and consecrated with the *saṃhitā* mantra, [are placed] in the vicinity of the fire.
Having covered [the sacrificial ground] with deerskin and other materials for one year, while remembering Śiva, the witness of all actions;
having purified the *saṃpāta* offerings according to the *Triśaptasaṃhitā*;
and having encircled the sacrificial pavilion and other structures with its thread and armor-mantra, he went into the presence of the Sun.

Having recited "Oṃ samasta... and so forth, one should offer fragrant flowers, sacred threads, food offerings (naivedya), and other items to that Śārṅga with his own mantra ending in "svāhā. Then, one should present offerings to the door-keepers, Brahmā, Mahālakṣmī, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) using the previously mentioned mantras.

Then, having recited two verses, one should offer the *pavitra*, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth to the Lord of the Pitcher (*Kumbheśa*) together with his limbs (*sāṅga*) using one's own mantra. Having gratified the Weapon (*Astra*), the Vardhanī vessel, Gaṇapati,
and the Gurus with food offerings and other gifts using the Astra-mantra, one should offer [the *pavitra*] to one's own *iṣṭadevatā* with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.
44a) The tooth-stick, twelve finger-breadths in length, should be produced from a *śrīmaya* tree,
a *kṣīra* tree, or even from a *nara* or *varmaṇa* tree, and used first [in the morning].
Ash should be applied on the right with the Rūpinī or Śikhā mantra;
clay should be applied on the west with the Sadyojāta or Hṛdaya mantra.
Oṃ hare! One should offer an āmalakī fruit to the God of gods, and water for purification with the Vāmadeva mantra or with the Śiras mantra.
In the northeast, with the Īśa mantra or the root mantra,
one should place fragrant water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) contained within a leaf-cup made of palāśa.
One should offer flowers in the northeast, Rocanā in the southeast direction,
agarwood in the southwest quarter, and saffron in the northwest.
All the materials for the fire-oblation, together with kusha grass, should be placed in the Sadyojāta [face];
the staff, rosary, loincloth, and alms-bowl should be placed in the Dakṣiṇa [face].
One should offer collyrium, saffron, oil, a probe, hair-cleansing powder,
betel, a mirror, and also yellow pigment (rocanā) in the northern direction.
One should offer a seat, sandals, a bowl, a yoga-band,
and a parasol in the northeast with the Īśāna mantra for the satisfaction of Īśāna.
44b) O man, in the eastern direction, one should mentally prepare an oblation of cooked rice (caruka) mixed with clarified butter and fragrant substances, as much as is available of these.
Then, having taken the purifier consisting of four hides and having meditated upon Śiva as before, [one should proceed].
Oṃ! For the sake of filling all deficiencies in the ritual procedures regarding this sacrifice, I invoke you, O Lord;
you are the one who brings about the fulfillment of my desires.
Know that the accomplishment of that mantra belongs to one who sacrifices; it is meditated upon by consciousness.
O Śambhu, salutations to you in every way and at all times; may you be gracious to me.
Having recited [the mantra] and performed the *āmantraṇa*, one should offer the *amṛtīkṛta* [substance] until the point of dissolution while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Then, having offered the water for the feet (*aṅghri-arpaṇa*) to Śiva, and having performed the food offering (*naivedya*), recitation (*japa*), prostrations (*praṇāma*), and so forth, one should present it to Durgā and Śāṅgā.
Thus, having worshipped Śiva even in the fire, offered oblations, performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and the *vyāhṛti* mantras;
and having worshipped Śiva and established him in the form [of the deity], one should unite him with the channel of Śiva worshipped in the maṇḍala through the connection of the channels.
Thus it has been said:
The channel, resembling a strand of wool, has emerged through the gate of joy;
it enters through the gate of non-arising, and having emerged, it proceeds through the gate of joy.
The Guru should not contemplate [the disciple] as being hostile when [the disciple's] own [inner state] has not yet arisen.
In this way, the unification should be performed everywhere by the Guru, the food, and the friend.
Then, having offered the oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt and having restrained the fire with the Niṣṭhura mantra, one should worship Citraṇa within and without the sacrificial pit.
Having dismissed the gatekeepers and others, as well as Śivāstra and Vardhanī,

one should then perform the inspection (*vīkṣā*) and other purifications upon a vessel made of pure bamboo or similar material, just as before. Having invoked the Dharmāstra-mantra with the Hṛdaya-mantra, and having placed all the *pavitra* threads upon it, one should touch them with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Furthermore, having covered the heart-mantra, the weapon-mantra, and the shields with one another using pure cloth,

having wound them with thread and worshipped them with the heart-mantra and the others, and having addressed [them] saying, "O Blessed One, out of compassion, may you protect these purifiers," he should offer them to the Śiva-pitcher; and likewise [he should worship] the seat of knowledge and the Guru as [one would] Śiva.

Having performed worship as prescribed, for the sake of [attaining] bondage one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth; for the sake of liberation, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa), singing, praise, prostration, and recitation (japa), remain awake, and eat with kuśa grass; furthermore, one should apply ashes and observe a fast—this is the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Having risen for that bath and observed the twilight prayers, abandoning desire for elephants and other such things,
one should worship with the eight flowers and, having taken up the purifying ring (pavitraka) from the heart, [proceed].
Having placed [the deity] in the north-eastern quarter of the mandala, one should dismiss Śiva.
After having worshipped the Brahmā-pitcher at the door, one should remove the floral remains (nirmālya).
Having spoken of Śrī, who is of the nature of both the expressible and the inexpressible, [one should worship] the guardians of the directions,
the water-jars, the Vardhanī vessel, the Gaṇas, the Guru and others, Maheśa, Śiva, and the Fire.
Having worshipped [the deity] with special care and having gratified him with mantras according to the ritual procedure,
he should then go near the sun, carrying dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).

Having placed a well-incensed *pavitraka* in the center of the joined palms (*añjali*), one should recite for each *tattva* everywhere the mantra beginning with "Oṃ kāla... and ending with "svāhā," followed by: "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ śaḥ, svāhā to Sūrya, the presiding deity of the *ātmatattva*. Then, having transferred [the merit] from the limbs as well, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) and other items.

And [offer] to the guardians of the doors and directions. Having offered to the pitcher-deity with the four principles (tattvas) and also to the limbs beginning with the heart, at the conclusion of the food offering and recitation, [offer] to the Vardhanī, to the limbs, to one’s own self, to Gaṇanātha, and to the lineage of Gurus. Having offered the food offering, the recitation, and so forth, and having requested permission from the Krama, then [proceed] a little further.
Facing the kalaśa, having meditated upon Śiva as one's own self and so forth, and having taken up the *pavitra* (sacred thread) accompanied by perfumes and other offerings;
46a) At the palate, the bindu, the aperture of Brahma, and the dvādaśānta: "O God, that which has been seen by you, whose self is Time (Kālātman), in my ritual procedure— "
What was done, what was afflicted, what was abandoned, what was taken away, and what was concealed—all that was done by me.
O Śambhu, by Your will, let that which was performed— whether afflicted, unrefined, done, or intensified— become purified for all these souls through this sacred [rite].
Oṃ, fulfill, fulfill! Svāhā to the Lord of the vow and observance of sacrifice (makha-vrata-niyameśvara). Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva, the sovereign of the principle of the self (ātma-tattva-adhipa).

Having meditated upon the *Ātmatattva* (the principle of the Self) as ending with *Prakṛti*, having Brahman as its cause, and extending to the end of *Māyā* while joined with the recitation of mantras, one should first perform the imposition (*āropa*). *Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva, the lord of the Vidyātattva.* The *Vidyātattva* (the principle of Knowledge), ending with *Vidyā*, has Viṣṇu as its cause and extends to the end of *Īśvara*, accompanied by the recitation of mantras.
Having meditated upon the second [syllable].
Oṃ hau& svāhā! To Śiva, the lord of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), svāhā!

Having meditated upon the third [level] as the Śivatattva ending with Śakti, the cause of Rudra, extending up to Sadāśiva, and conjoined with the recitation of the mantra: *Oṃ hauṃ, to Śiva, the lord of all principles, the sacred thread, svāhā*.
Then the yogin, having meditated upon the fourth [level] as the cause of all, the principle of all, the pervasive end of dissolution, by means of the recitation of the root-mantra.

Regarding the descent of the Gaṅgā (*gaṅgāvatāra*): one who desires liberation, being pure, should offer [the water] with the *Śivavidyā* mantra, the *ātman*, and all the *tattvas*, ending each with *namaḥ*. Then, having offered it to the limbs [of the deity], he should present the ritual food offering (*naivedya*) and the recitation (*japa*) to the Blessed One according to the rules.
Having joined his palms in reverence and meditated upon Śiva as being fully satisfied, he should address him with this petition:
Oṃ! You are the refuge of all beings; you are the foundation of the moving and the unmoving. By your movement within all beings, you cause them to flourish, O Supreme Lord.
Through action, mind, or speech, there is no other refuge for me than You.
Whatever has been performed by me that is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual, or deficient in devotion— [may it all be rendered complete through Your grace].
O Maheśvara, whatever daily rite of yours has been performed by me deficient in recitation, fire-offerings, and worship,
or left unperformed and lacking the proper words, please fulfill that for me.
O Lord of Heroes, you are perfectly pure and a purifier that destroys sins;
by you, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—is sanctified.
O Lord, whatever portion of my vow has been broken through the influence of deficiency,
may all of that become unified, expanded by the thread of your command.

Then, having performed the praise and other rites, the Guru should choose one from among the following durations: four months, three months, two months, one month, half a month, seven days, five days, three days, or one day.
Having undertaken the observance (*niyama*) to prepare the *vāyitrī* fan for presentation, one should offer it to Durgā.
Then, having worshipped the *pavitra* located in the fire as one would Śiva, and having performed the oblations up to the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Having united Śiva, who resides in the fire, with Śivā, and having removed the fire, one should present the offerings (*bali*) both inside and outside while holding the *pavitra*.

Having gone into the presence of Śiva, one should perform the offering of the ritual action (*karmasamarpaṇa*). Then, having worshipped the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) together with its limbs like a corpse, one should gratify it with food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth. At the end of that, one should worship the Guru like Śiva with garments, gold, purificatory threads (*pavitra*), and other things that cause satisfaction; likewise, one should worship the Lord and the twice-born (*dvija*) and others.
Having satisfied [them].
O Sadāśiva, may the Blessed One be pleased with me by means of this gift.
Thus one should resolve with the mind; this concludes the offering of the purifier.
Then, in the morning, having again performed the daily rites as previously described, and having worshipped [the deities] from Sūrya to Agni,
one should personally place the sacred threads (pavitra) at the beginning and the end, marked as before.
Having gratified Śiva in the fire with the full oblation, the knower of the purificatory rite performs the expiation.
Having cast away the fire of the *saṃśiva* rite and having performed the worship of Caṇḍa for protection,
the observer of the vow should go into the presence of Śiva and perform the offering of the ritual action (*karmasamarpaṇa*).
Whether seeking liberation or seeking enjoyment, according to this procedure, it is as follows:
"By your grace, O Lord, may this action be a bond for me."
"By your grace, may this rite of mine be effective in achieving its fruit. Then, having worshipped with eight flowers, he should place the *pavitraka* upon his heart.
Having dismissed Īśa and the others according to the ritual rule and having entered the pavilion,
one should then worship outside the sacrificial ground with waters mixed with *madya*.
He may be smeared with unguents, or clothed in garments, seated upon a throne, or depicted in a painting;
he may have three eyes, bear the crescent moon, possess a fierce and wrathful appearance, and have a lotus for his vehicle.

Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍāsana, hūṃ phaṭ! Having worshipped upon the seat of the sixfold arising, [one worships]: Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍamūrti, hūṃ phaṭ! His form has the luster of blue collyrium; he has four faces and twelve eyes (the number of the sun); he wears a serpent as a sacred thread and armlets; his mouth emits the radiance of the rising sun; and his flaming matted hair—half...
Having meditated upon her who is as dark as the moon, extremely terrifying, four-armed, holding a trident and a *ḍamaru* in her left hands, and a *ṭaṅka* and a rosary in her right hands,
and possessing the splendor of Rudra and fire, one should invoke the supreme [deity] with the root mantra.
Oṃ oṃ dhvani caṇḍeśvarāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having performed the rites of invocation, seating [the deity] within the heart, and so forth...

Oṃ caṇḍahṛdayāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ caṇḍaśirase hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ caṇḍaśikhāyai hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ caṇḍakavacāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ caṇḍāstrāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Having first offered the heart-mantra at the beginning of all [limbs], one should offer the others as before.

Having worshipped correctly [the limbs], including the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), one should then place the scented thread (*gandhapavitra*) upon the limbs starting from the principal deity with the root mantra, as in the case of Śiva, and perform the recitation (*japa*) and other rites. Then, taking up the thread: *Oṃ hāṃ, to Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara, the lord of the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. In this manner...

After the offering of the food (naivedya), taking all the purifying substances (pavitrāṇi) along with the [mantras] beginning with Vidyā and the limbs of the Ārūpya realm, [one should perform the rite].
Oṃ! By the command of Śiva, this food to be licked, sucked, and drunk, along with betel, garlands, and unguents—the remains of the offering—is bestowed upon you.
O Caṇḍa, by your command, I have performed this entire section on ritual action;
whatever has been done deficiently or redundantly through delusion, may it always be made perfect for me.
Then [the daily rite].
Whatever annual rite has been performed by me, whether deficient or excessive,
may it become complete through your command, O Caṇḍanātha.

Having recited [the mantra] and made the request, having offered the purificatory water, the food offering (*naivedya*), and so forth with the root mantra, and having prostrated, one should worship and satisfy the fire according to the occasion, then dismiss it, go outside, and establish the form of Caṇḍa. Oṃ.
Salutation to the form of Phe and Caṇḍeśa.

Having discarded the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) into a dark well or similar place, having purified the ground, and having bathed and worshipped Śiva, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). On the two days of the thirteenth and fourteenth [lunar days], on the thirteenth day...

On the fourteenth day, one should perform the *gandhapavitra* (fragrant purifier) and the *pavitra* (purifier) for the worship of Caṇḍa; likewise on both the fourteenth and the full moon days. On the fourteenth day, the *gandhapavitra*, and on the full moon day, the *pavitra* and the *upavīta* (sacred thread) are offered in the worship of Caṇḍa. Regarding the sanctity of the lunar day (*tithi*), it is the same on the eighth day as well.
And it has been said:
When one desires to perform the Pavitraka and other rites for Śambhu on a single day,
having performed the daily (nitya) rites, one should then perform the occasional (naimittika) rite once.
Having placed a purifying thread (pavitraka) upon the perfectly fragrant [object],
and having lifted it up and offered it, one should bathe the Caṇḍāpaliṅga and worship it.
One should worship the Lord on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila); this [following] procedure shall not apply to that [mound].
One should carry and lead forth a vessel containing water for bathing, along with fragrant substances, and a lamp held aloft by a Caṇḍāla.
And during the purification rites and other ceremonies, one should worship Caṇḍeśa according to the prescribed rule after having touched him.
In the same manner, one should offer the *arghya* with the *pavitra* and other implements; having released them, one should then perform the *ācamana*.
Thus purified and unconquered, one should never transgress the boundary.
Even a deity may otherwise attain success or fall at every step.

Vimala, Vimala, Vimalādiśiva, O you who are like the moon, O you who are the essence of the supreme, O you who are the lord of Uma— may he, the wise one who knows the ritual and the awakened one, ordain this supreme and purifying [state] for the Creator and for us.
In Vimalāvatī, this is the third rite of purification.
Volume 136.
The earth is the root, the ego-sense is the sprout, the subtle elements are the stalk,
the supreme reality is the upward-reaching stem, the knot of illusion is the four ages which serve as the feet for taming, and pure knowledge is the lotus.

We praise that lion-throne which rests upon the eight petals of the lords of knowledge, where Śiva and Umā are the filaments, Īśānī and Ambikā are the two rows of petals, and the seed-syllable is the pericarp.
Having performed the ritual ablutions and other rites on the seventh day of the dark fortnight or the thirteenth day,
one should go to the vicinity of the Adhyā [image] and worship it by beholding the Asādhya [deity] and so forth.
Having reflected, he should address him with these words of existence, as follows:
Oṃ! You who have arisen from the grace of Hara, be present through this mantra; for the sake of the work of Śiva, you abide here by the command of Śiva.
Having thus addressed him, one should go far away from the house while protecting [the site];
then, having brought back the earth that was situated in a vessel filled with clay and moistened with water.

In the house, one should meditate as before, remembering no deity other than Śiva. When the time of evening has arrived, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) according to the prescribed rite for the *pavitra*, and perform worship beginning with the Sun and ending with Fire.
Having made leaf-cups from *palāśa* leaves,
well-covered and joined together.

The five auspicious items, beginning with the root of *damasodbhava* (the *damanaka* plant), should be joined together; one should offer each individually with the *dhenumudrā* and other gestures, using the mantras beginning with "Sadyojāta" as appropriate.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta!
O Bhava, through Bhava, from the beginning, in Bhava, I worship you; salutations to Bhava, who has become the celestial self.
Or else, [one should offer] that which is named Bhavodbhava;
with this heart-mantra, one should place the root of the damana plant together with earth toward the west.
Oṃ, homage to Vāmadeva; homage to Jyeṣṭha; homage to Rudra; homage to Kāla; homage to Kalavikaraṇa; homage to Bala-pramathana; homage to Sarvabhūta...
Salutation to Damanāya and Manonmanāya.
With this head, one should offer a fruit of the vāsāmalakī; its stalk is for the north.

Oṃ, salutations to your non-terrible forms, to the terrible ones, and to those more terrible than the terrible; salutations to all your forms, O Rudra, from every direction and to each and every one of them. Salutations!
Or, with this [mantra] recited over the crest-lock, that leaf, like ashes, [should be placed] on the right.
Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva. May that Rudra inspire us. Homage!
With this armor-mantra, one should first offer that flower and the tooth-stick.
Oṃ. Īśāna, the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, the ascetic who is even greater than Brahmā—may he be Śiva; salutation to Sadāśiva. Or alternatively: Salutation to Sadāśiva.
With this root-mantra or with the Gāyatrī, one should offer that fruit together with fragrant paste to Īśāna.
Or, using the syllables of the deity as mantras; or in the case of *damana*, flowers, and fruits—if these are unavailable, one should substitute their leaves.
50b) Then, having placed the unbroken *damanaka* with its five parts in his joined palms and meditating upon Śiva, he should recite the mantra:
"Oṃ, you are invited, O Lord of Gods, by me at this morning hour, O Master."
These duties should be performed according to one's means, by the command of Pūrṇaparvata.

Having recited the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should plant [the dūrvā grass] from the limbs and so forth; then, having protected the purifying [grass] that has completely subdued [all obstacles] within the vessel, one should offer it for the sake of Śiva.
Having performed the purification as before and having partaken of the food, one should lead [the disciple] forward in front of Śiva.
Having bathed in the morning and performed the sacrifice to the Aṣṭakās, he should dismiss them as before;
thereafter, he should perform the obligatory and occasional rites, especially the specific ritual.
Having worshipped Śiva with five-limbed offerings consisting of broken pieces of food, one should take another portion;
then, being joyful, one should meditate on Śiva as having five faces, according to the Āgamas.
One should visualize the western face slightly turned upward toward the northeast;
the eastern face, Tatpuruṣa, is red and situated above the heart.
Ghora is on the right, Guhya on the left, and Ajā is white upon the back.
Oṃ Hrauṃ! To Śiva, the Lord of the Ātma-tattva, Svāhā!
Oṃ hau& to the Lord of the Vidyā-tattva, Śiva, svāhā!
Oṃ hau& to the Lord of the Śiva-tattva, Śiva, svāhā!
51a) *Oṃ hauṃ makheśvarāya makhaṃ pūraya 2 śūlapāṇaye svāhā*.
Having thus offered four handfuls [of oblations] with palms joined, ending with "namaḥ" or other [mantras], one should dismiss Śiva or the fire at the conclusion of the day.

In this context, the protection of the fire—from its consecration (*vāsanā*) up to its dismissal (*visarjana*)—must also be performed. For it is said: "For this consumer of oblations (*havi-bhuj*), the occasional (*naimittika*) rite ends right here; there is no [rite] born from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍaja*) beyond this, nor is there a daily (*nitya*) dismissal."
Thereafter, one should inform the Lord.
Oṃ! O Blessed One, whatever has been performed by me that is either excessive or deficient—may all of that become complete; may my festival be auspicious.
Then one should dismiss the sacrifice with a formula, as before, even if the subduing [of the disciple] takes only a single day.
One should always worship Śiva with offerings throughout all twelve months;
however, O Creator, this is due to the avoidance of even a single portion [of the rite] arising from the month of Caitra.
I shall describe the lineage of the most excellent gurus, encircled by Śrīkaṇṭhānanda;
by the mere remembrance of which the terrible fetters are severed from men.
On the bank of the Godāvarī, from Śiva, Maheśa, Vidyeśa, Śrīkaṇṭha, Īśa, and the others, [the goddesses] were born as their consorts.
51b) From Mādhava, Brahmā, and Skanda, there is a fivefold [emanation] born from the five faces;
through the division known as the meaning of the seed-syllables (*bīja*), it is twofold, marked by Śiva and Rudra.
The teaching spoken by you, O Śiva, which is divided into ten and eighteen parts, possesses various extensive elaborations and is connected with the stages beginning with *parā*.
From the sage Durvāsas, he received the descent of the Guru-Krodha [mantra].
Having reached the world-renowned site of Vāsuki, the lord of serpents,
at the illustrious Āmadāka-sthāna, one shall become a sovereign like the Lord himself.
Born in that lineage was Śakrani, the illustrious Raṇapaṭuka;
then his son was Andhagṛha, who possessed a thousand eyes, and after him was born another from that same line.
The Lord known as Śiva, who resides in the center of the primordial manifestation preceded by Śrī,
is the master of the five mantras and tantras, like the sovereign Sadāśiva.
The Guru, whose fame is sung throughout the three worlds, indeed sat upon the sacrificial altar in the form of a fire-pot.
He created Dhānāsṛj, the abode of sages, which was priceless and primordial,
like Kailāsa, the first mountain of Śiva, presided over by Viṣṇu and Viriñci.
He became Śiva—the sun that awakens the lotus of that lineage—tranquil, utterly serene, and auspicious;
though his form was appropriately seated upon the earth (Gonaya), he then manifested a transcendent form.
There was the minister Mahema, renowned and equal to Īśa; from him came the auspicious Prabodha;
and from him, through abundant austerity, there arose the illustrious and auspicious Kumāra.

In Saurāṣṭra, there was a brother-in-law named Śrī-Vāmana, who was born from the union of a woman of the Kucata and Agnyutthāyaka lineages with one of the Asmajā lineage; he ruled over three generations of his kin.
He who is praised by the name "The Three-Eyed One" (Trinetra), who possesses the three *yastakas*,
and who has properly resorted to this hermitage through this method— immediately thereafter...
The twelve principal queens of the king, led by Hāsyā and Nalāndī,
surrounded by a multitude of young women, spent their days and nights under the influence of pleasure; yet, with the king’s permission, they attended upon the great ascetic,
the unimpeded Vādīndra, who spoke as a spiritual preceptor.
Out of pride in his intellect, having conquered [his opponents] like a child, he broke through their rows of bone-seals.
Thus, by the power of his mantra and likewise through compassion, he touched the man who was untouchable;
then, at that very moment, the eyes of those who were the ornaments of his lineage became clear.
From that inconceivable source arose the Sun of Śiva, the Lord of Maheśvarī,
by whom this entire universe is bestowed through his wondrous rays.
Therefore, Sadyojāta and Śiva are to be worshipped; from him arose the venerable Ghoratara, who is Śiva,
the progenitor of those whose minds are terrified by the cycle of existence, residing within the midst of the venerable Mahānāga.

Although his disciples were many, he was like a fire at the end of an eon that has extinguished the great delusion; though his feet were placed by a Guru whose fame is infinite and who is bewildered by the directions, he possessed supreme authority.

In the evening, from the venerable Somaśambhunātha, who is immeasurable, [proceeded] the great-souled Dharmasambhu; from him came Gaurīśa and others, beginning with the Lord of the Serpents and ending with Tārkṣya, as well as the initiation into the Ṣaṭtarka system from the Guru.
May the Sun, Hari, Śiva, and Āryā protect me from this calamity;
having heard the remedy at the outset, the one born of Gauḍa, the teacher of all people, has arrived.
In that monastery, situated on the bank of the celestial river within the dwelling of the monks,
there was the glorious and self-controlled Ugratapas, whose crown was the sun and who held the lotus-feet [of the Buddha] in his hands.
He was a master of the extensive mantras of Īśa, one who had subdued his enemies, a wise and disciplined youth, beloved by the goddess Kīrti,
compassionate, a lord of true sovereignty, and profound with the boundless splendor of his penance.
