Of the Lord himself, who has come forth from the ocean of knowledge for the welfare of the world.

53a) For one whose mental fluctuations have become dazed by the arising of abundant and supreme bliss through the meditation on the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*)— which are the witnesses of virtuous deeds— [the state of non-duality is attained].
The king named Śrī Jayasiṃha was his disciple; from him arose the wonderful Śrī Vimala, who, intent on auspiciousness, took refuge in Śivapura (Vārāṇasī).

He was a poet who spoke with eloquence, whose intellect arose from the ocean of true meaning, and who, through his devotion to the Lord of the Earth, performed the worship of the deity with one hundred and eight thousand recitations.
Indeed, the preceptor of Malayasiṃha, the sovereign of Magadha,
was Śyāmavāra; he became a king of the goddesses through the hermitage of the Arhat,
being disciplined and performing ritual acts under the auspices of Śiva, such as Śrīkaṇṭha.
By whom, whose seed of saṃsāra has been burnt, various [teachings] were sought from the Teacher.
Now, it is said that for the purification of those performers of Śiva-sacrifices who have been seized by defects born of mind, speech, and body, there is this stainless expiation.
"Prāya" is said to mean penance, and "citta" is called resolve;
the combination of these two is proclaimed as "prāyaścitta."
The householder and the celibate student each have two types of expiation;
it should be understood that for each of these, there are two further varieties based on the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts.
One should prescribe double the purification for one who acts without desire in the presence [of the teacher];
however, for those who have taken lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika), the penance for materialists (bhautika) should be known as double.
One should not disregard the well-known relationships and duties;
by whatever the teacher bestows upon the disciple, through that there shall be purification of the self.
He too, O Lord, should give strength after considering the time, the recipient, the age, and the physical condition,
as well as the pain to his life-force and the resulting exhaustion, just as a man would do.

The inheritance should be given according to the essence of their respective actions, divided and apportioned in brief; or indeed, it may be distributed by others, even by brothers who are not of the same lineage.
O Bhairava, for those who are blind, elderly, afflicted by hunger, disease, and so forth,
as well as for women, a concise [instruction] should be given.
When one is able to perform the expiation for whatever has been cut off, then [it should be done].
Other prayers should also be performed, and as previously stated, the recitation and bathing should be done twice as much;
even if one is afflicted by pride toward the gods, one is purified through the practice of japa and ritual bathing.
Beyond that, fasting at night is prescribed for up to one hundred days;
beyond that, for one who has prepared [the food], there is a three-night fast or two [days] of subsisting on air.
One should perform the *homa* offering with one-tenth of the number [of recitations], and from the *gaḍḍuka* [vessel] with one-twentieth of the recitations;
having eaten at night with sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is completed.
The recitation of the *marujā* mantras is traditionally prescribed for one who has not observed the fast;
likewise, sesame, *maṅga*, wheat, and liquids are to be used properly, except for [the consumption of] meat.
Chinese silk, grain, and likewise all types of vegetables,
as well as cooked grain and whatever else is considered a group of alkaline substances, are declared to be of low value.
During processions for the gods, weddings, sacrificial rites,
and all festive occasions, the touching of those who should not be touched does not cause impurity.
Having rubbed [the body] with the wood of a bedstead, the female elephant [should be bathed] with a flood of grass and earth;
[this applies to] pilgrimages, marriages, and so forth, except for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
One should perform [the rite] for one year in the case of a great downfall;
otherwise, when the body is afflicted by disease, as well as by fear of kings and thieves.
Likewise, in cases of danger from fire or water, or for the purpose of destroying a woman in labor,
and when performing duties toward one's guru, deities, or the sacred fire, one incurs no fault even if there is a daily neglect of regular observances.
Purification for a Brāhmaṇa shall take ten days; for a Kṣatriya, it lasts twelve days;
for a Vaiśya, purification takes fifteen days; and for a Śūdra, it is monthly.

54b) Upon the miscarriage of a full-term fetus, purification occurs at that very moment; however, for one known as *cūḍā* (the tonsure ceremony), impurity due to birth lasts until the end of childhood.
But for those for whom there is *sūtaka*, there is no impurity from contact after the tenth day;
or else, it lasts immediately until the naming ceremony, or for one day until the eruption of teeth.

For the Cūḍā ceremony, it is declared that [impurity lasts] for three days; from that point until the Vrata, fire-purification is required. Therefore, purification occurs after half that time; this is the rule for all castes.
In the case of a corpse and similar instances, one should perform the rites separately along with those who have mastered yoga;
if it is not abandoned, he goes to that state, but then purification occurs after three days.
If one born alive should die, or if one who is dead should be born, no impurity (śauca) need be observed; rather, one should perform the purification rites for childbirth (sūtī-śauca).
An increase is purified by a corpse, but a corpse is not purified by an increase;
when all [transactions] have been increased, there is no impurity (sūtaka) upon entering the market.
In the case of a girl who is toothless, when she is given [in marriage], it shall be for two days;
this is to be understood regarding one's own paternal kinsmen, as well as in the case of the mother’s sister and the maternal uncle.
Upon the death of a brother-in-law, his son, a friend, a daughter's son,
a sister’s husband, or even a son-in-law and others, one becomes pure simply by bathing.
When a Śūdra dies before his teeth have emerged, or if there is a miscarriage, the impurity lasts for eleven days; having ascertained [the caste], one should determine it otherwise in other cases.

If one dies in another country with a separate funeral cake (piṇḍa), the bath [for purification] occurs without the Guru; likewise when those who have been honored, or those who have perished by leaping from a cliff, by fire, or in water, and so forth.

This distinction between the expression and the usage of words is explained in another tradition: "A mountain" (giri) refers either to a mountain or to a great river; that which lies at its foot is called the *veśānta*.
For those children who have not yet cut their teeth, and for those who have emerged from the womb,
there is no performance of the fire-rite (agnisaṃskāra), nor is there ever any ritual action such as the water-libation.

Upon the death of a child, the father shall observe a fast for one night and partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the prescribed rite; the mother shall observe this for three nights according to the rule.
Immediate purification is prescribed in cases of giving gifts, performing sacrifices, marriage, battle, the ten calamities, and even in times of extreme distress.
When one who is ill has undergone a bath, another who is not ill, having touched him ten times, should bathe outside; then he shall attain purity.
From the selection of the preceptor until the conclusion of the sacrifice,
there shall be no impurity due to death or birth for those who remain free from contact with others during this time.
For those initiated into nirvāṇa, there is no impurity (sūtaka) at all; however,
for others, impurity exists in accordance with worldly initiation.
The cutting of the top-knot does not exist elsewhere; therefore, initiation is known as worldly.
The internal sacrifice must be performed by those who have received worldly initiation.
Recitation, circumambulation, and other such rites must be performed with great effort,
even as one would during a period of birth-impurity, death-impurity, or when a woman is in her menses.
O Śuddhāyadrudra, her name is never [to be uttered] in any circumstance whatsoever;
on the first day she is a Caṇḍālī, and on the second she is a slayer of a Brahmin.
In the third [house], a washerwoman is declared; in the fourth, a threshing-floor is purified.
For one born under the asterism of Aśleṣā, there is the death of women at night and of living beings by iron.
The preceding day itself should be taken [as the time for the rite] until the sun rises,
in the case of children, the very young, the elderly, kings, and those afflicted by disease.
For women and for artisans, no expiation is prescribed,
whether [the offense occurs] out of disrespect, anger, affection, humiliation, or fear.
If a woman or a man dies after being removed [from the house],
those men go there to the hells named Aśuci.
When the Pūyamāna has been completed in the Atamasidāruṇa hell,
a man who has killed himself shall remain there for sixty thousand years.
56a) Pilgrimages to sacred fords, falling from a cliff, renunciation, and consuming fire—
these a consecrated person should not perform among the various classes of animals.
One who desires worldly enjoyment should avoid giving gifts and performing worship at night,
except when it concerns a meritorious eclipse or for the sake of spiritual practitioners.
Having worshipped through negligence, one should mutter the Gāyatrī eight hundred times;
for one who desires liberation, such worship of Śiva is never prohibited.
If the *pavitra* is lost, there are two hundred thousand [repetitions] of the *ghora* mantra; likewise for the *aindra-vrata*.
If meditation (*dhyāna*) is omitted, by the command of Śiva, he gains no merit from the month of Caitra.

Having inadvertently offered a cow [in sacrifice], one becomes pure by reciting the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times; having intentionally emitted semen, one should recite the Vāmadeva mantra two hundred times.
Having bathed after shaving, sexual intercourse, vomiting, or passing wind,
or having touched a corpse, smoke, a funeral pyre, blood, or being defiled by one's own crow and so forth, one should bathe.
One who has performed his daily rites but has bathed improperly without following the prescribed ritual,
or one who has eaten insects and the like, shall never worship the Lord after bathing.
If semen is discharged while one is sleeping unintentionally,
he should bathe with his clothes on as before and then recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times.
56b) Whoever recites [the mantra] once at the junction of the prior and subsequent limits— that is, immediately upon birth— the sin committed during the day and night perishes instantly, O God.

If one has uttered a falsehood through deed, mind, or speech, or if semen, urine, or feces have been discharged, or if one has sneezed during the recitation for the gods, one should mutter that [hundred] Guhyaka [verses].
He who recites the Aghora mantra even once at night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight is liberated from all sins; he becomes free from the pairs of opposites and free from disease.
By merely remembering [this] once, the destruction of all sins occurs;
by reciting it five times, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
By reciting [this] seven times here, one obtains the fruits of all sacrifices;
by repeating it twenty-one times according to the rule at the conclusion of worship.
One shall obtain the entire fruit of worship; there is no doubt in this matter.
There is no mantra superior to Aghora for bestowing accomplishment upon reaching the Kali age.
O-faced one, one who has been initiated should recite [the mantra] seven times for every mouthful;
by eating what is not to be eaten for a month, there is a twenty-fold penance, and for speaking what should not be spoken, a ten-fold penance.
One who has committed slander or defamation against the guru must remain submerged in water until death;
likewise for the theft of a deposit, and for sexual intercourse with my wife, one must remain so for seven hundred years.
Even if one touches something white, or eats five times, or eats alone after having anointed oneself,
that brahmin who recites the Rudra-mantra ten million times in the presence of Rudra [is purified].
Having recited that [mantra] even once, they are not worth a sixteenth part of one who,
out of delusion, would revile Śiva, his scripture, or likewise a yogin.
One who is ignorant of this mantra is not defiled by anything; he may eat insects and grass, and he should recite the mantra eight hundred times while rotating the wheel clockwise.
For one who constantly recites the Īśāna mantra during lunar and solar eclipses and during the Viṣṭi yogas, no sin exists.
Having committed evil through action, mind, or speech out of delusion,
one consumes garlic and other forbidden foods, as well as those grown underground and mushrooms.
Having recited [the mantra] over onions and garlic, one should remember Īśāna once;
however, for accepting a gift of a monastery, one should perform a formidable recitation of one hundred thousand times.
Where the place for the Guru is first and the arrangement of the temple (prāsāda) follows, that is called *tantra-yauvana*; otherwise, one should designate it as a monastery (*maṭha*).
When a confluence of all sins has arisen,
one should recite the five Brahmans or the one who possesses many forms.
Likewise, fasting, bathing, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the recitation [of mantras] a hundred times,
and the fire-oblation (homa) destroy all impurity arising from Śaṅkara for men.
In the event of the omission of a vow, a ritual act, or a restrictive rule,
one may again achieve such flawlessness by reciting the Gāyatrī eight hundred times.

If one fails to perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) even once, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times while remaining unborn [in body]. For the omission of the three daily periods, the penance is tripled; if done intentionally, it must be accompanied by fasting.
One who has missed the three twilight prayers attains purification by reciting the Śiva-ekādaśikā three times; even one who has omitted his bath should recite it.
Having killed a collection of boneless living beings, one should recite the Ekādaśikā;
and having killed all birds, one should spend three times the Ekādaśikā.
Having studied the five Brahma-fires, the limbs of speech, Śiva, and the supreme imperishable, one attains heaven; and having realized them, one is utterly liberated.
On a festival day, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, the Guru, and the Fire with devotion,
and having offered the bali-oblation there, one should recite the Śiva-mantra eight hundred times.
One who eats leaves, flowers, fruits, water, food, vehicles,
and medicine without first offering them, even if they are intended for one's own sustenance, [commits an offense].
One is purified by the recitation of the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times and by worship; however,
for the killing of a virtuous Śūdra, one should recite it ten thousand times.
He who, out of delusion, gives away the path prepared by his gurus,
and that other wicked-souled person who receives it— both of them shall go to hell.
Or, when one sneezes due to hunger or other causes, by touching the right ear with the hand and then touching the tip of the nose, one does not encounter obstacles.
At all times, during all activities such as sneezing or spitting,
by uttering "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," one is liberated from all sins.
One should avoid even the sight of those who have committed the five great sins; purification from conversing with them is held to require double that effort, and from touching them, twice again.
Purification comes from leaving the bed; one becomes pure by eating a hundred thousand times;
yet [impurity arises] from contact with Buddhists and Cārvākas, from reviling Śiva, and toward others.
In the company of those who corrupt the true scriptures, especially the fallen,
as well as with the naked ascetics (Digambaras) and others, the recitation of mantras becomes terrible.

The purification of conch shells and the like, as well as of the *śruva* and other sacrificial ladles, the *caru* vessels, and the pestle and mortar, is performed with cow's urine or with water churned by a *tūṣa* grass stalk.
The purification of winnowing baskets, cow-products, and vessels is by means of hot water;
that of horns, bones, wood, and ivory is by scrubbing with their respective powders.
One should cleanse copper with acidic water,
bell-metal with acid, or everything else with water containing *kāśa* grass or tamarind.

The cleansing of vessels touched by those who are impure from food remnants is achieved through sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) without doubt; for vessels such as gourds and those belonging to Caṇḍālas, it is done by scrubbing with cow-dung, cow-urine, or water.
Wood is purified by being scrubbed with metal or by planing;
leather and rope are purified by alkaline water, as is the purification for garments.
Daily purification is prescribed for those engaged in rites for the ancestors or the gods;
however, it is required upon discarding the lower garment or when impurity accumulates on the upper robe.
A cloth washed by a washerman becomes pure when washed again;
so too, the mind is purified by truthful speech, and auspicious actions are perfected through constant practice.
That cloth which has been beaten, that which is said to be of mineral origin, that which has been washed with clay,
and that whose fringes are uncut— this is traditionally remembered as most pure.
One who is naked has only a small portion of self; therefore, one should wear a loincloth and a garment.
One should not tie up the hair-knot quickly during rites for the gods or the ancestors.
Indeed, bathing with only a single garment, or one that has been worn by another, does not constitute a true bath; for one is thereby deprived of prosperity.
The purification of water-vessels is accomplished by carrying fire around them;
and whatever wood, such as a broom-handle or the like, is used, it becomes pure by being sprinkled with water.
By sweeping, by scraping, by sprinkling, by smearing with cow-dung, and by moistening with water—
thus five kinds of purification for the ground are known to those who possess knowledge.

One should discard the remains of offerings (nirmālya) immediately upon sight; a vessel produced from clay or cow-dung is purified by being washed with milk, and the purification of curd is likewise declared.
Having placed it inside a vessel of curd, one should scatter [the remnants] immediately thereafter;
thus, the food and other items are freed from contamination by the smearings, and the curd is purified by sprinkling.
The purification of well-heated clarified butter (ājya) is proclaimed to be through [heating];
likewise, the purification of molasses, jaggery, and other such substances is by means of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and contact with fire.

Upon touching the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one should discard minor substances as well as medicinal herbs, water that has undergone transformation, and likewise sugarcane, asafoetida, and cumin.
Having understood the relative strength and weakness of the substances— namely, saindhava and its group, camphor, kaṭuka and its group, sugar, ground sandalwood, and ash— [one should apply them].
Grain and other such items become pure by being sprinkled; one should observe this principle elsewhere as well.
This applies to cotton mattresses, pillows, flowers, and red garments.
Having dried these clean items, one should heat them; however, in some cases, barley is used for the removal of impurities from objects such as touchstones, arrows, lingas, and floral offerings.
59b) Having bathed the deity who is stationed here as if released from heaven, and having sipped water (ācamana), one should bathe [the deity].
Having sipped water from another vessel and having bathed [the deity] once more, one should worship;
this applies even to a moving or unstable image, preceded by bathing and sipping water.
Purification from the Aghora [mantra] occurs after thirty repetitions; purification occurs when the shadow of the liṅga passes through the opening;
and purification is twofold when it rolls over a thousand times.

When the linga has been displaced three or four times, or when it has turned over upon the surface of the earth, it is indeed impure; however, if it has fallen from its own base by less than a hundred thousand [units], it is pure.
If there is a violent impact within two *ayuta*s [20,000 *yojanas*], it will certainly occur nearby;
if there is the shaking from the touch of a foot, it is certain within three *ayuta*s, or half of that distance if accompanied by dust.

If one is defiled by saliva, thirty thousand [repetitions] are required; if by water from that [mouth], twenty thousand; and for water from the mouth during the recitation of a Sūtra, one becomes pure after two hundred thousand repetitions.
One should declare purification after fifty thousand [steps] from touching blood, semen, or menstrual flow;
and one is considered pure after seventy-five thousand [steps] from falling into a pit of excrement.
For the eradication of a firm [possession], one hundred thousand recitations are required; likewise, for purification and restoration, one hundred thousand;
for calamities, one hundred thousand; for a bad direction, one hundred thousand; but for a specific desire, ten million.
But when Sasamudgaka-Kaliṅga has fallen due to negligence,
half of thirty thousand (fifteen thousand) should be assigned to the hand; it may be less or more than that.
But if it is devoid of a casket, one becomes pure by [offering] twice the previously mentioned amount.
If its luster is not diminished even when licked by fire for ten thousand years, then it remains pure even when abandoned by another who is devoid of luster, even after a hundred thousand years.
When the meaning has been obscured by a shadow, or when it is carried away, lost, or fallen into a deep pit through negligence; or when it has descended from a lamp into a deep abyss.
If the linga has been licked by one's own dog, or has been carried away by pure persons,
or stolen by thieves, or even used by outcastes (svapacas);
If one touches two opposing groups, the rite of binding (pāśa) is prescribed;
one should then diligently recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and establish a restraint once again.
Once the worship on the sacrificial ground has been completed and [the deity] has been dismissed,
one should take those flowers with the mantra and offer five hundred oblations into the fierce fire.
One should recite five thousand [mantras] for the deity of the *liṅga*; if it is shattered, one should perform three hundred thousand according to the ritual procedure as before with total devotion.
If one moves the *liṅga* while reciting mantras, that man shall become a breaker of the *liṅga*.
This applies even to Śaivas, Pāśupatas, and those who observe the Kāpālika vow.
Even though he had coiled his body only once, he was able to slay the three worlds;
yet, by fate, he was not perceived due to the dense mass of his matted locks.
Likewise, having crossed over Mount Meru, one should mutter the Śiva-śāṣṭa (the eightfold mantra of Śiva) a hundred times;
thus [is the procedure] for the Vairākṣa-sūtra from the previously mentioned Liṅga-pāda.
The height of the bell should be one-eighth of the liṅga; in other cases, it should be like the liṅga itself.
By the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, their own desired liṅga should indeed be worshipped.
If touched by those ending in one, two, three, or four [syllables], one becomes pure after a hundred [repetitions].
Among the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, the lords of the *jātis* are Aghora, Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, and Īśa respectively; however, Aghora is common to all, while Īśa is the supreme common [lord].
If one's own chosen *liṅga* is touched by a group of fishermen, one becomes pure by performing the *yuta* rite;
if it is touched by Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, or Kaula practitioners, one should conquer [the impurity] through the *yuta* rite.
There is no fault if the linga is touched by those initiated in one's own tradition;
likewise, there is no fault regarding that which has been cooked for the purpose of a fire sacrifice, for the sake of the Guru, or for the sake of the linga.
If that evil-minded person should consume it out of delusion or craving, he must recite one hundred thousand [mantras] and a quarter of that; thus his purification will always be accomplished.
Alternatively, having offered the remains of Śiva’s offerings (nirmālya) or the water from the drainage channel (praṇāla),
one should recite [the mantra] thirty thousand times and offer eight hundred handfuls of water.
61a) However, one may be purified through intentional [confession]; unintentionally, it takes twenty thousand [repetitions].
This applies to those who revile their guru, or those initiated [into the Śiva path], or Śiva himself.
From that place he should go far away; he conquers hundreds of newborns.
Even by slaying those who revile him, he is not defiled by the act of killing.
The shadow of one who performs penance involving heavy fire is defiled even against their will;
for such a person, three hundred repetitions of the *ghora* mantra are required, while for a cow, a maiden, or a virtuous Brahmin, one hundred repetitions are prescribed.

If there is an omission of worship for one day, one should recite the mantra a thousand times as a middling penance; if done unintentionally or through negligence, this applies, but if done intentionally, one becomes pure by reciting it twice that amount.
They say that one is pure only after two fasts and not otherwise;
for those who perform worship three times a day, or even once a day.
The expiation for these shall be equal; it should be neither less nor more.
It begins from one day and extends up to ten days.

One should increase [the count] by three hundred through sprinkling, and likewise perform *gaḍḍuka* recitations on the left; furthermore, by omitting one [recitation] for each fortnight, one should mutter twenty thousand on the right.
But in the case of missing a month, one should increase it by twenty thousand twice over;
this is for the sake of purification month after month until the end of the year.
If there is an omission of the daily rites, one should prescribe an expiation;
for if the fire, though maintained, becomes extinguished, one should fast and mutter the Ghoramantra.
Even for the sake of auspicious liberation, having fasted for three nights,
he should either recite or offer oblations with the *vahurūpa* mantra for the sake of pacification.
Whatever ritual action is performed on the eighth day and so forth, such as worship, recitation, and fire-offerings,
one should transform it four or five times over.
If the vessel has not been released, or if it is broken, or if its contents have spilled,
one becomes pure by giving two hundred, a thousand, and half of that [five hundred] respectively.
Having eaten the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of an outcast, or likewise at a funeral feast;
having consumed the *sīmantonnayana* [initiation] meal, or the food of a teacher, or the food of a sacrificial post (*śamyā*), and so forth.
Having climbed up due to wandering or confusion, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred thousand times along with the *śrīdākṣiṇa*;
if, through negligence, one has consumed meat, fish, honey, or the like at night, one should recite it ten thousand times.
Where is devotion to Śiva, where is the worship of Caṇḍī-Kabha, and where is the drinking of intoxicants? Śaṅkara remains far away from those who consume liquor, meat, and blood.
If, by fate, one partakes even slightly of the vice of liquor, it leads to ruin because of its addictive nature; therefore, for such a person, *vāruṇī* is indeed a source of fault.
By the non-observation of the rules regarding sexual intercourse, food, and drink,
one is purified by half of the great *śrāddha* [penance] involving oil massage, foot-washing, clothing, and so forth.
Having resolved to sleep on the ground, one should recite the Lopāmudrā-weapon mantra a hundred times.
On the twelfth or eleventh day, one should recite three hundred *dakṣiṇas*;
on the eighth auspicious day, having eaten *dhūmrāla*, one should recite [the mantra] according to one's desire.
After eating the food of the Name-Initiation (nāmaprāśana) while free from desire, one should recite the Vaktra-śata;
but after eating the food of the Fourth Day (caturthikā), one should recite the Guhya-mantra as before.
In sacrifices such as the Pākayajñas, one should eat the food of the ritual site because it is purifying;
likewise, in the tonsure ceremony (caula), the vow (vrata), the Godāna rite, and the marriage, one incurs no fault.
Food should never be eaten by these three types of persons:
those who are devoted to the practice of purity and right conduct, those who are devoted to Rudra, and those who abstain from drinking liquor.
Indeed, those devotees who are intent on the worship of Rudra should be fed, even if they are born of the lowest castes;
for even they, having experienced the end of their restraint, may occasionally enjoy [liberation] through the power of their residual impressions (*upādhi*).
Having recited the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times while remaining self-controlled, one attains purification;
or, if the child born from an unworthy woman is abandoned, then, O Agni, there is suffering.
Having eaten [the food] of those who endure the terrible, one should recite [the mantra] for half [the duration], provided it was not done intentionally;
having eaten the food of those who carry skulls and wear lingas, one should instead cause the *putadīkṣā* initiation to be performed.
If one is touched by someone of one's own caste who has been initiated, one becomes pure by sipping water (ācamana).
If touched by one of one's own caste who has not been initiated, one should also sip water and recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
However, due to touching one who has been initiated nearby, the expiation is as before;
if he touches that initiated person, he should bathe and recite [the mantra] three hundred times.
In the same way, if there is an internal contact for one who has been initiated or is about to be initiated,
he should bathe and remain fasting, and then recite [the mantra] three hundred and four times.
Others, however, perform a penance reduced by one quarter;
for touching [the corpse] unintentionally, one should recite the *Sahasraśīrṣā* ten times over three nights.
A recitation of the *Kṛcchra-aghora* mantra ten thousand times must be performed for contact with a *caṇḍāla*.
Having recognized each instance of such contact, one should perform the expiation accordingly.

Having eaten the leavings of those of equal status, one becomes pure after fasting for a day; likewise, after eating the leavings of those who are ten thousand or even ten million times superior, or of those who are inferior, one becomes pure by fasting for half that duration.
Fasting for two or three nights is prescribed for eating food left over by one of equal caste;
however, it is recorded that for contact with the leavings of a lower caste, the penance is ten times greater.
If one who has been initiated into a particular caste eats food to which he has not been invited,
he becomes purified by reciting the mantras of the Lord of that caste and the Lord of his own caste together in one place.
63a) One, two, and three days respectively are for the purification of the recitation (japa) for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes.

The purification of the sense organs is twofold: through bathing and through the consumption of food. One who has committed a grave sin against the limbs [of the body] should fast and recite the mantra a thousand times.
A wise person should avoid bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, and worship when suffering from indigestion;
once the food is digested, however, one should bathe and then recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one should, through negligence, drink water remaining after it has been turned yellow,
the wise person should fast for one night and then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having drunk fresh water from the Nakha, Kaṇṭhaka, Matsya, Sambūka, or Kapardana rivers, one should fast and then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If it does not rain during the four months beginning with Pauṣa, one becomes pure;
however, water [received] from Vaiśākha onwards leads to great fault.
One who is naked, one who has not bathed after twelve days, one who lacks the nine limbs [of the body], a buffalo, a goat, or one who eats while devoid of the sacred thread during a Vedic recitation;
Having fasted and recited the Ghoramantra, he is purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the consumption of the remains of an offering (nirmālya) occurs through negligence, one should recite it ten thousand times.
63b) For one who is not Aghora, nor for any other [deity], purification does not occur through the practice of desire and so forth;
even if one violates the command of a fierce Guru, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.

The remains of offerings (nirmālya) belonging to the Guru, the sacred fire, the seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), the Mothers, the great serpents, the Yogins, the Mātṛs, the Yakṣas, and the like, are not [to be treated] as [ordinary] things are to Śiva.

In the case of images made of precious gems or bone, or of golden lingas, or in the circumambulation of a statue, or even during the oral exposition [of the Dharma], or in the case of a moving image or a painting, it is not at all improper to offer floral remains (nirmālya).
In the context of worship, fire, incense, and the like, as well as the radiance of scented water and lamps,
and even the flow of a river used as offering water, are never at all defiled.

One should always cast the remains of offerings (nirmālya) into still water, on dry land, or into a flowing stream; moreover, one should not recite the Gāyatrī mantra in water while wearing either dry or wet clothing.
Sūryā is eternally of the nature of fire (nalātmikā) due to the opposition between the two vowels *vā* and *ri*;
they are devoid of the twenty-four syllables beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *na*.
The Gāyatrī-arkā, when recited at the end of the Viṣṭāva within the solar maṇḍala,
accompanied by "Oṃ Hauṃ Hrīṃ" and ending with "namo," bestows desired boons and destroys sins.
In a *liṅga* installed on the same day, whether it is designated as mobile or immobile,
[the offering] up to the fourth day of the ritual period does not cause fault on the day of the *nirmālya*.

The property of the gods, the deity’s substance, the food offering, that which is presented as an offering, Caṇḍadanta, and the remains of offerings— even from the giving of these, one becomes a rākṣasa.
Success comes from eating the flesh of the Mātaṅga, while loss results from cutting it;
one who smells its scent becomes a wolf, and one who burns it improperly harms both himself and others.
In the case of sexual intercourse, it is the state of womanhood; and in the case of sale, it is the state of being a slave.
In the case of touching, the touch is equal; in eating and selling, they are equal.

That which has not been touched by flower-offerings (*nirmālya*), nor by a hand, nor by a person—therein the previously mentioned [penance] is reduced by one quarter; however, for touching or eating [such items], the same applies.
If sandalwood paste or other substances are inadvertently ground together with the *anuṣaṅga* (the remnants of the previous offering), that constitutes *nirmālya*;
one-fourth of it is [offered] to those known as *siddhaliṅgas* and so forth.
One should eat only one meal a day for three days, and for three days eat only what is unasked for;
one should always eat only at night for three days, and for three days indeed subsist on air alone.
One *ucchra* is known as the Mahāpadma, which belongs to Prajāpati.
One should drink hot water for three days and take food with milk for three days.
Having drunk hot ghee for three days and [fasted] for another three days—this is what some call the *taptakṛcchra* (hot penance). Now hear about the *atikṛcchra* (excessive penance).
For twenty-one days, one should drink three palas of milk,
remaining celibate, established in meditative concentration, and devoted to the virtue of patience.
One should not eat for a day and night; this is the characteristic of fasting. Abstinence from sexual intercourse and refraining from idle chatter are also required.
The characteristic of the holy life (brahmacarya) is the restraint of all the sense faculties;
it consists of celibacy, silent recitation, humility, patience, and moderation in food.
This form of penance is extremely terrible and [endures for] a moment;
fasting for twelve days is the Great Parāka, which is threefold [in intensity].
For half a month there should be an increase of one morsel [per day] during the bright fortnight, and one should decrease it during the dark fortnight;
thus are the two rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa prescribed, consisting entirely of water.
If one performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, consisting of two hundred and forty morsels of food,
beginning from today and ending on the new moon day;
One who is dependent on another's tradition must strictly avoid performing rites, vows, and observances prescribed therein that are not derived from one's own scriptures.
Whatever sin a practitioner of mantras who has mastered the Saṃhitās commits here,
he quickly reduces it all to ashes through the power of the mantra.
I have composed this [work] for him in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*.
This procedure for subduing those who are difficult to reach, as described by the seers, possesses inconceivable greatness.
This is the name of this excellent lion among men, who subdues the armies of gods and dānavas.
The fourth [chapter], the ritual of Dāmana in Vimalāvatī. [End of] section 244.
Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, distressed by various hardships in the grove of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, sought to liberate themselves from their state as sacrificial animals;
yet it was only by His grace that they attained initiation and, through ten million years of practice, manifested qualities equal to those of Śiva.
I shall describe that meditation, which brings about complete subjugation, performed within one's own abode of Śiva.
Even today, in that Devadāru forest, the sign is still seen:
by growing a tooth-stick sprout upon a living being, a great initiation has been performed.
Whoever—be they Brahmā or any other being down to the stationary objects—is initiated into the water, that initiation alone shall suffice for them; such a person is qualified for the worship of Hara.
From that time forward, he was rendered speechless whenever he was smelled by the will of Śiva;
however, he could not be recognized by others through signs such as initiation and the like.
The power of embodied beings falls toward the gods so that they do not turn back; this is their characteristic sign: an aversion to worldly existence and a longing for liberation.

65b) There is devotion toward the devotees of Śiva and faith in the ritual prescribed by their scripture; even for those of dull intellect, there is an inference based on the conduct of the learned, which serves as a cause [for conviction].
For those established in the yoga of increasing the sacrificial animal (paśuvṛddhi), there is an equal manifestation of two types of karma;
for those fit for the fruits beginning with Jyeṣṭhā, there is [the path] toward the eight liberations accompanied by qualification.
If one dies while still a disciple under Upāpāda or Ṛṣi, these three [stages] occur again;
however, in the case of Īśadadvanivarta, one proceeds toward the darkness of Rodhaka.
These signs appear when only a small portion remains for those who possess the power of the Lord; they become partakers of the state of Rudra, the Lord of Mantras.
Abiding in the state of *sthiti*, the one whose mind is fixed on consciousness (*ciddhata*) attains the Guru;
through the diversity of powers beginning with *manda*, he then reaches the states of *sālokya* and the rest.
Those who have gone from here and those who come from there, their own crests instantly become manifest;
they arise as the six-faced ones, the lords, or as the audāsas produced by Saṃskṛta.

In sleep, meditation, and likewise in wakefulness, the powers of Māyā—consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the mind (*manas*)—which are capable of manifesting objects, perform their respective functions; and whatever collection of entities exists, He projects it all according to its nature.
When, by destiny, one strives for the power of Śiva while remaining equanimous toward both dharma and adharma, then his meditation becomes fixed and initiation arises for him.
Reflecting repeatedly, "Of what nature is this ego, and what is this cage of suffering?", one who desires liberation should seek out a guru.
Having propitiated him and obtained the initiation of Śaṅkara from him when he was pleased,
one shall go to Śiva at the fall of the body, which is the gateway to enjoyment at that very moment.
Rudra, Rudra-śakti, and the Guru—these three are equal.
To him who strives with devotion, the initiation that transcends the cremation ground is bestowed.
Even by a disciple, that [instruction] should not be received when the teacher has been satisfied with his body,
wealth, knowledge, faith, ritual actions, virtues, and so forth.
Just as initiation is manifold through various distinctions such as that of the eyes and so forth, so too,
having closed the eyes and meditated upon the supreme reality which is perfectly stainless—
Then, for the sake of the twilight ritual, he should gaze upon the auspicious [deities] who are visible through initiation;
having first meditated on Śiva in his hand, together with the limbs of Brahmā and the head.
The Guru should touch the body of the disciple, beginning with the head;
in this way, the initiation by touch occurs, which effects dissolution, enjoyment, and awakening.
Having brought them into equipoise within the reality of consciousness,
one should utter the mantras joined together, augmented by supreme splendor; this is the initiation of speech, the instrument of the All-pervading Lord.

And that [knowledge] is eternal; it cannot be produced by anything else, whether by attachment or by a conscious agent. Relying upon a mental procedure, this knowledge belongs to one who possesses the mind.
Within the true tradition of the scripture, the initiation into the scripture (śāstradīkṣā) is indeed manifold;
it is said to be the piercing initiation (vedhadīkṣā), the entry-granting initiation (veśadā), the yoga-granting initiation (yogadā), and the one that bestows Śiva (śivadāyinī).
Through the grace of the Guru, all [obstacles] are overcome and abandoned;
for these initiations are indeed distinguished for those who desire distinguished fruits.
The delusion of living beings has been dispelled by the true guru for their benefit,
through thirty-six principles, half of that [eighteen], half of that again [nine], and then five.

By means of the three, or by the letters beginning with *ka*, *va*, *śrī*, *netra*, *bha*, and *ṣṭa*; and by means of the digits (*kalā*), the worlds (*bhuvana*), the phonemes (*varṇa*), the words (*pada*), and the mantras contained within the scriptures.
In these various ways—whether individually, collectively, or in detail—the Hotrī, who resides within the womb of the bride, is twofold: with seed (sabīja) and without seed (abīja).

That [state] is the seed (bīja) of speech, while those accompanied by it are "with-seed" (sabījakā). Those freed from these [states] are "seedless" (nirbīja), and the seedless state is further twofold.
67a) For there is indeed one [form of] immediate nirvāṇa, and a second, [attained] while still in the body; thus,
by the descent of power (śaktipāta), there are four types, which are equal with respect to their fruit.
Likewise, whether it be extremely intense, intense, mild, or even very mild,
one should meditate on that which leads to liberation from the ocean of worldly existence, accompanied by horripilation.
Having seen a disciple worn out by old age and afflicted by disease,
one should then speak to him and establish him in the supreme reality.
That [initiation] may also be of two kinds, with seed; among these, the first belongs to those whose nature is Śiva.
It is primary for the *putraka* and the *ācārya*, and it brings about the destruction of both merit and demerit.
For the practitioner devoted to sacrifices, charitable works, and the like, she is Lokadharmiṇī.
The root is the Śivadharma-āṇi, the fruit is the Śivadharma of prosperity, and the boat is that which is most beneficial and indestructible;
cross over the ocean of worldly existence by means of it.
In all the realms of enjoyment, she endures the results of her misdeeds;
for the sake of attaining other bodies and powers such as atomization (aṇimā), she follows the dharma of the world approved by the learned.
Whoever desires a share of the petals is appointed right there;
through the power of the mantra and by means of those respective principles, he becomes a partaker of accomplishment.
The fire sacrifice (homa) of mantras, mudrās, meanings, and substances is known as common;
it is distinguished, however, by the differences in the food consumed by the disciples and likewise by the teacher.
One should not look at those practicing celibacy, nor at one's father and so forth, nor at one's mother, nor at one's daughter-in-law and so forth, during the day.
One should initiate after having determined whether [the candidate] is a servant and so forth, or capable and incapable;
initiation is further divided into two types: that which possesses authority and that which lacks authority.
The obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites should always be performed according to the modified form;
that [initiation] is for the sake of qualification, while the higher [initiation] is for the sake of the adept (sādhaka) and the noble one (ācārya).
That son (putraka) is likewise, as is one who has been initiated without seed (nirbīja-dīkṣita);
because initiation possesses a single constant agent, it confers no authority upon them.

Children, women, the elderly, and those who are ill, as well as those who have been consecrated (dīkṣita), are entitled to a share of the food; however, those who are seedless (nirvīja) may eat according to necessity.
Furthermore, she becomes the Hotṛ priest in many ways through the differentiation of mantras;
she is known as the Brahmadīkṣā by means of the Brahma-mantras, and as Aṅginī by means of the ancillary limbs (aṅgas).
Initiation by the Śaktis is said to be through the Śaktis; initiation by the Heart is through the Heart-mantra;
initiation by the Mūrtis is through the Mūrtis; and initiation by the Cakras is through their respective presiding deities.
She was worshipped by the lords of the Gaṇas as Gaṇeśānī, by the world-protectors as their sovereign,
and by the Rudras, the Gaṇas, the Mothers, and her sisters in various places.
These and others are known as the mixed [mantras], which should be understood as being identical in nature to those [pure] mantras.

The Self is also said to be manifold; among these, the first is considered the Sakala (the conditioned), which is endowed with the impurities of *māyā* and *karman*, and is the locus of the principles beginning with *kalā*.
Among the impurities of karma, there is another, the *pralayākala*, within *māyā*;
above *māyā* and below *śuddhavidyā*, there is another who is covered by mere impurity (*mala*).
These [energies], however, abide in the state of the Jñānākala; they are easily grasped by the Supreme Self, Śiva, who is partless (niṣkala), due to the descent of his exceedingly intense power.
The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe, imperishable and of the nature of Śiva;
it is the single lotus within the Bilva fruit, subtle, beginningless, and undecaying, [presided over by] Īśvara.
The karma of the bound soul (paśu) is of two kinds, consisting of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma), which is to be experienced;
it is established through mental engagement (ābhoga) and is opposed to the two fruits arising from knowledge (vidyā).

That one is the root of all living beings—beginningless, dense, and vast; it stands as the source for each individual until the end of its own time, possessing a multitude of powers for the manifestation of mental afflictions.
The state of persistence consists in the authority over the impure power (mala-śakti), and it is further divided by the distinctions of cessation (nivṛtti) and other such divisions;
this manifoldness has been elaborated here within the Self.
For one who has been recognized through the descent of power (śaktipāta) as being of the nature of a limited soul (sakalātman),
Śiva, in the form of the Guru, should perform the *hautrī* initiation consisting of the constituent parts (*kalā*).

O Śiva, you who somehow attained the state of being bowed down to by the beautiful Goddess Siṃhāsanī— the daughter of Bandhuka, whose belly is like a lotus, who is radiant with the three coils of her serpent-king, and who is as pure as the subtlest essence of the rising dawn— [you who conquered] the demon Mahiṣāsura.
For liberation, one should offer [oblations] with the *pramathinī* and other mantras.
Just as a man's stain [is removed], so too is his state of ignorance;
through initiation, by means of the primary [rite] consisting of the realization of Brahman, he is purified on the balance of pure birth.
Just as poison destroys the body, so too does unrighteousness destroy the end;
for lack of discernment is his heaviness, while the destruction of the six [virtues] is his ruin.
By its very nature, it arises as light; yet through duality, it is perceived as such. Its essence is that of innate impurity, like copper enveloped in dense dross.
Through the application of the essence of initiation, one becomes Śiva, just as base metal becomes gold;
for just as the impurities of metals being smelted are burnt away.
69a) Likewise, even when they are burning, these [fires], having become like wind, are fully capable of consuming impurities; and that [wind],
by virtue of its continuity, is desired as the bringer of the fruit of felling trees.
The wheels of mantras proclaimed by Śiva, beginning with the Cumbaka and others, bestow one's desired goals when established [therein].
Therefore, first, for the sake of ascertaining the seed of initiation, there should be the general initiation consisting of the pledges (*samaya*) and so forth,
which serves as the ground, just like the purification of the site.

One should initiate [the disciple] in sacred fields, holy fords, mountains, forests, rivers, saline wastes, and the like; in the presence of a *liṅga* or other such objects; in a pleasing location; or elsewhere as well.
Exertion during the autumn and spring seasons is best for the performance of the rites of initiation;
in their absence, it is recommended even at other times, provided it is not during the rainy season.
However, [the month of] Pauṣa and Caitra are likewise [auspicious], provided there is a favorable planet on the day of Damanārka;
herein also occur the festivals of the Guru and so forth.

In the bright fortnight, that [day] is most excellent; in the dark fortnight, it is the fifth day. When joined with an auspicious yoga and muhūrta, and occurring in a quadrant (kendrādau), it brings about prosperity and grants great satisfaction.

[This applies] to the initiated disciple and the initiator who possess devotion, who act with constant assistance, who are endowed with [proper] lineage, appearance, and conduct, and who are both bound and liberated.
The eight factors of the Kārāṣṭaka consist of the [proper] waist-cloth, undergarment, and loincloth for those of inferior status;
correct knowledge of one's birth and conduct are the first two qualities of those two.
For whomsoever these [mantras] exist, O best of sages, they shall become the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The Brahmin is the foremost among the four castes; the Kṣatriya is superior to the other two;
the householder is the lord, authorized and fit for the performance of his duties.
Among the Saura, Vaiṣṇava, Pañcārtha, Sāṃkhya, and Ārhata systems, the Śaiva is the one who possesses authority over all; however, no one at all possesses authority over the Śaiva system.
Whether it be the destruction of the creator of the gods or worldly enjoyment, that upon which [the world] is established—
even if he were equal to Śiva— he is a true Guru who has burned away the hand of falsehood.
That guru who, out of greed, initiates those who drink liquor, those who are heroic [in battle], or those who are censurable,
shall be cooked for a long time in the Avīci hell along with those disciples.
If, out of delusion, one fails to attend upon a qualified guru while such a teacher is available within the guru’s lineage,
that person becomes burdened with sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and dwells for a long time in hell.
Wherever there are many people who, at that time, desire to receive initiation,
there the Lord’s own presence shall manifest among men.
Then the teacher, who knows all things, is solely devoted to the teachings of Śiva;
he wears white garments, has conquered the pairs of opposites, and performs the two-fold ritual placement of the sacrificial offering (arghya).
Then, before the sun has risen and before the morning [service] has occurred, one should worship with incense;
once the midday rites have been performed, having completed them, one should engage in the subsequent duties.
Surrounded by his disciplined disciples, adorned with white garlands and fragrant scents,
he drowned out all ill-omened sounds with the auspicious resonance of Vedic chants and musical instruments.
Having worshipped the site according to the prescribed ritual, one should extract any thorns or other obstructions;
for these are causes of suffering, grief, and so forth, and the ground here should be filled with that [extracted] earth.
With seventeen, eight, seven, four, eleven, and eleven syllables [per line],
it is symmetrical at the ears, equal, beautiful, square, and four-faced.
Having constructed a firm sacrificial altar adorned with pitchers and some sturdy wooden rafters,
one should worship the archways at the entrances.

Furthermore, having worshipped the mantras as if they were permanent— even if it be only for a single moment— having honored the deity within the city, one should cause the supreme [deity] to enter through the western door alone.
One should diligently block the three doors with a girdle and other such means;
then, having entered by the eastern door and circumambulated clockwise, one stands upon the altar on the right side.
Having expelled the pure wind, one should rest for a moment and then fill [the body] with pure air;
having first performed purification, one should always fill the body with pure wind.
The heart-lotus, which is facing downward, is opened by means of *pūraka* (inhalation);
having turned it upward by means of *kumbhaka* (retention), one should restrain the self within it.
Alternatively, having placed a white lotus facing downwards upon a mirror or elsewhere,
and having assumed the Śiva-body, one should employ the mudrā according to the [prescribed] manner.
The wise one should lead [the hands] from the two downward-facing palms to the heart;
then, with the faces turned sideways, he should lead them to the two *guru*s facing upward.
Renowned as Mahāmudrā in the practice of accomplishing the body,
she performs all actions for the sake of the yogis' attainment of yoga.
One should dissolve the wealth pierced by the arrow of Mūdrārāti with the net of mudrās;
through devotion and by taking refuge in Śiva, the mudrā causes it to melt and deludes [the senses].
The three mudrās pertaining to the three times arise from the mind, from the mouth of the Guru, or from the mantra born of Vāgbhava; they originate from the body through its limbs and gestures.

This mudrā is primarily used for invocation (āvāhana), obstruction (rodha), and dismissal (visarga); it is also employed for bringing about proximity (saṃnidhi) and for the removal of obstacles to the senses, speech, and mind.
In the body, on the ground, in the mere sacrificial pit, in the fire-ritual, and in the limbs as prescribed by the virtuous;

Then, facing east, that man should worship, offer oblations into the fire, and meditate upon Śiva— the lotus of the heart, the destroyer of ignorance, and the one who blocks the path to the lower realms.
One should perform all [the rites] or none at all for the purification of the Full Aṣṭakā;
[these consist of] sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
Intellect, mind, and ego—this is known as the inner group of eight;
for it has been said that one should worship Śiva after having become Śiva externally, starting from the eyebrows.
He who performs an external sacrifice without having first performed the mental sacrifice is to be known as inauspicious; he is not ordained for liberation.
For the purification of the site, having prepared the perfumed water (gandha) and the arghya with the heart-mantra, and the vardhanī vessel with the weapon-mantra (astra),
one should perform the special arghya as previously described and proclaimed.
One should install the sacrifice together with its constituent parts pertaining to the laity in that very place;
indeed, no one should move it, nor should anyone perform it otherwise.

One should perform the *calārgha* (moving arghya) for the worship of Śiva’s pitcher, the weapon, the guardians of the directions, Agni, and the others; and for the sake of fame and restraint, one should perform the *nirodhārgha* (restraining arghya) with devotion as before.
71b) For the sake of attaining the knowledge of Śiva, Agni, and Vidyā, having understood those three in their proper sequence somewhere,
one should [offer] all substances with perfumes, water for honor (argha), water for the feet (āstāda), akṣata, and auspicious kuśa grass.
One should scatter the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and perform the rite with the Sword of Knowledge as before;
whoever obtains the Uṣṇīṣa, gold, garments, and so forth, prepared and consecrated according to the ritual manual (saṃhitā).
Then, with the cord of the noose, the thread, the quality, the power, and the crest-lock,
one should fashion a sacrificial knife made of goat's horn, complete with its handle and sharpened.
[He should fashion] a small, sharp iron instrument from clay mixed with the juice of the *sadākārā* plant,
and a pair of scissors smeared with [the same substance], empowered by the seven-syllable mantra residing in the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Green, white, yellow, and black— these pure-colored cloths,
when consecrated with mantras, are joined with the peaceful, the transcendent, and the other [families].
One should worship oneself as before, according to the rule for the body of knowledge (vidyādeha),
and one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the five [limbs] by means of the breaking of the staff and the breaking of the skull.
Now, in which [deities] are there thirty-eight *kalās* joined with the *hṛdaya*, the *āveśa*, and so forth?
Likewise, the sixfold division beginning with *kalā* exists in the resonance (*dhvāna*) at Śukreśvara, as follows.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of Śānti, Atītā, and the others on the head and other parts, as well as the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and so forth on the hair and other parts, and having likewise performed the *saṃhitā* [mantra] as before, one should do the same for the jar and other implements during the supreme initiation (*paradīkṣā*).
72a) Then, having washed the hands with fragrant substances, one should form the *maṇḍala* with the left thumb and middle finger;
having worshipped Śiva along with his seat and limbs upon the hand, one should worship Īśāna and the others [starting] from the thumb down to the little finger.
Having projected [the mantras] starting with the heart, having worshipped them, and having performed the *saṃyūhana* (merging), one should again assign the possessor of limbs (*aṅgin*) and Śiva.
One should touch all the materials, such as flowers and so forth, with the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*), intensely,
for the sake of the perfection of the *yātrī* mantra and for the sake of fitness for liberation.
Alternatively, as before, one should consecrate the scattered offerings (vikirāḥ) and so forth with the mantra ending in *sadbhyaḥ*.

Then, as before, for the sake of purifying the path (*adhvan*) from Kālāgni situated below up to Hūhuka and ending with Śiva, one should sprinkle the pavilion with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the weapon-mantra (*astra*), perfumes, and special *arghya* water.

Having scattered the *vikira* offerings from the *vighurecaka* vessel, and having worshipped with the Heart-mantra the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances placed within the images, as well as the Earth and the *Vāstu* deity facing the Brahmins in the jars, and Lakṣmī— who showers dark flowers and syllables— one should worship them.

Having drawn [the deity] with the weapon-mantra using scattered offerings such as chowries and garments, and having established [him] for the sake of the weapon-mantra, one should [perform the rite] as before, either in the *prāṇa* or on the seat (*viṣṭara*).
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the bull-throne. With this, [one should worship] the seat, the white thread around the neck,

the perfumed chamber, the forest herbs and so forth, the cloth and the scriptures, the Gaṅgā and other [waters], O Ratnagarbha, the offerings and unbroken rice, the full golden vessel and so forth, and the mango sprouts and others, with the Astra-mantra.
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the *varmāstra* mantra and covered it, one should place the *śivakumbha* obtained previously from the root-mantra (*mūla*).

Having established the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) as being situated within the limbs of the supreme Śiva, one should, to its right, in the space between the fists, as before, [place] the *prāṇava* or [recite]:
"Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the Lion Throne (*siṃhāsana*). Thus, or otherwise, on the seat that has been consecrated, [one should perform the ritual].

Having purified [the site] with *mastrā* (astra-mantra) and worshipped it along with its limbs, one should worship the guardians of the directions as well. *Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ kṣauṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ sarvakṣetrādhipataye śrīkaṇṭhāya namaḥ.* Between Vāyu and Varuṇa, [there is] white or red [in color], holding a trident and a *ḍamaru* in the right hand.

One should worship Kṣetrapāla, who holds a skull-cup filled with the nectar of the head of Vāmeśvara, who has three eyes, matted hair, and a terrifying form; afterwards, one should mentally place two skull-cups joined to the sides of the pitcher as before, or otherwise, having placed a skull-cup in the hand of another [deity], one should install the sequence beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti in the place of the pitcher.

Having placed the water-pot (kumbha) upon the image of Śanaiścara and having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs, as well as the limbs [of the deity] in the directions starting from the southeast (agnyādi),
one should perform the eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the heart according to the requirements of the rite;
then, one should simply carry out the worship of the head and the other [limbs].

Then, having offered the pure food offering (*naivedya*) and the recitation (*japa*), and having joined the channels (*nāḍī*) within the vessel, one should project the form (*mūrti*) onto the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). As before, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), offer the food offering, and perform the recitation for one’s own mantra and the limbs with the *vaśāṅga* [mantra], just as in the case of the jar (*kumbha*). Then: *oṃ hauṃ*.
Saying "Obeisance to Śiva and Śakti" or "Obeisance to Śakti and Śiva," according to one's desire for worldly enjoyment or liberation,

he should touch [the disciple] as before, bestow the weapon of knowledge (*jñānāstra*), and [protect him] with the various hosts of weapons and missiles— such as the *vardhanī* vessel, the heated trident, the sword-blade, and so forth— which are blazing and have dispelled all internal obstacles until the completion of the sacrificial hall.
One should meditate [on the weapon-mantra].
At the end of the whirling of Śiva’s weapon, there is the worship of Indra and the other [guardians];
in some cases, for the sake of protection, there is the whirling around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should recognize the auspicious signs at the placement of the *śivakumbha*:
when flowers fall from the sky and deities stationed in celestial chariots appear.
A gentle aspect is seen in the bow [of Jupiter] in the sky for Indra and Rudra; there is joy from the pleasant sounds of peacocks,
cuckoos, and other birds, as well as from unctuous food and excellent sweets.
There was a great rain of rays and the attainment of fruit upon the body;
there was the sound of conchs, kettledrums, clouds, bark garments, and fruits.
O preceptor, foremost of Brahmins and kings: women, umbrellas, banners, weapons, milk and the like, unbroken rice, garlands, honey, meat, and sandalwood;
Having placed good earth upon the bull for lotus flowers and upon the cow, there is the sound of the trumpeting of a lordly elephant; and from those [flowers], there is the sight of jewels and lamps.
When there is the protection of palaces, essential trees, and virtuous people, then all things will become auspicious; just as when spring arrives, all things become auspicious.
Meteors, earthquakes, thunderclaps, comets, and showers of embers and bones;
great winds, darkness, smoke, rainbows, and blood;
There was a falling of dust and rains, and it was drenched with streams of blood;
there were the cries of donkeys, camels, buffaloes, serpents, ghosts, and naked ascetics.

Heedlessness is a terrible thing; a harsh word is like a stone striking the head. A quarrel between two horses is better than one between two men. Speech that is well-spoken leads to the highest good; one should always avoid speech that is fallen from virtue.
Indeed, in this case, whether the rite is auspicious or even inauspicious, the yoga of ghee must be performed;
for the sake of pacification, one hundred oblations should be offered with the Aghora mantra ending in the syllable *phaṭ*.

74a) Then, having performed the sacrifice for the Lord of the Gaṇas, one should worship Dharma and the other [deities] on the four corners of the altar, and Śiva— after purifying His residence in the *liṅga* or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)— in the manner of the daily rite (*nityavat*) using the mantra beginning with *āramata*, as stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*.
Beginning with the eastern face and proceeding to the southern, northern, and western ones,
as well as the center, the knower of mantras should thereafter present the *argha* offering.
Therefore, with the intention of the disciple, one should perform the unification within the mouth [of the teacher],
as was stated by the venerable Guru-pāda after rejecting the conjunction of the impure Īśvara and the pure Śiva.
Wherever and in whatever rite the application of whichever [limb] is prescribed, that has been stated by you, O Illustrious One:
for one desiring liberation, the head and the face hold primacy in initiation.
Know that the foot-unguents, the *janādi* [mantras], and those of various kinds,
all ending with Sadāśiva, should always be performed by those facing the eastern direction as before.
However, for killing, subjugation, and so forth, as well as for causing enmity and immobilization,
the fire offering performed at the southern face shall bring about success.
For rites of pacification and enrichment, as well as for [attaining] good fortune, attraction, and so forth,
one should always perform the fire offering in the north for the sake of achieving the ascent of fortune.
"In the west, the application of the daily rites is proclaimed.
(74b) Now, for the sake of a single disciple, [one should offer] five streams of rice and so forth; for each disciple, [the offerings] increase by one.
Having turned back the fire from the Śiva-pitcher, the weapon-fire, the *itthā* [fire], and so forth, and having offered honey and ghee together with clarified butter,
one should establish the marked [consecrated] items for the disciples and for oneself.
Then, as before, one should satisfy Śiva along with his limbs (attendant deities) in the fire.
Dust, clarified butter, a wooden ladle, chalk, and sesame seeds.
One should thoroughly purify his wife and others with the *mūla-mantra* and other mantras using the *sampāta* method;
however, if the *vāstu-yoga* has not been performed, one should [purify] the deities residing in the *vāstu* who have entered the body.
One should properly satisfy each [deity] in sequence with the five initial oblations during the demarcation of the site,
for the pacification of obstacles, and for the preliminary consecration.
In the purification of time, one must consider the causes such as deficiency or excess,
as well as the renown of the location and so forth, in relation to the requirements of place, time, and other factors.
At the time of the disciple’s entry, one should likewise employ either the root-mantra, the Aghora-mantra, or the Astra-mantra;
one should cause these mantras to blaze forth, reciting them a hundred times or more, according to the procedure.

Oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā. Having thus satisfied [the deities] beginning with the Heart-mantra up to the Full Oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should say: Oṃ hūṃ hrauṃ śivāya hūṃ phaṭ. Thus, having kindled the All-Self (sarvātman) and the others, and being filled with the final oblation, one should [offer] into the fire previously prepared in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), either in the east or the west.

75a) Having placed [the vessel] either to the left or between the *śiva-kumbha* and the *antarvalin*, one should offer oblations to each [deity] in the fire and present the *tarpaṇa* and *pūrṇāhuti*. Alternatively, having performed the satisfaction (*tṛpti*), the illumination (*dīpti*), the purification of the *rajas* and the site (*deśa-ādi-śuddhi*) on the left;

Having worshipped with the eightfold offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā) the Lord who is to be offered, the one situated in the fire, the one in the pitcher, the one in the stone, and the Lord of the ground, he should then make this request: "O Mahādeva, for what purpose has this yoga been brought forth?"
"Thus my animals stand here, peaceful and purified;
and in this matter, I have been commanded by you, who are the embodiment of the Guru."
Therefore, having now taken leave of me,
may the Blessed One himself, the Lord who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, grant them his grace.
Having conceived of himself as the Tortoise, as proclaimed by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin),
he should worship his own self as Śiva with flowers, perfumes, ornaments, and other offerings.
Placing his hand upon her head and abandoning all sense of dependence on another,
he should contemplate his own consort as non-dual with the Lord of Ambā (Sāmbhu) in the five locations.
I am the witness in the maṇḍala; I am the protector of the sacrifice residing in the water-pot (kumbha);
I am the consumer of the oblation in the fire; and I am the mover of the bonds within the bound soul (paśu).
I am the one who has been graced and differentiated through division;
I am that locus of conjunction, the supreme Śiva endowed with the six qualities.
Thus, with diligent effort, the Guru shall become most steadfast.
Having performed the sacrifice of renunciation (nisṛti-yāga) facing the entrance of the mandala on the left side,
and having offered unbroken rice grains (akṣata) along with darbha grass tips while reciting the Astra-mantra, he should draw back [the obstacles].
I am worshipped with the five-limbed prostration on a firm seat whose front is directed eastward;
[the worshipper] should approach wearing white garments, having bathed cleanly, and being fasting.
For the sake of enjoyment, one should place the disciple facing east, and for the sake of liberation, facing north;
having placed him with his head directed toward the summit of the meditative absorption (samādhi), while one remains oneself in the opposite position.
From the crest-lock down to the feet, this is for enjoyment; by the reverse, it is for liberation. This Self is called Śiva, whose bonds have been loosened;
by His own power alone, even this multitude of fetters is under His control.
Then the Lord appeared before him, possessing a copper-colored form, endowed with the manifestation of his own qualities, resembling a touchstone for jewels, and radiant with auspiciousness.
Having purified him through contact and washed away his impurities for a long time,
I shall make that one, who is free from qualities, the ornament upon the head of the hundred [sages].
Having intended this meaning, one should sprinkle the child with water from the *astra-mantra*;
by means of the *hṛdaya* and *astra* mantras, and with ashes, [one protects] above and below for three days for the sake of liberation and enjoyment.

Then, having recited the *Vikirā* mantra, one should scatter the offerings with water from the *Bhukya* vessel using the threefold weapon that brings about auspiciousness, so that the body of the disciple may become food for Śiva.

Then, with his skin, he should strike those who possess garlands of flames, who belong to the fierce Kula, and whose bodies are like the sky; thereafter, one should apply water to his limbs while reciting the mantras.
Sprinkled with that [water], those nooses become peaceful and fit for the goal;
with the tips and roots of the *kuśa* grass, the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra are recited three times, facing downward and upward, for the sake of liberation.

Having visualized the collection of nooses, one should then extract the face [of the mantra] from its own causal source by scraping it three times through those gates, and then remove it from the middle.
The individual soul (jīva), situated in the center of the four mandalas and struck by the weapon-mantra (astra),
becomes like the antarātmaka and abides within the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha).

Having separated [the deity] and taken it, one should bring it to abide within oneself; this is the procedure for the disciple. Having caused it to ascend into the heart, it should then ascend to the form, or else not go to the left.
Having worshipped Śiva, together with his limbs and attendants, upon a seat of darbha grass using white sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should apply [the mark] on the forehead.

Having placed a flower in his joined palms at the heart, one should offer it according to the ritual; in initiations such as the common ones, the hand-gesture (*hastaka*) is performed with the fingers of the fist.
Outside, near Śiva or even near the fire, one should offer [the oblation] once;
then, with that same hand, one should touch the heart and the back.
To bind him with a noose, one who knows the two-fold meaning should place it below the mouth;
then, there, one should take a fresh white cloth or one that is new and ten spans long.
The cloth is purified by inspection and other rites; flowers, perfumes, and so forth are consecrated with worship;
the hide is obtained through the root mantra and protected by the secret mantra.
Having firmly grasped his eyes with this [mantra] or with that [mantra] as before, or likewise his hands,
one should slowly lead this man behind the curtain.
One should place the five limbs in a clockwise direction on the seat, facing the six directions:
one's own duty, knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty.
Then, having placed that consciousness within his own heart-lotus by means of the form of withdrawal (saṃhāramūrti),
and having subsequently established himself as the fivefold self residing in the upper part [of the body], like the fire within the jar.
One should then perform the union of the channels with the root mantra and purify that body;
by means of the five door-breaths, one should fashion it into the body of Śiva.
The eye is the milk; otherwise, it is the vision of the "I.
From that vision arises the latent impression (vāsanā), which again becomes the seed of bondage.
Therefore, there is no obstruction of that eye-band by impurity.
Then, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord in his heart, navel, and *bindu*;
for the sake of the desired [attainment], one should place the child in the heart, the *bindu* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and [the other] below.
Pervading both outside and inside with its splendor, it is the Hand of Śiva;
it pierces the knots of the heart and other centers, being made manifest through the upward resonance of the root-syllable.
One should offer that [disciple] the attainment of Śiva’s power as the cause;
his impurities destroyed by the radiant energy that has entered the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
I shall go to the world of Śrīkaṇṭha, traversing the continuous path of coming and going;
then, O Śivā, [I shall reach] the infant [state] which obscures the light of the vision of the Sāra.
One should cast the flower with the root mantra and perform a prostration before the water-pot (ghaṭa).
One should lead [the deity] into oneself and perform circumambulation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) three times in a clockwise direction.
Having placed the vessel containing his own reflection on the right as before, and having placed a woman on the left,
he should place eight blades of kusa grass with their tips pointing upward in her hand.
One should gradually recite the tip of a *darbha* grass blade from its root to the end of the child's shanks;
[one should contemplate] the infant’s body as having emerged and dissolved into the three channels (*nāḍikā*).
Having performed the union as before and having worshipped, one should satisfy the three [deities];
indeed, having offered the root mantra eight hundred times for the sake of removing instability.
The head-mantras were brought together, and that which was performed by the mind was completed.
Having endured [the disciple's prostration] at his feet, he should cause the disciple—who has gone beyond Pūrṇa—to bow with his head;
thereafter, he should perform the worship of the fire, the crest-lock, and subsequently the twilight rites, the Sādhya-mantras, and so forth.
For one who observes the common pledges (*sāmānyasamayin*) should perform service and worship in this manner;
