otherwise, he shall not possess the authority for entry into all sacrifices and other rites.
The universal ascetic.
"After the ritual of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta-vidhi), there shall be the vow (vrata) beginning with the breaking of the fast (bhakṣaṇādika).
When this was said, the procedure for the subsequent observance (samayordhva-vidhi) follows in due order, as follows:

When the *sampāta* and other rites have been performed as before, Vāgīśa and Kāma become intensely enamored; they are then led by the root and subordinate mantras into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), assuming forms according to the six flavors and the ten regions.

For the sake of satisfaction through the presence of the archer (Śiva), one who has discerned the essence of the lineage should offer oblations upon the couch of the principles ending with Māyā, which has the impure self as its pillow.
In the lamp of knowledge, upon a bed of crookedness, having come together in union,
we two, red with passion, contemplated and entered the body of Bhava.
Then, having touched the disciple in the heart, he should sprinkle him with water from the weapon-mantra, using flowers over which the weapon-mantra has been recited seven times:
*oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ*. (78a)

Having struck and pierced [the heart] with the heart-mantra, one enters that heart through the left [nostril] by means of exhalation (*recaka*) with "Oṃ Hūṃ. Having separated [the deity] from the abode of Rudra with the thumb [finger] using "Oṃ Hāṃ Haḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ," one draws [the deity] forth with the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*) while reciting "Oṃ Hāṃ Svāhā," until the power (*śakti*) comes to rest within the abode of Rudra. Then: "Oṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ Oṃ."

I take hold of the self: *haḥ hūṃ phaṭ*. Having taken [the breath] with the left [nostril] by means of the *pūraka* (inhalation) and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], and having made it one with one's own self through *kumbhaka* (retention), one should then grasp that which stands at the tip of the root-mantra—resembling a blazing fire—with the *pūraka* in the *saṃhāriṇī*, piercing the knots from the heart upward and abiding in the *śakti*.

Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self (ātmane namaḥ). As before, with the *udghāta* and *rekhaka* breaths, while meditating on that seed-syllable (*deśabīja*) with the left [nostril], one should join it for the purpose of meditating on the womb within the womb of Vāgīśī; having worshipped it during the yoga and the satisfaction, and having offered oblations with the root-mantra (*mūla*) and the *svānūna*, this twice-born one, possessing the purity of the seed and the place, is fit for the food of contemplation (*bhāvāhāra*).

"O portion of Rudra, by your grace, may there be Sadāśiva"— having thus entreated him, one should offer two hundred and ten oblations with the root mantra and ten oblations each with the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*).
Now, one should purify him through the fire-offering (*homa*) beginning with the consumption of his foot-dust.
As they have said:
Having discerned the multitude of the disciple's sins through various signs such as the presence of excrement and so forth,
he should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) for the pacification of those evils.
Having thus performed the self-abasement (*ātmān-namaskarṣa*) regarding one's birth as before,

and having established the state of Śiva through the root mantra for both oneself and the disciple’s body, and having effected their essential identity (*sāmarasya*), one should place [the mantra] upon his head, dismiss Vāgīśvarī, and perform the non-dual full oblation (*pūrṇādvaya*).
One should give a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of the bark of the *svajātīśāla* tree. Even a *śūdra* householder may employ that [thread] for rites such as ritual bathing; as it has been said:
O child, one who has received the specific initiation or is endowed with another initiation—
even a Śūdra— should wear the sacred thread during worship for the sake of spiritual prosperity.
Then, having caused him to offer oblations with the root mantra as prescribed in the *Kulārṇava*,
and having performed the prostration with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-nati*), he should, out of devotion, address him consolingly:
"Now you have become fit for hearing the scriptures, for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and for study."
Then, for him, he taught the eight rules of conduct, each beginning with "first," as follows:
One should not revile Śiva, the scripture, the Śiva-fire, the practitioner, or the Guru; nor should one ever, under any circumstances, even step upon their shadow.
One should avoid eating the remains of offerings (nirmālya), giving [such things] as gifts, and fasting; however,
the worship of Śiva, the sacred fire, and the Guru must be performed for as long as one lives.
If one is unable to abandon all these objects of attachment, one should indeed restrain them through the intellect.
In the fire, one should worship Nandin and the others, as well as the ten splendors who are the lords of the directions from the end;
having crossed over [the obstacles] and invoked them, one should offer two hundred oblations with the root mantra for the sake of the disciple.
Having given the full offerings and dismissed these [disciples], who are bound by the fetters of conventional conduct, one should [dismiss] the castes according to their established order,
or even the stages of life (āśramas) as appropriate.
One should always establish [the fires] in the northeast, following the sequence of worship and prostration to the Guru.
In this interval, to one whose soul is dispassionate and who has been tested for a very long time,
and who desires to become a shaven-headed renunciant (muṇḍa-pravrajita), one should grant the vow according to the prescribed rite.
One who possesses a staff, a loincloth, ashes, a sacred thread, a topknot, and a rosary,
and who carries a begging bowl and other such limbs and appendages, is merely one who knows the meaning of words.
Having shown the *liṅga* and informed [the disciple] for a moment about its protection beneath the water-pot, the preceptor,
having received permission from Śiva, should give it to the practitioner who has performed his duties.
Having said, "Great grace! with eyes filled with tears of great joy, he should receive these [offerings] after having propitiated them; then he should assign their names.
The disciple [is designated] according to the falling of the flower or by his own choice, and not otherwise.
The name "Śiva" belongs to the twice-born (the Brahmin), while that called "Kavaca" belongs to the king (the Kṣatriya).
For Vaiśyas, [the rites] are known to be divine; for Śūdras, they are prescribed as being [performed with] white [implements].
Indeed, those who are intoxicated by delusion should be treated like Vaiśyas;
however, those born of noble lineage who always abide in righteousness are not to be considered as such.
Since even Śūdras achieve success, why should there be any hesitation in this matter? A Śūdra does not become a Jaṭila, nor one who lacks knowledge, nor one who is prone to negligence.
Neither a woman, nor one who is very young, nor one who is old, nor one who is diseased, nor one who is deformed [should perform it];
moreover, there shall be a single lock of matted hair on the head for a Śūdra—such is the determination regarding castes.

Having divided the number of syllables, letters, purifying limbs, and the counts of *kalās* and *tattvas*, one should distribute them by means of the *vibhajyaka* [method] and join each with the auspicious *saṃhitās*.
One should bind [the cord] in front of Vrateśvara with the splendor of Śiva, having correctly understood the lineage of the gurus; otherwise, one will become subject to obstruction.

The two observers of the vow were worthy of being honored with garlands and ointments; white with ashes, their feet touched the ground adorned with sectarian marks, forehead streaks, and cloth banners.
Whether they be Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, or those with forehead marks made of cloth-paste, they are liberated;
this is the fourth stage of life according to the determination of the stages of life (āśrama-nirṇaya).
One who bathes at the three periods of the day, subsists on alms, wears a girdle, an antelope skin, and carries a staff;
who worships Śiva and the sacred fire, practices meditation, observes celibacy, and wears a topknot— such a person is known as a *brahmacārī*.
A householder, avoiding sexual intercourse with others' wives and devoted solely to his own wife, is indeed [virtuous].

A forest-dweller with matted hair who worships the gods, the sacred fire, guests, and mendicants, is devoted to his own duties; he is a performer of the *hotṛ* sacrifice and, possessing good fortune, subsists on fruits and other such forest produce.
Bathed three times a day, wearing bark garments, free from worldly attachments through his own duties,
he should be known as one who has taken up the office [of the stage of life] and is a guardian of the fourth āśrama.

Endowed with matted hair, a loincloth, ashes, and so forth, self-controlled, and acting according to his own nature, he may have matted locks, a shaven head, or a single topknot; subsisting on alms, he remains free from possessions.
Compassionate toward those who have become silent, the ascetic should possess a tranquil mind;
having entrusted his own duties to the disciple, he remains free from attachment when there is nothing more to be done for the heart.
One who has renounced [worldly life] would be ineligible [for such rites], and his food would not be fit to be eaten;
however, those residing in the Śiva-āśrama, being established in that state, are eligible for the bestowing of blessings.
Except for those who, out of love, have been composed by me for my devotees,
[this work] is intended for those established in the worldly, the Vedic, the spiritual, and indeed the super-marginal paths, O Śiva.

Even those three who are preeminent in knowledge do not attain liberation while wandering through future births; rather, one attains the cessation of rebirth by remembering one's former state as an ascetic.
He who asks about one's former country, caste, name, and so forth, or he who tells them, [is not purified] by such acts as touching water, ritual contact, or ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*).
Then one should perform the Brāhmī rite; thereafter, the Śaivī, the Gṛhasthā, and likewise the Hotikā.
The lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), however, should perform only the Śaiva twilight worship and no other;
the same applies to the detached householder and even to one who observes the materialistic vows.
The Śaiva twilight rite is said to occur at the arising of Śiva, and not the Brāhma one;
it pertains to the Preceptor, the Mantravṛtti, the Putraka, and the Samayin.
These four are the Śaivas: the Vratins, those who are still under vows, the Sādhaka, the Lokadharmī, the Putraka, the Snātaka, and the Gṛhī.
Those who have previously taken the vow (samayin) and those who remain steadfast, though they may be Śaivas devoid of excellence,
are declared by the twice-born and others to be worthy of honor through initiation when [the teacher] acts out of delusion.
One who has violated the samaya.
Now, in all cases of initiation, according to the *Tṛptidīpana*,
once the striking of the bonds (*pāśatāḍana*), their binding (*bandha*), and so forth have been performed, [the disciple] is brought into the presence of Śiva.
Having gone there and worshipped him along with his disciples, he should then address him thus: "O Blessed One, this [place] has been examined by me while remaining under your command."
Of noble birth and long established in the Rudra-śiṣya tradition,
he was afflicted, longing for nirvāṇa, and like a child tormented by his own suffering.
Therefore, for the sake of this liberation, remain with me;
the Lord has attained his desired resolve and is empowered by the majesty of Śiva.

Having worshipped the disciple as before—standing in his own right-hand position at the center of the universe, facing east and so forth, with palms joined at the heart and seeking refuge in the Teacher— (Note: *sāthanyāśam* is interpreted here as *śāstary-āśam*, "seeking refuge in the Teacher," based on the context of ritual initiation.)
Having brought about the end of the channels and performed the oblation for that purpose,
one should then wear the consecrated thread upon the Susumṇā.
The weapon (śastra) should be placed near oneself, consecrated by sprinkling (prokṣita), and worshipped with the root mantra;
then, while engaged in the movement of power (śakticāra), one should perform [the rite] at the tip of its blade with the root mantra.
For the sake of the two-fold prosperity (bhūti), one should lead [the breath] from the big toe of the left foot up to the crown of the head;
for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), it should be led from the big toe of the foot to the crest-lock (śikhā) and so forth, starting from the forehead.
The teacher, being cautious, should place [the disciple] on his left side and restrain him with the root mantra:

*oṃ hauṃ iḍāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hauṃ piṅgalāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hauṃ suṣumnāyai namaḥ*. Then, either from the heart center or by means of exhaled breath, he should draw [the vital energy] from the body of the disciple through inhalation (*pūraka*), [visualizing it] as resembling the fibers of a lotus stalk.
Having placed [the mantra] upon the *saṃsāriṇī* thread (81b), having worshipped it, and having restrained it, one should perform the *snāna* (bath) and other rites.

In that thread which represents the future continuum of all bodies, one should worship the triad of mandalas beginning with the Sun at the heart with the mantra: "Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śakti. Having worshipped [the thread] with the Niṣṭhura and Āruṣa fire as before, in some places the worship of the Cause (kāraṇa) is also mentioned. And as before, by means of the Tātana and other [mantras], the consciousness of the disciple [is projected].
One should join the vowels beginning with *vā* to the consonants beginning with *mṛ*, as stated in the Sūtra: And it has been said:
There are three powers (śaktis) of Śambhu: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā;
they are unimpeded in their energy in all matters—whether in binding, releasing, or uplifting.

Having worshipped the self as all-pervasive, having contemplated it, and having veiled it with the armor-mantra (*varman*), one should perform the purification through the presence of Nala and so forth. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the cause of the experience of the impure bonds.* It is like the darkness of night.
*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the karmic bonds which are the causes for the experience of pleasure and pain.* [Visualize them] in white and black forms.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Māyāpāśa, the cause of the body and its objects; [the color] is variegated (karvura).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva-śakti, the presiding deity of the noose (pāśa). Having meditated upon her form, having taken [the thread] from the disciple, having fixed it upon the cord, having worshipped it, and having offered it into the fire, one should perform the grinding and so forth. It is as follows:
Their power belongs to Maheśvara. The auspicious ones (*śivāḥ*) are those who uplift all.

Because they follow after *dharma*, O God, they are metaphorically designated as "bonds" (*pāśa*). Then, having placed the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) upon the pervasive thread: *Oṃ hau*, [salutation] to the crooked power (*kuṭilā śakti*) that causes concealment (*tirobhāvikā*).

Homage! Having worshipped Bhāvikā in the fire, [one performs] the *arcāri*: Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, homage to the bond of the *kalā* Śāntyatītā. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hauṃ hāṃ, homage to the two principles (*tattva*) of Śakti and Sadāśiva. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, homage to the twenty worlds situated within the powers beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Nivṛtti.

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hauṃ hauṃ! Salutation to the state of *yauṃ*, which is endowed with the *turyātīta* (beyond the fourth) that transcends all [levels] of *nāda*. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ! Salutation to the letters beginning with *aṃ* and ending with *kṣaḥ*, from *a* to *kṣa*. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hāṃ haḥ hāṃ! Salutation to the mantras of Śiva and Śakti. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ...
Hāṃ! Salutation to Śaktiviśālā. Oṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ! Salutation to the two channels, Kuhū and Saṅkhinī. Oṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ! Salutation to the two winds, Devadatta and Dhanañjaya.

Oṃ hā& hau& hā& salutation to the two sense organs of hearing and speech. Oṃ hā& hau& hā& salutation to the object of sound. Oṃ [hā& hau& hā&] salutation to the quality of resonance. Oṃ hā& hau& hā& salutation to the sphere of space (vyomamaṇḍala), whose essence is the vacuity of the crystal-like light.

Salutation to the Bindu, Nāda, and Śakti, which is perfectly circular and measures ten million *yojanas*. OṂ HĀṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ, salutation to the cause of Sadāśiva. One should consecrate each of their respective forms—white, topped with a crescent moon, and consisting of the nature of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kuṭila* (the curved letter)—according to the ritual procedure, from the crest (*cūḍā*) to the end of the face. And it has been said:
One should always place the mantras beginning with Śiva upon the head;
likewise, one should apply the half-moon (ardhacandra), the bindu, the nāda, and the śakti for the sake of illumination.
The half-moon is like the appearance of a crescent moon; the point (bindu) is circular like the solar disc;
within the two points is the staff-like (daṇḍa) appearance, which is the power of sound (nādaśakti), residing in the three faces.

O Dear One, through union with the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth, conjoined with the syllable, the half-moon, the person (puruṣa), and the point (bindu); Sadāśiva is to be expressed in the resonance (nāda).
Because the pure power (vimalā-śakti) dissolves into the entirely pure Śuddhādhvan,
the subtle Śiva is proclaimed as the Savior (tāraka) of all.

In this interval, some, having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each subsidiary part (kalā) and the root-mantra according to the prescribed rite into the fire, should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Oṃ hā& hya& hā&! Salutation to the noose of the Śāntikalā. Oṃ hā& hyai& hā&! Salutation to Īśvara and the Vidya-tattva. Oṃ hā& hai& hā&! Salutation to the thirty-one worlds beginning with Icchā and ending with Vāmā, presided over by Śakti. Oṃ hā& hyai& hā&!

Salutations to the twelve words beginning with "bindurūpātīta kuryānvitebhyo vyādhina" and ending with "ityadhyānāhārāya. Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ kṣaṃ haṃ, salutations to the two syllables. Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ heṃ hāṃ, salutations to the two mantras of Tatpuruṣa and Kavaca. Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to the object of touch. Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two qualities of sound and touch. Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ, salutation to the wind-maṇḍala, which is black, powerful, the destroyer of the six, possessing six corners, and extending for a hundred thousand million *yojanas*. Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ, salutation to that which has Īśvara as its cause.
Homage! To Syāmālā, from the heart center to the end [of the body], beginning with bliss.
Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the Vidyā-kalā. Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, [obeisance] to Māyā and the others (63b).
Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the twenty-seven worlds beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra and ending with Vāmā.
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the twenty-one words beginning with "oṃ matyādi" and ending with "divyomin," which are accompanied by the state of deep sleep (*susupta*) in the form of the letter *ma*.
Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the syllables *sa*, *ṣa*, *śa*, *va*, *la*, and *ra*. Oṃ hāṃ.

Hruṃ Huṃ Hūṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the two mantras of Aghora-śikhā. Oṃ Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the seed-syllable Ra. Oṃ Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the two channels Pūṣan and Hastijihvā. Oṃ Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Vyāna and the wind-nāga. Oṃ Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ...
Salutation to the two organs of sight and smell. Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the object of form.

Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the qualities of sound, touch, and form. Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the red fire-maṇḍala, whose nature is burning, which is called Svastika, which has three corners, and which measures ten million yojanas.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, homage to Rudrakāraṇa. In the Lord, from the heart to the navel, [is] oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ, homage to the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā. Oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ, homage to the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Water.

Oṃ hāṃ hvāṃ hāṃ, homage to the fifty-six worlds beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Lakulīśa. Oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ, [homage] to all those beginning with Vyādhinī, who are endowed with the state of sleep within the syllable *u*.
Salutation to all the thirty-two syllables ending with *khaṃ*. Salutation to the twenty-four syllables beginning with *oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ yaṃ* and ending with *khaṃ*.
Salutation to the two mantras of Vāmadeva and Śiras: *oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hiṃ hāṃ*. Salutation to the seed-syllable *va*: *oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ va*. *Oṃ*.

Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Gāndhārī and the *sumnanāḍī* channels. Oṃ Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Samāna and the Udāna vital airs. Oṃ Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the tongue and the sense organ of taste. Oṃ Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the object of taste. Oṃ Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ...

Salutation to those possessing the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste. Oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the aqueous mandala, which is white, liquid in nature, marked by the lotus, moist like the moon, and extending for thousands of crores [of yojanas]. Oṃ hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the cause.
The *śūtras* [are recited] from the navel until the end of the twice-born.
Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, homage to the noose of the *nivṛtti* stage. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, homage to the earth principle (*pṛthvī-tattva*).

Oṃ, salutation to the one hundred and ten worlds beginning with Alpādi and ending with Kālāgni. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the twenty-eight stations beginning with Bhava and Bhavādi, which arise from the syllable 'a' and end with the syllable 'au'. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ kaṃ.

Salutation to Varṇa. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two heart-mantras of Sadyojāta. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ la, salutation to the seed-syllable. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two channels, Iḍā and Piṅgalā. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two vital winds, Prāṇa and Apāna.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, homage to the sense organs of smell and generation. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, homage to the object of smell. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, homage to the five qualities beginning with sound and ending with smell. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, homage to the yellow earth mandala.

Homage to the firm, diamond-marked, square and elongated [earth], extending for ten million yojanas. Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, homage to the cause of Brahmā. [The earth] has a golden luster from the knees down to the tips of the big toes.

85a) Thus, in all cases, having firmly established the disciple from the very beginning through the cultivation of the sixfold mantra and mudrā according to their respective divisions, and having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings, one should restrain them even in the fire, each being present individually.

And one should offer oblations during the libation (*tarpaṇa*). In some places, the sacrifice is desired through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities Water, Air, Fire, Varuṇa, and Indra. Others, however, consider the offerings to be distinct for the *mātrās* beginning with *Ādi*, for the yogas beginning with *Sarvātīta*, and for the states (*avasthās*) beginning with *Turyātīta*. In some instances, however, [the offering is made] to the principles (*kalā*), categories (*tattva*), levels (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, and worlds (*bhuvana*).
It has been explained both in sequential order and otherwise.

Having made manifest with the mind— by means of the non-differentiation from the thread of the child’s body— the entire fivefold collection of time-paths (*adhvan*) pervaded by *kalā* and accompanied by impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and the illusion of *māyā*, one should contemplate and place [the mantra] upon the thread in the fire: "Oṃ hauṃ,
salutation to the Supreme Lord’s power who presides over the bond of *kalā*."
One should satisfy [the deities] with: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the noose of the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta-kalā-pāśa).

Having thus satisfied [them], one should likewise satisfy the [deities] beginning with Peace (śānti) and so forth. Then, with: "Oṃ hūṃ hauṃ, hūṃ phaṭ to the noose of the kalā beyond peace," one should inflame them, and the [remaining] rites for Peace and so forth are as before.

One should anoint the crown of the head, the mouth, the heart, the navel, and the knees. That thread, for the sake of pervasive awakening, extends to the top of the skull. Having offered into the fire, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and sever [the connection], beginning with the *ākaṇa* and so forth.

Then, having visualized the entire path (adhvan) from Earth up to Śakti within the Child (Śiśu), as pervaded by Kalā as before, [one should recite]: Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ! To the one who possesses the principles (tattva), the worlds (bhuvana), the words (pada), the phonemes (varṇa), the mantras, impurity (mala), karma, Māyā, and the principles belonging to Māyā; to the one whose form consists of the three powers (astrī-rūpa); [Salutation to] Nivṛtti.

Homage to Kalāpāśa. Having observed [the disciple's] body as being pervaded by oneself, one should offer libations. In this manner, with the heart-mantras enclosed by their respective seed-syllables, one should likewise project the levels of *pratiṣṭhā* and the others as before. OṂ HĀṂ HLĀṂ HVĪṂ!

Homage to the two *kalās*, Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā, at the end of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth. [This is performed] through the pronunciation of the short and long vowels.

One should likewise perform the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) for those [deities] by means of the *vidyā* and *śāntātīta* mantras during the twilight [rituals], beginning with the fire-worship (*agnipūjā*). Having recited from "Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ" up to "to the one whose form is the *tattva*s," one should utter:
"Haḥ hūṃ phaṭ to the bond (*pāśa*) of the *nivṛtti-kalā*."

86a) Having thus distinguished the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, one should offer [the oblation] into the fire. Here, for the purpose of laying out the threads (*sūtravinyāsa*), one should further perform the *lokasāti*.
OṂ HĀṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ; obeisance to the noose of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta-kalā-pāśa*), ending with the form of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth.

Having meditated upon and visualized the nine principles beginning with *tattva* and ending with *māyeyā*, which pervade their respective stations, and having likewise contemplated the [five kalās] beginning with *śānti*; then, having uttered "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ," for the sake of severing the bonds of the *kalā* beyond *śānti*, one should say "haḥ hūṃ phaṭ. Then, with the *savyaprasāri-nārāca* mudrā, one should satisfy the [deities] beginning with *śānti* by offering oblations into the fire.

Oṃ hā& hau& hā&! Homage to the bond of the *kalā* Śāntyatīta, which designates the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth. One should enter [the fire] and worship even the [levels] beginning with Śānti within the fire. Oṃ hau& hā& hau&! At the end of the principles and so forth, I seize the bond of the *kalā* Śāntyatīta: haḥ hū& phaṭ. Or: homage. By means of the filling-in (*pūraka*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

The [mantras] beginning with Śāktī and ending with Dhruva, encapsulated by the root-heart (mūlahṛdaya), should not be recited from the beginning; rather, having grasped them starting from the principle (tattva) and so forth up to the end of the form (rūpa), one recites [the mantra] ending in "śāya namaḥ" as belonging to the Śāntyatīta [kalā].
In the arising of exhalation (*recaka*), there is neither pacification (*śānti*) nor other [rites];
*hāṃ hāuṃ hāṃ*, the form of reality (*tattva*) beginning with reality (*tattva*). *arpa*.

Homage to the noose of the Śāntyatīta-kalā. One should also satisfy Śānti and the others within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). OṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ HAUṂ! From the principle (tattva) and so forth, up to the form of the principles, I bind the noose of the Śāntyatīta-kalā here: HAḤ HŪṂ PHAṬ! With this knot, one should likewise bind and satisfy the eight [kalās] beginning with Śānti. OṂ HĀṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ...

At the beginning and end of those [mantras], one should offer obeisance with "Namaḥ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya. Having worshipped the Sūtras and the [deities] beginning with Śānti, one should satisfy them all in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with five initial oblations ending in "Svāhā. [The sequence of rites is:

sprinkling (tarpaṇa), illumination (dīpana), attachment (rakti), worship (pūjā), oblation (homa), inspection (vilokana), union (sandhi), piercing (bheda), gazing (īkṣaṇa), entry (niveśa), grasping (grahaṇa), and joining (yojana).

In the sixteen [sections] beginning with Kalā, ending with the propitiation of the Knot (bandha), one should worship on the thread or in the fire with the mantra: *Oṃ Hauṃ, salutation to the Supreme Lord’s Power who presides over the noose of Kalā*. Having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should place the portion [of the thread] upon the shoulder of the disciple. Otherwise, the knots would be forgotten. One should offer a hundred oblations of the root-mantra into the directions.
Then, having seated the disciple and placed the thread upon his head, he should perform the *saṃpātana* (sprinkling) with the *Saṃhitās*,
according to the teachings of the *Śrīrudra-śakti-āgama*.

Having contemplated that, according to the *Śrīdīkṣānirṇaya* and other texts, the thread should be placed within the hollow of the copper vessel belonging to the person; it is then enclosed by the *pranītā* vessel, brought forth from the heart, and placed within the heart-vessel. Having established it in the heart and performed the oblation (*iṣṭvā*), one pours [the liquid] over it according to the *Śrīnaya*. Then, taking that, the disciple [is adorned with] five colors.
One should move with the ritual thread (*sūtra*). Having shown [the site] by the Guru’s command, one should offer the *liṅga*.

Then, having worshipped the sacrificial pots (*kalaśas*) and so forth, and having covered the courtyard, one should prepare the entrance to the mandala with cow dung facing east. One should place the remaining [substances] to the south of the eastern, northern, and southern [sections].

Having drunk a handful of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) twice or thrice; then, in the second [rite], by means of the three-fold [mantra],

one should consume eight mouthfuls of unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and caru-oblation, the size of a peacock's egg, without touching them with the teeth and remaining silent, according to the white [textual] instruction, placed upon leaves of the *palāśa* and *aśvattha* trees, for the sake of liberation.

One should feed [the guests]. At the conclusion of the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), one should take a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and recite the root mantra twice over it. Having struck it with the "royal tooth" (the index finger), one should cast it forward. Wherever it falls at a distance from the ground, that is the sequence for the end-points of the directions.
Peace, heat, death, gain, the ninefold state, the guru, the lineage, prosperity, increase, enjoyment, liberation, the higher and the lower, victory over past difficulties, and constant [success]—
for the sake of wiping away the faults born from falsehood regarding the root-mantra recited face-down, one should offer a hundred oblations of ghee according to the scriptures.

A hundred-fold oblation with the root mantra is prescribed for the protection of the body and so forth; [oblations] numbering one hundred are performed with the mantras born of body, speech, and mind, namely Śiva, Aghora, and Ruru.

Having offered three oblations, one should satisfy the Root-mantra with a thousand or a hundred [recitations]. According to the opinion of Vāsuki, this should continue until ten parts of the mantra have been completed, or until the end of the full rite. Having presented the *caru* and other offerings to him, and having prostrated, one should cause him to lie down. "O Lord, this stream of water of Dharma from the sequence of sacrificial rites must be drunk by you for the sake of severing the bonds of those bound by fetters."
Otherwise, there is proximity [to the deity]. Having offered the arghya with the mantra of cessation (nirodha), one should cause the deity to enter the state of cessation.

One should perform the rite of the linga until its cessation on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila). Having dismissed the desired [deity] without transgression, one should place the fire into the jar for Śiva, and having established Śiva therein, one should purify the earth and worship the divine jar and the weapon (astra).
One should plant [the seed]. At the descent of sleep, one should release the Gaṇa into the jars at the summit of the sun, which is the guardian of the directions.

Having subsequently smeared, protected, and fumigated [the ground], and having made it provided with white flowers, fresh kuśa grass, and four steady, blazing lamps, one who has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) should then spread the earth silently. Upon its completion, one should spread a layer of ashes consecrated with the hundred-weapon mantra (*śatāstra*), and within that, one should place the child of another.

Separately, having performed the evening worship and meditation, with water reaching up to the navel, and having tied the topknot with the *śikhā* mantra, [one should recite] for the boy during sleep: "Oṃ, salutation to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul; salutation to the Left-handed One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Sleep."

O Lord of the gods of gods, tell this to the one who has sought refuge, as well as his extreme distress: "Whatever tasks are situated in the heart, place them all within [this] dream. *Oṃ hrīṃ hili 2 śūlapāṇaye svāhā*. Having recited this seven times over the water for sprinkling according to the rule, he should be covered with a garment obtained from the *kavaca* [mantra], protected by the *varma* and *astra* [mantras].
One should cause [the deity] to arise from the heart as before, reciting the mantra one hundred times, marked with yellow orpiment (rocanā).
Then, with ashes, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, white mustard seeds, and [other] substances, one should surround it on all four sides.

Having performed the austerity with the four staffs (*caturdaṇḍaka*), having meditated upon [the site] with yellow pigments (*rocanā*), having enveloped it with a hide, and having offered [oblations] to the lords of the directions while reciting the mantras, and having performed his daily rites, he should meditate on Śiva, whose body is the totality of all that exists.

Having cast the body [of the disciple] into the ritual fire with mantras, he should himself, remaining self-controlled, sequentially perform the offering of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth,
while recollecting the entire sequence of initiation as if he were the disciple.
Having seen a good dream concerning grace, the power of the Saṃhitā, Vyomavyāpin, or the primordial [deity], neither the disciple nor the guru should sleep again.
One should diligently conceal a bad dream with sound sleep;
or else, having performed the afternoon rites after the dedication of one's actions (karmārpaṇa), one should engage in worship.
The *pañcagavya* and other substances are for the children of Śiva’s lineage;
the mental [practice] consists of the *pañcagavya* and so forth; anything else is immediately a calamity.
Having properly prepared the pure mandala and having commanded the others, the procedure for that—
characterized by firmness of hand and self-devotion— is now described.
Having prepared an altar in the center of the sacrificial pavilion— anointed, mirror-like,
and complete with all the required characteristics— one should place [the deity] in its center.
For the purpose of establishing a square, one should first lay out a cord extending from east to west.
Having stretched it out with its center marked, one should then place two bindus;
then, using a thread of equal length from their tip, [one should mark] the north and south.
Having laid down a cord in the middle of the two fish arising from the two marks,
one should [measure] eight cubits toward the east and north using a cord equal to half the intended field.
One should establish the Matsya diagram; having drawn four lines in the four directions and two diagonal lines (karṇas), one should perfect it within the fire, rakṣas, and wind sectors.
The cord extending from corner to corner is known as the ear on the third head;
that [cord] shall be divided into four, eight, sixteen, or thirty-two parts respectively.
In the middle of that, having omitted the portions belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, one should draw a lotus with threads of equal intervals,
extending to all the cardinal and intermediate directions and the center of the wall.

Having divided this [circle] thirty-two times, one should draw four equal circles; with a radius of one finger-breadth on the outside, one should rotate [the lines] by one cubit. Within the central circle is the pericarp (*karṇikā*), which is yellow.
89b) Adorned with nine blue-colored, very soft filaments,
the second [petal] is likewise; the substance is as before, though otherwise.
At the base, middle, and front, with white, tawny, and pale-yellow [lines],
three straight, even, and well-knit petals each should be fashioned.
The joints of the petals should be fashioned above the third circuit;
however, in the fourth [circuit], the tips of the petals should be divided according to their distinctions.
For those seeking liberation as well as for those desiring enjoyment and liberation, [the practices] are joined together;
however, when they are not joined, each of them is praised as being threefold.

Among those, the mature [mantras] are for the sake of liberation in rites such as enjoyment and liberation; the youthful are for the attainment of powers such as the power of becoming small (aṇimā); and the infantile are for the sake of wealth.
And regarding their modes of arrangement,
it is also said that from the field at the tips of the petals, sixteen half-moons are to be produced.
By revolving around both sides, those facing upward and likewise those facing downward—
altogether sixteen in number— are indeed the petals of the full-blown lotus.
The tips of the petals should thus be joined together by the omission of the remaining [parts];
however, when not joined, the tip of the petal is extended by ten [units].
Having abandoned the enjoyment [of the petals] from the two sides, one should rotate the tip of its own petal by a measure of half the joint-line behind it.
In the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, it is said that the lotus has a sharp point and is fresh.
One should rotate the tip of the petal through the middle and end of the joint like a half-moon;
the thread extending from the two joints forms the filament, and this is one's own mandala.
It was white and very soft, with the spaces between its petals colored blue by pollen;
it was slightly bent by the hoods of the king of serpents, which were coppery-red.
Adorned with eight yantras according to the Kubjikā tradition,
the fifth line is drawn thickly from the left, while the celestial line (vyomarekhā) is sometimes ninefold.
In some places, the lotus is described as manifold; in others, it is described through its various divisions.
For one seeking liberation, the straight stalk is for enjoyment, while the inner petal-tip is for transcendence.
For all the Vidyeśvaras, [the tip is] like that of a cow's ear in the case of Bṛhaspati;
for the sacrifice beginning with Kāma, it is sharp-tipped; and for those belonging to the directions, it is blunt-tipped.
Just as for Gaurī, Devāpi, Patramra, and others, [the lotus is drawn] like the front of a maṇḍala;
having thus prepared the lotus, one should draw a square outside of it.
Having surrounded the path with a portion according to his word,
he then constructed four Khaṇḍarudras in the four directions.
90b) Having erased two [squares] in the middle by removing four squares diagonally, Khaṇḍarudra stands below; from there, one should lead [the lines] upward in the four directions.
Having abandoned one part on each side of the base of the pillar,
one who is instructed by Aurva-Āśika should fashion two [pillars] for each direction of the linga.
Below and across, it should have four lines with [six] spaces;
above that, two; then the neck with four; and the upper fillet should be six [spaces].
Above that, one should fashion the *liṅga* from the middle of the two [parts], extending on all sides;
furthermore, there is a single part situated on the outer side of the *liṅgas* for the purpose of the *cyuti*.
Having formed four lotuses in the corners with twenty-five squares each,
one should then place two [squares] marked in the center of the corners between the two liṅgas.
One should protect the chamber with three parts increased by one for the sake of beauty;
furthermore, the pathway (vīthī) below the base of the liṅga shall consist of one part.
One should draw a thread downwards from the center-line and horizontally across to form four squares;
then, one should remove the lower squares in the four cardinal directions.
On the sides, one should lead three squares each by means of two [lines] according to the Vedas;
it is beneficial that two squares are made horizontally below the corner.
One should perform the binding of the corners of the ten squares with the remaining [colors]; this mandala of the Fire-altar (citi), however, is devoid of a door.
Since the measure of the lotus is the same as that of the gate, its projection is half of that half;
when this has been done, one should scatter various colored powders upon it.
A straight line should be drawn, free from any overlapping;
one should know that in a case of overlapping lines there is strife, while in a case of broken lines there is conflict.
If it is excessively thick, there is the disease of existence; if mixed with [other colors], there is constant affliction;
through the drops, one incurs fear from the side of enemies, which brings about decay.
If [the thread] is made there, there will be loss of wealth; if it is severed, there will surely be death;
and if it becomes detached, there will be separation from one's beloved person or from one's cherished possessions.
He who should draw the mandala according to his own whim without knowing [the rules]—
in the corners from the southeast to the northeast— are the red, white, and dark-colored [lines].
One should place colored powders in the form of lions within the mandala at the Arka and Yamunā;
one should decorate the various lingas and other elements according to their beauty.
Outside, one should wrap [the chariot] with lotuses, mirrors, lamps, fragrant incense-sticks, and cloths, beginning with those of a hundred petals.
He who beholds this mandala, worshipped and known as the arising of the lotus-liṅga, through twenty-four efforts, in that way bliss is produced.
Even one who is crowded with the great sins of men, being liberated from the fetters, attains the state of Śiva.
Victorious is that supreme worship, which flows with the outpouring of transcendental bliss, wherein all the thrones of worldly existence dissolve the moment the throat-gate is opened.

In the abode of the sacrifice to Jupiter and Mercury, the initiation of objects is said to be like one's own; according to the ritual procedure, the pair of mantra and mudrā is declared to be supreme.

Having heard the child’s dream occurring during the three watches of the night, one should examine it at dawn according to its sevenfold nature; then, for the sake of welfare or prosperity, one should declare its meaning.
O Abhinanda, rejoice; this auspicious [teaching] has been revealed to you as being like a dream.
It arises from thoughts and so forth that have not been previously seen, and likewise counteracts the other.
It indicates the future prosperity, worldly enjoyment, liberation, and desired or undesired outcomes for the disciple.
It is not perceived through sight or hearing, nor has it been experienced; it is sought after and is thus considered fit.
Among these, its excellence is at the end of the night, while its mediocrity occurs at midnight.
92a) The calculation for the remaining portions of the three watches [of the night] involves lightness due to the onset of dusk;
what can those striving for wealth do against the lords of men who sit in the circle?
The summoning of those to be slain, as well as causing enmity, killing, driving away, and bewildering;
likewise, the subduing and favoring of fevers, planetary spirits, and poisons.
"O you who are known by the name Samastajanavācchakhya, this lowest success has arrived.
Arise! [Take] the sword, the netherworld, the ointment, the collyrium, and the sandals."
Invisibility, the extraction of essences from the earth, the power of movement, the withering of trees,
and the eightfold production of proof— these are the intermediate supernatural powers (siddhis).
The attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā*, the wealth of the enjoyment of the sky-farers (*khecarī*),
and the attainment of the state of a Vīreśvara— this is the most excellent of accomplishments (*siddhi*).
I consider egoism, fear, anger, pride, sacrifice, and straightforwardness, as well as envy and the production [of wealth], to be based upon one's mode of conduct.
O wandering women, [they experience] mutual hatred with their teachers, as well as hatred toward the philosophical systems, and they cause suffering to their sons, wives, and families.
This suffering is internal; beyond that is the divine [suffering], such as the terrible fear of cold, heat, and so forth, and the destruction of wife and sons.
Furthermore,
for those whose wealth consists of the knowledge of exhaustion, there is a swift attainment of excellence; [however,
this applies] except for that which arises from fear of predatory beasts, fire, thieves, lions, tigers, elephants, and the like.

Furthermore, the mental affliction arising from kings and so forth, as well as that which is established externally, is threefold; liberation is said to occur from below, except for the supreme [liberation].
Having performed the preliminary rites such as the *nitya* [recitation] as before,
and having offered the *arghya* for the purification of the mantra, one should stand before the mandala and sprinkle it with the water from the weapon-vessel (*astrakalaśa*).
Having performed the purification, inspection, and so forth, one should deposit the five kalās there—
namely Nivṛtti and the others— at those locations [starting] with Kṛṣṇa and the rest, along with their respective consorts.
Then, one should perform protection with the Āveśa, Varma, and Astra mantras;
subsequently, with the root mantra and the Praṇava, using the Śakti mantra eight hundred times or more.

For the pacification of defects such as dust and the like, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times; having worshipped the Linga or the altar (pīṭha) according to the detailed procedure, one should worship the lords of the directions beginning with Pṛthivī.
One should worship the weapon-mantra in the four directions of the mandala, starting from the east;
the eastern direction is situated at the eastern ghaṭa, and the southern mandala is in the south-western corner.
One should not worship with flowers and other offerings outside [the fire] during the descent of the flame into the pit of prosperity;
likewise, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth should be performed in the fire during the sacrifice to the site (*vāstuyāga*) and similar rites.
For the pacification of bad dreams and the like, one should offer one hundred oblations to Indra with the *digbāṇa* mantras, beginning with the best [mantra].
Having offered oblations to the root-mantra and others for the sake of satisfaction and so forth, and having worshipped Śiva, one should meditate and request the disciple’s entrance as before.
Then, having understood [the procedure] regarding Nandi, Śikhin, and the others, one should perform the *śivahasta* (the hand of Śiva);
by means of that, one should perform the sprinkling (*ālabhana*), as well as the grasping (*grahaṇa*) and the joining (*yojana*).
Having contemplated the non-duality of Śiva regarding their separation, as well as their emergence and the cutting of the bonds, one should then exit from the pavilion.
At the conclusion of all the previously mentioned rites, one should lead the disciple to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit;
having seated him there and worshipped him, one should perform the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).

Having offered oblations with the root mantra and its subsidiary mantras as before, and having invoked the presence [of the deity] by uttering "Hūhū," he should then place the head [of the effigy] on the ground with the *śiva* mantra.

With a glance, they are satisfied by the other [offering] and honored; within the *kuṇḍa*, the mantras beginning with Pāśa and ending with the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*)—these, when accompanied by the three pairs at their ends, grant the attainment of satisfaction and bestow Śiva.
Having performed one hundred oblations and more until the completion, he should be raised up again;
having caused oblations to be offered into the fire with the root mantra while proclaiming bliss, [the rite is concluded].
93b) Having performed worship upon the pitcher and so forth, on the mandala, in the fire,
and also on the sacrificial grass, one should offer salutations to the Lord of the Pitcher and likewise perform the formal supplication to him.
One should cause the disciple, the Lord of the World, and the others to bring the cord of nooses;
having purified the path therein, O Śiva, one should worship and satisfy them as before.
One should bind that cord of the *śampā* noose attached to the topknot;
having worshipped the disciple and drawn it out from his body according to the previously mentioned rite.
One should not worship the *nāḍī*s and so forth in the thread, nor during the *sandhāna* and *sannidhi* rites;
having performed the *tṛpti* (satisfaction) rite, one should contemplate the path within the body as being situated in the thread.

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of the root mantra at the junctures of all the paths— projected upon the self, the sacrificial pit, the maṇḍala, and so forth— in accordance with the teaching of the Āryākośa.
Having placed the Śakti in the vessel (kuṇḍa) along with the bearer of the banner, and having worshipped and gratified her,
one should perform the rites of inspection and so forth in the sequence beginning with Nivṛtti.
Just as the state of neither pervader nor pervaded exists beyond nirvāṇa,
so too here the words of mantra are entirely pervaded on all sides by the phonemes.

The worlds are pervaded by the castes, and those [worlds] are pervaded by the principles (*tattvas*); likewise, the collection of principles is pervaded by the *kalās*, and from that, the *kalās* [are pervaded].
It must be purified with effort and its internal inclusion should be conceived:
94a) Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the bond of the *nivṛtti*-kalā at the end of each reality-level (*tattva*) and world-level (*bhuvana*).
Having visualized the fourteen-fold creation of beings, beginning with the immobile and ending with Brahmā, situated in their own place;

having uttered "Oṃ Hāṃ Hlāṃ" and the [other] principles (tattvas), [one should recite] "Hūṃ Phaṭ," which removes the bonds of the Nivṛtti-kalā. Having thus severed them from the cord of bonds at the end of the letter 'Rā', one should enter with the mantra ending in "Namaḥ" and separate them with the mantra ending in "Phaṭ."

Having drawn [the breath] in with a blade of *kuśa* grass using the mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having performed the ritual procedure for the beginning and end of the principles (*tattva*) with *oṃ hauṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ hauṃ*, one should grasp [the cord] from below the knees while performing the *kuṃbhaka* (retention) that withdraws [the elements], using the mantra: *nivṛttikalāpāśāya haḥ hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*.

Having recited "tat tvā" and so forth, [one says] "namaḥ nivṛtti-kalā-pāśāya. Having placed [the deity] into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) through exhalation (recaka), having worshipped [him], having honored [him] with the mantra ending in "svāhā," having established [his] presence, and having offered libations, [one says] "oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ.
Having performed the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, [one says] "bho * * *? dhiko * * *".

Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hauṃ! To the reality (tattva), the worlds (bhuvana), the stages (pada), the phonemes (varṇa), and the mantras; to the karma, māyā, and the offspring of māyā (māyeya); to the one accompanied by investigation (savicārā); to the fetter of the kalās (kalāpāśa); to the pervasive one (vyāpakā); to Vāgīśvarī.
Homage!
Having placed the menstruating woman, dressed in red garments, within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should display the *yoni-mudrā* at the conclusion of the worship. [Recite]:

"Oṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvara. Having invoked him—four-armed, with five faces, the agitator of all wombs—into the pit, and having meditated upon the union of the two [deities] through the offering of eight flowers and so forth; |||

Oṃ hā& ha& hā& haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ. Having offered oblations ending with "svāhā" through the channel into the flower for the sake of piercing—the animal-consciousness situated in the Nivṛtti [kalā]—[one recites]:
Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ. Oṃ hā& vāmāyai namaḥ.
In each vessel, at the beginning of the worship and other rites, [the consciousness] is bound by the syllable *HŪM* through the left [nostril] and exhalation.

*OṂ HĀṂ HAṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ*. *OṂ HĀṂ JYEṢṬHĀYAI NAMAḤ*. As before, having continuously separated the consciousness of the sacrificial victim (*paśu*) from the body by means of Jyeṣṭhā, [one recites]: *OṂ HĀṂ HAṂ NAMAḤ*. *OṂ HĀṂ RAUDRE NAMAḤ*.
Having extracted the individual self from the *kuṇḍalī* and other centers, which resembles the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, and having placed it within the power at the *dvādaśānta*,
[one recites]: *oṃ hyaṃ*.

HĀṂ HAṂ HĀṂ HŪṂ OṂ PAŚUCAITANYAṂ GṚHṆĀMI HAḤ HŪṂ PHAṬ. Having offered oblations into the fire with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and having taken [the soul] along with the *pūruka* by means of the *raudrī* and *ariṇī* [kalās], one should— separating it from its location and its constituent measures (*mātrā*)— unite it with the Self according to the previously mentioned procedure, and having established it in a state of peace, [place it] in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having worshipped Vāmā and established her there, [one should recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ! O Self, be united with Naśiṣa for the purpose of conception (garbhādhāna) in the womb of Bhuvanā Vāgīśvarī, who possesses manifold forms and wombs, and who is free from lameness and other defects due to being differentiated by the various distinctions of numerous bodies simultaneously; [this is] for the sake of ultimate perfection. Having thus joined them, [one should recite]: "Oṃ."

Hāṃ Hāṃ Hāṃ! Salutation to the Self. One should perform the worship and other rites in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Indeed, for the sake of generating radiance for this [deity] whose name begins with such-and-such and who is engaged in the ritual, one should offer oblations of the sense-objects.

Then, having offered five oblations with the root mantra for the sake of the union (*yaugārtha*), one should contemplate with the *hṛdaya* (heart) mantra: "By means of simultaneous union, may the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) of this animal be performed at one time within its many wombs. And with the *śiras* (head) mantra: "I perform the birth of the animal from all its wombs simultaneously."

"O beast, I shall exercise authority over you," so says the *Sikhavā*. "I shall bring about the experience for the beast, whose karma has arisen from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within beginningless saṃsāra," so says the *Carmanā*. "I shall effect the dissolution of the beast," [so says the *Śiraḥ*].
With the root mantra.

For the sake of removing the karma that initiates those streams which have forms similar to illusion, [the officiant] thinks, "I shall perform the purification of the stream for the bound soul (paśu).
As before, he performs this with the Astra-mantra ending in *svāhā* for each individual, and with the Hṛdaya-mantra for the purification of the principles (*tattva*).
For the sake of purification, he recites the Hṛdaya-mantra one hundred times while gazing at the bound soul, as if [seeing] the cessation [of bondage] like an arrow shot from a bow.

"I perform the concealment of the impure soul," [he says] five times with Śiva. Holding it with the index finger and thumb, he effects the loosening of the bonds by moving the cord of the bonds of the impure soul five times with the Astra-mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*. "I sever the bond of the impure soul," [he says]. *Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ* [for the purification of] the principles (*tattva*) and so forth.

At the end of the word "rūpa," one should recite: "I sever the noose of the kalās; hūṃ phaṭ! For the weapon, hūṃ phaṭ! Having recited this mantra for the weapon, one should cut the noose with a blade consecrated by that same recitation.

Or else, as it has been stated: one should first consecrate the knife seven times with the *kṣurikāstra* mantra; having purified it with the fire of Śiva, one should join it with the three sweets. (96a)
One should purify the bonds by means of that [wisdom] through skillful means, and certainly not through impurity;
for those bonds, which are the joints of the aggregates, are severed from delusion.
In the world as well, one who possesses the secret key (sandhimat) breaks open a lock with a key, a chain, and so forth;
by the statement "crushing the bonds" (pāśamṛdnām), one should crush with both hands the bond that has been previously cut into pieces by means of the aforementioned mantra.
Thinking, "I am making the noose round," one should indeed make it circular with both hands as previously described.

Thinking, "I give the noose," one should place the thread on the tip of the *śruva* ladle filled with ghee and burn it with the mantra beginning with *oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ tattva* and ending with *rūpam*. [One does this] with *hūṃ* for the purpose of obstructing the power of the noose.
One should offer five oblations with the *phaṭ* weapon-mantra for atonement, or eight; then one should satisfy Brahmā with libations:
*Oṃ hāṃ, O Brahmā, accept these elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—along with sound and touch as the fee, svāhā*.
Having offered five oblations, [one says]: "O Brahmā, by the command of Śiva, you must again perform the ritual preparation of this sacrificial animal."
One should not create an obstacle regarding one's own sphere of action; rather,
having first made a formal request while facing east, one should release [the victim] with the thought, "I am performing the liberation of the sacrificial animal."

Having offered five oblations with the root mantra, one should separate oneself from the self by means of the left-hand [channel] which is most excellent; then, having placed it in the *raudrī* [channel],

one should meditate upon it as being like a cloud fallen from the mouth of Rāhu in the solar orb, being swallowed by the nooses of *pratiṣṭhā* and the others, and then project it onto the thread located within the self for the sake of satisfying the self situated therein.

Having performed five oblations with the root mantra, for the purpose of the disciple’s study, one should contemplate the form of the deceased upon the head of that [disciple] ending with *vauṣaṭ* using the root mantra; then, having applied a drop of water with the ring finger, one should satisfy the ancestors beginning with the ten [classes] with oblations, dismiss them, and offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). *Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hrīṃ hāṃ nivṛtti*.

Salutation to Pratiṣṭhā and Kalāpāśā. Having performed the union of the pure and impure states by means of the short and long rays of light, extending from the heart to the end of the self and from the end of the self to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the yogi should offer five oblations with the root mantra for the sake of its stabilization. One should likewise offer them during the rites of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth. And [this applies] to Kuñci, Śrī, Vṛddhi, and Bhārgava.
Thus, for each reality (tattva), the guru of the disciple-beast should perform the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) in order to eliminate the threefold speech and attain the state of Śiva.
The application of reality consists of accepting self-beating, the non-arising of the unwholesome, authority, enjoyment, and dissolution of the streams.

Purification, the purification of reality, the concealment of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), the severance of the fetters, their covering, and their burning— these are said to be the ritual actions.

The destruction of the cause and the removal of the animal [oblation] occur through these very [mantras]; others also, along with all the intermediate consecrations, are to be understood as being performed with the *pūrṇāhuti*.

And in the subsequent consecration (pratiṣṭhā), having meditated upon Śiva as before, and having performed the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites for Viṣṇu at the beginning and end of the visualization, [one should say]:
"O Viṣṇu, in this office, I shall initiate this disciple."
"By the command of Śiva, may you be favorable to me, O servant of Śiva.
Having thus entreated [the deity], and at the conclusion of the invocation of Vāgīśī and other rites, one should offer a hundred oblations from the head for the sake of expiation.
At the end of the previously mentioned ritual, Viṣṇu or another [deity] should be worshipped first.
Oṃ hā& Viṣṇu, with the companion of the other path, by means of that which pierces; Oṃ hā& hvī& hrū& hā&, salutation to the junction of the bonds of the *pratiṣṭhā* and *vidyā* kalās.
97b) Having performed the inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and other rites for the *vidyā*, and concluding with the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Rudra,
[one should contemplate] this seeker of liberation who desires to ascend upward within this office of Rudra-hood.
"I initiate you; have compassion according to the command of Śiva.

Having performed the invocation of Bhāgīśa and Caura as before, and having worshipped them, he should then offer a hundred oblations with the *śikhā* mantra at the conclusion of the worship of Rudra and the others: "Oṃ Hāṃ! O Rudra, [accept] the other paths, companions, form, and fragrance as the toll (*śulka*)."

"Take [it], Svāhā! Having announced it as before: "By the command of Śaṅkara, you must no longer impose restraint upon this Rudra, who has been freed from bondage and desires the auspicious abode. At the beginning and end of the prayer: *Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ haiṃ hāṃ, [we offer] to the bonds of the Vidyā and Śānti Kalās.*
One should join together.
Peace (*śānti*) is also as before, and light (*āloka*). Having performed the rite [of initiation] which has neither beginning nor end, the two lords (*īśvara*) [say]:

"O lords, regarding this authority over you, I shall favor this child who desires liberation; show compassion toward him within your own domain. Having thus petitioned, having summoned Vāgīśā, and having completed the worship and other rites, [he addresses] the son: "O one free from anger..."
98a) Having performed the root five oblations for the two seedless [fires] at the beginning of the worship of Īśvara and so forth:
*Oṃ hāṃ! O Īśvara, accept this offering of clarified butter along with the moon, the wind, the intellect, and the ego; svāhā!* Thus, having offered.
O Lord, since this animal’s noose has been completely burnt away by Your sovereignty, it can no longer act as a binder within Your own domain,
O Master.

Thus, at the beginning and end of the study, having performed the placement of the thread (*sūtra-nyāsa*) and so forth upon the Self—which possesses some knowledge, is of the nature of Vivasvat, and is liberated from the bonds of the *kalās* such as Śānti and Śāntyatītā through the mouth of Svarbhānu—one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ haiṃ hauṃ hāṃ, salutation to the bonds of the *kalās* Śānti and Śāntyatītā. One should then meditate.

And for Śāntyatītā, the invocation of Hṛdaya, Aghora, Śiva, and even Sadāśiva is also performed according to the previously mentioned ritual variations. [The officiant says: "I am initiating this seeker of liberation who has attained the state of Sadāśiva;
you, being compassionate, must be favorable toward him."
Having thus petitioned the two Lords of Speech (Vāgīśau) and invoked them as before, and having performed the worship and the entire visualization,

he should again offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), followed by five oblations to Śiva for the sake of the teacher and his son; then he should cause [the deity] to disappear.
By the previous rite, [the offering is made] at the end of Sadāśiva.
(98b) O Sadāśiva, accept the toll of the other paths, the consciousness of the mind, the drop (*bindu*), and the trident; svāhā!
One should announce one's qualification, as it has been stated in the Śrīmūḍhā and other texts.
One should abandon sound and touch in the Brahma-station; one should indeed abandon taste in Keśava;
one should abandon form and smell in the Lake (Hrada); and one should abandon intellect and ego in Īśvara.
Having uttered "Manobindu Śiva," one who is liberated by these becomes Śiva.
Then, within that: this Śiva acts. Drawn forth, he becomes the transcendent one;
having accomplished his purpose, O Bhavodbhava, you should always restrain the Self. Having informed Sadāśiva and released the principle of the Self—

Having contemplated everything up to Māyā within one's own mantra, during the rites of destruction (naṣṭi) and so forth, the practitioner should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra upon the image (arcā). For the principle of Vidyā (vidyā-tattva), ending with its respective vowel, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra upon the dust (pāṃśu). For the state of Śiva (śivatva), ending with Śakti, and for the knowledge-principle (jñāna) and so forth, one should perform a hundred mental oblations with the root mantra; thus, for each of the three principles, there is the attainment of perfection.

Or one should perform the rite of filling (*pūrṇatvita*). Some say that this mental recitation of the ritual mantra is the purification of the *kalpa*. One should [visualize] the self within the heart-lotus of the disciple’s body as being stainless, radiant, and complete, like the autumnal moon.

99a) And having placed the two Lords of Speech (Vāgīśvarau) at the tips of the tufts as before, one should satisfy them with eightfold devotion. Then, [one should say]: "O Parents, for the sake of my disciple, you who have been invoked by me—having looked upon me with compassion, please return to your own abodes."

The master, having recognized [the disciple], having dismissed [the obstacles], and having given the full offerings, should say: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hauṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śakti of the Kalā Śāntyatītā. He should then dissolve the impure Śakti of Śāntyatītā and unite [it].

Oṃ hā& hau& hā&! I cut the crooked power (*kuṭilāśakti*) that causes concealment; *hūṃ haḥ*, for the weapon, *hūṃ phaṭ*. Having recited this seven times over a razor-sharp weapon-mantra, one who desires liberation [should apply it] eight finger-breadths above [the head], while one who desires worldly enjoyment [should apply it] ten finger-breadths above, acting as an assistant to the fragrance of the self-blaze.
Having placed a wick made of cloth soaked in ghee and honey into a vessel filled with ghee at the tip of the *śruk* spoon during the Puṣya constellation,

he should offer oblations, saying, "I sacrifice according to what was previously stated. Having washed the *śruk* and *śruva* spoons on the outside with hot water and having bathed the disciple with pure water, he himself should bathe for the sake of the ritual purpose.
Having sipped water with ashes and earth according to the rule, and having duly entered the temple,
the practitioner of mantra, having performed the worship ending with the "Hand of Śiva" (śivahasta), [should proceed].
In the mandala and other rites, one should first request Śiva according to the previously described procedure for the fulfillment of desires.
O Blessed One, by your grace, the group of six has now been established;
having gathered the bound souls and purified them, [the rite] concludes with the severing of the topknot and the final submission.
This arrangement of your face has been fashioned by me through poetic suggestion;
by means of this power of yours, one must quickly go to that auspicious state.
Now, O Lord, grant me the command for that which must be performed by me in obedience to your instruction; I shall unite this disciple with [the goal].

Having offered oblations to Śiva in the fire of the *labdhājñā*, one should sprinkle the disciple as before; then, having performed the rites ending with the *kākalī* [mantra], one should perform the worship of the junctions of the channels (*nāḍī*) along with the limbs, accompanied by oblations.
Having performed [the ritual], one should purify the mantras; these belong to the qualified practitioner who possesses all parts.
Therefore, the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making complete) for the sacrificial animal is never performed through the fire-oblation (*homa*).
After initiation, when future karma is to be obstructed, one should offer a hundred oblations at the root;
then, having taken up the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles, they should be smeared with unguents and worshipped until the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having visualized the flame of fire blazing forth and performed the striking of the disciple and other rites,
one should bring oneself, radiant as the blazing sun, into the lotus of one's own heart.
Having personally brought about the state of equal flavor (samarasa) and having resorted to the path of the equinox (viśuvat),
the senses are filled with joy, and the elevation of the body is accomplished.
One should slightly lower the tongue so that its tip does not touch [the palate] above;
one should open the mouth just enough for speech, without touching the lips.

Likewise, the rows of teeth here are seen devoid of vision above and below; indeed, they are obstructed by the door being blocked at the Śūdra-gate. One should contemplate a single door flowing through the head.
Meditating on the mantra abiding in the *nāda*, relying upon the fundamental ritual procedure (*prakriyā*),
and employing the divine instrument, he is endowed with the supreme state.
Having extracted the sixfold [deity] from the disciple, the self, the pitcher, the fire, and the mandala,
and having performed the installation (ādhāna), one should place it within the ladle (śruva) located at the tip of the vital breath.
Just as the mantra is first articulated from the *kanda* at the base of the spine and so forth, it proceeds through the *mūlādhāra*,
the *kanda*, the navel, the heart, and the hollow of the throat.
The tip of the uvula, the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā,
the crest-lock, or the limit of twelve finger-breadths— these ten are the knots of movement.
100b) For the sake of the liberation of mantras, they must be understood by the teachers and others;
having pierced the knots in due order with the trident of the root mantra.
Having led the Self from the tip of the crest-lotus of serenity down to the base of the navel,
and having abandoned it there, one should contemplate the further shore endowed with the nature of pure consciousness.

Meditating upon that Śiva— who is complete with the six attributes, a mass of consciousness and bliss, and supreme— one should cause him to dissolve gradually, dropping [the breath] into the full [state].
One should remain in that state with the *kumbhaka* breath-hold as long as the clarified butter has not been consumed;
and when stability in the *yojanikā* [posture] is achieved, one should again offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Or, like a prince who has fallen from his position, one should manifest the six qualities of a child through the rites of initiation,
the offering of clarified butter, sesame seeds, and the breath-control of the wind, according to the rules of natural liberation.
Oṃ hāṃ! O Self, become omniscient; svāhā! Oṃ hīṃ!
O Self, become eternally satisfied; svāhā! Oṃ hūṃ! O Self, become beginningless awareness; svāhā!
Oṃ hauṃ! O Self, become independent; svāhā! Oṃ haḥ! O Self, become one whose power is withdrawn;
svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ! O Self, become one of infinite power; svāhā!
Having extracted the self, one should offer it into the center, which blazes like the sun.
101a) Then, O Keśin, one should place a drop of nectar upon the body of the disciple;
this is for the sake of pacifying the fatigue produced by the intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
In this manner, the teacher of the *putrikā* should initiate the practitioner for the sake of his purpose;
having purified the triad beginning with *nivṛtti* as previously described, and then *śāntyatītā*.
Having invoked and worshipped Sadākṣamā, one should then place the Śuddhaśakti within the disciple;
then, by means of the kumbhaka breath-retention joined with the recitation of the Śakti-mantra, one should [place] the guṇas.
One should produce, in due order, the three effects arising from the cause, such as the merchant and others, which have two causes,
as well as that which arises from the instrument, just as before.

Oṃ hāṃ! May there be for the self the power of atomization (aṇimā), svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ! [May] greatness (mahimā), lightness (laghimā), attainment (prāpti), irresistible will (prākāmya), mastery (vasitva), and wherever one desires (yatra-kāmāvasāyitva) reside in the white feet of Śrī Sadyojyotis.
The powers are: atomization (aṇimā), levitation (mahimā), magnitude (mahattva), and lightness (laghimā).
The attainment of all desired objects effortlessly;
the power of will (icchākāma); and the power of irresistible desire (prākāmya) accompanied by celestial women.
101b) Sovereignty is autonomy, being the master over all things without exception;
and there is neither emptiness nor contentment in that which is desired. All this is established by the Lord.
Wherever there is an opportunity for desire, there the manifestation of everything occurs;
by means of the form of wealth and worship, he himself causes the emergence of the *liṅga* and so forth.
As previously stated, one should eat together with the disciples according to the rule in the *Bṛhatsvāyaṃbhuvatantra*;
even at the end of the meal, one should prepare a mouthful of food (*gaṇḍūṣa*) from which [the leftovers] flow.
The food and other items that have been discarded are for the consumption of one's own deceased ancestors, such as *pretas*;
[the offering] begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ends with *svāhā*, directed toward those dwelling in the realm of *pretas* and hell-beings.
Blinded by that, one should cast away that mouthful of water upon the earth;
and on the following day, at the end of Caṇḍapāśa, one should offer the sacrificial cakes and other offerings to the Supreme.
Or else, one should perform the Caṇḍeṣṭi once at the beginning of the Guru’s [initiation];
those born from the maṇḍala of the Guru, purified by initiation and Gaṇapati,
possess bodies resplendent with the maṇḍala of the rising sun through the mantras of the Siddhas.
Having enjoyed their pleasures, they are accompanied by hosts of celestial women; with their longing for worldly power faded, they become intent on the path of Śiva and do not return to existence.
Nirvana.
Then, on the following day, after the daily rites and so forth, Śiva should first inform [the disciple]:
"O Great Lord, you have been commanded by the one who is the embodiment of the Guru."
O you of excellent vows, this yoga consists of initiation and its applications for the sake of non-interruption;
it is the thorough knowledge of one's true birth, which has been correctly explained by you to me.
It should be given for the sake of one's own accomplishment immediately after the *śiraḥśikhā*;
by your grace, this [accomplishment] has now arrived.
Therefore, I shall initiate him with the second commandment;
thus permitted, he should initiate the child who has performed his daily obligatory rites.
Having worshipped Indra and the others, they carry [the deity] outside from the sacrificial site;
then, in the northeast, the north, or the east, [one places] the ten-faced one.
And having caused a bathing pavilion to be constructed here facing east,
one should prepare two altars, quadrangular in shape, situated from south to north.
It is four cubits in width, equal in its proportions, and one *śūrya*-finger (twelve fingers) in height;
alternatively, it may be two, two, and one cubit, or eight, eight, and eight fingers in height.
Having adorned that place with auspicious Svastikas made of white mustard seeds and sprouts of barley,
one should place a beautiful seat there.
Thereafter, on both altars, O gentle one, he should station the physicians in the cardinal and intermediate directions and in the center, and likewise the jars possessing the proper characteristics.
From those endowed with the previously mentioned qualities, seated upon complete seats, and possessing beautiful limbs of a single uniform color— one should place eight oceans among them.
In the center, one should place sweetmeats, wine, sugarcane, clarified butter, curd, milk, and parched grain;
and in the northeast, as well as in some cases starting from the east (Indra's direction), one should place auspicious items.
When one worships Sadāśiva at the end of the eight Vidyeśvaras,
one should worship Ananta and the others in the four directions, protecting them with the lords Īśitṛ and Aruṇa.
And in the corners [of the mandala], one should place Ekarudra and the others— Sita, Asrik, and Nīlalohita— as well as Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Ekanetra.
And [he saw] Ekarudra, the form of Tryambaka, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin;
all seated upon lotus-thrones, gentle, four-faced, and bearing tridents.
He holds the weapons of Śiva, has three eyes, and possesses ears and a sword; he may have five faces or one face, and has three eyes and wears a digit of the moon.
The Lord stands upon a lotus, wearing a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of severed heads;
in his left hands, he holds a water-pot, a noose, a kusha-grass broom, a bell, and a trident.
Having meditated upon Śiva as holding a trident, a vajra, a rosary, and a discus in his right hands, one should gradually abandon all these [attributes].
Joined with Śiva and the power of Śiva like a jar of Śiva,
[the practitioner] should perform the recitations and oblations obtained from the root mantra eight hundred times according to the count.
