As before, one should worship [the deities] starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending with the east (Pūrva) in reverse order, O Lord; or else, one should worship Śikhaṇḍin and the others, beginning with Ananta and ending with Ājñārāda, in the jar that blazes.
Alternatively, O Lord, when five jars are well-positioned in the east, south, north, and west,
the reversal of the [usual] procedure occurs through the recitation of the Śāntyatītā and the other [Kalās].
One should worship with [offerings] joined by two oceans and accompanied by two Vidyeśvaras for each;
or else, one may worship five or nine in a single vessel as previously described.
Having placed the seat consisting of the six [elements], he should hold the child upon a gentle throne;
as before, having performed the ritual of the parts (sakalīkaraṇa) while facing the east or the north, he should cause him to arise.
Having worshipped Indra and the other deities with divine weapons, one should [offer] dūrvā grass, earth, ashes, and cow dung;
sour gruel, nine-colored rice, and black gram and so forth in shallow bowls.
The householder is rubbed by women; one should hold water in three ways with eight [fingers].
Śiva is the ocean; in the process of creation, it is salt-water, and in dissolution, it is milk-water.
One who is engaged in the practice of retaining the *payūṣa* should throw away the jar and leave the remainder.
Having struck the bull, one should lead the garments and other items to the southern altar;
there, one should worship Śiva, or rather, his garment together with the bull and other [attendants].
Having performed the *ārātrika* ritual with the waving of lamps, curd, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth,
one should wave them three times and then offer three handfuls of cool water in succession.
One should joyfully offer gorocanā, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, flowers, curd,
milk-rice, barley, and white mustard seeds.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the eight auspicious signs, he should take [the vessel] in his hand and cause it to circumambulate the sacrificial hall three times.
One should place that worship of the mandala to its south,
upon a seat that is auspicious in every respect and worshipped with colored powders and parched grain as previously described.
Having worshipped him while he is seated there, one should offer to him as a preceptor a well-strung rosary,
along with a parasol and a meditation belt.
A water-pot, sandals, a small vessel, a thread, a pair of scissors,
the *śruk* and *sruva* ladles, a ring, *darbha* grass, elephants, a palanquin, and so forth.
Then, having worshipped the Uṣṇīṣa as before, one should worship Caṇḍa as is appropriate;
[one should worship] the Pinākin with the first letter of his own name, the limbs of the Vidyā, and the left [hand].
Dakṣanareṣṭa, Vaikāṣya, Gotama, Eka, and Mālin—
these are said to be within the Śivabhakta [section] of the illustrious Mukhabimba.
From the east to the northeast, he is always accompanied by his wife and ends with his guru;
he has three eyes, sits upon a lotus throne, is gentle, white in color, and holds the moon and a conch in his hands.
Vāmana has eyes on his right side; the wielder of the trident has two arms.
He holds a rosary and a trident, and is adorned with tiger-skin and other ornaments.
Śrīkaṇṭha is praised as one thing, while in this [rite] they are said to be different; those [deities] should be invoked again.
Having offered all [oblations] to the fire-eater (Agni), one should then perform the recitation (japa) in the fire according to the prescribed number.
Having taken a portion of the wealth [offered] for the sprinkling of Indra, and having placed flowers, incense, and so forth— which have been perfumed—
into the joined palms [of the disciple], one should cause [the disciple] to perform the offering and then recite the following for them in sequence:
O Caṇḍa, you who are authorized, O dear child, [you must maintain] the supreme reality and the pledges in the presence of the Guru,
as they have been transmitted through the lineage of Gurus.
The poetry concerning the obligatory and occasional rites should always be composed by one residing in a good country.
Having carefully deliberated on what must be done from this day forward by the command of Śiva,
he too, trembling with devotion and faith, should place his joined palms upon his head.

Then, being devoid of authority and smelling like a mere disciple, he bowed before those [gurus] in the presence of the pledges (samaya) and so forth, and performed one hundred auspicious full oblations (pūrṇāhuti).
Having seated the disciple to his right with palms joined in reverence,
he should worship the Yoga-pīṭha, the pair of forms, Śiva, and the limbs.
Having offered ten oblations for each of the *daśās* beginning with Śanaka,
one should offer a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand oblations of the root mantra for the sake of its satisfaction.
The preceptor should mark the fingers of the child’s right hand, starting from the thumb,
with burnt darbha-grass using mantras, once the ground has been rendered barren [of impurities].
Having fashioned its three spokes and its central hub like the hand of Hara,
one should worship it with the *yogapīṭha* and other rites, and perform the fire-oblation as before.

Having placed flowers and other offerings in his hand, one should cause him to perform worship, prostration, and so forth; finally, one should offer the merit of one's own stainless splendor, beginning with the jar and ending with the self.
This very same procedure is to be performed by the practitioner as well;
however, this [procedure] is the "scissors" (kartarī) that accomplishes all tasks when conjoined with the mantra of the one to be accomplished.

Furthermore, one who has abandoned the Sūtras, even if he has established his residence in a proper place, may perform his vows according to his own will; yet he should avoid marrying a woman of the Strī-nyāya class.
The Guru, too, should remain for three days in a state of restraint; thereafter, he may join the desired mantra to the sādhya, provided no one else does so anywhere.
If a lifelong ascetic (naiṣṭhika) should fail in his vow and mentally desire a woman,
he should be expelled from his vow according to the prescribed rule if he is attached to sense-objects.
Likewise, having extracted the Pāśupatas and others from their vows, one should make them householders;
or else, those who remain under vows are not qualified [for this].
In all ritual activities such as initiation (dīkṣā), and in matters such as eating in a single row, [the same rules apply].
In the case of Nala, one should eat [only] the remains of the sacrificial offerings at five lotuses;
having offered a hundred oblations for each of the rites according to the number of vows, the practitioner shall remain fasting.

The Śaśor-vrata: Having first performed the *śikhā-mantra* according to the sequence of creation as prescribed in the *Jātaka-kalpa* and other texts, and having worshipped Caṇḍa, one should cast the components of the vow (*vratāṅga*) into the water.
105b) One should clothe [the disciple] with a garment, just as others do upon the completion of a vow;
those who abide in the reality of the Buddha-mind (buddhitattva) are always struck by the three qualities (guṇas).
The Vedāntins [worship] in Prakṛti; the Bhāgavatas and others in Puruṣa; the Pāśupatas in the principle of Māyā; and the Mahāvratinas in Sadvidyā.
Furthermore, other places of liberation for those wearing sectarian marks, such as the Buddhists and others,
are [located] one, three, or five *rātras* away from the fasting ascetics who wear such marks.
For those who remain outside the pavilion and are performing penance,
one should extract the *liṅga* after worshipping Śiva as before.
Having established the principles (tattvas) in the fire, beginning with the mortal and ending with the final one,
one should worship them with their own respective names, or else knowing them as one, in due order.
Then, having drawn up that consciousness from the previously mentioned method of the convergence of the channels,
one should offer it as an oblation into the fire with the root mantra, ending with "svāhā."
O Śveta, you practice that dharma which arises from the worship of the gods;
[you have] a thousand-fold weapon multiplied by eight, [and] the mantra for each individual liṅga.

For the sake of liberation through the realization of reality, one should again extract the five [elements] from each of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva, and join them together auspiciously.

106a) For the sake of remaining established in that yoga, one should first offer one hundred and eight oblations into the fire of Śiva, and then cast [the materials] as previously described as part of the ritual observance (*vrata*).
Even for one who has been initiated but is not a devotee, one should perform the rites possessed by Śiva;
for the sake of pacifying defects, one should perform the Niṣkala-saṃhitā-homa up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should cause the descent of the Śiva-mantras, beginning with Kālāgni, by means of the power of wrath.
Even one who has taken up the life of a householder lacks the authority for the sprinkling of the son;
however, the mantra is the rule for the sake of one's own self.
The noble one, authorized and consecrated, who has severed the bonds of the bound souls,
should perform a small amount of recitation and offer a small amount of oblation into the fire during the day.
One should always observe this vow for the sake of the preceptor;
in the absence [of the preceptor], one should offer oblations into water or other elements according to the prescribed rite.
Or else, for the sake of accomplishment, having performed [the rite] mentally at the "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta) and so forth,
there should be oblations of water mixed with ghee and milk, equal in measure to the water [offered].
Therefore, she too is considered superior to all other oblations;
however, a blind person should not perform the daily worship of the supreme deity in a linga or similar form.

One who performs the ritual according to both the mixed and the non-mixed tantras with equal application should here complete the eightfold procedure; yet he whose intellect is deluded acts in such a manner.
Or else his ear may burst, and he shall meet with destruction along with his very roots,
if he performs consecrations or studies in a place belonging to those observing vows within the Śiva tradition.
But birth, wealth, and learning are not the causes for seniority;
rather, even a younger person is senior to one who is present [but lacks these], by virtue of being sprinkled with the [initiatory] water.
Furthermore, between one who has been initiated by a teacher and another who was initiated later by that same teacher,
they should address one another with the word "sir," except for the act of formal salutation.
Neither the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) nor those who follow the Krama tradition perform the praise of the Teacher, the Śiva-scripture, or Śiva himself.
Whosoever enters whichever stage of life (*āśrama*), Śambhu, remaining right there, protects him through the eight auspicious initiations (*dīkṣā*) and the Śiva-dharma.
Having undertaken the state of a religious student, it is indeed merely a matter of designation;
for here, the true essence lies solely in the duties of the stages of life, not in the stages themselves.
By initiation, initiation is destroyed, as is the previous initiation; however, by means of the specific [initiation], the common [initiation] is indeed overcome by the Guru alone. 107a)
Having initiated [them], both the teacher and the disciple go to hell— [even if they were] as perfectly liberated as Bhārgava— by transgressing the *svatantra* and other [rules].
Those should be known as gurus only so long as they are observers of proper conduct;
however, one should abandon conduct that has been corrupted, for it would become like a broken reed.

Or rather, due to the fault of speech, one should worship the two serpents who have resorted to the navel, having fallen from their state by embracing [the world]. One should show compassion toward those who approach.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the purification of the body and other preliminary duties;
then, one should daily contemplate that embodied Śiva, who possesses three eyes and the crescent moon upon His head.
Having performed the recitation while remaining in the same posture, one should offer three hundred oblations each;
having bathed in water with a paste of *śākāviṃ*, one should be firm in effort.
From the sixth month until the end of the year, he should then perform the completion of the vow;
with the water from the auspicious pitcher, he should consecrate himself by means of his own self.
One should recite the *saṃhitā* in sequence, beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Śiva;
having performed this vow of the teacher, one should examine the mantra.
Just as there is no flame without fire, and likewise no fruit without a tree.
The paralyzing of nooses, the destruction of the great ripening [of karma],
the transference of poison, and likewise the rendering [of it] seedless.
And the destruction of planetary fevers occurs through these eight conditions.
Having thus completed the initiation, one should initiate oneself through the knowledge of all ritual actions as before, or else by means of the nature of higher consciousness (vijñāna).
O Sandalwood, by simultaneously dissolving the bonds of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted,
and by once uttering the *sūla*, one should unite oneself with the Self.
Since you have been urged by me for the sake of the disciples and the purpose of the teaching, O Blessed One, may the wise ones then attain success through the eternal qualities.
Therefore, forgive me out of compassion as I carry out your very command;
then, having released [the deity] from the fire, he should enjoin him within the mandala.
Having placed [the deity] residing there into the water-pot, one should lead the deities to their respective abodes;
then, even after releasing the two Śiva-pots, one should sprinkle the child with that water.

Having eaten from the auspicious vessel (śivaghaṭa), one should perform the self-consecration (svayamabhiṣeka) for the sake of satisfying those residing within one's own body, offering it to the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) in the reverse order.
By that which removes all obstacles and the like, through the mouth of peace, it is as follows:
let there be the destruction of misfortune through the intentional recitation of mantras.
That which has become scorched and dried up by fire is not equal to the pacification rites for animals;
even when the linga and other items have been discarded, contact with them remains a source of harm.
The remains of the offering (nirmālya) shall not be discarded as long as the Śiva-vessel remains;
likewise for the Linga, the Mandala, and the Fire, once they have been worshipped with libations for Śiva.
Having discarded the *nirmālya* of Caṇḍeśa, everything else indeed becomes light upon contact; at that time, it even ascends upward.
The consecration.
For the deceased gurus, sādhakas, and sons, purification through the principles (tattva) is prescribed;
for those who have violated their commitments (asamayastha), the concluding rite (anteṣṭi) is said to destroy their defects.
Alternatively, having otherwise cast the supreme *parāśu* of the yogins of Śiva, one should,
by the power of one's strength, fashion it as an adorned palanquin for Śiva.
Wearing red garments, with the resonant sounds of fluttering banners,
those whose wealth was their asceticism followed slowly behind him.
Likewise, he is carried along by non-relatives and others whose heads are covered with their garments,
who are driven by whips, and who are of the same caste as dogs and jackals.

One should cause those initiated disciples who wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder and contemplate the weapon-mantra and other rites to rest for half the time, or one should place them near the water.
On the ground, the head of Śauri (Viṣṇu) should be fashioned by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
it should be four-cornered, one cubit in measure, and have a single girdle six finger-breadths wide.
Having prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should fashion a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) using the earth from that pit in the northwest direction;
or, even to the south of the pit, one should construct a square altar measuring four cubits.
Having bathed in the confluence, which is two or three finger-breadths deep and three [finger-breadths] wide, the practitioner, whose self is the mantra,
should proceed to the south;
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the rules for the dry land, he remains protected there.
Having first placed the life-prolonging [substance] at the edge of the vessel of the silent one's mind, [he should perform the rite].
One should sprinkle the vessel with that liquid and worship the food according to the prescribed rite;
then, having offered oblations for the sake of dispelling obstacles, one should perform the consumption with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having first established the site for the funeral pyre, one should fashion the nine [deities] beginning with Carakī, each occupying one square;
these extend from Earth up to Ākāśa, colored according to their respective five colors.
109a) Having adorned that [site] with flowers and other offerings, one should worship the deities of the site (vāstudevatā).
One should worship Brahmā together with the Earth in the five central squares.
Viṣṇu, accompanied by Ambu, is in the square of the Vedas in the southwest;
Rudra, followed by Agni, is in the four squares located in the southeast corner.
Īśvara, together with Vāyu, is in the corner square of the wind;
and Sadāśiva, joined with Vyoman, is in the square of the northeast direction.
One should worship Indra and the other deities, located in the eastern and other quarters within the square grids, four by four;
then, having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) and searched for it, one should seek the site of the funeral pyre within the domain of the Lord of the Earth.
In the *vardhanī* vessel, one should duly place the weapon-mantra within the range of the directions starting from Īśāna,
followed by the trident and so forth ending with the purifier (*pavitra*), and likewise the discus and lotus in sequence.
Then, having worshipped [the deity] upon an altar (sthaṇḍila) mixed with sesame seeds, ashes, and so forth,
one should install the sustaining power (dhārikā-śakti) as well as the seat of sovereignty (aiśvarya-āsana) and the rest.
One should worship the host of powers beginning with Manonmanī and ending with Vāmā; thereafter, one should worship Śiva along with the limbs of the Vidyā in reverse order.
Having duly prepared the fire and worshipped the Lord therein with the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having satisfied the deities,
one should [insert] the sacrificial pegs made from dry wood or metal in sequence on the right side.
One should bury red threads and so forth, obtained from a woman who has bathed after her menses and directed downwards,
in the corners starting with the southeast according to the teaching of the *Śrīvajradeha*, and then the fire-pit should be filled with fuel.
Having worshipped together with sesame seeds, flowers, and *kuśa* grass, one should worship with the *astra-mantra*;
thereafter, with the *viparīta-paṭacchadman* [mantra] and with the *sṛṅga*, *mṛd*, and *ambhas*.

Having bathed the corpse and sprinkled it with water, one should not look at it; O Lord, in the case of a reversal [of status], one should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder and place the sacrificial vessel on the right.
Having led [the soul] out as before, one should then extract the pure body and place the *jīva* [within it], with the *mahājāla-mantra*: OṂ HŪṂ HĀṂ HAṂ HAUṂ HŪṂ, obeisance to the self of [Name].
One should apply the mantra "namaḥ" even upon the body: to the head, the face, the heart, the navel, and all the limbs.
One should offer the five *kalās*, the *vidyātattva*, *śakti*, *haṃsa*, and likewise *śiva*,
one hundred times with the root mantra, in the presence of Consciousness.
Whether sequentially or simultaneously, having assumed the *nivṛtti*-kalā and the others,
and having placed them in the fire and worshipped them during the invocation of Śiva and the other deities;
According to the procedure prescribed for initiation, one should perform the striking and other rites upon the individual soul (jīva),
whereby its present, past, and future merits and demerits, and so forth, are destroyed.
110a) One may practice as if attaining immediate liberation, or one may act through the self, the doors [of the senses], and so forth; then,
at the end of the experience of the fruits of merit and other such commenced actions, one should cast off the body.

The "good enjoyment" (*subhukti*) that follows is initiation (*dīkṣā*), which also possesses the seed-syllable (*bījavatī*). Then, at the conclusion of the "joining" (*yojanikā*) and other rites, it belongs to one who has worshipped the station of fire.
Having placed the corpse on the funeral pyre with its head to the south,
he joined the sacrificial pit with the sounds of the three oblations.
Having kindled the funeral pyre, O gentle-faced one, standing at the head of the corpse,
he should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with this mantra, using an offering ladle filled with honey, clarified butter, and milk.
Oṃ! O Agni, you who are the southern direction and time itself;
at this very moment, accept this great oblation, joined with the mantra, which has the target as its essence.

One should cast the *śruk* and *sruva* ladles there with their openings facing downward, or perform a circumambulation to the right; then, taking the vessel containing the weapons situated on the left side of oneself, one should discard them in sequence.
Since the internal self (pratyagātman) is extracted from its states by means of these [elements], one should hold fast to it there;
then, having gone near water, one should not look back.

Having bathed and crossed over, with the sacred *darbha* grass placed over the left shoulder (*napasavya*), he should place three handfuls of water on the riverbank and offer them according to the ritual procedure accompanied by the appropriate mantras.
Oṃ hāṃ! O pure self, become Īśa. Oṃ hāṃ! O pure self, become Sadāśiva.
Oṃ hāṃ! O pure self, be peaceful; svadhā. Having bathed, the preceptor should mutter the terrible [mantra] one hundred times, like Śrī Hāṭakeśa.
Then, the two hundred givers of the shoulder [offering] should go to the hermitage.
There, for the duration of a year, they should perform the worship of Śiva dedicated to him.
If one is unrelated [to the deceased], having touched the corpse or even smelled it,
or having bathed in pure water, or having muttered the *rūpi-śata* mantra, one should bathe and worship Īśvara.
After cremating the corpse of one who was staying in the bathhouse, the female bird (the ascetic woman) should either remain there for two days or follow the ascetic on his journey through the world.
Nevertheless, one should follow after even a person of low caste who is established in a vow;
having followed him and bathed in water, one should mutter the hundred names of the Lord at the mouth [of the water].

Even for a householder who has withdrawn his mind from worldly objects, gambling always brings about a state of impurity lasting until the moment of purification; even that [impurity] flees away through bathing.

Those who are related to a single teacher or a single disciple should abandon their ritual duties for three days; others [should abandon them] for one day. Among them, those established on the Śaiva path—whether householders or even non-householders—should fast for one day, and they are consecrated by that for the sake of purification.
Householders, remaining on the worldly path, must again transcend the worldly conduct;
therefore, those who have been initiated should act while conforming to worldly conventions.
And that [impurity] lasts for two days according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures;
therefore, they should perform the doubling of the period for guests and so forth, as well as the impurity following a birth and other such occasions.
A householder who always eats only what is offered and who does not cause distress to others by seeking food from them should, out of necessity, avoid all other activities.
The horse, however, being independent, should go behind it, following its path;
[this applies] to the lay initiate who is devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*.

Worship should be performed by those initiated into the Dharma using materials previously intended for the purpose, even during periods of birth-impurity or death-impurity, as well as with items produced for that specific occasion.
The first [rite] occurs on the twelfth or eleventh day; that is the *piṇḍīkaraṇa*. This ritual duty must be performed by a householder, but not by anyone else.
Whether it belongs to one who has taken up worldly duties as a householder, or to one who is initiated, or even to a common person—it must be performed; thus it is stated in the Bhargaśikhottara.
The words of Śiva are manifold: they are stated, prohibited, and then reconsidered; they are dependent and independent.
Since differentiation therein is traditionally held to arise through the distinction between actions and so forth,
therefore, whatever has been taught in a particular way should be performed accordingly, and not according to another system.
One should perform the extraction of even water that has been long afflicted and spoiled;
thus ends the rite for the deceased.
Then, for all those whose minds were agitated by various ghosts of wealth born from their transgressions,
he immediately performed the *śrāddha* rite, which grants desired boons and brings about the destruction of obstacles.
In that regard, [the teacher may be] one-eyed, bald, lame, hunchbacked, or similar;
he should be chosen according to availability from among those who are senior, middling, or junior, based on their merit.
One should offer the hand and speak words of affection with *elā* and other substances, saying:
"Oṃ, this [food] has been consecrated by me; [partake of it] in the evening with a restrained mind."

"I shall perform the Śrāddha for you all, impelled by the power of Śiva. [Having said this], in the afternoon, with Kuśa grass, he should place his hands facing eastward, with the palms slightly apart.
In the southern and northern directions, the two deities are square and have two circles;
likewise, in the west, the two ancestral deities (paitra) are circular, [anointed] with cow-dung and water.
Then, one should draw lines across the four corners;
from the circular characteristic [of the center], one should place much sand in the two mandalas made of clay.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) with the two southern [mantras] preceded by the word "nyasya," and the two northern ones with the heart-mantra,
one who knows the ritual procedure for the śrāddha should worship the two mandalas with these very flowers.
Two [pots] are for the gods and three for the ancestors; they should be arranged in order starting from the eldest.
When the rite is completed with water containing sesame and *darbha* grass, one should offer them with the common *arghya*.
With barley grains properly crushed at the Devatīrtha of the gods.
Ending with "svāhā," while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should circumambulate clockwise;
subsequently, standing on the ground with his right knee [touching] it, he should perform [the rite] for the sake of happiness.
The ritual for the ancestors is performed with sesame seeds and broken kuśa grass;
it is conducted with mantras ending in "svadhā," with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apavīta), and without circumambulation to the right.
One should not perform the rite facing south while touching the ground with the left knee.
In rites for the gods (daiva), the right side is the beginning and the north is the end; in rites for the ancestors (pitrya), the east is the beginning and the west is the end.

Oṃ rudrāya svāhā. Having offered the arghya on the right side, [one says] Oṃ dvirudrāya svāhā. One should wash the feet with clay from the Gaṅgā and other sacred sites. Likewise with the name Ananta: Oṃ īśāya svadhā. Having presented the arghya on the left side, [one says] Oṃ īśāya.

*Svadhā* is as before at the beginning; likewise for the two [sections] ending with Sadāśiva. (112b) Then, having caused everyone to sip water (*ācamana*) in the two intermediate maṇḍalas, and having himself entered within, [he addresses] Viśve.
For the sake of the gods, two [offerings] facing east: *Oṃ hiṃ rudrāya svadhā*;
*Oṃ hiṃ anantāya svadhā*. For the sake of the ancestors and others, three [offerings] facing north: *Oṃ hīṃ īśāya svadhā*; *Oṃ hiṃ sadāśivāya svāhā*; *Oṃ hiṃ sadāśivāya svadhā*.

Having sat down comfortably upon a pure seat as before, one should prepare a special *argha* offering— filled with water, fragrance, flowers, *kuśa* grass, dūrvā grass, and unhusked rice (*akṣata*)— facing any direction starting from the east, using the *hṛdaya* and other mantras as well as the *brahma-mantras*; then, with that water...

Sprinkle the ritual substances with the Astra-mantra; consecrate the incense and flowers with the Hrdaya-mantra, the lamp with the Shikha-mantra, and the garment and sacred thread (yajñopavīta) with the Varma-mantra, as before. Then, using the left hand, place water in vessels made of gold or other materials; with the Sadyojāta-mantra, place barley; with the Shikha-mantra, place scented water; and [place] dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and flowers.

Having placed a blade of kuśa grass with its tip intact and a middle *brahmagranthi* knot measuring a span (*prādeśa*) cut by another kuśa blade, one should consecrate it with the heart mantra. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*dakṣopavītī*), one should offer two sets of water for presence (*sāṃnidhya-argha*) as before for the deities and the ancestors.

113a) Having performed the threefold *argha* offering due to the presence of the local deities (*tilākṣi-khāsāṃnidhya*), with palms joined in reverence (*vadhāñjali*), he says: "Oṃ, today, together with Rudra, the Lord of All Gods (*viśvadeva*), I shall perform [this rite] among you. When this has been spoken:
Oṃ, "Do so," when thus authorized. Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Rudra. Having placed a seat of kuśa grass with its tips pointing north on the right side, [he says]: "Oṃ, I shall invoke Rudra, the Viśvedevas.
When [the officiant] has said this, [the other replies]: "Oṃ, invoke them. [He then says]: "Oṃ, svāhā to Rudra. Having invoked [them].

Oṃ hiṃ rudrāya svāhā. One should perform the installation and so forth. Oṃ hiṃ rudrāya svāhā. Protection is provided by waving barley all around with the hand while circumambulating clockwise. Oṃ huṃ rudrāya svāhā. Having first placed a blade of kuśa grass, one span in length, with its point facing oneself into the joined palms (añjali) of his right hand—

Then, having offered the *sānnidhya-argha* with cupped hands and holding that vessel beneath it, with both knees resting on the ground, one should repeatedly tread upon its limbs from the feet up to the head, saying: *oṃ hūṃ rudrāya svāhā*. Worship it with barley grains: *oṃ hūṃ rudrāya svāhā*. [Worship] with perfumes and flowers: *oṃ hūṃ*.
To Rudra, Svāhā! With incense and lamps.
(113b) Oṃ Hāṃ, to Rudra, Svāhā! And with garments and purifiers. When it is said, "Oṃ, may everything be complete," [one says] Oṃ.
One should say, "May it be complete. In this same manner, [the rite is performed] with the names Ananteśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta.

However, for the ancestors, protection is performed with sesame seeds in a counter-clockwise direction; or, in the case of Ghora, worship is performed with sesame seeds by means of destruction. Then, the *saṃsrava* (residue) held in their hands, having fallen from the tips of the hands into the vessel at the heart, [is offered] to Nairṛta.

Having said, "Oṃ, you are the seat of the ancestors," one should place [the vessel] face down for the sake of the downward-facing deity. One should omit the *arghya* offering and the application of collyrium to the eyes for the deity. Having performed [the rites] with the three-syllable mantra and having given the hand-washing and other services to all, one should purify the site, avoid the defect of the lines by means of [drawing] rows, and provide the vessels.
Taking the finest of all cooked foods, along with sesame seeds and ghee, and having said, "Oṃ, I shall perform [the oblation] in the fire," and being told by them, "Oṃ,

do so," he offers three oblations into the fourfold purified fire according to the rite for the ancestors (pitṛyajña). Then, having dismissed [the deities], he offers an abundance of rice boiled in milk, along with ghee, soup, condiments, and the like.
Oṃ haṃ, svāhā to Rudra.
Having placed barley in the vessel, devoid of licorice, one should set that vessel aside for the sake of purification.

Having touched it with the *aghora* mantra and consecrated it, one should place the lamp upon the food while reciting either the *mṛtyuñjaya* or *vāmadeva* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, holding the thumb of the right hand downward and the other fingers closed in the fist; thus, one should very slowly raise the lamp. The same applies for *ananta* as well.

Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Īśa. The householder should offer [the food] along with sesame seeds as before, up to the end of the consciousness that is equal to himself. This applies likewise to Itthaśada and Āśivaśānti. Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Rudra.
Having thus offered to Īśāna and having placed [the portion] into the hands of all, he should say: "Oṃ juṃ, eat! They too—

As before, they should eat until satisfied. When the time has arrived, having determined the lunar day (tithi), one should receive [the guest] with the thought that he is none other than Śiva—excluding the formal mantra—and honor him as previously described by feeding him and so forth under that name. [The deities are: Śiva, Umā, Arka, Acyuta, Brahmā, and Skanda.

On the ground for the *dharma* and other [deities], one should move about in the form of a guest (*atithi*). Having reflected upon that guest-day (*tithi*), one should protect the food and so forth from its half. In the absence of a guest, one should give even that to cows and the like.
Then, while they are eating, one should stand facing north and recite the Īśāna mantra.

Then, having taken some food from the remainder of the meal, when asked, "Oṃ, are you satisfied?", and they reply, "Oṃ, we are satisfied," one should request, "Oṃ, may the remaining food be distributed as alms. Oṃ.

"May the remaining food be eaten by those who are dear and worthy. When this is said, having placed five portions of fire on the ground in sequence, saying "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Rudra," and having offered a stream of water,
one should form three circles near the leavings with the palm of one hand moving around them, with the lines pointing toward the south.

Or [one may offer] ten [stalks] with their tips pointing northward. Having performed the ritual placement (*āropaṇa*) with "Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Īśāna," and so forth; or alternatively, having scattered sesame seeds and other offerings with "Oṃ hīṃ, svadhā to Īśa," and so forth, one should thereafter take water and all three *piṇḍas*, hold them in the left hand as they are positioned, and impel them with the root-mantra of the ten [fingers].
Oṃ, svadhā to the father Īśa. In this manner, proceeding in order with the right hand, one should offer [the oblation] into the ten spaces situated within the eastern, central, and western mandalas.

"Oṃ hīṃ, svadhā to Īśāna. Having thus offered a stream of water and honored [the deities] with flowers and other offerings, first [offer] the water for the weapons (*astra*), and afterwards offer the two [types of] water for sipping (*ācamana*) in reverse order. When requested, say "Oṃ, may there be well-being (*svasti*). When requested, say "Oṃ, may there be well-being. When requested, say "Oṃ, may there be inexhaustible water (*akṣayodaka*). When requested, he should say "Oṃ, so be it. Oṃ.

For the purpose of the installation of the ear-ornament of Rudra, the Universal Deity, I give this dakṣiṇā of gold to you; he should place it in the right hand along with ten new barley grains as before. "Oṃ Svasti," the priest should also say. This same procedure applies to Ananta as well. For Īśāna and the others, [he should offer] sesame and turmeric. "Oṃ Astu."
Having obtained permission from those worthy of honor, and while pouring a stream of water upon the ground, he makes this prayer: "Oṃ! May the gods and Rudras be satisfied;
may they always bring us auspiciousness. Having thus requested and received permission, he says: "Oṃ!
May the donors increase, as well as the lineage of Śiva; may there be faith, freedom from disease, and much to be given."
"It is not so. As before, when they were thus addressed by those who had been requested, [he said]:
"Oṃ! May everything be offered to the gods. Oṃ! May they remain. To the ancestors, it is requested that they partake. Oṃ.

Having said, "May you attend [upon us]," and having bowed down with affection, he should first dismiss the ancestors and the girdle (mekhalā) in this sequence: "Oṃ haṃ, svadhā to Śānta. Then, having dismissed the two deities at the end with "Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Ananta," and having turned the vessel for the ancestors placed as before face upwards, he says: "Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Śānta."

Having dismissed the three with "Svadhā," and having anointed the eyes with the water-offering for the deities (*devārgha*), one should say: "Oṃ Hāṃ, svāhā to Ananta. Having offered the two [libations] and the argha-vessel, one should cast all that—including the flowers and other items—upon the cloth-covering. Then, saying "Oṃ, may you be pleased," and "Oṃ, we are pleased," one should offer words of conciliation to those [deities].
Having circumambulated [the vessel] clockwise, one should give the middle *piṇḍa*—or the central *piṇḍa* with its root-end—to the Brahmins and others;

or, for the sake of obtaining a son who is a portion of Rudra, one should give it to a woman. Having also wiped away the remnants from oneself and sipped water, one should eat the remaining food together [with the guests]. In some places, immediately after the word "givers" (*dātāraḥ*),...
The dismissal of the ancestors (pitṛvisarjana) is performed by bowing down with the mantra beginning with "pitṛdevaviṣargādyantānata. (116a) The dismissal of the ancestors.
The purpose is to briefly summarize the offering of water (arghya), food (anna), poison (viṣa), and the rice-ball (piṇḍa), as well as the avoidance of [inappropriate] attachment (*abhirati*).

This consists of either five absences or two pairs. In that very context, the Viśvedevas are located on the two arms—the right and left. Elsewhere, the ancestors (pitṛs) are located by means of the division of the two limbs—the right and left—and the head.

Then, in one vessel for the *saumya* [deities], one should place two arms and two *skandas* on the heads [of the vessels] as before, and also invite the gods and ancestors (*devapitṛs*). Here, for each individual, one should say, "I shall perform the *śrāddha* for the Viśvedevas and the ancestors," and so forth. Even in the case of using one or two vessels, this should be done according to one's own discretion.
And the *saṃśravā* [vessel] is placed first; or else, with both knees bent, O Lord, there are two for the gods and one for the ancestors and so forth.

That [offering] is a gift, either across [the altar] or by means of a vessel; and the three *piṇḍas* are placed upon a single blade of *kuśa* grass—at its root, middle, and tip—respectively in the order of north, middle, and south; and in some cases, also in the fire.

One should perform three oblations for the purification of the parents and others from the lord of the *sārṇa*. Then, having consecrated the *cūrṇikā* (the powder) starting with the chest and so forth, one should worship it with:
*oṃ hauṃ cūrṇikāyai namaḥ*. Then: *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*.

[With] *cūrṇī* [and] *adakṣavāhu*: *oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Adharma; [on] the left arm. Having taken that [substance] as before with fire, from the *dvādaśānta* into the fire of the vessel: *oṃ hāṃ*, may this be the fire of Śiva—thus one should join [it].
There too, having invoked Agni and the others: *oṃ hāṃ*, svāhā to Agni; *oṃ hāṃ*, svāhā to Soma; *oṃ hāṃ*.
Svāhā to Savitṛ! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Bṛhaspati! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the gods! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Viśvedevas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!
Thus, at the end of the full oblation, one should offer three oblations into the fire as in the daily rite, beginning with the eight syllables and ending with the word *bhāva*.

Having given [the offerings] and dismissed the fire, one should perform the previously mentioned rites. One should not perform the *śrāddha* with the *pūrṇāhuti* and so forth in this manner during the festival of the Guru. The *pārvaṇa* rite for the five [deities] beginning with Rudra and Īśa is always incumbent. Even while one's own Guru is present, the ascetic should perform the *śrāddha*, because he has bathed [purified himself] from the cause of this transmigratory existence.

Even one who has performed the rites for the deceased, though bound, should act as a husband for the sake of the cow; likewise, this [duty] should be performed by a householder even if he is a seeker of liberation (nirvāṇin), provided it is offered in such a manner. This is the superior [path] for householders, [known as] Nandikā.
But in the Pārvaṇa rite, Kārttikeya is worshipped;
furthermore, the Pitṛs, Skanda, Caṇḍa, and the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa) are worshipped together.
Then there are two portions for the two [deities], and three portions for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva respectively.

Having offered a single pinda, purified water (arghya), and oblations to the gods and Agni, and having discarded the vehicle, one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder; this is the purification for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite that a householder should perform.
He who performs a *śrāddha* in this manner, being mindful of the proper place and time,
shall deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage and himself attain the state of Śiva.
Those lords of their own people who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for those in a former stage of life remain in hell until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.

May that sprout of liberation— which arises from the seed of the true initiation born of the surging wave of the descent of power (śaktipāta) from the Lord of the Unrestrained (Uddāmeśvara), and which brings forth joy— be produced through faith, the nourishment of the field, meditative absorption, recitation, observances,
ritual performance, sacrifice, and vows.
He should protect [the mind] by means of the practice of the "antidote" (kaṇḍuka), beginning with the sphere that reaches to the end of life.

The lord Śrī Dharmaśiva, who acted as the sole cause for the cries of fearlessness, was the author of numerous compositions consisting of golden elephant-pearls for the ears of the great lords of poets;
his disciple Vimala [composed this] together with Śivendu, Yavana, Śrī Rājyapāla, and others.
Having performed a prostration to those who eat with virtuous conduct, I obtained this initiation.
117b) The fifth [chapter], the ritual for initiation in Vimalāvatī. [End of] 800 verses.
That in which all play— the entire range of effects beginning with earth, water, and fire, produced by the primordial power— exists,
and which at the end of the aeon and at the creation of reality becomes once again joined with the worlds and so forth; that is the eternal Linga.
Having bowed to the incomparable, stainless, primary, secondary, and even further secondary [deity],
he describes the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), which is the cause of liberation for those who enjoy the slopes of Mount Śiva’s peak.
The primary *liṅga* is without support, eternally manifest, and indivisible;
the secondary is the nature of sound (*nāda*), and the further secondary is Śadāśiva.
Because devotion resides in the individual, that word [of "Bhagavat"] is applied to whatever has been fashioned by us—
whether manifest or unmanifest, whether in the form of fear, or even in arrows, horses, and so forth.
The manifest [form] has a distinct head, neck, face, and the region from the navel downwards;
the unmanifest is characterized by four equal, circular portions.
The manifest and the unmanifest, the one adorned with four, three, and one lotus-like faces—
the Lord Sadāśiva, Bāṇa, Bāṇa, and even the god Bāṇa.
Because it was fashioned by him for him, it is therefore known as the Bāṇaliṅga;
like the Svayambhūliṅga, the Bāṇaliṅga is for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The fruit of establishing and worshipping [the deity] in this manner is said in the Liṅgārṇava to be a thousandfold greater than that of other [forms of] Vāṇaliṅgas.
Those which grow on the backs and flanks of rocks, bestowing all accomplishments, are said to be worthy of worship; they originate from rivers and springs.
Having approached a crystal liṅga, the sacrificer attains sons, long life, prosperity, servants, and whatever else is desired by the mind.

The manifestation of the phallic emblem (liṅga) brings about spiritual perfection, liberation, or wealth; it may even bestow external sovereignty upon a ruler. Therefore, one should practice the worship of the liṅga.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and likewise the two Aśvins,
having worshipped the Liṅga according to the prescribed rites, attained their most desired state.
One who possesses faith should worship an image fashioned from clay, ashes, cow dung, flour, molasses, or wood for the sake of consecration; such a person attains the highest state.
Whether made of stone, clay, wood, or metal, or even fashioned from a painted image, a Liṅga established with faith and devotion shall become the desired bestower of fruits.
The sacrificial fee for that linga is one hundred [gold pieces]; it is honored even by its installation in the north.
118b) The superior one is the best fruit indeed for embodied beings;
for the feet are the primary support of both the door and the heart.
The installation of that which is born from the eightfold aggregate is recorded as being fivefold.
Whatever [rite] such as the offering of *argha* occurs therein, it is included within that very [process].
The sacred seat (*pīṭha*) consists of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), while the Lord consists of the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*).
The consecration (*adhiṣṭheya*) of those two [the disciple and the deity] consists of the sacrifice accompanied by the cultivation of mantra;
it is the ritual for the attainment of the Lord, which is joined with the principles of vision (*dṛk*), action (*kriyā*), and stability (*pratiṣṭhā*).
The specific presence, according to the prescribed rule,
of the Supreme Pervasive One within the consecrated image— that is what constitutes installation (pratiṣṭhā) and the like.
That upon which the Brahma-stone and other elements extend for one *yojana* is the foundation;
its installation occurs on that pedestal (*pīṭha*) where the ritual procedures, such as the placement of the arrows and so forth, are performed.
The installation of great reciters (pāṭhakas) is established;
the installation of images, world-lingas (lokaliṅgas), and [other] lingas is performed by Śatakratu.
In the rite of raising [the image], it should be old and so forth; for a child, it should be joined with two doors.
Thus, there are five ways. Now, the protection of the ground is described:
the earth of the Brahmins and others is red, yellow, and likewise black.
Ghee, blood, cow urine, and liquor are respectively unwholesome for the sense of smell.
Even in the absence of the desired color and other qualities, one should effect the application of color and so forth using *darbha*, *śara*, *śakāśa*, and well-polished, resonant materials. (119a)
O Lord, in the east and in the north, may the earth everywhere be firm for those who float upon it.
Just as when a hole dug by the hand is filled and not even a single particle of earth remains [outside], so too is the earth,
tested by water, considered most excellent when it is level with the surface.
One should thoroughly purify the ground so that it is free from bones, charcoal, and other defilements,
by means of various types of plowing, digging, and the dwelling of herds of cattle and the like.
Where a river that formerly flowed eastward becomes filled with ant-hills and tangled weeds, it is inhabited by carnivorous beasts and birds.
There, one should cause [the ground] to be sprinkled with sesame seeds mixed with honey, gold, and the hundred-fold [substances].
Then, having performed the rites such as the establishment of the sacrifice according to the prescribed method, [one should proceed].

Having completed the ritual actions— such as the worship of the door and other elements in sequence, along with the offerings for the satisfaction of the deities— he should perform a thousand oblations throughout the day and night.
On a level ground that has been smeared with cow dung, one should purify the directions on the earth;
having performed the ritual of the site (vāstu), one should worship these deities, beginning with Indra, in a clockwise direction.
One should worship the full pitcher situated in the northeast compartment from the center;
then, like Śiva, one should thoroughly sprinkle the site with its waters.
Then, having worshipped Kuṣmāṇḍa and the others outside, one should protect against the Rākṣasas and Grahas;
thereafter, one should worship the sword, the earth, and so forth in the ten directions.
Likewise, one should cause the worship of Uddālaka and the others to be performed upon his cloth;
O Teacher, it should be done with honey-smeared *kundā* flowers by one who has been consecrated.
Then, one should cast the great storehouse toward the western direction with portions of earth;
subsequently, one should pour water from the pitcher into the pit and sprinkle the ground on all sides.
The Brahmin should have the second pitcher, the cloth, and so forth, covered;
then, standing in the east for a moment, he should sprinkle the marked stones with muddy water.
By circumambulating clockwise as far as the northeast corner while rotating the water-pot,
the formal acquisition of the ground through the gift [of the earth] shall be established in the presence of people.
Having worshipped Vāstu in the Āśivakumbha, one should place four lamps— white and so forth— with wicks, in a shallow bowl filled with ghee, positioned at its openings.
Through the persistence or destruction of that reality or unreality, one should indicate the gain or loss of the caste;
likewise, whether equal, inferior, or superior, it obstructs the previous abode and so forth.
By performing [the rite], one obtains a clay vessel and a temple or the like from the deity;
the height of both should be double [the width], and their respective widths should be diminished in sequence.
One should place his foot in front, behind, and on both sides; by means of the syllables *kha*, *hra*, and so forth,
there is entry into the sequence at the divided navel, or through the speaking of arrows at the undivided navel.
One should clear the ground for the purpose of the temple until reaching water or gravel;
or, for the excavation of the temple site, it should extend down to the knees or to the depth of a *vāṇaliṅga*.
In the house, one should contemplate the earth element as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) extending to half the height of the wind;
then, by means of one's own power, [one should contemplate] the knee, ending at the navel, the private parts, and the mouth.
Or rather, as long as there is purification of the ground, such as the moon, the speaker, the water for sipping (ācamana), and so forth—
this has also been stated for the sake of the abode in the *Bṛhadvirodhana* and other texts.
One should perform the rites for the armor, such as the *śilpācārya* and others, according to the rules stated by Piṅgala;
or likewise, during the laying of the foundation lines (*sūtrapāta*), one should perform the placement of the *svajasvaka* and other elements.

One should spread clear knowledge among people through means such as the *praśvekā* and protective charms (*varma*), using words, scratching, and various activities; yet, one should remain free from agitation at times.
Having touched that which is named with effort, one should listen to that which consists of beginning and end;
this has been described merely by way of direction—nearby, at the edge, or in the middle.
The tree of consciousness, the golden peak, the pearl, the jewel, and the wealth; the conch and the oyster shell—these are the death and immortality of the elements.
There, for the sake of all accomplishments, one should repeatedly perform the ritual of raising [the deity] at all times.
Having smeared the pit in the ground, one should worship the Vāstu deities with a hundred blades of kuśa grass.
Having scratched the ground and likewise sprinkled it with fragrant water, |||

One should worship the Earth, who has the Vedas as her ears, the Viśve-devas as her form, and who is adorned; she whose feet are the excavated pits, who is filled with the sky, and who possesses the power of the constructed pavilion.
The sacrifice is satisfied by the mantra; let him go to the bathing pavilion.
The pedestals for the temples and lingas, designated as *dharmādi*, should be made of stone;
they should be one *vitasti* in length, four fingers at the top, one finger high, and firm.

[The pillars] are made of wood, brick, stone, or earth; they are raised to the height of a *vasu* (eight units), measured by the hand, consisting of nine parts, and marked with symbols such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*).
All [the pedestals] should likewise be adorned with five lotuses or svastikas;
they should have a width equal to half the length of the hand, and a height of eight aṅgulas in the middle.
In a house as well, there are five types of ninefold arrangements according to the wood used for beauty:
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Pūrṇā, Ajitā, or Parājitā.
Vijaya, Maṅgala, Dhanya, Dharanī, Vāstu, Mānava, Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sunanda, and Puṣpadantaka.

Jaya, Vijaya by name, and likewise Kumbha and Uttara; these five, along with Vasu and Nidhi-kumbha, are as follows: [The names of the five are: Jaya, Vijaya, Kumbha, Uttara, and Vasunidhi-kumbha. Thus are the five.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Raktā are for the Pūrṇas; Vimalā and Utkaṭā are for Padma, Mahāpadma, Śākha, and Marakata-muḍraka.
Having bathed all the stones, which are smeared with unguents and covered with cloths,
one should place them upon the bed of the child in the sacrificial chamber, or alternatively, one may place two of them there.
In that which follows his teaching, flowers, sandalwood, and so forth are smeared [as offerings];
when the vital breaths have been withdrawn, one should contemplate the reality from Īśvara down to the earth through its own designations.
Having offered handfuls of flowers upon the upper, middle, and lower sections of the stones,
one should place the forms of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman above the pedestal.

Above that, having brought the presiding deities (mūrtipās) into proximity and having clearly visualized them, one should meditate upon the three sections (khaṇḍas) in sequence, either ninefold or fivefold.

The mind extends as far as the end of the heart; therefore, the limit is the mind alone. From the horse (the tip of the nose) to the edge of the earth, this is the state of the Self consisting of the Śiva-vidyā.
Or else, one may perform the three principles (*tritattva*) within the mass of knowledge (*jñānapuñjaka*) at the end of all ritual actions;
or it may be performed upon the central stone, or even upon other [stones].
The union with the single form [of the deity], the meditation on the principles (*tattva*), and so forth, are as previously described.
Prior to that, there is the satisfaction of the principles, the touch of purity, the recitation of mantras (*japa*), and so on.
In each of the three realities, one should subsequently prepare [the offerings] joined with jewels and the like,
filled with clarified butter and honey, and consecrated with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having worshipped the presiding deities of the directions from the copper pitcher, [one should proceed].
One should perform the oblations in their presence, sequentially by the respective owners;
one should likewise contemplate the presiding deities for all the stone slabs as well.
With smiling faces, possessing the luster of pure gold, bearing the forms of knowledge,
and adorned with various beautiful ornaments, they then [perform] the rite for the purification of the site and so forth.
One should offer oblations starting from fifty and ending at one hundred with the root mantra, or until the completion of the rite;
having thus measured out the temple, one should fashion the entire Vastu deity.
One should draw this four-petaled lotus as before using sixty-four squares;
having placed two *vaṃ* syllables in the corners, one should lay out twelve cords from the corners.
One should worship those two-footed and six-footed beings there as the *vāstu* (site-deity) according to the rule;
for through neglect in worship, [the world] perished during the interval of the Cākṣuṣa Manu.
A terrible and most extraordinary being, composed of darkness, indeed came into existence;
the immortals stood there, having bound him firmly with bamboos and ropes.

Indeed, in that body of Nandikeśvara, there are two channels carrying the individual soul (āṇava), which are inverted and shaped like demons; they are the upward-moving path and the body-consciousness.
122a) During the worship, one should contemplate the site (vāstu) as having its head at the bottom and its body extended; it is a man adorned with ornaments, facing downwards.
With the *brahmāṇī* [drum] as his mouth, the *piṇḍapādī* as his head, and the *apavaktṛ* and *kathatadvat* as his neck;
bearing a pair of *koṇa* [cymbals] as his two arms, that *jayāditya* is a *yugmaka* [pair].
The meanings of the words *diti* and *parjanya* constitute that *yugmaka*.
Indra and the others [are situated] in the pairs of directions starting from the east; in the two directions, there is a pair of Rakshasas.
Mitra, Viṣasvanta, Aruṣa, and those known as Adakṣiṇa; then Roga, Pūśa, the two Jānus, Marīci, and Avani-bhṛt.
Jaghanya, vitatha, śoṣa, and the others are thus worshipped for the benefit of the site;
Brahmā is in the center on four squares, and Marīci is in the east on six squares.
Sāvitrī is below Sūryavṛddha; Antaka is in the two squares [occupied by] Vahnikoṣṭhaga; Indrā and Upendrā are at every step on the southern side of the six squares.
Furthermore, Valabhadra stands upon the mud in the southwest;
Rudra and Kārtika are in the west, and thereafter in two adjacent compartments in the northwest.
In the north are Meru, Ṛṣabha, and Malaya;
this Īśāna is the lord of half a square (padārddha), while Parjanya and Kāśyapa occupy one square (pada).
Indra, Savitṛ, Dharma, and Kāma are situated in the eastern direction;
Ākāśa and Agni are in the south-eastern corner, traveling from one step to another.
Pūṣan, Dharmāṅgāraka, Yama, Nārada, and Bhṛṅgin;
Then, in the southern row, in the half-cell of the Rakṣas, there is the one called Mṛga;
and in the western half is Piṇḍa, according to the mention of Śālaṅkāyana.
Then Ānanda, Mahārka, Garuḍa, Ura, and Aruṇa are in the [southeastern] quarter; Rāhu and Śanaiścara are in the western direction and the northwest, as before.
The two wings were fashioned by Vāsuki and Viśvakarman;
the tail was fashioned by Kuvera, and the head by Ananta and the others from the waters.
Īśāna, Vyarakī, Vidārī, Putanā, Pāparākṣasī,
Skanda, Yamajambha, and Pilipiccha are said to be stationed in the cardinal directions.
Thus, those who call themselves reciters [of mantras], having failed to worship these deities residing in the site (vāstu) with sacrificial offerings, fall among the animals or even into hell.

He who performs the rites of conciliation and so forth against that Asura who acts in opposition [should do so] after having worshipped, with faith and in due order, the deities residing in the site (vāstu).
On all auspicious days as well, one should perform the ritual actions from beginning to end;
this is declared to be for a permanent dwelling, and also for a temporary one in some cases.
In the months beginning with Bhādrapada, his head faces east;
in those beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, his head faces south; in those beginning with Phālguna, he faces west; and in those beginning with Jyeṣṭha, the Lord indeed faces north.
The house with a boar's face should be placed on the lap of him who reclines on his left side;
otherwise, it must not be done by one who desires his own welfare.
Alternatively, one should prepare the site for the purpose of a house using eighty-one squares;
therein, the lines consist of three squares and six squares, forming nine compartments.
The two shoulders are in the middle; Brahmā always occupies nine squares.
Marīci and the others occupy six squares, while Āpa and the others occupy two cells.
All those beginning with Īśa are single-word [mantras], and those beginning with Carakapāda are from the Vākya [text];
all those beginning with Ekāśīliya and Aśurāra consist of sixty-four words.
One should worship Durgā in ancient ruins, cities, towns, villages, and hamlets;
on beds, seats, and palanquins; and in both movable and immovable dwellings.

In places of accomplishment, in monasteries, mansions, sacrifices, and the like; in [mantras] such as *kha* and *hram*; in step-wells, wells, ponds, and the like; and in forests, mountains, and so forth.
Among all those mentioned and unmentioned, there is then the hundred-pada site-plan;
by the mention of the abodes of Brahmā and the others, as well as the portions of Candra and the rest, it is thus established.
One should worship the planets and spirits with offerings of water and grain;
one should always worship the twelve great Maruts upon the walls and other such surfaces.
Alternatively, one should offer all things, such as vajras and so forth, outside the field (*kṣetra*). Then, having offered three oblations (*āhuti*) for each deity in due order:
Having offered an oblation to the spirits (bhūtas), one should place the stone at an auspicious moment;
in the central pit, one should install the Śakti and the water-pot known as Ananta.
Having established the root-mantra mounted on the letter *la* right there upon a stone slab,
one should [place] the eight jars, beginning with the Svatantra, in the directions starting from the East and so forth, in due order.
Once the powers have been deposited into the bright [deities], one should deposit the mantras of Śakra and the others;
for the image-protectors, the stones such as Rāṣi and Nandā should be placed first with the syllable LŪM.
One should place them upon the walls so that they stand in the middle of the wall; in the intermediate and cardinal directions, one should likewise place Dharmarāja and the others.
In the [mandalas] beginning with Subhadra, the four goddesses beginning with Nandā are considered to be in the directions starting from the southeast;
likewise, those beginning with Ajitā are in the east and so forth, while those beginning with Jayā are honored in their own respective positions.
Having placed Brahmā above and the all-pervading Maheśvara,
one should contemplate the future path situated within the palace of space.
Having again offered the oblation to the spirits (bhūtavalī), one should worship the remover of obstacles caused by weapons;
this is done even upon the five stones placed atop the ocean-vessel (samudrakalaśa).
One should place the full stone (pūrṇāśilā) in the center, and then [the others] in the cardinal and intermediate corners in due order;
likewise, Nandā and the others should be placed upon the lotuses and so forth, while the Lord himself is in the primary directions.
The four intermediate states are proclaimed as the true nature of the Mothers:
Oṃ! You are Pūrṇā, the Great Vidyā, characterized by the gathering of all things.
Perform all [the rites] here in their entirety; let the essence (rasa) proceed in due order.
Oṃ! I establish you, Nandana and Nandinī, as a pair, right here.
Remaining joyful in this palace as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure,
grant to embodied beings their desired lifespan, prosperity, and bliss, O son of Vasiṣṭha!
Therefore, O Kāśyapī, you must always diligently perform protection over this palace:
"Oṃ! O Bhadrā, may there always be welfare for the worlds!"
O Goddess who bestows longevity, O Goddess Kāmadā, and O Śrīpadā, be ever present! Om Jayatrā, O Goddess, remain forever; you have been installed by me.
O Mistress, be ever present for victory and prosperity with the Bhārgavas;
Oṃ, O auspicious one, who destroys the defect of emptiness and bestows success and liberation!
O you who abide in all places at all times in this form of the moon,
having accepted the sacrificial fee in all sacrifices, one should release the rite.
Having firmly filled the excavation, one should then perform the binding of the pedestal (pīṭhabandha).
There too, having worshipped the Vāstu deity, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (jagdhya).
The section on the precepts.
Now, the time and other factors conducive for the installation of deities are described.
In that regard, O knower of the gods, when liberation has been accomplished, it results in the liberation of all deities.
During the Caragna and other such periods, when the sun has entered its northern course (udagmārga), [the deity] is to be worshipped;
however, during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), worship is to be performed for three years, as beyond that it brings danger.
Having first performed some auspicious act, it later becomes the bringer of misfortune;
when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu, the subjects are afflicted by Indra and others through speech and so forth.
The prince is greatly afflicted and fears for his daughters;
likewise, a very great and terrible wrath arises among the kings.
The destruction of the doer and constant sorrow become terrible within the house;
one should engage in the worship of the auspicious Umā and Gaṅgā according to the words of Svarasvāmī.

On the first day of the three-fold causal conjunction (*kāraṇa-tritaya*), when there is the rising of a planet that is neither malefic nor a preceptor [in the *kāraṇa* system], the sixth lunar day is not empty; it is drinkable provided it is free from the forbidden days of the week and so forth.
Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Śatabhiṣā, Śravaṇa, the three Uttarās,
Rohiṇī, and Anurādhā are auspicious for stable undertakings and great success.
The Ascendant, Leo, the Staff (Sagittarius), Taurus, Virgo, Libra,
Aquarius, and Scorpio— these are the best signs according to Śrī Sundara.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Hastā, Puṣyā,
Śravaṇā, Punarvasu, and Dhaniṣṭhā— these are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa.
Citrā, Śravaṇā, and Uttarā-Āṣāḍhā are for the king; Uttarā-Bhādrapadā and Aśvinī are for the Vaiśya; and Svātī and Pūrvaphālgunī are for the Śūdra.
Or, at the crest of that commonality of the one of excellent complexion,
a pavilion should be constructed in front, leaving a space of five finger-breadths on the ground.
From one shrine to another, or from one flight of stairs to the next, there should be ten varieties;
for the liṅgas, starting from one and ending at nine finger-breadths, they increase by two each time.
From the twelve directions up to the twenty-sixth and twenty-eighth,
as before, there is a half-altar for the purpose of bathing, which is provided in the ritual procedure.
In that [mandala], the piercing (vedha) is performed with two, three, or four [units], and it is considered inferior or superior;
there may be a single archway (toraṇa) facing the east, or there may also be four archways.
In the northeast or the north-eastern direction, there should be either a principal [shrine] or even a pavilion;
for a liṅga measuring one, two, or three cubits, [the dimensions] are equal to eight, ten, or twelve [cubits].
The pavilions (maṇḍapas) are four cubits [in size], or they may increase by two cubits each;
they are Ghanoghora, Virāja, Artha, Kāñcana, Kāma, and Rāmaka.
125b) He established other names such as Suveśa, Urdhvaroman,
and Rodakṣa; and [the measurements] of the liṅgas and human forms, including those with intervals, starting from the hand.
There are twenty-seven [types] with eleven syllables, increasing by two each time;
they occur at the beginning of *vāṇa*, *roha*, *amya*, and *aja*, or they are well-illuminated by the sun (*arka*).
In the Piṅgalāmata, it is stated that for a domestic liṅga in front of a house, one should set aside the space between the door-posts,
and the pavilion (maṇḍapa) for the recitation of mantras should measure sixteen cubits.
The extensive and vast confusion consists of three great serpent-pavilions;
fifty-five [units] have been declared, except in some cases where they are five cubits less.
Candra, Agni, and Arcimān are the three pavilions for the Bhūtakaras;
they are distinguished as inferior, middling, and superior according to their great supernatural powers.
The best [measurement] begins from sixteen cubits; for inferior [measures], there is no calculation of prosperity.
Just as a pavilion of sixteen cubits is used for all rites, so it is here.
A small hut for the purpose of the residence pavilion should be screened from the covered area;
for the sake of utensils, it should be situated in the east and protected by the western direction.
The pavilion for the mandala may be equal in size to the root pavilion;
however, according to the rules for the tilaka of the eldest [disciple] and others, there should be ten, eight, or nine divisions.

126a) A pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed with equal and well-set pillars, provided with arches and other ornaments; one should make it of bricks, measuring one hundred times its width, and having a low roof.
Above the four-pillared pavilion, it is covered by five layers consisting of six [materials]:
namely, with firm, unbroken bamboo, and with branches of trees and the like.
There should be four pillars at the corners, two on each side of the doors,
and other pillars as desired for beauty, starting from a height of two cubits.
In the center is a four-cornered altar, with four pillars at the corners;
these are eight finger-breadths in height, each reduced by one thumb-breadth.
One should increase the measurement by one-quarter both in width and in height, even in the intervals;
the altar (vedī) is obtained by dividing the maṇḍapa by eight and taking the central square.
The remaining width of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is half that of the great altar (vedi); they are square on all sides, with a length and width equal to that of the linga.
Above the hand (hasta), the altars (vedī) increase by six finger-breadths (aṅgula) at each stage;
leaving a space of one foot (pāda) between them, there are nine or five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
Three [kuṇḍas] are for the purpose of inducing sleep; one is before [the fire]; and another is either in the northeast or the southeast for the disciple.
For the installation of the Unmanifest (Avyakta), the pit should be circular and located in all directions.
Then, during enjoyment, liberation, nourishment, and digestion, the doorways are especially [active];
in the manifest, the four ages, the eight-angled, the unmanifest, and the unmanifest-unmanifest, there is the turning back of Śrī.
He is free from fear in all directions and intermediate points, and is devoid of pride and the like.
One should offer these— quadrangular, triangular, crescent-shaped, triangular, circular, hexagonal, lotus-shaped, and octagonal— in order from the east to the northeast.
For the subjugation of enemies, for tormenting foes, for killing, for inciting disease and anger,
for longevity, prosperity, nourishment, and fortitude, and for the increase of fortune and intelligence.
These are prescribed in sequence in the directions for the attainment of all desires; the ninth is to be known as situated in the center of the east, remaining as before.
Half of the Vedas (four) are indeed circular, while the eight corners are in the cardinal directions according to their form; all others are square, or alternatively, they are said to be circular.
The hand [is placed] upon the handless; the others, along with their limbs, are understood as pairs.
Having written the sun, the king, and the letter *cha*, one should place the letter *ya* eightfold.

A finger-breadth (aṅgula) multiplied by twelve is the best, while that multiplied by ten is middling and inferior; this is the measurement for the fingers and joints of the Lord of Śavarī, known as Prādeśa.
The *vyāma* and *prādeśa* are measured by the thumb and the forefinger; the *tāla* and *arati* by the middle finger; and the *vitasti* and *karnaka* by the ring finger.
127a) In the Śiva-āgamas and other traditions, however, a *vitasti* is measured by the span of the hand;
whereas in the *aiṣṭika* (ritual concerning fire-altars), a *vitasti* is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) measured from the little finger.
A cubit consists of twenty-four finger-breadths; a *rantī* is twenty-one [finger-breadths];
a *kiṣṇu* is two *rantīs*; and a *nārāyaṇa* is four hundred and four [finger-breadths].
Four cubits (hasta) make one bow-staff (dhanur-daṇḍa); two pairs of nālikās [make] one dhanus;
two thousand dhanus make one krośa; and twice that [krośa] is a gavyūti.
O best of the Kośalas, eight thousand *dhanus* make one *yojana*;
it is traditionally held that [the width] is six, seven, or eight *yavas*, or measured by four *śatadhūs*.
When measuring the three [types of] measures— inferior, middling, and superior— the inferior consists of three *aṅgulas* of sesame seeds, while the superior consists of eight barley grains (*yava*).
Alternatively, one may divide either the sacrificer’s own hand or twenty-four [finger-breadths].
Or it may be joined with four finger-breadths, according to one's own hand as it naturally is.
The thumb of the eldest [finger] measures twenty-four [units];
one should cause a perfectly level sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be made on the head [of the altar], with its horizontal and vertical girdles (mekhalā) being equal.
In the *Śrīskanda*, *Vijaya*, and other such texts, however, the visualization is not otherwise:
one finger-breadth outside the neck and one finger-breadth on the left side of the neck.
Its girdle is in the shape of a bowl; it is equal in width and height.
As before, its fivefold nature is formed by increments of two, three, two, one, and four finger-breadths respectively.
From the point called the girdle [the *mekhalā*] to the navel, the width is three and a half finger-breadths;
from the base to the tip, the stalk is one finger-breadth in height at its lower part.

Or, they may be raised as high as the sky; when the girdles are shaped like the leaf of a *svastha* tree, the height of the thumb [of the handle] should increase by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) at each successive half-unit of its curvature.
The shape of the womb-pit (yonikuṇḍa) is indeed that; in its center, there is a single-aṅgula mark.
The navel of the eastern, western, and southern pits faces north, while those of others do not.
For the remaining [deities], the pit should be located in the northeast corner, facing east;
it should measure twelve or twenty-five finger-breadths and possess three girdles.
In the *śata* [measure], it is called five hundred *muṣṭi*-hands; in the *sahasra*, it is one hundred;
in the *ayuta*, it is ten hands; in the *lakṣa*, it is four; but in the *niyuta*, it is six.
In the case of ten million oblations (*koṭihoma*), [the altar] should be eight cubits; one should not make it larger than that.
With the syllables *raṃ* and *praṃ*, [one measures] with fire-purified fingers, and likewise with fingers [measured] by the fist.
The first [section] consists of two, one, and four cubits; the second consists of three, two, and one cubits;
the third consists of two, three, and two cubits; and the fourth, known as the *turya*, consists of eight, six, and two cubits.

The girdle is desired to have eight, six, five, or one [strands], and the yoni is as in the case of the elephant-stable (hāstika). It is also praised when accompanied by the Rudras (eleven), the Aṣṭakas (eight), and the Ṣaṭs (six), or with eight, ten, and eight [units] respectively.
128a) Or else, there may be an increase of two finger-breadths at a time in both width and length;
the fire-pits for the mantras beginning with Indra have not been mentioned here due to their extensive nature.
To the Bodhi tree of the Vaṭa and Udumbara, to the Pūjāstāraṇa Mūrti,
and to the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees situated in the east and other directions.
One of these should be taken when available;
namely, the *nyagrodha*, the *palāśa*, the *udumbara*, or the *siddhaka*.
The Aśvattha, Vāpī, Mādhūka, and Bilva are to be worshipped in sequence;
these are specified for the eight gates, being fresh and capable of delivering [the devotee] across [samsara].
In the directions of the Lord (East), Fire (South-East), and the other corners, there are three doors facing east;
in the West, South-West, and North-West, there are three facing west.
In the north, the northern face [is directed] toward the north, and the right face toward the south;
all the arches (toraṇas), moreover, may be rectangular, square, or circular.
The [measures] for the junior [disciples] are five, six, and seven cubits;
for the middling and the superior, they are increased by eight and sixteen finger-breadths respectively.
The excavation for the smallest of the archways (toraṇas) measures one cubit;
for the three situated in the middle, it is increased by four finger-breadths (vedāṅgulas).
The excavation for the three types of stupas, beginning with the *tuttama*, should be known as one and a half *karas*;
or it may be determined by a fifth part of the circumference of the base, or according to the available space.
128b) On the branch [of the hand], the distance between the fingers should be one finger-breadth in height, or even more;
the breadth of the two [hands] or of the forehead should be six finger-breadths.
In another [tradition], it is five cubits in measure, with an increase of two or one finger-breadth;
the *śalya* is eight fingers at the beginning and sixteen fingers at the end.
The side-ribs of that [pedestal] have a width of one-fifth [of the total];
their projection should be two finger-breadths, increasing by one finger-breadth in sequence.
In the center are Śrī, a svastika, a lotus, and a blue water-lily for Lakṣmī and Keśava;
the supporting pillars are equal to the arches, and the altars are eightfold and very lofty.
At the doors, plantain trees are desired, as well as water-jars containing barley;
