the pedestal should be twice the height of Brahmā and made from a milk-producing tree according to its width.
It should have four sides, be marked with a lotus, and be eighteen finger-breadths in height;
or else, its height may be double its width.
The auspicious seat for the Kanyāśās is twice as wide in some cases;
for others, it increases by four finger-breadths in successive order.
In the Rauravottara, three pedestals are prescribed for the nine [deities];
the banners should be seven cubits long, and the flags likewise five cubits.
The banners, made of nine cubits of cloth and twenty fingers in width,
are considered by the sages to be of the highest quality when measured in rows by the digits from one to nine.
The width should be two cubits, or in the case of the most excellent [temples], three cubits.
Thereafter, the banners and flags stand with a width of two cubits, then decreasing by half successively, until they have a width of only one cubit.
In some places, there are forms with mouths two cubits long and a width of only one cubit;
they are yellow, bearing the weapon of Indra (the thunderbolt), and are eastern banners and small flags.
In the southeast, at Nāradeśvara, they are smoke-colored, pale, or the color of fire;
in the south, they are saline, black, or auspiciously resembling the color of smoke.
In the southwest (Nairṛta), they have a golden luster, yet are blue-black and emit a foul odor;
in the west (Vāruṇa), they are pale-white, bright white, or like the color of fresh blood.
O Goddess, in the southeast they are white; in the southwest, green; in the northwest, yellow; and in the northeast, red and resembling clouds, O Yāmalā.
Therein, for Brahmā, [the colors] are red in the east and blue in the southwest; in the center they are white or variegated, while the goddesses are delighted by their respective colors and so forth.

In pacification (śānti), all [planets] are very white; in prosperity (saubhāgya), they are like vermilion; in subduing (māraṇa), they are like collyrium. In auspiciousness (śubha), they have the luster of turmeric.
The staffs should enter the hand of the banners measuring five cubits;
the streamers should enter at the fifth [mark], measuring ten cubits.
One should arrange garlands of mango sprouts and the like in such a way that they are beautiful.
Then, from within that [area], with fabrics, powders, and ointments,
a canopy was fashioned above the altar at the edge of the pavilion in some places.
From the square [mandala], one should place the jars and the pit according to their respective numbers;
upon the head [of the deity] is the jar of Sleep (Nidrā), while Śiva’s jar and the vardhanī vessel are for the weapon (astra).
Joined with a cavity for the destruction of urine and so forth,
it is twenty-five finger-breadths in thickness and twenty-seven finger-breadths in height.
The mouth of the pitcher should be eight finger-breadths wide, and its circumference ninety finger-breadths;
even if it is reduced by one-eighth of this measure, it serves as the enemy-pipe for the *vardhinī*.
Or else, both [the base and the top] should be made firm as is aesthetically pleasing, but not with protruding parts and so forth;
they should be eight finger-breadths high and equal in length and width.
In the worship of Acyuta, the vessels should have eight long handles made of refined iron;
or alternatively, they should be five units high, eight units wide, and twelve units long.
Then, as before, one should perform the great rite with Vāmadeva joined with the staff;
this is for the sake of seizing the two arrows, or for the purification of the lineage on the long staff.
To the west of the staff, one should place a water-filled cup;
likewise, in a large vessel, there should be a square excavation made according to its beauty.
The sacrificial fuel, born from sacrificial trees, should be blameless and of even thickness.
Even the smallest [fuel stick] should not be thicker than a span; they should be equal in size to a prādeśa.
[The recommended woods are: Arka, Palāśa, Khadira, Vapā, Mārga, and Pippala.
For the pacification of the Sun and other deities, one should offer one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-seven oblations of Udumbara wood, sacrificial grass (samidh), Dūrvā, and Kuśa.
Twenty-eight blades of kusha grass, each individually shorter than that, grown in a pure place, glossy, neither too thin nor too long, should be taken.

The parrot’s shadow, the *sāgramūla* trees, the *saptaparṇa* not grown from seven seeds, and those born on a path or on a funeral pyre— even in the cremation ground— serve for the libation of the ancestors.
In the funeral pyre, the food offerings, and the rice balls, seven blades of *kuśa* grass should indeed not be used;
rather, well-dried, auspicious fuel fit for sacrifice should be employed.
For the purpose of pacification, one should offer a bilva leaf from a sinful tree along with honey, milk, and ghee; in the absence of these, sesame seeds should be offered to Vāyu.

The vessel for the highest [offering] should be made of fifty palas of gold, that for the middling of half that amount, and for the lowest of twenty palas; it should be provided with its mechanical fittings.
The sacrificial vessel for the *homadravya* and other offerings should not be made of ivory and the like, nor of conch or mother-of-pearl;
likewise, it may be made of gold, silver, and so forth, shaped like Mount Meru, a bull, a tortoise, or a lotus.
The earth is the back of a tortoise, and the lotus is sometimes made of eight metals.
Sandalwood, sesame oil and the like, a vessel, lamps with bowls,
a pair of golden lids, or silver ones that hold the external honey.
For the fulfillment of the fruit, the application of oil to the feet is prescribed;
for the sake of Lakṣmī and for the purpose of the madhuparka, two golden rods [are required].
In Āśiketa, there are three, two, and one [liṅgas] respectively, beginning with the Jyeṣṭha-liṅga;
likewise, the excellent collection of materials is always filled with the eightfold arghya offering.
The vessel for eating should be provided with a lid, free from cracks,
and equipped with two supports for placing it over the fire.
He [held] a firmly supported stalk and a well-prepared vessel of clarified butter;
there was also a bell with a beautiful sound, a lamp, and a garland placed upon the balance and other implements.
The *ārātrika* lamp is well-constructed, provided with nine wicks,
and consists of four copper vessels with lids, fashioned from the sight of the *sthālī* [offering-pot].
He burned incense from copper vessels; his livelihood was new. He possessed household utensils made of copper and likewise copper tilakas.
Furthermore, for the purpose of bathing during a sacrifice, one should use a small portion of *vṛtsva*;
for the rite of the copper jar (*tāmraghaṭī*) on that path, it should be combined with turmeric and oil.
Many pairs of mirrors made of bell-metal and bronze, as well as many yokes.
At Kumbhāghātaraṇa, there are various offerings of six kinds of food;
and a couch with a rug, a woolen coverlet, and two pillows, covered with a white upper cloth.
The eyes, the headband, the chowries, the two swords, the two shields, the sword-belt,
the two small cloths, the two lotuses, and the fruit accompanied by the pair of moons.
A cloth made of various fabrics is called *apaṃṭī*; *jalapatraka* is a water-leaf;
*madhūka* is a type of collyrium; *kāṇḍapaṭa* is a screen-curtain; and *kāṇḍadhanu* is a sword-blade bow.
For the purpose of the mandala, one requires the ritual materials, such as a hide from a deer or similar animal,
a lotus leaf produced from a sheath, and many sacred threads made of muñja grass.
The musk-deer, the water-jar, the tall plantain tree, the swing, the pedestal, and the stone;
the mortar and pestle, the auspicious grain, the broom, and the dye-pot, and so forth.
The white-staffed umbrella, the household utensils,
the sacrificial rice, the red thread, the ritual implements, and the sandals.
Iron tongs, bamboo tubes,
arrows with feathers, the application of yellow pigment (rocanā) and the like, conch-shell vessels, and vessels made of gold and other such [precious metals] are inauspicious for holding [food].
A bed, a cloth for the hips, a yoga-cloth, a head-cloth, and so forth— these are possible;
there should be fifty-five sandals with ten successive fruits at their ends.
The Kumbha and other [vessels] belong to those with different sectarian marks (liṅga), and the Vardhinī is for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
For a stable linga measuring one cubit, the bathing pedestals (guṇḍikās) should be eight, sixteen, or twenty finger-breadths [in height],
corresponding respectively to the inferior, middling, and superior types of eyes.
With eight *gaḍḍukas* increased by one *kara*, there would be one *prastha*;
with an increase by fruits, there would be a *mūrti*, according to the number of *piṇḍas*.
Those who recite the *saṃhitās*, those who recite the *śastras*, and those who chant the hymns (*stotra*)—
they are exceedingly skillful in that regard, and even a small amount [of their practice] is sufficient for the propitiation of Yakṣiṇī.
For each pit, there should be an arghya-vessel, a side-dish, and implements such as the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles;
these should be made from trees such as the *śrīparṇī*, *panasa*, *aśoka*, *śāka*, or *asvattha*.
With a middle face, a wide back, and roots of the fangs shaped like lotus buds, they should be made starting from eight barley-corns and increasing up to twenty-six finger-breadths.
Alternatively, for the sake of aversion [to the enemy], one may decrease by one, two, or three [finger-breadths] at each point;
or in some cases, the arms may be as measured in the Gaurī Tantra, where the śruva-ladle and the arm are thirty-six finger-breadths in length.
For the sake of increasing the purity of the income, one should add a single auspicious element;
at its base, there is a jar nine finger-breadths in circumference and two kalās in height.

In the *Vṛhadvidyā-purāṇa* as well, it is stated that the staff, which emerges from its mouth, is seven finger-breadths in circumference and equal in length to nine finger-breadths when measured around its base.
Six or seven [fingers] on the pitcher, and likewise with the neck-ring.
Indeed, it is twenty finger-breadths in length, with the mouths of the crocodiles and other figures at the bottom;
in the best [quality], it is one finger-breadth more, in the middling two finger-breadths more, and in the lowest three finger-breadths more.
By increasing the middle one in this manner, three ladles of equal size are formed;
these are used for rites performed for specific desires, occasional rites, and daily obligatory rites, according to Śrī Nārāyaṇa Kaṇva.
The secondary altar (upavedī) should be twice as long as this [main altar] and four finger-breadths higher than its back;
in the middle of this, the auspicious Lakṣmī, with four limbs and facing forward, is beneficial.
On its two outer sides are two lions, exalted in their prowess;
the altar is [constructed] with seven or eight rays according to the measurement of the largest finger and so forth.
Immediately after spreading the Veda [mantra] over it, one should dig three finger-breadths into its center.
There, however, according to the respective measurements, it should be filled with four, two, or three *palas*;
it may be circular, square, or adorned with an eight-petaled lotus.

Therefore, in a circular pit with a rim one barley-corn high, one should place a lotus seed-vessel (karṇikā) that is slightly elevated, provided with a seed-syllable, and accompanied by the syllables *sa-īśa-dā-śiva*.
The altar is variegated, and at its edge, on the back, there are ten pitchers joined together;
the middle of the two thumbs should be seven finger-breadths in length.
The face is as wide as the altar, measuring one mātrā of a horse's hoof;
it is six barley-corns in the best and other [sizes], according to the *Durgāhṛdaya-ḍāmara*.
In front of that, the width [of the pedestal] should be one-third of its length, or equal to the diameter of the *golaka*;
the altar (*vedī*) at the front tip of the mouth of the flute should have a width of one-third [of the total].

Having brought out the little finger from behind and having drawn it forward, the exit should be made with an iron rod; this should be done for one whose mouth is wide open and who possesses equal splendor.
The *śruva* ladle is made of wood, its source being the *śrī* tree;
it is excellent, prescribed by one's own scripture, and may be twenty-four finger-breadths in length.
It should be as thick as a grain of rice, four finger-breadths in height, and half of that in its lower portion; in the middle, it should be determined by proportion to the thread.
The smooth *ūrṇā* of Śrī Caṇḍabhairava extends from its tip to its base; the staff should be like a curved horn, and the *syāṇu* should be three finger-breadths in circumference.

There, a single depression in the shape of a deer's footprint, two fingers deep, exists; within it is a pit capable of holding a *karṣa* of water, and inside that is a bridge leading to the Lord of Elephants (*Gajendra*).
On the back of two jars placed together, a staff twenty finger-breadths long should be fixed;
alternatively, it may be made of guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter, or even of sandalwood and other suitable woods.
133a) A mass of flowers with their stalks removed is what I have prescribed for the collection of flowers;
camphor, saffron rubbed [with water], and sandalwood are for the ointment.
Sesame, barley, and other grains for the purpose of the *homa* sacrifice, as well as *gorocanā* and honey for the bath,
or five tawny cows, should be placed at the four gates within the pavilion.
From their milk and so forth, one should perform the necessary rites, such as the cooking of sacrificial porridge (caru),
or other substances such as ash, cow dung, cow urine, curd, ghee, sugar, and the like.
One should take the well-ground inner bark of the Udumbara, Vaṭa, and Āmra trees,
as well as a decoction of all types of earth, excluding that which contains hair or fragments of broken pottery.
From the center of the field of Dvīpāvṛṣa, from the two riverbanks, from a mountain,
from the Śarāsuta tīrtha, and from Valākāmṛdu— eight handfuls of earth were well-dried and ground into powder.

O King, earth from a cow-pen, from a crossroads, from a palace gate, and even from a boar’s lair— these twelve types of earth, when combined with the previously mentioned earth from Govinda, are [to be used].
Water fragrant like sacred fords, likewise seasonal water, the eight kinds of fruits,
all medicinal herbs, gold, gems, crops, flowers, fruits, and water.
One hundred and eight varieties of flowers, including those from the Śāśṛṅga plant,
as well as milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar, constitute the fivefold sweetness.
With sesame, rice, and the various body-parts [of the deity], along with *kṛśara* mixed with jaggery;
one hundred and eight jars for the bath, and likewise five jars.
Sahasraśravadhārā, the two excellent jars (kalaśau), the hundred medicinal herbs (oṣadhī), Sahadevā, Valā, Pāṭhā, Lakṣmaṇā, and Śatāvarī.
Vijayā, balāvṛddhi, guḍavṛddhi, and suvarcalā are separately prescribed for the purpose of bathing; and siddhārtha and others are for protection.
The powders of wheat, barley, and bilva are also used for drying;
likewise, local earth for scrubbing, or brick powder such as that of *vajra* and other minerals.
Vaiḍūrya, vajra, padmarāga, puṣparāga, and pearls, along with exceedingly deep blue sapphire and sūryakānta— these are the eight [jewels], each consisting of eight [units].
Uśīra, śaṅkhinī, kuṣṭha, viṣṇukrāntā, śatāvarī,
śrīkhaṇḍa, aguru, and red sandalwood constitute the collection of medicinal herbs.
Gold, silver, brass, copper,
tin, lead, iron, and steel— these are the eight metals (loha) in the *Kāṣṭhakūṣṭaka*.
Mercury, sulphur, fire (cinnabar), realgar, mica, orpiment,
talc, realgar, gold, and pyrites— these are the eight minerals.
Barley, sesame, mung beans, green gram, kidney beans, wheat, and raw rice; nīvāra, āhrīhaya, and uṣṭrtha—these are considered auspicious when they are not otherwise [prepared]. 134a)
Eight handfuls make one *kuñci*, and eight *kuñcis* make one *laṃ*.
Four *puṣkalas* make one *āḍhaka*, and four of those make a *droṇa* and so forth;
thus, when the five sets of eight have been obtained, one should take up the five substances.
When there is a lack of all [materials], such as necklaces, bracelets, golden palm-trees, or even barley, then one may use silver or mercury in the rituals.
Just as the ghaṭikā revolves at the gateway of time when the hour is established,
so too, upon completion, the six supreme words— daṃ, lā, ra, mā, gu, and ru— are elevated.
One should immerse it in water, having inserted inside it a copper needle twelve *vistā* wide and four *aṅgula* long, with a gold *māṣaka* weight at its tip.
When sixty *daṇḍas* are complete, it is called a *padādaṇḍa*; thus, a day and night (*ahorātra*) consists of sixty *daṇḍas*, occurring in two twilights and two dawns.
Eight kṛṣṇalas weighing ten māṣas constitute one śāstra-śuvarṇaka; two karṣas make one śuvarṇa, and four karṣas become one pala.
During the bathing, consecration, worship, and installation rites, one should offer garments in pairs; this applies also to the head, the hands, the stone, the altar, and the bull.
With earrings, crowns, necklaces, seals, armlets, and bracelets; with golden sacred threads, bangles, villages, jewels, and vehicles.
One who lacks wealth should honor the preceptor with excellent offerings;
likewise, one should honor the Brahmins, such as those representing the deities (mūrtidhara), with offerings slightly less than those given to the preceptor’s feet.

One should cause the chief artisan to enter like a crow quarreling with a sparrow, and likewise others according to their strength; one should not admit those born of other stages of life (āśrama) into the performance of rites belonging to another.

Then, one should install the archways (toraṇas) named Śānti, Bhūti, Bala, and Ārogya, starting from the eastern direction with the deities Mūrti, Yava, and so forth, at the doors of the Śāntikalā and others.
Then, to the right of those [archways], one should place Nandī and Pālī.
Bhṛṅgin and Bhāsya, Vṛṣa and Skanda, and likewise Devī and Caṇḍa in the north.
Bhr̥ṅgī was seen with three eyes, his head bound by veins, possessing a bold beard, holding a trident,
clad in a white loincloth, aged, bearing a bull, and wearing a topknot.
A bull, or one resembling a bull, white, with three eyes, and covered in filth;
or a man with the face of a bull, carrying bells and chowries—such a being appears somewhere.
He has two arms and one face; he holds a banner in his right hand and a spear in the other. He has copper-colored crests and a red body, or he may have six arms and hands like the rays of the sun.
He holds a trident, a spear, a sword, a vajra, a bell,
and a shield, respectively, with his six right and left hands.
In the six and three [fingers], the noose and sword are joined with the index finger on their respective sides.
And in her right hand she holds a peacock feather, a bow, a shield, a banner, a [gesture of] fear, and a cock; likewise with six [objects] in her left hand.
Endowed with the form of the six-faced one, youthful and adorned; in the middle [of the mandala] is a young woman with a golden luster, slender-waisted and possessing full breasts.
She had large eyes, a rounded face, arms that were not to be looked upon, and blazing splendor;
yet she held two jars, cool and tranquil, placed at the base of her tree's branches.
One should worship the eight [deities] in the sequence starting from the east: Parjanya, Aśoka, Sañjñā, the two Bhūtasaṃjīvana and Amṛta, Dhanada, Śrīprada, and Avasthama.
When there are eight arches (toraṇas), the assignment (nyāsa) is as follows for each pair:
one bestows prosperity and fame, while the other bestows growth and nourishment.
Agni and the others, residing in the directions of peace, should be worshipped in sequence with their respective mantras;
in each world-grasper (loka-graha), there are two pairs of Śravaḥ-stones situated upon the eight-petaled lotus.
Bhānu, Trayam, Yuga, Veda, Alakṣmī, Gaṇapati,
as well as the gods Dhamī and Yāgaukas, are stationed at every archway.
With devotion, for the sake of destroying the flood of obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice,
one should worship in sequence the guardians of the directions, beginning with Vajra and ending with Cakra, along with their banners.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ! To the Vajra, hūṃ phaṭ, and salutations! Thus [it is said].
By reciting the initial mantras beginning with Śakti and ending with Agni, [the following are named]:
Kumuda, the one called Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Saṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, Suprasiddhaka,
and Supratiṣṭhita— these are the deities of the banners, whose images are most formidable.
With these collections of mantras beginning with "Oṃ Kauṃ, obeisance to Kumudā," as well as the eight guardians of the fields (kṣetrapāla) together with billions of bhūtas; |||
Hetuka, Tripuraghna, Vahni, Āyama,
Ājihvaka, Kālakarālin, Ekāṅghri, Bhīma, and Atibhayānaka— these are the [eleven Rudras].

One should worship the five elements, beginning with Earth, in the throat, the tongue, the teeth, the joints, the bamboo-like spine, and the pillars, using the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta as before.
The pavilion is the abode of Śaṅkara, consisting of the digits beginning with Nivṛtti;
its interior is the principle of Sadāśiva, characterized by banners and powers.
Beholding reality with the vision of truth, and having first entered [the ritual space] and performed the purification of the self and other elements,

one should worship one's own self and others, and then install the principles (*tattva*), the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*), the forms (*mūrti*), and the lords of the forms (*mūrteśa*) upon the forehead, the throat, and the feet respectively.
136a) These Śiva-mantras, which have become the instruments [of action], bestow Śiva-hood;
and this triad of principles consisting of the forms and the lords of the forms constitutes the body.
Having purified the pedestal of the *liṅga*-Brahman stone and having realized its nature as the object of awakening,
and having thus reflected on these matters, one should likewise worship the deities of the directions beginning with Dharma.
Then, having first worshipped Vedyādhidaiva, Ananta, and the others at the Āluka of the Vaghāṭa,
one should worship Śiva in the mandala, on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in the water-pot (kumbha), or in the fire.
For one who recites the *saṃhitā* while focused on the form of his own mantra,
even those who recite other mantras in incalculable numbers are surpassed by that reciter of the weapon-mantra alone.
Then, they recite the Vṛṣākapi, the Yavamānī, the Śrīsūkta, and the Maitraka hymns before the initiated and skillful Brahmins standing at the intermediate directions.
A Brahmin learned in the Ṛgveda should recite [the hymns] in the northeast or the south;
one learned in the Atharvaveda should recite the Stambasūkta, the Atharvaśiras, and the Nīlarudra.
O Lord, [I have studied] the Ślokādhyāya, the Yajus-pratyagrudra, the Muktaka-brāhmaṇī, the Antara-sāman,
the Vrata-sāman, the Bṛhat-sāman, the Rathantara-sāman, the Jyeṣṭha-sāman, the Soma-sāmans,
the Yāsānikā, the Puruṣagati, and the Vṛta-suratānekaroditnit.
If he is a follower of the Rigveda, he should be on the east; but a follower of the Samaveda should be on the south.

The follower of the Yajurveda should recite from the west, and the follower of the Atharvaveda from the north; then the Guru, having prepared the sacrificial fires, should generate the fire within the pit.
Having placed that [image] into the fire-pit according to the command while it is submerged,
and having performed the purification of the earth with the recitation of the weapon-mantra (astra-japta) along with the visualization of the deity's form, one should proceed.
Having poured the arghya-water for the elements into the vessel, along with kuśa grass, unbroken rice, and a conch filled with water, he establishes the aforementioned permanent seat (dhruvāsana).
Then the Guru, having performed this, [establishes] the fire according to the method described in the Nisvāsaśekhara.

In the daily (nitya) rite, [the mantras] should begin with Īśa and end with Aja; in the occasional (naimittika) rite, it is otherwise. In the optional (kāmya) rite, they are born from Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, and Aja, along with Vāma and Aghora.

The unification of the faces consists of Īśāna, Aghora, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Puruṣa; they are joined with their respective seed-syllables, positioned above, in front, below, to the right, and within.
Bathing, the twilight prayers, worship, recitation, and fifthly, the fire-oblation—
these are declared to be the five constant limbs [of daily practice], as well as the sacred thread and the *damanaka* rite.
Initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā)—these two constitute the occasional rites (naimittika).
Furthermore, the attainment of powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, as well as the rites for specific desires (kāmya), are also explained in detail.
The movement of the breath is said to extend from the beginningless knot to the tip of the sprout;
in the *Brahmayāmala*, it is taught that the "knotting" consists of each individual syllable to be accomplished by mantra.
By means of two [syllables], one mantra-syllable, and one [syllable of the] name, there is a single *vidarbhaṇa*.
To the left and right, the mantra of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is placed within the Himālaya;
then, the mantra of the lotus-pedestal (padāmantra) is enclosed as a *saṃpuṭa* in the four directions according to the Kāmika-tantra.
The object to be accomplished should be placed at the beginning of the mantra-yoga; in the opposite case, it should be at the end.
*Svāhā* is used for pacification (*śānti*), *svadhā* for the two enclosures (*puṭa*), and *vauṣaṭ* for the visualization and worship.
ṬHA ṬHA for paralyzing, PHAṬ for slaying; CĀRYA for killing, GHĀṬAYA twice; VAṢAṬ for summoning—this is the [mantric] birth, though others have explained it differently.

Granthana is prescribed for pacification (śāntika), while vaśya, ākarṣaṇa, and vidarbha are [used] for subjugation; stobhana is for obstructing a fortress, and sampuṭa is for paralyzing and pinning down.
In the *yoga* season, one should perform acts of sowing dissension and eradication; in the *pallava* season, the act of killing (*māraṇa*);
in the *hemavanta* season, rites for nourishment (*poṣṭika*); and in the *śiśira* season, the supreme act of killing.
Subjugation is effective in the dark fortnight and during spring; in summer, it brings about great enmity;
in the rainy season, it effects great eradication; and in autumn, I resort to the peaceful rite.
Likewise, they know winter to be in yoga, early morning as the cool season (śiśira),
spring in the first watch of the day, and summer at midday.
The rainy season lasts for three fortnights, as does autumn; the winter lasts for six [fortnights].
Then, having divided the number of fire-pits (kuṇḍas) into parts starting from the eastern direction, the Guru [proceeds].
In the sacrificial pits starting from the east, the invocation of the deities (piśācāhvānana) and other rites are performed.
Having performed and meditated upon it, they attain the auspicious state of their own true nature;
and the teacher, too, by means of the ritual fire, attains the infinite.
Having meditated on [the deity] as far as the heart of the stalk, one should worship Śiva upon the lotus situated there—
beginning from the east and ending in the northeast, and including the center— according to the sequence of the tongues of flame.
She who burns away the gift of Rākṣasas, she who bestows death upon [her] mother, she who destroys enemies, she who brings others under control,
she who performs great eradication, she who bestows wealth, and she who accomplishes liberation.
Since she who grants all desires resides in the center, one should therefore perform the oblation in the center.
One should offer two full oblations; for if the tongue is afflicted or the deity is not present, [the rite] is performed by Śiva.
The seed-syllables beginning with *la* and ending with *kṣa*, situated in fire (*ra*) as the sixth,
resting upon the goddesses (*ī*), topped with a half-moon and a bindu, and having *jihvā* as their crest, are the [seed-mantras] for the Vedīs.

One should offer oblations into the sacrificial pit starting from the east with *narādyaiḥ* and *vacādyaiḥ*, and likewise in the center with *indhī*, *śaśivān*, and *bhyaṃ*, as well as in the nine directions and so forth.
In the nine [circles] beginning with Indra and Agni, [the deities are worshipped] with Narasimha and others, and with Dayā (Compassion) and others;
in the sixteen and so forth, [they are worshipped] with the faces and limbs; for all [these], there may be a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

138a) Having performed the *vāstu-homa* and other rites, as well as the *bali* offering and the *caru* oblation as before, one should present them before each sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) while performing the *nāndī-śrāddha*.
The Guru, having performed the *nāndī* rite, should first be worshipped as before;
the bath known as *koṣadhvaja-vitāla* is prescribed for the temple.
There, having struck the Linga of Aśaninya with the Astra-mantra and the Varma-mantra,
and having performed the scraping, one should worship it with the Bhuva-mantra.

For the sake of purifying the source of one's conduct, one should clearly perform the impurity-bath (mala-snāna) for the images, lingas, and so forth, ending with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, according to the two Āgamas.
Having offered oblations with the ashes of a dead snake, cow-urine, Śaṅkha-powder, and thorns,
one should then worship the abode of the hide with white flowers.
But with the common *anuvākya*, as before,

having placed [the victim] on a bed that is to be known by the inward-facing [priest], which is not fixed and which destroys the portion of the food with a thread of *sṛṇa* grass, one should perform the sacrifice.
O gentle one, when the teacher has sprinkled the auspicious signs with milk from a horn,
the craftsman should then cut them with a tool at that very same time.
O protectors of the earth, if even in the midst of conceptual distinctions such as honor, measurement, and proof,
the presence of Lakṣmī has arisen, her residence there is certain.
From the worship [of the image], there are three hundred and sixty-four auspicious descents of Lakṣmī.
Having divided a barleycorn into nine parts, the lines for the cubit-sized [image] consist of eight parts.
The dimensions of the limbs of the image are measured by *aṅgulas*, *yavas*, and parts of *yavas*;
the lines [of the body] enter into the body of Lakṣmī and are likewise extended in width.
In the *sāntara* [sections], there should be an increase of two *yava*s at the shoulders respectively;
and in the body of the *lakṣma*, there is the descent of three parts of the line.
When that [number] is equal to eight times the division, yoga occurs by the exclusion of two;
and there, a conjunction should be made between the two sides like a serpent’s noose.
In the third division, by abandoning the half, there is either the vow that grants all desires;
or [it is so] in the Vāma, Cāla, Lobha, Īśāna, Cāla, and Roha [divisions].
Their own form is their characteristic; in those jewels, the brilliance is radiant, and even in the images, the opening of the eyes is performed by means of three stars.

Then, having filled that line— which is characterized by the syllables "tatryaṃ śā kyā ti" and is devoid of other vowels— with honey and clarified butter, one who has conquered death [should proceed].
To remove defects of craftsmanship, one should bathe [the image] with clay and other substances;
having fumigated it and offered oblations, one should worship the artisan and [worship the deity] with a vessel of clarified butter and a probe.
Then, if one has the capacity, five cows should be given to the installer.
Having worshipped the *liṅga*, one should perform recitation (*japa*) with sesame oil and a hundred stalks of *dūrvā* grass.
That noble lady, accompanied by eight pure-born sons of her husband who were singing,
touched [the vessel] with kusha grass along with a thread wound clockwise and counter-clockwise.
Having bathed her and applied yellow pigment (rocanā), they should diligently perform the ritual of exorcism (nirmatsana).
To them, one should give dried ginger, pippalī, salt, and jaggery.
Afterward, the preceptor, accompanied by the image-bearer, should apply vermilion, saffron, turmeric, lac-dye,
and collyrium with the Heart-mantra or the Aghora-mantra.

One should perform the preliminary purification with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)— consisting of horn, dung, urine, curd, and milk— along with ashes, and with the waters of the five barks and medicinal herbs.
One should bathe [the deity] with the Rudra-hṛdaya or the Guhya-mantra, using the five sweet substances,
water infused with śatapuṣpā, and water from eight various fruits.
Then, with powders of barley, wheat, and bilva, along with urvāruka and agaru, and with eight pure, fragrant substances, as well as all the auspicious medicinal herbs;
With water from jewels, gold, cow-horns, grain, and the Gaṅgā; with jars containing the hundred streams and so forth, and with sandalwood water.

Having thoroughly wiped [the vessels] with a white cloth, one should perform the offering of water for the feet (pādya) using the eight jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara), the jar of Śiva, and the jar of Śakti, according to one's capacity, in the presence of the enclosure.

Having performed the *sadya* rite and worshipped with the Brahma-mantras, one should perform the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* on the feet. Then, having invoked [the deity] and smeared [it] with clarified butter, fragrant substances, camphor, and sandalwood, one should clothe [the image] in a deer skin or one dyed red, and then adorn it.

Having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) with the multiformed deity (*bahurūpa*) using heaps of *īśena* flowers and marked with *siddhārtha* seeds as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), one should offer the water of honor (*argha*) with the eight-limbed prostration (*puṣpāṣṭāṅga*).
Having worshipped the Lord, whose self is all-pervading, with the Īśāna mantra, and having performed the recitation and praise,
one should raise the liṅga from the heart with the Bhava and Viṣṇu mantras.
Having placed it upon a well-controlled chariot, one should cause it to circle the city with the clamor of battle-drums and the like;
or else, exerting effort, one should hurl it into the city from a palace.
The officiating priest, having placed brass vessels, gold, and the other seven types of grain along with flowers,
should proceed in front of the chariot through the consecrated area.
At every step, one may obtain the fruit of ten million horse-sacrifices;
even those who are the five great sinners attain the supreme goal.

Having circumambulated clockwise, one should worship and offer the *arghya* with the heart-mantra to [the deity] seated upon the auspicious throne at the western door of the sacrificial hall, facing east.
Having properly performed the rite for averting obstacles, one should enter with a focused heart;
then, one should place a wooden plank made of excellent wood upon the middle of the altar in front of the deity made of *kauśika* grass.
Then, having dragged a bedstead with its crest, covered with a head-covering and a garment,
one should thereafter spread a mattress with Ananta and Dhruva.
Having offered the previously mentioned seat there, one should raise the Lord with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
then cause him to rest with the *śiras-mantra*, and finally bow with the head or prostrate with the crown of the head.
Having offered the portion of the altar from its western edge up to the heart with the *tāra* mantra,
and having worshipped it, one should place the water-pot in the northeast of the deity.
Having recited the mantra known as Nidrā one hundred times with the Vāśinī [vidyā],
he should again smear the liṅga with the heart-mantra, fumigate it, and cover it with the Vāśasā [mantra].
O Lord, having offered various kinds of food offerings (naivedya) into the armor,
one should now offer household utensils, swords, lamps, and so forth.
One should perform anointing at the region of the feet with vessels of honey and clarified butter;
or, by means of the *hṛdaya* and *aṅgagīta* mantras, one should offer the most excellent [oblation] within the *ghora* and *nātha-liṅga*.
Worshipped like the Linga, bathed, known as Kriyā, embodied as the sacred seat (pīṭha),
anointed, clothed in garments, and marked with the vulva (bhaga) located within her prepared apertures.
Having performed the placement of the seats as previously described, one should worship with the head;
one should always place the *liṅga* in the east and the center, facing west toward the abode of Dhātṛ.
The *piṇḍī*, the *brahmaśilā*, and so forth, are placed in the west or facing east;
because of the reversal of the ritual requirements, everything thereafter, including the *brahmaśilā*, is likewise reversed.

One should place the five jewels and other offerings upon the base of the *liṅga* after it has been worshipped; and one should install the consecrated bull, which has been well-sacrificed, to the north of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
In this manner, one should offer four [oblations] with the *dhruva* vessel according to the ritual logic of the *āpādya*;
then, having invoked [the deity] with *kuśa*, *bhasma*, and sesame seeds, one should proceed with the *ghorāstra* and *kavaca* mantras.
One should offer a flower-arrow placed in the directions for the sake of the threefold wisdom.
Standing at the heart and the other [limbs] of the preceptor,
one should lead him [to the state of] non-duality by means of the three mantras ĀṂ, ĪṂ, and ŪṂ, which possess the pervasion described in the initiation.
In the squares, the triangles, and the circles known as the "hair" (keśa),
[the deities] were created in sequence from the east onwards, according to their respective divisions.
O Śiva, one should install the forms of the deities as Earth, Fire, Sun, Wind, Moon, and Sky; and the mantras for these are Narasimha and the others.
Then all the masters of the forms— Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra,
Bhava, Īśāna, Mahādeva, and Bhīma— were made his precursors.
One should employ the Bhairavas as lords of the forms (mūrtipatis) for the sake of pure enjoyment, for the sake of purification, for the worldly path, and for the sake of minor disciples.
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetāvalotkaṭā,
Dhātrī, Vitvī, Caya, Uṣārthā, Sthāpanā, Mūrti, and Nāyakā.
Alternatively, his eight forms are Kṣamā and the others, or the group of eight beginning with Dhārikā;
furthermore, his forms are Vāmā and the others, and these forms are also present in the five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).

Kṣāṃ, Vuteja, Maruṅga, Keśa, Īśāna, Śada, and Aśiva are the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) for the sake of enjoyment; Nivṛtti and the other [kalās] are indeed the lords of the parts (kalā-īśas) for the sake of liberation.
Then, the deities such as Mūrtidhara and others are worshipped with female hymns;
among Vāmā and the others, some perform the ritual action while others [exercise] will—such are their lords.
These forms are situated in the windows (vināra): Ugra, Ardhānānta, Māhoha, Ghora, Arati, Apajvara, Mūrtinā, and Mūrtayaḥ Sadyaḥ; thus one should install these eight [forms] in five ways.
141b) He whose form is darkness, who destroys the objects of the senses and brings about delusion;
he who is the leader of passion, obstructed by initiation, resides as the Bindu within the cavern of his form.
The marks and so forth are the establishers, being the sole causes for the commencement of the subtle body (liṅgadeha);
therefore, [one should meditate on Him] as non-different from the Self of all, possessing the luster of the autumnal moon.
The Guru, having specifically assigned the thirty-eight kalās to the self in the form of the *liṅga*, likewise [assigns] Śiva as its presiding deity.
The Lord, together with his consort, wore earrings and other ornaments as if they were eternal;
the Puruṣa likewise wore collyrium, excellent sandalwood paste, and a mirror.
The waist-thread, the sacred thread, the mace and other implements are offered by Rūpin;
and the canopy, the chowrie, the parasol, the banner and so forth are offered by Guhyaka.
The substances to be licked, sucked, or offered as oblation (haviṣya) and so forth are presented with the *sadya* mantra or the *hṛdaya* mantra.
In this manner, the *pīṭha*, the *brahmaśilā*, the bull (*vṛṣabha*), and the various stones are consecrated.
The yogi should perform the placement of the forms and so forth upon the plane of the power of action (kriyā-śakti),
using the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, conjoined with either of the seed-syllables *oṃ sūṃ* or *hūṃ*.
At the conclusion of the dance, O Lord, one should invoke and worship [the deity] with the mantra: "Oṃ Hrīṃ Śamahāgaurī Padāntaraṃ Rudradayite Svāhā."
142a) Then,

having meditated on the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), which has been fashioned as the universal support-form (viśvādhāramūrti) and so forth, possessing the power to form the mass of Mount Mandara and Mount Airāvata at its extremities;
Having worshipped with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the power of knowledge residing in the path of the assembly," and having brought her into presence, one should clearly contemplate her with the mind.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma"—with these words, one should offer salutation at the heart.

One should worship the pervasive Kriyā-śakti as a bull. Within the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), O Supreme Lord, one should contemplate the Śevī-kriyā-śakti at the girdle (mekhalā) and the Sound (nāda) at the navel. And one should contemplate the lip.
By those situated in the fire, by those situated in the vessel, and by the guardians of the forms, [they should be worshipped] mutually.
One should perform the joining of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhānaka), adorned as before with blue banners and flags;
having invoked the forms and the lords of the forms into the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should also [invoke] the vehicles of the forms.

The yogin should satisfy the full and the severed [forms] through the inherent nature, the form, the capacity, the pervasion, and the conjunction, respectively, by means of the Brahmā-aṅga and the Brahmā-aṅgeśa mantras.
Then, in their presence, having performed the *saṃhitā-homa* with the desire for success,
and having touched [the disciple] with the water from the *śānti-kumbha* along with *kuśa* grass while reciting the *brahmāṅga-mantras*, [he should proceed].

The preceptor, who effects the union of all things and abides in nine ways, should offer oblations according to the number of the [mantra] syllables. 142b) He should perform the offering for his own limbs, the ten directions, and the head.
Then, like a yogin, having externally projected his own form as the Lord of Forms (Mūrtīśāna) by means of his own breath;
One should perform oblations with the root mantra and its limbs; having asked for peace, one should sprinkle with water from the *ghaṭa* vessel.
As before, one should recite the *brahmamantra* for the purification of the portions, and thereafter the preceptor and others [should proceed].
With the pairs beginning with *auṃ*— namely *lūṃ lūṃ*, *rūṃ rūṃ*, *sūṃ sūṃ*, *ṣūṃ ṣūṃ*, *vūṃ vūṃ*, *yūṃ yūṃ*, *kūṃ kūṃ*— joined with the salutations (*namaḥ*) for Earth and the other elements,
one should perform the union of the pure and the impure through the external [mantras] beginning with *dhruva*.
The creation and protection of those who possess the nature of Brahmā and Acyuta are always characterized by righteousness.
The Māyā of black and red [colors], pervading the reality of the region,
should be joined with the heart itself for the purpose of obstructing the path and veiling.
Thus, those who possess the wisdom of Viṣṇu should join together with Hari by means of the armor of withdrawal (saṃhāra-varmaṇā),
which is exceedingly white and intensely radiant, in due order.
Then, by means of the nature of Kuṇḍala established in his control,
he gradually resolved that pure Śiva-tattva into the Supreme.
If there is a deficiency or otherwise, one should offer a hundred oblations for the purification of the root-mantra;
[performing] actions impelled by Your power, may I be blessed by Your permission.
143a) We have now turned back from this; furthermore, we declare the end of the season.
Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, to Rudra! O you who are fierce as Rudra, homage be to you!
Whether complete or incomplete, let it be accepted according to one's capacity with the mantra:
*Oṃ hrīṃ śāṅkari pūraya pūraya svāhā* for the *piṇḍī*.
They should announce [the offerings] with the ears and worship the Liṅga with the two types of knowledge;
likewise, one should install the Śakti on the Kriyā-pīṭha and upon the Brahma-śilā.
One should perform the ritual of suppression (saṃnirodha) and so forth; this detailed procedure applies even when the rite is small.
Having placed the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) [upon the vessel], having worshipped it, and having offered three oblations (āhuti), [one should proceed].
The three principles (triratna), as before, are all-pervasive and endowed with the cognition of their respective forms;
they consist of the thorough knowledge of cyclic existence and are joined with the capacity for liberation.
Then, having worshipped with one's own mantras or with the root mantra, one should perform the libation;
one should place the Eye of Knowledge upon the *liṅga*, and the supreme body and hands upon the *liṅga*.
Having invoked [the deity] into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), worshipped, and offered oblations, one should perform the purification upon Jayadratha;
some say that one should perform the recitation (japa) upon the Liṅga as before, when Govinda is seated.
One should perform the junction of the two [mantras] and the placement (nyāsa) with Keśinī and the others;
for the sake of purifying the initiation, these [rites] declared by the Kalpanā should be performed upon the liṅga.
If he is not a devotee of Maheśvara, one should initiate him with matted locks; otherwise,
one should perform the preparatory rite (adhivāsana) for one, three, or five days.
Either immediately or every day, one should perform a hundred oblations with their respective mantras;
having restrained [the spirits] from the fire-site and so forth, one should offer the bali-oblation to the bhūtas as previously described.
Having performed the vigil at night and the ritual procedures for the *liṅga* and so forth, one should sleep during the *vyāyana*.
This is the consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Then, as before, another [form] is established on the second day;
the Lord of the Veil (Samurtipa) is beyond Śiva by half a [unit]; that is Śambhu, the Kuṇḍaliṅga together with its pedestal.
One should offer [the oblation] into the eight locations as before, starting from the Kaśīlatā;
having thus gratified the fire, Śiva, being informed of that, shall proceed to the two suns (Svarau).
Having established three lines within that space, one removes the defect of *vedha* (piercing).
From the mouth of the altar, however, one should draw a single line situated in the middle of the *vedha*.
It has been stated that when the moon and the laugh (the *viccandra* and *hāsa*) are joined,
through their union, the destruction of the middle [element] becomes the highest good.
Non-deception for the sake of no harm, with Śrī, Vāyu, and the others delighted;
the determination of the Brahma-place as thirty-six hundredths of the door.
With sesame or half a sesame, one should place [the deity] slightly leaning toward the northeast;
thus, the powers (śaktis) such as Jñānā and others, beginning with the one called Kūrma, were previously fashioned.

Having deposited [the seed-syllables] along with *rasa* (6) and *kūrma* (1), one should likewise deposit the *iṣ* (5) and *vaṭā* (8) upon the *brahmaśilā*; O Lord, this is for Śiva up to the end of the *śakti*, according to the previously mentioned *kaśilā*.
Oṃ, salutation to the pervasive, stable, immovable, and firm one; then one should recite:
"Laṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā" to her who is known as Ānanda and who holds the stream [of the teachings].
Having meditated upon the stable foundation of Śiva, the Guru should establish the Brahma-stone through emanation; he should then contemplate the entire path as having ascended into it.
You alone are the Supreme Power; you alone are the bearer of the throne.
By the command of Śiva, O Goddess, you must remain here forever.
Having worshipped those [deities] in the directions of fragrance and the left, as well as Śarva, Indra, and the others in their respective directions,
one should place in sequence [the substances] ending with jewels, medicinal herbs, metals, minerals, and seeds.
Indeed, [these wheels] consist of brilliance, health, physical vigor, satisfaction, and power;
whether in the world or through the wheels and mantras, they are all-pervading everywhere.
Even though previously described as being without [the lotus], it should later be joined with a lotus;
this is for the sake of the prosperity of the wise and the increase of glory, provided it is golden and filled with kṛsarā.
A water-pot, yellow orpiment, dūrvā grass, gold, a horn, earth from a mountain peak,
wheat, a stone from a natural cleft, and a bull [should be placed] facing the entrance.
He established the common characteristics of the four castes in the Nandana grove.
For the increase of four-footed animals, for constant prosperity,
or for the growth of one's country, one who desires fortune should apply an ointment made from honey and *madhūka* powder.
And one should place Mount Sumeru there for the prosperity of all beings;
likewise, one should offer everything along with the Earth, the seeds, and the unblemished [sacrificial materials].

One should offer earth from a field that yields crops easily, from a place of prosperity, from a riverbank, or from the soil of a great river; likewise, one should offer a pair of shoes, silver, and barley.
One should cause [the image] to be mounted by a tortoise; their measurements are now described:
for those beginning with the lotus, it is one cubit (hastika), and for those ending with the elephant-toothed (sonadantika), it is nine months' [length].
In the case of an elephant as well, medicinal herbs and so forth named *guñjā* should be placed as before;
thus, one of these alone should be inserted into the middle of the womb.
Then, by means of the jewels and so forth, or by the mantra of Mahānanta, or by the heart-mantra; in the Sanatkumāra-śāndra [tantra], the placement (nyāsa) of these is likewise performed in sequence.
Having thus completed the ritual placement of the Brahma-stone according to the prescribed rule,
one should then smear its surface with milk-rice (pāyasa) or with honey.
Having covered it with an armor and an eye-cloth, one should sprinkle it;
the hole of the stone-thread should be filled with food or with ash for the sake of pacification.
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to the gods who have entered his body, as well as to the deities of the site (vāstu).
Having performed the satiation as before, at the conclusion of the full oblation— whether at night or during the auspicious consumption [of food] by day—
one should raise the liṅga, which has been worshipped with dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains, and move it as previously described.

Then the preceptor should proceed ahead from there, while the sacrificer, accompanied by his friends, follows behind, touching the image of the deity in its various forms as it moves through its respective directions during the festivals.
Others, measuring only a *devamātrā*, should align the palace with the front of the doorway;
there, the door should be well-proportioned, leaving a space for rest except for the auspicious [central] portion.
Or one may cause it to enter by means of the door-measure; or else, at the door, it should be devoid of the *śikhā*.
The entrance should be half the measure of the door, and everywhere, moreover, it should be [marked] with the crescent moon.
One should lead the Lord, who is stationed there, through the middle of the door by touching it;
having been released from the mouth of the door, he should remain steady upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
One should wash it with ash until it is bright white,
and then, having removed the cloth and installed the complete seat, one should smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances.
One should support the liṅga with a mechanical device using suspensions so that it is made straight;
for the embodied Guru and Śakti, as well as for those possessing armor and its attributes, [the same applies].
One should contemplate non-differentiation as the root, moving through the limbs until the end of dissolution, as before;
one should enter [the state] by means of emanation, for that is meditated upon as the appearance of the sacred site.
Having filled the pit with full sand using eight long leaden pegs driven into the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should install the pedestal and other components.
And one should install the pervasive supreme reality in the liṅga as before, provided it is not cracked,
trembling, rotating, decayed, or crooked in any way.
Having arisen from the defects such as the worship of his wife and so forth,
he was then led away by the one possessing form through the root mantra, like a river flowing to the ocean.

If the fire being kindled within the linga should become extinguished at night, it becomes defiled; by offering a hundred oblations with the *vigīśānu* mantra and with the *dhāman* mantra, it is purified.
Then, having informed the virtuous ones, one should lead Pūrṇa to the root as before;
whether the collection of faults has been mentioned or not, the Śaiva pacification (śānti) is desired.
One should worship Śiva within the principles (tattvas) that constitute the embodied Brahman;
when the liṅga is protected by the armor and weapon mantras, its characteristic is that of mutual interpenetration.
The lunar Śakti, white-robed and covered with a pair [of garments], performs the ritual action;
having bound the pedestal, one should raise the piṇḍikā with the mantra "vinā yomā."
One should contemplate the previous mantra ending with the syllable *Śaṃ* as before;
having established the northern channel, one should install it according to the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
Just as the digits of nectar [the moon] reach a state of oneness when in conjunction with the sun and the moon.
In the same way, one should clearly meditate upon the movement of both vision and action;
otherwise, for one who is not upright, there are a hundred obstacles in setting her in motion.
Alternatively, one should perform twice as many oblations with the root mantra according to the teaching of Kailāśa,
using iron filings, milk, and flour mixed with *sarja* resin, cooked together.
Having filled the cavity of the womb with oil and sand, one should bathe it with water for pacification,
with the five sweet substances, with the eight pacifying [substances], and with scented waters.
The Lord should embrace the *piṇḍa* with the previously mentioned line and touch it;
having realized the food of Śiva through the mantras of the principles (*tattvas*), he should [worship] the triad of lords.
Having performed the placement of the form, one should meditate upon the Liṅga as having the nature of the Vidyā-ātman and perform the placement;
then the supreme reality and its limbs, which consist of Jñāna-śakti and Śiva.
Having invoked the ritual action upon the pedestal and established it there, one should then worship;
having adorned the deity with garments and other offerings, one should burn guggulu resin mixed with ghee.
Having assigned Śiva, who is all-pervading, in the directions and the limbs as in the daily rite,
one should thus effect His presence everywhere through the assignment of the living soul (jīvanyāsa).

If there is sudden dancing, playing, or other such signs, that is certainly a sign of [the deity's] presence. Having offered food (naivedya), performed recitation (japa), and made a formal request at his feet, one should ask for forgiveness.
As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth remains.
The mantras and the world-protectors must remain there by the will of the Lord;
[they occupy] the pedestal, the base, the head, the belly, and the back of the liṅga.
If a wound occurs, death will eventually follow, as well as the ruin of the kingdom and the mendicant;
its pacification occurs when one hundred and eight oblations of ghee are offered.
After the auspicious announcement has been made, or subsequently with the *praṇavas* recited by oneself,
having offered oblations into the fires and performed the sacrifice for the Bull (*Vṛṣa*), one should present a bountiful *bali* offering.
If there is a deficiency of one hundred [oblations],

then for the sake of pacification, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with a hundred fuel-sticks (samidh) consecrated by the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, along with Śiva-mantras, and with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having restrained himself with the heart-mantra or the terrible mantra, he should again address Bhava:
"Whether through ignorance or lack of knowledge, whatever has been prescribed in the scriptures has not been performed by me."
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, may all that be fulfilled;
then, one should properly bestow the means of subsistence (saṃvṛtti) for the sake of Amukeśvara."
One should perform the gift of food and a great festival for four days;
on the second day, the image-bearers (mūrtipās) [should offer] a hundred [oblations] each into the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
They should perform a fire sacrifice with the Aghora mantra for the sake of expiation and for the attainment of wisdom;
on the third day, for the sake of pacification, they should offer one hundred fuel sticks smeared with clarified butter.
Alternatively, one may perform two [offerings] for each vessel, or at the fourth or the first;
or one may perform them in pairs or in threes, with the fourth rite performed as the remainder of the ritual action.
Having prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the mantras of Vāgīśī and the Brahmās along with their respective limbs, as prescribed,
[he should offer] a thousand [oblations] into the fire-pits purified by the residual drops (saṃpāta), together with the Bahurūpa mantra.
Alternatively, having offered oblations with Śiva as the possessor of limbs (the deity), one should present the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the temple of the deity;
thus it is stated in the *Liṅgakalpa* and other texts that the fourth [rite] purifies the action.
The wives of the gods and others [should be bound] by means of the Samvara and other [mantras].
Then, having worshipped the deity and fumigated him with another [substance], [one should act] with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should dissolve the consciousness of the external liṅga into one's own subtle measure;
by means of the Praṇava, the seat and other elements are not even to be projected (nyāsa) or worshipped.
In this [rite], the emission (visarga) is the state of Śakti; the manifestation (vyakti) consists of the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth.
Afterwards, one should perform the rite with two jars according to the procedure prescribed for the Śiva-jar.
Having brought the remains of the offerings, one should bathe the Lord with a single pitcher;
then, having bathed Him with milk and other substances, one should worship the Lord as before.
Having prostrated and made this request repeatedly as before, one should worship Caṇḍa:
"O Lord Caṇḍeśvara, take refuge in you; what cause for fear could there be for you?"
Therefore, those who have taken refuge in the path of Śiva possess inexhaustible means of propitiation,
by which [the power] of Brahmā and the others, though it had fallen into disorder, was restored.
Even though Śambhu himself is of fierce form, he restrains even that which has been committed [as a transgression] by means of bathing,
fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth, once [the image] has been consecrated according to the prescribed ritual.

Having joined the form together with its faces and limbs, one should place the support—the Śakti—within the lotus; then, by means of the path of the vital breath (prāṇa), one should establish it within oneself in its own place.
Outside the enclosure wall in the northeast, on ground measured equal to the interior of the temple,
one should place the *khakhrama* and address that leader of the staff (*daṇḍanāyaka*) regarding the pledge (*samaya*).
Remaining on the path and always protecting the auspicious substance in the presence of Śiva,
one should abandon clothing, ornaments, and even the use of flower-remnants for one's livelihood.
Having worshipped the mouth of Śiva, one should make this request with devotion:
"O Lord, whatever has been done by me, whether through ignorance or lack of knowledge, that which was deficient or otherwise improper—"
"May all this indeed be complete; be satisfied and forgive me.
As long as this deity remains with his linga, so long must you remain in his presence."
The ritual arrangements for Caṇḍa are recommended for a stable image that is clearly manifest and designated by the name of a hundred thousand [deities],
as well as for the unmanifest primary Liṅga.
The Caṇḍeśvara [linga] may be self-manifested (svayambhū) or situated within the earth; however,
when it is fashioned upon a pedestal (piṇḍikā) or a base (jagatī), the Caṇḍeśvara does not exist in a mobile state.
It was established by the great ones upon a self-manifested bāṇa-liṅga.
And when joined with the non-dual mantra, Caṇḍa shall not be empowered;
having recited the weapon-mantra one hundred and eight times, one attains Śiva through the mastery of mind and speech.
Having bowed and offered oblations in the cardinal directions,
one should then restrain the earth until the Lord is present here together with the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
As long as he has become present and established, you who have cultivated yourselves should remain;
when [the deity] finally departs, it is taught that one should offer seven oblations beginning with the "Stable" (sthirā).
For it is stable, immeasurable, beginningless, unassailable, eternal, all-pervading, indestructible, and contented; these seven are its qualities, beginning with stability.
For the sake of fulfillment, for the ritual procedure, for satisfaction, and for the sake of the one who possesses many forms—
for Śiva, O gods, oblations are considered to be offered in his presence at certain times.
Then,
he should bathe the single Guru in the form [of the deity] with the water from the eastern jar, or on a lotus seat, or on the ground, or on a small vessel.

Having worshipped him as if he were Śiva, the performer should give him a generous sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Having offered his own head at his feet, the disciple should make this request: "I am a sinner, O Lord, a vessel of all sins; I have transgressed the command of my guru and the scriptures. O ocean of compassion, grant me refuge; O Lord, protect me who am fallen into the ocean of worldly existence. Thus having requested, the disciple should remain standing with palms joined in reverence. Then the preceptor, having performed the purification of the body (tanuśuddhi) and the like, should perform the ritual of the five fires (pañcāgnisādhanā) for the sake of the disciple. He should then offer oblations (homa) into the fire with the mantra *tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam* and other mantras, as well as with the *mūlamantra*. Then, having performed the rite of the *pūrṇāhuti*, he should place the disciple within the *brahmāṇḍa* (the cosmic egg) and, having sprinkled him with water from the *kalaśa* (vessel), he should lead him out. Then, having performed the rite of the *kavaca* (armor), he should bestow upon the disciple the *mantra* of the *sudarśana* discus. Then, having performed the rite of the *netra* (eye), he should bestow the *mantra* of the *triśūla* (trident). Then, having performed the rite of the *astra* (weapon), he should bestow the *mantra* of the *vajra* (thunderbolt). Then, having performed the rite of the *varma* (shield), he should bestow the *mantra* of the *śakti* (spear).
