Then, having performed the rite of the *pādya*, he should bestow the *mantra* of the *pādya*. Then, having performed the rite of the *ācamanīya*, he should
O Lord, my birth has become fruitful because I have been rescued by you from the great ocean of saṃsāra; I forgive you for the suffering you endured on my account.

Then the worshiper, being joyful, should joyfully offer [the merit] to him according to the procedure prescribed for the offering of recitation; [he thereby obtains] the fruit born of the installation.
One should give two full sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) in the form of a pair at the conclusion of the initiation (dīkṣā),
the installation (pratiṣṭhā), and the sacrifice, as well as when a sacred festival day (parvan) has arrived.
Upon obtaining a mantra and for its accomplishment, worship of the Guru is highly recommended;
however, those who recite mantras while serving as temple priests (mūrtipās) who, out of delusion, fail to worship their Guru, [fall].
One obtains no fruit at all; that [fruit] belongs only to the one who established [the shrine]. Without a teacher, there is no sacrifice or mantra; without contemplation, there is no kingdom.
Without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one would destroy both the Dharma and the sacrificer;
therefore, the purified implements of the sacrifice and the sacrificial pavilion should be accepted from the preceptor.
The bathing pavilion for the principal artisan, along with his tools, should be one thousand [units];
however, for a self-manifested [liṅga], it should be half of that, together with the deities and others.
When a sacred field is established by men through their emblems, it becomes as vast as a hundred hands;
even one of sinful conduct who dies therein attains the supreme goal.
The field of the self-born Rāśavāṇas extends for a yojana in every direction,
as does that of the great rivers, which bestows movement upon all things moving and unmoving.
At its end, one should designate a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) with water for the sake of peace, such as the "eye of Śiva" (śivākṣa);
for in the absence of the Revā and other rivers, that alone is a great purifier.
Let the palaces of the god be according to his desire as determined by the wood;
however, the faces of the Puruṣa and the others abandon their positions in the directions starting from the east.
Whether a *liṅga*, an image, or something else is fashioned, one should worship Śiva facing north at each respective place of sacrifice.
The primary consecration.
One should perform everything as before with the stationary and moving *vāṇaliṅgas*;
however, the characteristic of the *nokṣila* is not mentioned here, as it has already been consecrated by the gods in the past.
It is perfectly formed or irregularly shaped, always bestowing all accomplishments; it is never at all subject to conceptualization, and it resides upon the pedestal of every temple.
In this case, one may or may not perform the conceptualization of the form and the lord of the object;
for prosperity, there is a fire-oblation here, and no conceptualization of Caṇḍa with the dative case.

There is never a confusion of mantras due to their connection with both the common and the extraordinary; nor can anything else, even if mobile, ever bring about stability in that which is inherently unstable.
The proximity of Raudrī should be established, or else a consecration like that of the Bāṇaliṅga;
[this applies to] Bāṇa and the others.
In the case of a mobile liṅga, one should place it on a separate pedestal, whether it has been consecrated or not;
having meditated upon the power of knowledge and action within the liṅga and the single pedestal.
It is not even placed upon a pedestal; rather, it is consecrated through non-duality.
One should join together crystals and other materials with the desired mantras according to the ritual procedure;
or else, one may collect everything previously mentioned here within the pavilion.

In a ritual procedure, one should employ the fourth case ending and so forth; in the suppression of an obstacle, what need is there for vowels? But in a general sense, there should be a visarga, since proximity to the specific [object] always exists.
One should first divide the [space] beginning with the jewels into five or three parts;
then, one should place either two or one part upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā) at the banyan tree.
In the ocean of recitation (*japārṇava*), one should offer a portion for worship according to one's means or as is appropriate;
it may be made of gems, minerals, or wood, whether originating from its own source or from another source.
Having understood the characteristics for the installation of the *liṅga* as previously described,
one should perform the placement of the stone, jewels, and so forth, as well as the joining of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
In this case, everything mental that was previously mentioned remains as the remainder;
[this applies] to seats made of gold, silver, bronze, copper, or wood.
When pure, withered lotuses, or *sviṣṭakṛt* flowers along with *mudga* beans are unavailable, one should worship using half a cloth, or in some cases, even a piece of bark.
At the conclusion of the worship, that [image] should again be placed in a casket wrapped with flowers;
having placed it above the head of the bed, people should offer a cloth covering.
Having placed it upon one's shoulder, one may go on a journey oneself or have another lead it;
this is the rule for as long as one lives, out of a desire to obtain the fruit of true merit.
That [liṅga] must always be protected with effort for fear of the need for expiation;
if one’s own desired deity is present in a common liṅga, then [it is so] during the sacrifice.
"This is the command of the Supreme Lord regarding beings who have not received initiation.
[This refers to] crystal and so forth.
Regarding the worship of manifest [deities], the previously mentioned procedure applies, with the exception of Caṇḍeśvara;
their installation should be preceded by the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
In the fourth *kharba*, which consists of seven times seven limbs (*aṅga*), is the station of Brahmā;
in the third, that of the heroes (*śūra*); and in the second, that of human beings.
And in the first portion of the Vasus belonging to the Piśācas, between Bhānu and Durga,
in the midst of gods and humans, lies the station of Pidhri to the north of Kaca.
There, the Brahma-stone pedestal should be made with a width equal to half the [total] breadth, and its height should be half of that; it should be adorned with jewels and provided with a hollow.
Whatever fivefold set beginning with jewels and ending with tortoises has been proclaimed— that entire collection should be placed within the pit of the pedestal upon the surface of the kaśilā stone.
O Grandfather, when one proceeds in sequence through the various meanings below,
the words for the Rakṣasas, Maruts, and Ādityas are located in the Skandha and Pauṣkara sections.
An image that is joined with a wall, situated in a place inhabited by rākṣasas,
or whose intention is poorly conceived, will bring about the complete ruin of the artisan, the installer, and the patron.
In the five [groups] beginning with the eyes, situated in the sky during the upward sacrifice for those who sleep and eat,
there is sometimes an image of a cow made of the letters starting from *ka* up to *ha*.
Beyond this, one should move upward through the families beginning with Jayā, which are the upadravas;
[these are] the trees, the species of dice, and the excellent dwellings of the garden of mantras.
One should perform the bathing and other rites for the tridents and the archway bells as previously described.
The manifest and so forth.
Having fixed a firm cloth that has destroyed [all] white [impurities] according to the rule,
one should place Sadāśiva within it, in the lotus, upon the pericarp.
With palms joined in reverence, one should show [the deity] who has a great white serpent as his sacred thread;
one should show the three faces, but Īśāna should not be shown.
One should draw Śveta in the middle with the shadow of Īśāna, and then Tatpuruṣa, who has a white face, is radiant, and whose three eyes are motionless in meditation.
Non-terrible yet terrifying, with fangs and a formidable face, he is marvelous;
he resembles a mass of crushed collyrium and blazes with eyes emitting flames.
And one with tawny eyebrows, body hair, and hair, who carries a staff on his right shoulder.
Vāmadeva is very fair in complexion, possessing the luster of a woman's face, playful, three-eyed, and smiling beautifully; he wears a tilaka and earrings on the left side of Sambhu.
Below the deity, at the base of the feet, is Manonmanī within the pericarp;
extending from the east to the northeast are the gentle powers, beginning with Vāmā.
The heart is located near the right knee in the direction of Agni;
the head is situated near the left knee in the direction of Īśāna.
To the north of Dakṣa, near Uśanas, and in the vicinity of Cūḍā and Carma,
one should place the fierce yellow weapons in the directions starting from the east, as before.
In the gates, the castes, and the square mandalas,
one should place the nine or eight limbs together with the regions, facing forward.
Then, one should place four lions starting from Agni in the peaceful corners;
thus, one should install them starting from Indra below the deity and extending to the northeast (Īśāna).
May Brahmā be situated above Īśa, and Keśava also above Nairṛta;
may the Earth and Puruṣa be between Rakṣas and Varuṇa.
Vidhi and Śrī are situated [therein], and Kṣetrapāla is located in the middle of the wind; all these should be meditated upon facing Śiva.
Indra and Dakṣiṇāmūrti stood there, while Nandin and Kāla were in the eastern direction.

The *stava* (hymn) should be performed from the northeast to the north; and those beginning with Bhṛgu up to Caṇḍa should be performed outside the pavilion, starting from the east and ending in the west, with the *hṛdaya* mantra at the end.
Outside of that, [the deities] such as Gajagokarṇa and others, or alternatively with ornaments, are situated in the intermediate directions;
they stand with palms joined in añjali-mudrā.
To the right of the deity is Brahmā, seated upon a swan;
likewise, to the left is the Yakṣa Ananta, seated upon a tortoise.
Between Śakra, Aryaman, and Īśa, there is likewise Bhāskara in the fire;
below Nandī and Indra, one should place Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī at the proper time.
Alternatively, O gentle one, for the sake of the glory of Śrī, one should place Gaṇa and Vāṇī in the middle of Dakṣa; Nandī and Gaṅgā to the right of Deva; and Kālā and Arkajā on the left.
Alternatively, [the site] where the Gaṅgā flows to the south and the Yamunā to the north-west, where there is the suppression of weapons by Mahālakṣmī, and where there is a Brahmastambha nearby; |||
Outside [the circle] at Nandī, beginning with one's own guru, and outside [the circle] at Kāla, beginning with *ṭa*;
furthermore, this should be known as the western door according to the sequence of the letters.
He is first perceived as being situated in the eastern direction;
one should then draw Gaṇapati in the east within the row above [the directions] beginning with Nairṛta.
One should worship Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Gāyatrī, and Bhāskarī in sequence; then Durgā, Caturitā, Vaidyanātha, and Heramba according to one's desire.
Tvaritā has a lion’s face and is distinguished by peacock feathers;
she bestows all goals swiftly and grants boons and protection with her two left hands.
Consisting of white nectar, three-eyed, with a lotus, moon, and water-lily for her seat, she is exceedingly gentle, adorned with matted hair and the moon, and graced by all ornaments.
Four-armed and youthful, she should be meditated upon as bestowing boons and protection with her right hands, while holding in her left hands the full moon and the nectar-pot.
This is the highly auspicious form of Mṛtyañjaya Vaidyanātha;
what more need be said? It is for the accomplishment of all that is desired.
Bestower of all accomplishments swiftly, son of Hara and Ambā, destroyer of all obstacles; moon-like, fair, full, and gentle, you who possess five faces and five streams.
Clad in a tiger skin, wearing the sacred thread, with arms reaching to the horizon, adorned and with matted hair;
in his right hands he holds the boon-granting gesture, a garland, an axe, and a mallet.
In her left hands she holds a noose and a skull-cup containing sweetmeats;
she is seated upon a lotus, and as he beholds her, she is white in complexion and smiling.
Having sat down with her left foot placed upon a lotus and the other foot extended,
she should then, as before, deposit the syllables of the Guru and her own *svāhṛti* within the *caṇḍānta*.
Paint with diligence according to what is beautiful, according to the color, according to the hue, and according to the proper position,
making it radiant with various colors.
Half [of it] should be protected with vermilion (hiṅgula), provided with a staff and a fringe;
the fringe should be attached above, hidden, and joined with a cord for binding the staff.
Having mentally fashioned such a cloth [of the deity] that increases the delight of the mind,
one should perform the purification through sprinkling, the ritual of warding off obstacles, and the pure ablution, all with the mind.
Or, having bathed [the deity] in mirrors and so forth, as with one's own body and the like,
one should arrange the placement of jewels and other offerings, even if it is merely a new meeting [of the deity].
One should worship this in detail so that the desired goal is not lost; this has been stated by the illustrious Navī Vimalēśvara regarding cloth-paintings and other such supports.
One should [perform] the pacification of all obstacles with mantras found in one's own scriptures,
using either the initial letters of one's own name or as appropriate, distinguished by the vowels.
The intellect of Brahmā extends up to Prakṛti; these three principles belong to the Lotus-born.
Within the Egg of Brahmā, his authority shall consist of the portion characterized by the qualities (guṇas).
And this has been stated in the *Hiraṇyagarbha* regarding the nature of the *stobha*.
The triad of the subtle elements (tanmātras), the manifest (vyakta), and the principle of the person (puruṣatattva) is for the attainment of Viṣṇu;
the form of Viṣṇu should be established in front, and Tārkṣya [is for] the moment of the deity's departure.
There, situated upon the pedestal (pīṭha) with the three pillars ending in the mind, intellect, and ego, [he] stands firm,
having raised up the earth and the other elements up to pride, as well as the human, boar, and bull lineages.
Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Nṛsiṃha, and Vāsudeva.
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Rāma, Rāma, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the incarnations beginning with the Earth. (10)

Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhughna, Trikamā, Mana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara— these [names] consist of the elements beginning with Earth (kṣmā) and ending with Śiva. 12.
Tryakṣa, Umāpati, Sthāṇu, Nīlakaṇṭha,
Vimohana, Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Saṅkara, and Nīlalohita.
Īśāna, Dhanada, and Bhīma are the Rudras [worshipped] starting from Mārgaśīrṣa up to Kārttika. ||12||
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, ego, and the faculty of action;
primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual soul (puruṣa), power (śakti), and Śiva—these exist like the sun, the Rudras, and the gods. 12.
Māyā, along with the principles up to Sadāśiva and Śakti, belongs to the Śivas;
however, this triad of principles is otherwise [classified] according to the Vīrāvalīkrama.
The three principles (tattvas) of the Sun—Māyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—dissolve into the principle of Śakti;
his great enjoyment occurs in the plane of Vidyā.
The domain of the Sun is also like a location on the path of purity;
Hari, Hara, Ardhanārī, and Sāmā arrive at Vijayottara.
The necklace of the Sugata, the stone of Īśāna, and the dwelling;
the pride of the mother, the limit of qualities, and the establishment of the Jina—these are the three.
The rivers situated on the earth, including those of the oceans and sacred fields,
as well as Yamunā, Varuṇā, Ambhodhi, Gaṅgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.
Even the great rivers remain fixed in their courses; otherwise, they might flow anywhere.
But for the mothers of the hosts of Nādyas, who possess fortune and dwell within the caves, there is no such restriction.
Impurity (mala) ending with impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā) consists of three principles (tattvas) within the "grasping" (grāsa);
those beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin are said to belong to the principle of the Self (ātmatattva).
The Brahmās reside in Śuddhavidyā; the limbs of Śiva reside sometimes in Śiva;
Dharma and the others reside with the Vidyeśvaras; and Śuddhavidyā belongs to Bhānin.

In the Śiva-śāna [rite], by reciting the names of Vīrabhadra and others, the limbs of Śiva are to be installed according to the prescribed ritual; likewise, those who have fallen from the Śiva-sacrifice and others [are restored].
Śiva is not present in other sacrifices, since he stands above all as the supreme.
The pervasion [of consciousness] beginning with Brahmā.
Having leaped over the courtyard, the threshold, and so forth, and having covered [the ground] with her own hair, she should lie down upon a bed and place her three [limbs] as before.
One should place the [remaining] digits (kalās) in the middle, below, to the left, and at the very top;
and having diligently satiated them, one should deposit the drop (bindu) consisting of those digits at the gateway of the bath.
Having performed the sacrifice, having confined [the spirits], having offered oblations, and having recited mantras, one should [establish] the site at the base of the door.
Having worshipped Ananta with mantras, one should deposit the jewels and other items there;
then, having performed the pacification rite as before, one should perform the all-encompassing protection for the sake of preservation.
Cow dung, white mustard, the lord of diseases (ginger), barley, white mustard, lakṣmaṇā, sesame, gorocanā, krāntā, vṛddha, and mṛtamohanā.
Having first placed curd, dūrvā grass, and kuśa grass upon them,
the Guru should fashion a *pāṭṭali* [seat] with an upward-pointing *udumbara* lotus using the *dhruva* mantra, established as the *dhruva*.
Having led [the breath] slightly upward and properly fixed the door,
one should place the reality of the Self, known as Vidyā, below the two branches.
In the sky is the Śiva-tattva, all-pervasive and omnipresent;
or rather, that which extends a hundred-fold below, reaching down to the branches of the manifest form.
One should offer seven oblations called *mantra* for the pervasive head in the evening;
likewise, one should perform the self-pervasion through the names of those stationed at the doors, beginning with Nandin, who have been bathed.
Having performed the preparatory rites, one should then offer one hundred oblations with the heart-mantra;
then, having consecrated the thread with the weapon-mantra, one should perform the offering to the quarters to remove all defects.
"Even when released, it may cause burning; thus, there must be a placement at the entrance."
Now, the relationship between the body and the self is described;
and that [relationship] would be completed by direct perception from the time of conception within the womb until the end of life.
According to Kaśyapa, the rites of bathing and the installation of an image made of gold or silver should be performed exactly as prescribed for the aforementioned [clay] image.
One should prepare a vessel made of copper or any other single metal, like a *śivakumbha*,
filled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), honey, milk, and scented water.
The wise one should place the jar, which resembles a heart-lotus and has become manifest in form;
and having gone to the white-eared [deity], he should place that lid, which is like a fruit, upon it.
Having taken up that reality of the self-nature of protection— which is of a form inseparable from the self of all—
by means of inhalation (pūraka), one performs a kumbhaka (retention) through one's own breath.
Having awakened [the disciple] by means of the command (ājñā), one should contemplate the twelfth [letter] at the end;
having taken that from there, which has the luster of a star, one should place it into the image-vase.
One should cast off the body that perceives those qualities as a vehicle for this [state];
and one should cast it off by means of the Lords (Īśvaras), beginning with Kalā and ending with Śaṅkara, using their respective names.
Likewise, specifically, there are one and a half channels in sequence beginning with Prāṇa;
these include Iḍā and Alambuṣā, as well as the ten Mātrās and the Śavas.
The five [breaths] ending with *prāṇa* are shaped like tortoises, as before; they are the accumulation of the five, six, and the intellect for the two [groups of organs].
The organs of action are Viyu, Agni, Cakra, Acyuta, and Caturmukha.

Samitra, Diśāmanu, Sūrya, Pracetas, and Svindva are likewise to be employed as the presiding deities (adhiṣṭhātṛ) over the organs of perception (buddhīndriya) during sacrifices, under their respective designations.
By virtue of fulfilling its own function, it regulates the initial time;
by virtue of accomplishing its own goal, it is due to its non-differentiation from the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa).
One should place Śiva and his pervasive nature within one's own body according to their respective [mantras];
then, having briefly described it, one should offer the all-pervasive vessel.
Salutations to Prakṛti, from Pṛthivī up to Pradhāna among these principles;
then they bow to the divine Lord of Umā, who pervades her interior.
One should assign the *puṃs-mantra* for the sake of all prosperity, and with the syllable *maum*,
one should satisfy these mantras for their presence and the pacification of defects.
Having first offered the portion set aside according to the ritual procedure, he should release the partless Śiva from his heart.
Īśāna, being identical with that [Liṅga], should always be made equal to the root-liṅga;
in the case of the Nṛsiṃha [liṅga], the cūlaka should be like the liṅga in length or in width.
When the width of the neck is divided into three parts, the *cūlaka* (top-knot) is one and a half [parts];
its length is three [parts], and it is either as wide as that or slightly more.
The width of the neck should be one-third of its length,
and its expansion at certain points should be one-tenth of its diameter, with the thickness being proportionate to its strength.
When enveloped by the power of grasping, it takes the form of a jar;
above the jar is a trident, and its crest is the ever-grasping [consciousness].
When someone shows a seasonal portion above the pitcher, that which is devoid of the root is like this: such is the kīlaka of Īśāna.
When the kalaśa is empty, one-third of it is designated as the visible portion, half of that is the śāra portion, and at that very time, the śivacūlaka is situated in the remaining half.
Just as the protection of crops is diligently carried out according to the field so that they may ripen well,
so too here, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, its growth is likewise taught.
The width of the base of the temple should be half of that, or even more.
In a temple made of brick or wood, [the image] should be made of wood starting from the northeast;
in one made of stone, it is considered to be made of stone; and in some cases, it is worshipped by the hosts of Śūras.
In this [rite], the fourth [deity] Caṇḍakṛṣṇī is prescribed for Suparṇaka;
one should perform the rites as stated for the Liṅga, preceded by the placement of the faces and limbs upon the image.
For the sake of a specific purpose, one who possesses knowledge should perform the entry into half of the Brahma-portion, even if it is devoid of ritual action;
furthermore, he should perform everything else as previously stated. He would be successful in his goal, and his banner [of victory] would be equal to that.
Jaghārcalambā, Jaghāntā, Daṇḍamāna, or he may be Dṛḍhabhūta, Naṭa, Dvastra, Pīṭhaveśī, or Mahādhvaja.
Alternatively, the extent of the hand-spread may be one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight cubits;
or it may be half of that at the commencement of the sacrifice, just as previously described for the planet Venus.
It is extended by its own sixteenth part at the forest of Śiras;
for the sake of attaining liberation, it is desired by those who seek their own goal.
Adorned with tinkling bells and yak-tail whisks, rising upward marked by his own vehicle,
he assumes the form of his respective deity, slightly embellished according to his own power.
In the largest [temple], the pinnacle (śikhara) is three parts; in the medium-sized, it is one-quarter less than that;
and in the smallest, it is half of that. This is known as the staff (daṇḍa).
In some cases, according to the sequence beginning with "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) and so forth, when the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are joyful,
there may be an increase in that lineage (*vaṃśaja*) and in virtue (*dharma*).
It is firm, smooth, soft, and free from all defects of trees.
If a knot, a facial joint, or even a fine jewel is placed upon a virtuous person, and it is broken while being honored,
the king’s life would come to an end.
In that regard, a fierce affliction caused by malevolent planets is said to occur;
it may affect the back, the house of the flagstaff, or even the northeast or northwest.
With a thread [measuring] five bow-lengths and a tip [of one bow],
starting from the top, [the measurement is made] either in the eastern half or subsequently at the end of the core, once the abode has been constructed.
Having bathed [the image] as before and beautifully adorned it with perfumes, garlands, garments, and so forth,
one should install the sustaining power (dhārikā-śakti) in the form [of the deity], beginning with the faces, as previously described.

Having installed the entire auspicious *Ātmavidyā* from the middle and upper portions [of the diagram] using the previously mentioned mantras, and having recognized it, one should perform oblations in its presence.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Sambhu, the bestower of prosperity, and having restrained [the breath] as prescribed,
one should contemplate the multitude of principles (tattvaugha), beginning with Ananta and ending with the Supreme Lord (pareśa), which is well-established therein.
One should join him to the world with the linga and pedestal as if they were joined;
having bathed him, one should sprinkle the vajra with the cloth from the crest-staff.
As before, one should worship the ritual procedure for the bed situated within the pavilion and other structures.

The pentad beginning with the couch (śayyā) should be placed in the staff (daṇḍa), and the partless (niṣkala) in the banner of Śiva (śivadhvaja). Furthermore, one should place Ātman and Vidya in the staff, and the Śiva-tattva in the banner.
Behind the two banners at the Cūlaka and in the storehouse,
one should offer oblations with the Saṃhitā mantras ending in "Ṣaḍanta" for the sake of the banners.
Having restrained the mind through excellent worship, or by means of the Brahma-mantras or the Śiva-mantras,
and having understood [the nature of the mantra], having recited it a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of times, and having offered it [to the deity].
Having placed the jewels and so forth upon the flagstaff, and likewise the food as before,
he should lead the manifested form with the Sadyojāta mantra and offer it to the staff.
Then, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon that banner,
he should install the partless Śiva (niṣkala) and worship him along with his limbs (sāṅga) according to the prescribed method.
Those wise ones who have mastered the principles and are protectors of their own weapons—
meditate upon all of them as the removers of obstacles.
O Teacher,
even one who performs a circumambulation while clinging to a great banner that has been suspended attains the fruit of benefit.
Thus has the sequence been stated; now it is explained by means of [the following] verses:
having projected [the deities] into the previously mentioned *vāsana* according to their portions as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
In some places, the forms (*mūrti*) and so forth are taught, while in others, the remainder [is taught].
Therefore, having first recited [the mantra] that many times, one should perform the concluding rite (*astaka*) with that same number.

One should offer the perfumes and other articles with the Brahmamuṇḍa mantra, and the offering to the presiding deity of the Vidyā with the [same]; however, the food offering (naivedya) and the bali-rite should be performed with the Hṛdaya mantra.
And as before, one should install that staff, which has become an embodiment and possesses the form of a weapon,
together with a banner consecrated by the weapon-mantras.
Meditating upon him as endowed with the previously mentioned limbs, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns,
with a roar like the clouds at the dissolution of the world, and with blazing eyebrows, beard, and hair;
With teeth blazing like fire, he was not to be provoked;
his tongue was like a flash of lightning, and he wore a serpent as his sacred thread.
The previously mentioned [deities] such as Dhvaja and Vaktra, who crush the beloved ones,
[reside] within the temple, the linga, and the pedestal, as many as there are supreme atoms.
For as many thousands of kalpas as there are [trees], one enjoys the fruit of the performed enjoyment;
when a great flagstaff is erected, that merit shall be ten million times greater.
Even when the conditioned has decayed, there is merit in this nectar of the crest of the gods.
Having cast everything inside, one should fashion a liṅga made of metal or precious gems;
it is the supreme [object] upon the temple pinnacle, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Or one may place the trident of the abode of Maheśa and Caṇḍikā upon the pitcher.
Therefore, it should be equal in size to the *liṅga* or the seed-syllable, or even according to another characteristic;
thirty-two finger-breadths is the best, while the middling and inferior are measured at eight and ten [finger-breadths] respectively.
Or, having consecrated [an image] made of gold or silver, one should discard it as before;
[one should likewise discard] the triad of powers—Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—together with the body.

Alternatively, the knower [of the tradition] should perform a firm drawing of the wheel upon the back of a Karīra tree using the *śivāruta* (the cry of the jackal), which is endowed with power and known as the "secret desire."

The staff is equal in length to the height of the living being (jīva), and its thickness is one-twentieth of that; this is indeed the opinion of Hari. For the Sun, however, it is considered to be a lotus in the sky.
One should always install the deities of the Svāyudha-dhanya [mandala] with their respective mantras;
the deities of the Cūlikottara [mandala] should be installed according to the tradition.
If the cause of sensation were long, then the eight subtle elements (āśavas) would be coarse;
having examined the Guhyasūtra and other texts, this is called "coarse" (sthūlaka).
The raising of the banner.
It is shaken, moved, broken, shattered, and split;
it is burnt, deficient, excessive, low, on a wrong path, and likewise marked with various signs.
Relying on such signs of defects as being fallen into the womb, decayed, afflicted by wounds, or cast down, the rākṣasas and others [attack].
Therefore, having extracted the essential characteristic, one should display it as something possessed of excellence.
A jewel [image] that was consecrated by Daityas who knew the reality,
even if it is dilapidated or broken, one should not move from its place according to the ritual rules.
Furthermore, that linga which is covered by a cloth, or which has not been consecrated by those who know the divine signs,
or by artisans and others, [is unfit] for one seeking initiation into Śiva.
Furthermore, one should perform its consecration according to the previously prescribed rule;
in the northeast and to the south of it, there shall be a single archway for the western door.
To the northeast of the temple entrance, one should construct a well-adorned pavilion for the placement of the feet;
having performed the world-offering (loka-yajña) as before, one should worship the Vāstu deities upon the drum.
Having worshipped on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should satisfy the mantras with libations and cause them to blaze;
O twice-born ones, one should also feed those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgins) and the likes of Mitra and Upendra.
Having been satisfied by the multitude of offerings, you are equanimous like Śiva;
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, this [act] does not bring about any fault in you, O Protector.

"The sign of this [obstacle] is that there will be peace upon its removal"— such would be the statement. Therefore, let the confusion arising from its removal be stilled, and may they preside over it.
Having been addressed thus by Śiva with eight hundred [mantras] and so forth,
one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) using sacrificial fuel-sticks, durvā grass, milk, ghee, and other substances.
One should offer a thousand oblations with the *ghora* mantra for the sake of moving the *liṅga*.
Then, having gone near the *liṅga* and bathed it, the Guru should perform the sacrifice.
Oṃ, ending with "namo" for Vyāpakeśvara, is the expression of the root mantra: Oṃ, salutation to the pervasive heart; Oṃ, salutation to the pervasive head.
In this manner, one should worship the mantra, the crest (śikhā), the armor (varma), the eye (netra), and the weapon (astra) in sequence;
with these, one should worship the liṅga and the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) upon the fixed seat (dhruvāsana).
Then, while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*), he should cause the being residing there to hear it;
that being, having assumed the form of a *kaupīna* (loincloth) or a *cilliṅga*, remains stationed there.
May he who has abandoned the latent tendencies of the linga go there by the command of Śiva;
there, Sambhu will be joined by the Vidyeśvaras.
Having thus commanded, one should then recite the Astra-mantra over the arghya-water and dismiss it;
and having performed [the rite] a thousand times with the Astra-mantra according to the previous sequence.
Then, having performed the sprinkling and touching with the Śānti-mantra and having recited the Astra-mantra according to the rite,
and having offered [the oblation], one should dismiss the attendants of the Mūrtis.
Or one should dig with a hammer, gold, a spade, or a sword;
[the earth] is encircled and shattered...
May Skanda protect you firmly at Gayā.
The sages [state that] one may carefully extract either the *liṅga-pīṭha* alone, both together, or the entire assembly;
having extracted it with effort, one should bestow peace upon the worlds and lead it outside.
Accompanied by those very [implements], one should cast [the image] into water or outside the house;
it may be made of stone or clay, but never of wood, for that would be terrible.
One should cast [the image] made of iron right there and offer oblations daily;
one should abandon a burnt, fallen, or shattered gem or [metallic] object.
Afterwards, having offered the oblation to the quarters with mantras as previously described,
he should consecrate the previously measured linga within the womb-chamber (garbha) in the same manner as before.
Having established [the deity] in its own place, one should worship it according to the root ritual;
in some cases, the procedure for other deities and their installation is also stated.

Then, one who desires success should offer a thousand oblations with either the Astra-mantra or his own specific mantra; thereafter, the restoration of the worn-out [linga] must be performed again as previously prescribed.
Having deposited those mantras upon the sword through the extraction of the worn-out [mantras], one should worship it up to the Prāsāda mantra; one should diligently protect the liṅga.
Once this is accomplished, he should perform that yoga by drawing [the essence] from the sword.
That substance, which is of the same measure as the previously mentioned *khahrama* and is undigested, [is the means].
Furthermore, that which consists of eight substances is the best, while that produced from inferior materials is very low.
Through contraction there is death; through expansion, exertion. Having extracted what is worn out and having replaced it, one should perform oblations for the sake of expiation.

Having worshipped the venerable one with undivided, full water from the *khadadyoja* [vessel], and having prostrated before him, he should seek forgiveness while offering blades of grass and drops of water.
Whatever has been performed by you out of ignorance regarding existence,
whether it be the command of the Lord or the installation of the *liṅga* and so forth— that, O Parameṣṭhin, you must forgive.
"O Maheśvara, you are the lord of King [Name];
O Bhava, be well-pleased with our craftsmen and those of others."
Then,
having [offered] that sword, one should give a bracelet, a cow, and two bulls with their horns intact.
* *?rṇe is the door.
One should construct the maṭha twice the size of the earth;
having left the jagatī on the outside, [it should be] in the south or the west.

As before, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Having worshipped the Śiva-pitcher (*śivaghaṭa*) and smeared it [with unguents], one should... [perform the remaining rites].
The Brahmin, having performed the circumambulation together with those preceding him,
and having entered after [the time] of two lava-s have passed...
